Investigation carried out by the SEBI revealed that certain directors and employees of SCSL had connived and collaborated in the overstatement, fabrication, falsification and misrepresentation in the books of account and financial statements of SCSL. The investigation also noted that the statutory auditors of SCSL had connived with the directors and employees of SCSL in falsifying the financial statements of SCSL. Show-cause notice was issued to PW Bangalore and its two partners who signed balance sheets of SCSL, seeking to take action for violation of sections 12A(a), 12A(b) and 12A(c) read with regulations 3(c), 3(d), 4(1), 4(2)(a), 4(2)(e), 4(2)(f), 4(2)(k) and 4(2)(r) of the SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations. The SCL inter alia alleged gross negligence and recklessness in conducting an audit in accordance with the accounting standards and repeatedly deviating from the mandated course of audit especially in relation to items of significant materiality; and failure to consider the direct confirmations received from banks with respect to the figures of fixed deposits while blindly relying on the indirect confirmations received from SCSL which showed higher balances. It was also mentioned in the SCN that PWC International Ltd. had approved 11 partnership firms consisting of Chartered Accountants as their partners to use the name 'Price Waterhouse' in India and that the 11 firms had common branch offices located in New Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurgaon, Bhuvneshwar & Ahmedabad and there were several common partners in these firms. These firms shared resources, manpower, offices, revenues, etc. amongst themselves and, for this purpose, the 11 firms had entered into an agreement in 2000 for resource sharing. It was further stated that the members of the "engagement team" which worked on the audit of SCSL was on the payroll of Price Waterhouse Kolkata and Lovelock & Lewes Kolkata.

Two writ petitions were filed before the Bombay High Court, first by PW Bangalore and second by ten other CA firms along with their partners who were using the brand name Price Waterhouse in India, for quashing of the SCNs on the ground that SEBI lacked jurisdiction as it was encroaching upon the jurisdiction of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI)

The Bombay High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that it could not be said that SEBI at that stage, had no jurisdiction to issue a SCN simply because the appellants were professional Chartered Accountants. The Bombay High Court, however, set out the scope and extent of SEBI's power under sections 11 and 11B, read with regulation 11 of the PFUTP Regulations to act against Chartered Accountants and the circumstances under which SEBI could issue direction to Chartered Accountants acting in their professional capacity. The Bombay High Court emphatically held that the jurisdiction of SEBI in the instant case would depend upon the evidence which was available during the investigation and that if there was only some omission without any mens rea or connivance with anyone, in any manner, then SEBI could not issue any further direction.

Thereafter, the WTM held that failure to seek external confirmation of the bank balances, fixed deposits, failure to detect fake invoices without adopting the rigorous procedure mandated by AAS drew an inference of gross negligence and inference of involvement of appellants in the fudging of the accounts. This gross negligence amounted to an act of commission of a fraud for the purposes of SEBI - Act and SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations for which mens rea was not required to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt but could be based on a preponderance of probability.

The WTM held that (i) entities/firms practising as Chartered Accountant (CA) in India under the brand and banner of Price Waterhouse (PW) would not directly or indirectly issue any certificate of audit of listed companies, compliance of obligations of listed companies and intermediaries registered with SEBI under the applicable laws for a period of two years, that, (ii) individual auditors, namely, 'SG' and 'ST', would not issue an audit certificate or any certificate of compliance with respect to a listed company for a period of three years; and that (iii) G, T and PW Bangalore would jointly and severally disgorge the wrongful gains of Rs. 13,09,01,664/- along with interest at the rate 12 per cent per annum from 7-1-2009, till the date of payment.

The other issue is whether the intra group charge for such services for tax purpose should be in accordance with the arm's length principle. The OECD Guidelines inter alia also provide that the allocation of the group cost might be based upon the turnover or staff employed or some other basis. It mentioned that whether the allocation method is appropriate may depend upon the nature and use of the services. A reading of this OECD Guidelines makes it abundantly clear that contrary to the revenue's argument, the using of allocation keys for allocation of intra group services is not alien to international tax jurisprudence. Further, the allocation of concerned group expenses to different accounting units is a duly accepted accounting procedure. Furthermore, the assessee has used a CPA certificate for the allocation of intra group services from the AE. The authorities below have rejected the CPA certificate on the ground that underlying documents on the basis of which the CPA certificate has been issued has not been produced before them. In this regard, it is noted that the CPA certificate is quite specific and has been duly authenticated. Hence, the evidence for international transaction can be duly supported by public accounts and financial statements relating to business affairs of the AE. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustment - Others) - Assessment years 2015-16 and 2016-17 - Assessee-company had made payment to its AE towards central service charge - TPO held that assessee-company had not explained exact nature of services which were categorized under central services and there was a vague description of services without any details being available and further assessee had not submitted any evidence in relation to actual receipt of services - It was found that assessee had given all detailed submission and analysis not only demonstrating rendition of central services but also commensurate benefits derived from such services to assessee - Whether, accordingly, TPO was not justified in holding that either there was no rendition or no benefit from said services and adjustment made by TPO was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 18] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee-company had made payment to its AE, viz., towards central service charge.

The AE had granted a non-exclusive license to assessee; firstly for using technical documentation, information, technical know-how and improvements; and secondly, for central services vide common-technology, trademark license and simple service agreement.

The assessee had benchmarked the transactions using CUP method.

HELD: Before the authorities below, the assessee has given all the detailed submission and analysis not only demonstrating the rendition of central services but also commensurate benefits derived from such services to the assessee. Accordingly, it cannot be held that either there was no rendition or no benefit as observed by the TPO. Apart from that the CUP analysis done by the assessee by taking four comparables in both the assessment years in providing advisories, management advisory, strategic planning, business administration services, marketing plan, protocols, procedures, etc., wherein mean margin determined was 2.75 per cent in assessment year 2015-16 and 5.75 per cent in assessment year 2016-17; whereas the assessee has made payment at 0.50 per cent in assessment year 2015-16 and 0.75 per cent in 2016-17. HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustment/Adjustment - General) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee was engaged in manufacture of electric power steering for four wheelers - Assessee had made payment of royalty for technical know-how and documentation charges to its AE against certain services - TPO concluded that no independent party would have made such payments and that transactions were not for benefit of assessee - Assessee was dependent upon its AE, even for carrying out research and development activities and providing manufacturing technology and it had produced all invoices and proof of payments in respect of services rendered by employees of AE - Whether since commercial expediency was recognised, it could not be held that transactions were really not for benefit of assessee; and that technical service fees paid by assessee to AE was not at arm's length - Held, yes [Para 6.7] [Matter remanded]IT/ILT : Where assessee had produced all invoices and proof of payments in respect of services rendered by employees of AE, and commercial expediency of said payment was recognised, it could not be held that technical service fees paid by assessee to AE was not at arm's length

FACT: The assessee was engaged in manufacture of electric power steering for four wheelers and also had a non-exclusive right and license for the know-how and intellectual property rights in respect of designs, drawings, standards, specifications and all other technical data relating to various products.

The assessee had made payment of royalty for the technical know-how and documentation charges and testing charges and training charges and technical support charges to its AE's.

The TPO concluded that said transaction were not realty for benefit of assessee no independent party would have made such payment of technical fee and the TPO referred to OECD guidelines with regard to intragroup services and calculated the arm's length price.

DRP confirmed said order.

On appeal:

HELD: The principal activity of the assessee is to manufacture the automated product being power steering. On perusal of the Technical Collaboration Contract and Technical Personnel Dispatch Agreements dated 16-10-2006, it is observed that the assessee depends upon the technical support received from the technical personnel sent by the AE. It is also clear that, had the assessee not entered into a technical collaboration agreement with its AE, it would not have been able to make any sales whatsoever using the technology. These agreements are approved by the Ministry of Commerce, Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, including the payment of royalty and lump sum technical know-how fee. Article 5 of the Technical Collaboration Contract provides that, technical assistance would be provided by the AE, which shall include, dispatch and training of technical personnel. The very existence of the assessee's business depended upon the Technical Collaboration Contract and the technical Personnel Dispatch Agreements. [Para 6.1]

Further the transfer pricing study explains the nature and terms of the international transaction entered into by the assessee with its AE. The assessee was dependent upon its AE, even for carrying out research and development activities and providing manufacturing technology. Further the paper book narrates the details of the technical fees paid for the year under consideration. Whenever international transaction of such a nature is undertaken, it is a combination of technical know-how, royalty and technical assistance through deputation of employees. Merely by importing machinery or designs and drawings, it cannot be said that the assessee would be competent to make use of such machinery. No doubt that the technical know-how of the able personnel is needed under normal circumstances. [Para 6.2]

The evidence had been submitted before the authorities below showing rendering of certain services against the payments made to the AE. [Para 6.4]

So far as the segregation of international transaction is concerned, it is assumed that the various international transactions were entered into with respect to the final commercial venture undertaken by the assessee, be it the manufacture and the sale of the goods or provision of services by it. The assessee has priced the royalty and the technical services provided by the AE separately, and they were all provided under 2 different agreements which constitutes an International Transaction. TPO on one breath does not doubt the existence of services being rendered by the personnel sent by the AE, while on the next breath he has denied that technical support fees paid by the assessee to its AE, on the ground that no independent enterprise would pay such expenses under similar circumstances. [Para 6.6]

HEADNOTE: Section 92C, read with section 40A(2), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Section 92C v. Section 40A(2)) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether when assessee had chosen to use transfer pricing provisions to demonstrate its claim that expenditure for availing data service was at arm's length and that same was not excessive or unreasonable, revenue authorities were bound to rebut this claim of assessee and when transfer pricing reports submitted by assessee were not rejected, it was to be concluded that assessee had discharged burden of proof that lay on it as regards said payment - Held, yes - Assessee-company derived income from business of providing advisory and consulting services to companies engaged in business of general insurance and life assurance - It entered into an agreement with Amway, a foreign company and availed data processing services - However, Assessing Officer determined total income of assessee by making a disallowance under section 40A(2)(b) of data processing charges paid to Amway - It was found that assessee had filed Transfer Pricing Reports justifying price paid by it for services obtained, after conducting a Transfer Pricing Study and Amway as well as assessee were both assessed at maximum marginal rate and said transaction was tax neutral thus was not made with an intention to evade tax - Further no comparative data or instance was available and no exercise was made to arrive at a fair market price by Assessing Officer - Whether on facts ad hoc disallowance made was arbitrary - Held, yes [Para 14] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : When assessee had chosen to use transfer pricing provisions to demonstrate its claim that expenditure for availing data service was at arm's length and that same was not excessive or unreasonable, revenue authorities were bound to rebut this claim of assessee and when transfer pricing reports submitted by assessee were not rejected, it was to be concluded that assessee had proved that price paid for said services was at arm's length

FACT: The assessee-company derived income from the business of providing advisory and consulting services to companies engaged in the business of general insurance and life assurance. It entered into an agreement with Amway, a foreign company and availed data processing services. Assessee had filed Transfer Pricing Reports justifying price paid by it for services obtained, after conducting a Transfer Pricing Study.

However, the Assessing Officer determined total income of assessee inter alia making a disallowance under section 40A(2)(b) of data processing charges paid to Amway.

The FAA upheld the order passed by the Assessing Officer.

On appeal:

HELD: From Circular No. 6-B, dated 6-7-1968 of the CBDT, it is clear that the provision was made specifically to check tax avoidance. Thus when there is no tax avoidance, the applicability of this section would not be appropriate. [Para 12.4]

In the case the revenue does not dispute the fact that Amway as well as the assessee were both assessed at the maximum marginal rate and said transaction was tax neutral. Thus it was not made with an intention to evade tax. In fact the income of the Payee Company is much more than that of the assessee. Thus, Circular No. 6P dt. 6-7-1968, apply to the facts of this case. What is the amount that should have been paid for these services is to be decided by the Assessing Officer by keeping in view the requirements of business and the point of view of the businessman. [Para 12.9]

No basis or factual justification whatsoever is given by the revenue authorities in both these cases for this ad hoc disallowance. The factum of rendering of services is not in dispute. The requirement of payment of fees is also not in dispute. Only on the quantum of charges, the Assessing Officer is of the view that it is excessive and unreasonable. No comparative data or instance is available. No exercise is made to arrive at a fair market price by the Assessing Officer. Those ad hoc disallowances, are based on surmises and conjectures. [Para 13]

In the case on hand, there is not even an allegation that the assessee has evaded payment of tax.

In the case on hand the ad hoc disallowance made by the Assessing Officer is arbitrary and without any basis. The Assessing Officer had not given a finding as to what as per him, is the fair market value. Even if it is assumed that the payment made is excessive and unreasonable, such arbitrary and baseless, ad hoc disallowances cannot be upheld. On this ground also the assessee has to succeed. [Para 14.1]

HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act 1952 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transaction/allowability of expenditure ) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee-company had entered into agreements with its AEs - In terms of which, AEs would recharge on actual cost incurred towards rendering of services with 10 per cent mark-up and AEs would raise invoices on assessee towards support services rendered - TPO proceeded to compute ALP of transaction at Nil, for reason that evidences submitted were inadequate, need for availing services not substantiated break-up of cost was not submitted - Assessee had submitted substantial documents in form of agreements with AEs, details of cost recharged, employee wise cost details allocated to assessee, details of employee wise time sheet evidencing time spent by various employees towards rendering services to various countries including assessee in India, e-mail correspondence in support of nature and benefit of services rendered - Whether once availing of various services from AEs was duly substantiated by documentary evidence and cost allocation among group companies was also on basis of a well-accepted allocation key method, there was no basis in upholding transfer pricing adjustment made by TPO/Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether thus, TPO was to be directed to delete TP adjustment - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 12] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where availing of various services from AEs was duly substantiated by documentary evidence and cost allocation among group companies was also on basis of a well-accepted allocation key method, there was no basis in upholding transfer pricing adjustment made by TPO/Assessing Officer

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act 1952 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transaction/allowability of expenditure ) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee-company had entered into agreements with its AEs - In terms of which, AEs would recharge on actual cost incurred towards rendering of services with 10 per cent mark-up and AEs would raise invoices on assessee towards support services rendered - TPO proceeded to compute ALP of transaction at Nil, for reason that evidences submitted were inadequate, need for availing services not substantiated break-up of cost was not submitted - Assessee had submitted substantial documents in form of agreements with AEs, details of cost recharged, employee wise cost details allocated to assessee, details of employee wise time sheet evidencing time spent by various employees towards rendering services to various countries including assessee in India, e-mail correspondence in support of nature and benefit of services rendered - Whether once availing of various services from AEs was duly substantiated by documentary evidence and cost allocation among group companies was also on basis of a well-accepted allocation key method, there was no basis in upholding transfer pricing adjustment made by TPO/Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether thus, TPO was to be directed to delete TP adjustment - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 12] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of providing manpower recruitment and consultancy services to clients in India. It entered into various international transactions which included payment towards shared services availed from its AE and fees for such services was charged by AE at actual cost plus 10 per cent mark-up.

The TPO proceeded to compute the ALP of the transaction at Nil, for the reason that the evidences submitted were inadequate, the need for availing services was not substantiated and break-up of the cost was not submitted.

Before the Commissioner (Appeals) the assessee submitted additional evidences such as time sheet of employees, various documents to substantiate the benefits received, e-mail correspondences, marketing materials. etc. The Commissioner (Appeals) called for the remand report from the TPO. The Commissioner (Appeals) after perusing the remand report and the rebuttal of the assessee upheld the determination of ALP at Nil and confirmed the T.P. adjustment.

On appeal :

HELD: The assessee has submitted substantial documents in the form of agreements with AEs, details of cost recharged, employee wise cost details allocated to assessee, details of employee wise time sheet evidencing the time spent by various employees towards rendering services to various countries including assessee in India, email correspondence in support of nature and benefit of the services rendered. From the perusal of these records it is evident that the assessee before the lower authorities have submitted evidences in support of rendering of services, the benefits derived, basis of allocation of cost i.e. allocation key etc. and therefore, lower authorities were not justified in holding that no services were rendered by the AEs in respect of which payments were made by the assessee. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Methods for determination of - Most appropriate method, determination of) - Assessment years 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Assessee entered into service agreement with an entity to avail certain services in areas of business strategy, value based management, legal, marketing etc. - It paid consideration under said agreement - TPO computed TP adjustment by applying ad hoc estimation of salary cost and man hours - Whether while determining ALP of international transactions entered into by assessee, TPO cannot adopt any other method except methods prescribed in section 92C(1) and, therefore, impugned adjustment was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 17] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee has entered into service agreement with CEPT for availing certain services such as business strategy, financial planning and accounting supply chain, co-ordination and planning human resources legally and marketing, etc. It had made a payment towards availing these services where the AE has charged cost plus 5 per cent for providing the services.

The TPO computed TP adjustment by applying ad hoc estimation of salary cost and man hours.

The DRP confirmed the said TP adjustment.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: It is noticed that the TPO while arriving at the ALP has used the estimated salary and also used earlier year's man hours to determine the current year man hours spent. In the assessee's own case for assessment year 2009-10, the co-ordinate bench of the Tribunal has considered the issue of determination of ALP by the TPO and has held while determining ALP of international transactions entered into by assessee, TPO cannot adopt any other method except methods prescribed in section 92C(1) and, therefore, the TP adjustment made by the TPO is not tenable. Therefore, following the above decisions of the co-ordinate bench, impugned TP adjustment was to be deleted. [Para 17]

IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Whether company providing services of testing of various chemicals as well as consultancy in field of pollution-control and in which case segmented data is also not provided would not be comparable to assessee engaged in provision of business support services to its AE - Held, yes [Para 23] [In favour of assessee]

VII. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments - Comparable/Illustration) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee-company rendered ITE services to its AE - Whether where nature of services provided by a company required application of knowledge and advanced analytical and technical skills, it was incomparable to assessee - Held, yes [Para 99] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section  92C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer Pricing  -  Computation of Arm’s length price  (TP Adjustments - Illustrations - License fees) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee-company, engaged in providing integrated facility management and catering services and also low-end IS&T services to its AEs, received allocation of third-party IT software licence and support costs from its AE amounting to about Rs. 59.30 lakhs, reported in Form 3CEB - TPO, holding that assessee failed to substantiate receipt of intra-group services and tangible benefits, applied CUP and determined ALP at NIL and proposed TP adjustment, which was sustained by DRP - It was found that assessee had furnished inter-company invoices, third-party agreements and cost break-ups evidencing receipt of services - Whether, since assessee had demonstrated actual receipt of services through documentary evidence, imugned adjustment was unjustified - Held, yes [Paras 9 to 9.2] [In favour of assessee]

IX. Section  92C , read with sections  92  and  92CA , of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section 165, read with sections 161 and 166 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Transfer Pricing - Computation of Arm’s length price (TP Adjustments -  Illustrations  - Support Services Fee) - Assessee paid its US AE for marketing, regulatory liaison and customer support services, reimbursed on cost plus 20 per cent basis, and benchmarked transactions under entity-level TNMM showing higher margins than comparables - TPO held entity-level TNMM inappropriate, proposed to treat AE as tested party, questioned necessity/benefit and documentation, and determined ALP of service charge/markup at Nil - CIT(A) recorded that assessee had substantial US exports and multiple ANDA filings, that services were actually rendered and costs were certified by an independent CPA, and that TPO had not brought comparables or disproved rendition; disallowance of mark-up was deleted - Whether ALP cannot be determined at Nil in absence of contrary evidence; services accepted and TNMM sustained; adjustment deleted - Held, yes [Paras 19.21 to 19.28] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Technical services fee) - Assessment year 2008-09 - DRP held that transaction relating to payments of intra group services and technical fees is treated as separate transactions and not aggregated with transaction of manufacturing activity - In light of above, it was held by TPO that assessee has failed to prove that it has actually received services and such services have benefitted assessee - Therefore TPO opined that it is appropriate to restore matter to file of Assessing Officer with direction to find out as to whether any service is rendered by AE to assessee and from which assessee has drawn any benefit from it - Whether authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits and that aspect of exercise is left to Assessing Officer therefore, TPO restoring matter to file of Assessing Officer to find out as to whether any service is rendered by AE to assessee and from which assessee has drawn any benefit from it is not correct - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits as that aspect of exercise is left to Assessing Officer therefore, TPO restoring matter to file of Assessing Officer to find out as to whether any service is rendered by AE to assessee and from which assessee has drawn any benefit from it is not correct

V. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - High end service providers) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether a company engaged in high end services cannot be compared with captive service provider like assessee - Held, yes [Para 51] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether where assessee provided services related to accounts payable management, payroll, processing invoice processing and handling of related queries to its AEs as a captive service provider, a company undertaking software testing and validation activities, could not be accepted as comparable - Held, yes [Para 59] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments) - Assessment years 2007-08 and 2008-09 - Whether in transfer pricing proceedings, role of TPO is to determine arm's length price of a transaction but he cannot reject entire payment made to AE under provisions of section 92C - Held, yes - Whether in order to determine ALP of service fee paid by assessee to its AE, it is irrelevant as to what benefit assessee eventually derived from said services but in such a case, actual determinative factor is as to what assessee would have paid for those services if same had been rendered by a non-AE - Held, yes [Paras 96  102] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : In transfer pricing proceedings, role of TPO is to determine arm's length price of a transaction but he cannot reject entire payment made to AE under provisions of section 92C

IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether company engaged in providing placement services, which fall under head of business support services, in absence of any contrary material on record to show difference between profiles of assessee and company would be comparable to assessee engaged in providing business support service to its AE - Held, yes [Para 36][In favour of assessee]

I. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arms length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transactions/Allowability of expenditure) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee-company had entered into a multilateral service agreement with its Associated Enterprises for various intra-group services relating to strategic inputs such as product information, marketing field engineering services, scientific and laboratory services, logistic, administrative, etc. - TPO held that evidence submitted by assessee were only data excel sheets of cost allocation and further, these were duplicative in nature and a shareholders activity and therefore, he determined ALP of such services as nil - Assessee had submitted agreement showing description of services and benefit received therefrom and various e-mail correspondences were submitted which said that services had been rendered by AE and received by assessee and certificates of various AE were produced to show basis of allocation and exact cost allocation to assessee and employee wise cost sheet which showed distribution and allocation of such cost - Whether, on fact, assessee had reasonably sustantiated benefit test, need test and rendition test for said intra-group services and there was no justification in determining ALP at nil - Held, yes [Para 16] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where intra- group service received by assessee-company was supported by proper agreement and substantial evidences with respect to services rendered by Associated Enterprises also demonstrated benefits received therefrom, AO was not justified in determining of ALP of said service at nil  TRANSFER PRICING : Transfer Pricing Officer should restrict addition/TP adjustment only to International transactions

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Legal and professional fee) - Assessment years 2012-13 to 2013-14 - During relevant years, assessee made payments of legal and professional fee to its AE - In transfer pricing proceedings, TPO taking a view that no benefit was derived from services rendered by AE, determined ALP of said payments at nil - DRP confirmed order passed by TPO - It was noted that there was an agreement between parties for rendering of services - Besides, evidence of rendering of services was also brought on record - Whether in aforesaid circumstances, ALP of services rendered by AE could not be taken as nil and, thus, impugned order passed by authorities below was to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 8] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING: Where there was an agreement between assessee and its AE for rendering legal services and evidence of rendering of services was also on record, ALP of such services could not be taken as nil by TPO by applying benefit test

III. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Consultancy service providers) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Whether where assessee was rendering project support services to AE, a company engaged in providing custom/excise and service tax related services, was not acceptable as comparable - Held, yes [Para 13.2] [In favour of assessee]

III.Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparable - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether where 95.06 per cent of export revenue of a company was from software services, it satisfied export filter of 75 per cent as applied by TPO and was thus comparable - Held, yes [Para 32][In favour of assessee]

Section  92C,  read with section  92CA,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer Pricing  -  Computation of Arm’s length price  (Adjustments - Segmentation) - Assessment year  2018-19  - Assessee, engaged in testing, inspection and certification (TIC) services to third-party customers in India and to AEs, also provided ITES support and shared services to AEs - For transfer pricing, it prepared segmental accounts showing AE margins of about 15% in ITES, shared services and certification segments, a 4% margin in non-AE certification services, an overall margin of about 6%, and ITES revenue of about Rs. 4.53 crores out of total revenue of about Rs. 124.81 crores (non-AE certification about Rs. 97.40 crores; AE certification about Rs. 15.09 crores; shared services about Rs. 7.79 crores) - In its TPSR, it benchmarked ITES transactions of about Rs. 4.5 crores under TNMM using OP/OC with a margin of 15% - On reference, TPO grouped TIC, shared services and ITES together as ITES, rejected assessee's segmental results stating that HR, finance, operations, legal and admin costs were not allocated to AEs, computed a consolidated margin of 4.44%, rejected TPSR and proposed a TP adjustment of about Rs. 26.18 crores - Whether since for earlier AYs TIC and ITES services were benchmarked separately, as TIC services and ITES services did not share same FAR, and TP Order did not explain why TIC and ITES services were being grouped together, combining TIC and ITES services for benchmarking was not justified - Held, yes [Para 24] [In favour of assessee]

V. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - High-end service providers) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether a company engaged in high-end services could not be compared with low end BPO service provider like assessee - Held, yes [Para 27] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - ITES services) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Whether Company which has an abnormally high RPT filter of 82.92 per cent could not be considered as comparable to ITES service provider - Held, yes (Para 26) [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Support service fee) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee company was engaged in business of developing, installation, commissioning and service of captive power plants - In course of transfer pricing proceedings, TPO found that assessee had rendered marketing support services to its AE in supplying gas turbines to Public Works Department (PWD) in carrying out construction for Common Wealth Games (CWG) - He thus made certain addition to assessee's ALP in respect of said services - Tribunal examined relevant clauses of contract and noted that eligibility condition for participating in tender was submission of registration under Delhi Value Added Tax Act, 2004, besides submission of certificate of being original equipment of gas turbines - Admittedly, assessee was not a manufacturer of gas turbines but AE was - However, AE did not have VAT registration certificate - Therefore, for participating in tender and for obtaining contract bid was submitted in assessee's name - However, Tribunal found that there was nothing on record to suggest that assessee had provided any other services to its AE for sales of its gas based turbines either to PWD or to other customers in India - Tribunal thus, deleted addition made by TPO - Whether since finding arrived by Tribunal was based on appreciation of evidence and materials on record, impugned order did not require any interference - Held, yes [Paras 24, 25 and 26] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had not rendered any marketing support services to its AE in supplying gas turbines to Public Works Department (PWD) in carrying out construction for CWG, impugned addition made to assessee's ALP in respect of said services was to be deleted

III. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Whether a company engaged in valuation of various assets which is highly technical involving huge expertise would not be comparable with assessee-company engaged in provision of business support services to its AE - Held, yes [Para 21] [In favour of assessee]

III. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Technical support service provider) Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether a company engaged as commercial testing house in running laboratory testing, chemical testing and services which are highly technical in nature who offers services like testing of products and also offers services in field of pollution control as allied activity cannot be compared with assessee company who were purely in nature of marketing support services and not engaged in providing technical services- Held, yes [Paras 21 to 23] [In favour of assessee]

III. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Whether where assessee was providing back office support services to its AE, a company which only earned 0.14 per cent income from export and, thus, failed to satisfy export filter of 25 per cent as applied by TPO, was not acceptable as comparable - Held, yes [Para 2.4.2] [In favour of assessee]

VI. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Business support services) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether where assessee was providing back office support services to its Associated Enterprise, a company providing full range of geospatial services was not comparable to assessee - Held, yes [Para 14] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustration) - Assessment years 2007-08 and 2008-09 - Assessee rendered marketing support services to its AE - Whether a company engaged in providing testing services for various products and also offering services in field of pollution control, was incomparable - Held, yes [Para 13] [In favour of assessee]

II.Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee was rendering Call Centre services to its associated enterprises - Whether company operating as an IT enabled, knowledge based Back Office Processing Centre which served needs of financial content sector, was not comparable to Call Centre services - Held, yes - Whether RPT being more that 25 per cent, said company be excluded from comparability analysis - Held, yes - Whether when export revenue of a company was 74.45 per cent as against TPO's filter of 75 per cent, said company could not be excluded for such a minuscule difference if it was otherwise comparable - Held, yes [Para 14-15] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparability functional similarity - Consultancy service providers) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether in case of assessee engaged in rendering business support services to AE, a company providing financial consultancy services, was not acceptable as comparable - Held, yes [Para 24] [In favour of assessee]

IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparability factors - Related party transactions) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Whether a company having RPT filter of more than 15 per cent cannot be compared with captive service provider like assessee - Held, yes [Para 12D] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section  92C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer pricing  -  Computation of arm's length price  (Adjustments - Others) - Assessment year  2021-22  - Assessee was involved in main business of advertising agent for its various clients as well as providing media planning services to its clients - Assessee-company had paid a certain sum to its Associated Enterprise (AE) towards intra group services, namely, Global information services (GIS) - TPO determined ALP of intra-group services at nil on ground that need and benefit test was not satisfied by assessee and made adjustment - It was noted that assessee had submitted relevant agreements showing services rendered, obligations of parties, fees to be charged, allocation of cost, etc.- Whether since assessee had reasonably satisfied various tests, i.e., need test, rendition test, benefit test, duplicate test and shareholder's activity, TPO was not correct in arriving at ALP as NIL without giving any contrary findings with regard to various documents including TP study submitted by assessee - Held, yes [Para 12.2] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Advisory services) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Whether in case of assessee providing marketing support services to AE, a company, which basically aimed at providing advisory services on procurement and also carrying out procurement audit, was not acceptable as comparable - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables-Illustration) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee-company provided marketing support services to its AE - Whether where a company was providing end to end solution and was into commercial testing and analysis laboratory engaged in analyzing food and agricultural products etc., it was not a valid comparable - Held, yes [Para 17] [In favour of assessee]

Section  92C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer pricing  -  Computation of arm's length price  (Adjustments - Benefit for transaction/allowability of expenditure)) - Assessment year  2021-22  - Assessee-company, engaged in recruitment services, had made payments to its AEs towards Business Support Services and Business Technology Services (Intra group services) - TPO noted that assessee had not been able to substantiate need for such services, benefits derived from same and quantification of service payments in relation to same and, thus, determined ALP of such services as nil and made transfer pricing additions - It was noted that assessee had submitted detailed description of various services availed, copy of relevant agreements, inter-company invoices, cost allocation workings as well as a description of each category of services along with need and benefit derived from each of said services - Further, assessee had furnished details of employees on its payroll and it was noted that assessee did not have any personnel on its payroll to perform support functions - Moreover, assessee had carried out primary benchmarking analysis taking foreign AEs as tested party and secondary benchmarking analysis taking assessee as tested party - Whether since assessee had discharged burden to satisfy that need, purpose, rendition and benefit test for relevant previous year by furnishing relevant documents and details during proceedings before TPO, transfer pricing addition was to be set aside with directions to TPO to compute ALP as per corroborative benchmarking analysis after verifying computation of PLI - Held, yes [Paras 15, 16 and 19][In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price - (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustment - Whether where Payment was made by assessee for services rendered by its at but - TPO had not carried out exercise for computing arm's length price on plea that assessee did not provide agreement with ANCR, whereas assessee claimed to have provided a copy - Since to determined arms length price of benefit, service etc. as per most appropriate method as envisaged in section 92C(1) matter be remanded back - Held, yes [Para 7] [Matter remanded]

IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustments - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether a company providing consultancy services to financial institutions in and out of India couldn't be compared to company providing market support services - Held, yes [Para 22][In favour of assessee]

Section 92CA, read with section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Reference to TPO (Section 37(1) v. section 92CA) - Whether jurisdiction of Assessing Officer under section 37 and TPO under section 92CA is distinct and, therefore, a referral made by Assessing Officer to TPO for limited purpose of determining ALP does not take away power of Assessing Officer to determine as to whether payment made by assessee to its AE for services rendered was basically an expenditure incurred for purpose of business so as to allow same under section 37(1) - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]IT/ILT : Jurisdiction of Assessing Officer under section 37(1) and TPO under section 92CA is distinct and, therefore, a referral made by Assessing Officer to TPO for limited purpose of determining ALP does not take away power of Assessing Officer to determine as to whether payment made by assessee to its AE for services rendered was basically an expenditure incurred for purpose of business so as to allow same under section 37(1)  IT/ILT : Authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits; therefore, TPO cannot determine ALP of payments made by assessee to its AE at nil taking a view that assessee did not derive any benefit from services rendered by AE

IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricingComputation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Marketing/sales support services)- Assessment Year 2010-11 - Whether a company providing advisory services can be no match with a company providing actual marketing support services - Held, yes [Para 11.29] [In favour of assessee]

IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer Pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparability factors - Export turnover) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee was a BPO service provider - It was also providing services to customers of its holding company abroad - It had selected a comparable in its TP documentation - However, TPO had excluded comparable on ground that it had failed export filter - Whether since entire turnover of said company was attributed to exports, there was no reason for exclusion of this comparable and, thus, it was to be included in set of comparables - Held, yes [Para 25] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether where assessee provided services related to accounts payable management, payroll, processing invoice processing and handling of related queries to its AEs as a captive service provider, a KPO engaged in providing high-end services such as data analytics, data solutions services etc. was not acceptable as comparable - Held, yes [Para 58] [In favour of assessee]

facts.text:
The assessee was a practising chartered accountant. The revenue levied tax on certification service holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

On appeal :

The assessee was a firm of chartered accountants. The original authority confirmed demand of service tax on the assessee for the period 16-10-1998 to 31-7-2002 under the heads ‘Practising chartered accountant’, ‘Manpower recruitment service’, ‘Management consultant’ and ‘Business auxiliary service’. Modifying the findings of the original authority, the Commissioner (Appeals) found that the assessee was not liable to pay service tax under the head ‘Business auxiliary service’. He affirmed the demand on the assessee in respect of other categories of services. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that it had rendered services as management consultant and man-power recruitment agent which were exempt in terms of Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998. The assessee also contended that Commissioner (Appeals) had wrongly held that the Notification No. 15/2002, dated 1-8-2002 which inserted an Explanation to Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998, had come into effect from 16-10-1998.

The Income-tax Department’s case was that when a Chartered Accountant is authorised in terms of section 288, the authorisation, if in the form of power of attorney, is required to bear stamp duty of Rs. 50. It was further contended that an authorisation of a Chartered Accountant or an income-tax practitioner by a person to represent his case in income-tax proceedings is not an instrument subject to payment of court fees under the Court Fees Act. That being so, such an authorisation could only be considered as a ‘Power of Attorney’ as defined in section 2(p) of the Kerala Stamp Act, 1959 in respect of which stamp duty is payable as specified in article 44 of the Schedule thereof. Accordingly, while a Vakalatnama signed by an advocate is chargeable to court fee under the Court Fees Act, an authorisation in the case of a Chartered Accountant or an income-tax practitioner is only a ‘Power of Attorney’ which is subject to stamp duty under the Stamp Act.

On writ :

Assessee PWH was an independent firm of Chartered Accountants managed and controlled by its partners who were individuals and residents of India.

It had entered into an agreement with Price Water HouseCoopers International Limited (PwCIL) a company incorporated in the United Kingdom to become member of PwCIL. The member firms of PwCIL were collectively known as PwC Network.

PWH had become a member firm of PwC Network, at the same time it was a separate independent legal entity whose affairs were managed and controlled only by its partners.

Price Water HouseCoopers Services BV, Netherlands(Services BV) was the central services entity of the PwC Network and operated exclusively for mutual benefit of all PwC Network member firms. Neither PWH nor any of its partners was a shareholder of Services BV. Services BV had not conferred on PWH any right regarding use of any brand name as Services BV itself did not own any brand name.

During relevant year PwC received a non-refundable loan to strengthen PWH's audit practices in India. Such loan was received under contractual arrangement existing between Services BV and PWH and PWH had shown it as business income in its return.

On scrutiny assessment, the Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax (R-3) issued notice requiring PWH to file its computation of income and tax for year, audit profit and loss account and balance sheet, tax and audit report issued under section 44AB. PWH filed all the necessary documents

Thereafter R-3 issued a letter to PWH informing it that a reference had been made to the TPO and called upon PWH to file details requested for in earlier notices.

PWH contended that TPO regulations did not apply to PWH as it did not have a relationship of being AE with any overseas network entity. It further contended that it had never entered into any international transaction envisaged under section 92B, and hence, it was unable to comprehend the reasons for which reference had been made under section 92CA(1) to the TPO. Further the fact that the transactions between PWH and Services BV were not international transactions had been accepted in the previous assessment year and hence there was no justification for R-3 to take a different view on same set of facts and law.

Facts

The assessees had provided chartered accountant's services prior to 1-4-2012 and raised the bills therefor prior to that date, levying service tax at the rate of 10 per cent.

Up to 1-4-2012, Chartered Accountants services were governed by rule 7 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011 wherein point of taxation was determined based on date of receipt of payment.

With effect from 1-4-2012, rate of service tax was increased to 12 per cent and services of chartered accountants were excluded from Rule 7 ibid.

Circular No. 158/9/2012-ST dated 8-05-2012 and Circular No.154/5/2012-ST dated 28-03-2012 had provided that since, prior to 1-4-2012, services of Chartered Accountants were covered by rule 7 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011, hence, point of taxation of services provided prior to that date will continue to be governed by said Rule 7, as it stood before that date. Accordingly, in case of services provided and invoices raised before 1-4-2012, the point of taxation would be date of payment and if payment was received on or after 1-4-2012, revised rate of service tax viz. 12 per cent would apply.

The assessees argued that point of taxation, in their case, was determinable as per Rule 4 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011.

Therefore, the assessees challenged the said circulars as ultra vires the Constitution and the provisions of the Finance Act, 1994 and rules.

Issue Involved

Whether Circular was ultra vires the Act ?

The applicant, a tax resident of Hong Kong, belongs to X group of companies. The group entities are engaged in the business of inspection, verification, testing and certification (IVTC) services to various customers. The X trademark is owned by ABC (Parent Company), who had entered into a trademark license and Support Services Agreement (Support Services Agreement) with all its group entities, separately, including the applicant. The support service agreement is stated to bring uniform standards, procedures and policies described therein to IVTC services. It is stated that the inspection services are generally performed either at the load port or discharge port of a product or activity and are based on scientific and internationally accepted techniques and as per the clients' requirements. Verification services are used to evaluate whether the product services are system complaint with given regulation, specifications or condition. Testing services are used to determine the quality of the product or services as per the customer's requirements and are carried out in laboratories owned by respective X entities which are accredited to international bodies. Certification services refers to the confirmation of regulations, standards or contractual specifications of a product or organization or training. The applicant provided IVTC services to Indian Customers either directly or through X India. The applicant states that the IVTC Services are provided to the Indian Customer outside India if there is a direct arrangement between the customer and the applicant and the payment is made on the invoice raised by the applicant. But when the arrangement is not direct and is through the X India, then the invoice is raised either on X India or the Indian customer. Explaining it by an example, the applicant states that where a customer approaches X India to have its goods inspected in India and outside India, then X India sub-contracts the inspection to its applicant and the applicant raises invoice on X India for services provided by it and a consolidated invoice is raised on the customer. The applicant sought advance ruling on the question as to (i) whether the payments received/receivable the applicant in connection with transactions under taken/proposed to be undertaken in relation to the (a) inspection and verification services (b) testing/analysis services; and (c) certification services are chargeable to tax in India as 'fees for technical services' (FTS) under section 9(1)(vii)( b) and (ii ) whether payments received/receivable in connection with procurement of goods/services and reimbursement of other expenses proposed to be incurred for and on behalf of X India are chargeable to tax in India. The applicant also raised issue relation to withholding of taxes under section 195 and filing of return under section 139.

The assessee has entered into service agreement with CEPT for availing certain services such as business strategy, financial planning and accounting supply chain, co-ordination and planning human resources legally and marketing, etc. It had made a payment towards availing these services where the AE has charged cost plus 5 per cent for providing the services.

The TPO computed TP adjustment by applying ad hoc estimation of salary cost and man hours.

The DRP confirmed the said TP adjustment.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The AO had made a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) under section 92CA. Pursuant to this reference, the TPO passed an order under section 92CA(3) accepting that the international transactions entered into by the assessee with its Associated Enterprises were at an Arms Length Price. In other words, the TPO made no variation.

■

The Assessing Officer passed a draft assessment order under section 144C(1) and thereafter passed a final assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C(3) and section 144B.

■

On writ:

■

The assessee, engaged in providing basic market research and testing services to its associated enterprises (AEs), reported international transactions in Form 3CEB. The matter was referred to the TPO for determination of the arm's length price (ALP).

■

The TPO, by order passed under section 92CA(3), proposed a transfer pricing adjustment of Rs. 16.13 crore. On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal.

Price Waterhouse (PW) Bangalore, a CA firm, was given the audit for auditing the books of account 'SCSL', which was regarded as one of top IT outsourcing firms in the world.

In the year 2009, the SEBI received an email from the then Chairman of SCSL stating that the statements of accounts of SCSL were not true and fair. The e-mail basically revealed that there was large scale financial manipulation in the books of account of SCSL, namely, that the balance sheet of SCSL as of 30-9-2008 carried inflated/non-existent cash and bank balances.

Investigation carried out by the SEBI revealed that certain directors and employees of SCSL had connived and collaborated in the overstatement, fabrication, falsification and misrepresentation in the books of account and financial statements of SCSL. The investigation also noted that the statutory auditors of SCSL had connived with the directors and employees of SCSL in falsifying the financial statements of SCSL.

Show-cause notice was issued to PW Bangalore and its two partners who signed balance sheets of SCSL, seeking to take action for violation of sections 12A(a), 12A(b) and 12A(c) read with regulations 3(c), 3(d), 4(1), 4(2)(a), 4(2)(e), 4(2)(f), 4(2)(k) and 4(2)(r) of the SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations. The SCL inter alia alleged gross negligence and recklessness in conducting an audit in accordance with the accounting standards and repeatedly deviating from the mandated course of audit especially in relation to items of significant materiality; and failure to consider the direct confirmations received from banks with respect to the figures of fixed deposits while blindly relying on the indirect confirmations received from SCSL which showed higher balances. It was also mentioned in the SCN that PWC International Ltd. had approved 11 partnership firms consisting of Chartered Accountants as their partners to use the name 'Price Waterhouse' in India and that the 11 firms had common branch offices located in New Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurgaon, Bhuvneshwar & Ahmedabad and there were several common partners in these firms. These firms shared resources, manpower, offices, revenues, etc. amongst themselves and, for this purpose, the 11 firms had entered into an agreement in 2000 for resource sharing. It was further stated that the members of the "engagement team" which worked on the audit of SCSL was on the payroll of Price Waterhouse Kolkata and Lovelock & Lewes Kolkata.

Two writ petitions were filed before the Bombay High Court, first by PW Bangalore and second by ten other CA firms along with their partners who were using the brand name Price Waterhouse in India, for quashing of the SCNs on the ground that SEBI lacked jurisdiction as it was encroaching upon the jurisdiction of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI)

The Bombay High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that it could not be said that SEBI at that stage, had no jurisdiction to issue a SCN simply because the appellants were professional Chartered Accountants. The Bombay High Court, however, set out the scope and extent of SEBI's power under sections 11 and 11B, read with regulation 11 of the PFUTP Regulations to act against Chartered Accountants and the circumstances under which SEBI could issue direction to Chartered Accountants acting in their professional capacity. The Bombay High Court emphatically held that the jurisdiction of SEBI in the instant case would depend upon the evidence which was available during the investigation and that if there was only some omission without any mens rea or connivance with anyone, in any manner, then SEBI could not issue any further direction.

Thereafter, the WTM held that failure to seek external confirmation of the bank balances, fixed deposits, failure to detect fake invoices without adopting the rigorous procedure mandated by AAS drew an inference of gross negligence and inference of involvement of appellants in the fudging of the accounts. This gross negligence amounted to an act of commission of a fraud for the purposes of SEBI - Act and SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations for which mens rea was not required to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt but could be based on a preponderance of probability.

The Assessing Officer referred the determination of ALP in respect of the aforesaid transaction to the TPO under section 92CA.

Prima facie, the Explanation added in amended Notification No. 15/2000 ST, dated 1-8-2002 purported to add to the tax liability of a PCA, Practising Company Secretary and Practising Cost Accountant, by providing that the exemption under Notification No. 59/98-ST would not be applicable to services provided by these professionals, which may fall in any other taxable services defined in clause (90) of section 65. The legislative intent was amply clear. Prima facie, taxable services under clause (90) of section 65 were sought to be excluded from the scope of exemption. It is well settled through series of judgments of the High Courts and Supreme Court that writ jurisdiction of the High Courts in exercise of powers under article 226 of Constitution of India is extremely wide. If a jurisdictional error is pointed out or it is shown that an authority has acted wholly without jurisdiction, the Court can, without relegating the petitioner/assessee to the departmental or even statutory remedies, strike down exercise of such powers. Therefore, if it is found that the action of the TPO or a part of it which can be severed from the rest is wholly without jurisdiction, such order or part thereof is to be struck down even though statute provides certain appeal remedies to the aggrieved assessee.[Para 4]

It is indisputable that by virtue of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, in case of an international transaction, the TPO would have an authority to examine any international transaction which comes to his notice during the proceedings, whether a reference in this respect was made by the Assessing Officer or not and whether the assessee had reported such transaction under section 92E or not. However, in view of specific non-inclusion of the specified domestic transaction under the said sub-sections, in so far as the domestic transactions are concerned, the situation would be vastly different.[Para 13]

In plain terms, in absence of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, the TPO would get jurisdiction to examine a transaction whether it is international or specified domestic transaction, only upon reference being made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1) of section 92CA. Sub-section (2) of section 92CA provides that where a reference is made under sub-section (1), the TPO would serve a notice to the assessee requiring him to furnish details in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction referred to in sub-section (1). Thus, the jurisdiction of the TPO to issue a notice to the assessee would be in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction for which reference is made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). It is precisely for this reason that sub-sections (2A) and (2B) provide a deeming fiction where they provide that in case of an international transaction not referred to the TPO or an international transaction not reported by the assessee, which comes to his notice during the proceedings, the provision of the Chapter would apply as if such international transaction was one referred to in sub-section (1). In absence of this deeming fiction, it would not be open for the TPO to exercise the powers under the said chapter in relation to the transaction not referred to him. The reference to be made by the Assessing Officer is not an empty formality. Said reference has to be made only on approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. Legislature, requires the Assessing Officer to obtain an approval from senior Revenue Authority before a reference is made. Such requirement cannot be jettisoned by the TPO exercising suo motu jurisdiction over the transaction not reported to him.[Para 14]

Inescapable conclusion that is reached is that in relation to a specified domestic transaction, the TPO can under take transfer pricing study only in relation to those transactions which are referred to him under sub-section (1) of section 92C. Sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92C are confined to international transactions and with the aid of any interpretive process, the said provision cannot be applied to empower the TPO to examine any specified domestic transaction not referred to him by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). Any other view would be doing violence to the plain language of the statute.[Para 17]

The revenue is correct in pointing out that in the instant case, the assessee did not report such transaction at all and therefore, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to notice such transaction as specified domestic transaction. His reference, therefore, was necessarily confined to the reported transactions. The TPO noticed this anomaly, he proceeded to determine the arm's length price after full opportunity of hearing to the assessee.[Para 18]

The jurisdiction of the TPO cannot extend to decide the basis of charge/allocation of expenses. CIT [2017] 78 taxmann.com 50 (Chennai - Trib.), the co-ordinate Bench of Tribunal held that allocation of cost partly on the basis of turnover and net profit cannot be considered as a factor to propose transfer pricing adjustment. Further, it was held that where the PLI of the Appellant under TNMM is at arm's length and it is not possible on the part of the department to identify a comparable, which is rendering similar services, the question of considering CUP method would not arise at all. [Para 20.12]

CIT [2016] 76 taxmann.com 147 (Chennai - Trib.), the Co-ordinate bench has held that any payment which is systematically subject to deduction of tax at source cannot be said to be non-genuine. Section 92CA(1) empowers the Assessing Officer to make reference to TPO for the computation of arm's length price of international transactions. Further, the TPO as defined in Explanation to section 92CA to be the person authorized by board to perform functions of Assessing Officer specified in section 92C. In sub-section (3) of section 144B, roles of Technical unit is clearly spelt out according to which, functions of technical unit includes assistance or advice on transfer pricing issues. During the course of performing such function, the technical unit can obtain advice from the TPO on the issue of determination of arm's length price of international transaction as they are expert in this field. Thus, the reference by technical unit to TPO is in accordance with the provisions of the Act and therefore, consequent orders passed are not barred by limitations. [Para 10]
