LAST WORD : NOTIFICATION NO. 25/2006-SERVICE TAX

V.S. DATEY

Partial justice to practising CA, CWA and CS

Services provided by a practising CA/CWA/CS in his professional capacity are taxable with effect from 16-10-1998. Till 28-2-2006, all non-statutory services provided by practising CA/CWA/CS were exempt from service tax. This exemption was withdrawn w.e.f. 1-3-2006. The practising CA/CWA/CS are providing non-statutory services like tax consultation and acting as representatives of clients before various statutory authorities. If the same service is provided by other professionals like an advocate or a non-qualified person, the services will not be taxable. This created discrimination. Many representations were made to Government by ICAI, ICWAI, ICSI and other bodies. Writ petitions were filed by many practising members in their personal capacity.

Finally, partial relief has been granted and service relating to representing clients before any statutory authority has been exempted vide Notification No. 25/2006-ST, dated 13-7-2006. However, there is no relief in case of other services like tax consultation, preparation and filing of tax returns and accounts writing work.

Background

1. Services provided by a practising CA/CWA/CS in his professional capacity are taxable with effect from 16-10-1998.

Any service provided or to be provided to a client, by a Practising Chartered Accountant, Practising Cost Accountant or Practising Company Secretary in his professional capacity in any manner, is a taxable service [section 65(105)(s), section 65(105)(u) and section 65(105)(t) of Finance Act, 1994].

Thus, this covers statutory as well as non-statutory services provided in his professional capacity.

Constitutional Validity of Levy - Constitutional validity of service tax on CA has been upheld in Chartered Accountants Association v. UOI 2000 STT 64 = 115 Taxman 543 = 179 ELT 129 = 252 ITR 53 (Guj. HC DB) - same view in All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. UOI [2001] 116 Taxman 418 = 256 ITR 401 (Bom. HC DB) * All Kerala Chartered Accountants Association v. UOI [2002] 121 Taxman 486 = 258 ITR 679 (Ker HC DB).

Services of non-qualified persons not taxable under this head - Though the definitions of practising CA/CWA/CS are ‘inclusive’, a person who is not qualified CA/CS/ICWA and do not hold certificate of practice cannot give statutory services in fields of chartered accountancy, company secretaryship or cost accountancy. However, services of firms of CA/ICWA/CS will be taxable, since the word used in inclusive part is ‘any concern’.

1.1 Distinction between tax on services of professional and other services - In case of all other taxable services, the service tax is on a specified service, while in case of practising CA/CWA/CS, the service tax is based on person who is providing the service and not the type of service.

This creates discrimination, since the service provided by practising CA/CWA/CS will be taxable while same service provided by others (like advocate, non-professionals) will not be taxed.

1.2 Exemption to non-statutory services till 28-2-2006 - In order to remove the discrimination, non-statutory services provided by practising CA/CWA/CS were exempt up to 28-2-2006, unless they fall in some other head of taxable service.

As per earlier Notification No. 59/1998-ST dated 16-10-1998, service tax was payable only on following services provided by PCA/PCS/PCWA -

(i)Accounting and auditing

(ii)Cost accounting and cost auditing

(iii)Secretarial auditing

(iv)Certification under Companies Act

(v)Certification for exchange control purposes under FEMA and

(vi)Certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets under wealth tax.

If any service provided falls under any of aforesaid category, it will be taxable. Service provided other than those specified in Notification No. 59/1998-ST was exempt from service tax, unless that service falls under some another specified category.

the following illustration:

"The service provided by a practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant in connection with the management of any organisation in any manner or recruitment of manpower in any manner shall be deemed to be the taxable service provided under the category of management consultant or manpower recruitment agency, as the case may be. Therefore, no exemption under this notification shall be applicable to such practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant." So, w.e.f. 1-8-2002, it was clarified that only those services are taxable under service tax which are either covered under Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 or covered under any of the other categories of services. And not all services, which are not covered under Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998, are exempt in case of these professionals, as was the thinking of these professionals. The Central Government, in principle, has accepted the representations of ICAI, ICWAI and ICSI that certain specified services rendered by these professionals should be exempted from service tax till the other professionals (e.g. Advocates) rendering these services are also brought into the service tax net. This can be seen from the Government’s Press Note. Therefore, based on these considerations (i.e., to maintain a level playing field), the Central Government has by Notification No.25/2006, dated 13-7-2006 exempted representation services (i.e. services relating to representation before statutory authorities) rendered by these professionals from service tax. The author argues that the logic for exempting representation services applies equally to tax consultancy services, filing of tax returns which constitute the main source of income for many CAs in non-metros and small cities and makes a passionate plea for exempting tax consultancy services and filing of tax returns also from service tax.

Backdrop

1. The Finance Act, 2006 has removed the exemption notification issued with respect to exemption to the Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost Accountants from the services other than audit, accounting and statutory certification services. The above exemption was given through Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax, dated the 16th October, 1998. This Notification was withdrawn w.e.f. 1st March, 2006 and from this date all the services including taxation services rendered by a practicing CA/ICWA/CS in his professional capacity are now covered by service tax. Auditing, accounting and statutory services of the Chartered Accountants were under the scope of service tax since initial stage of imposition of service tax on these professionals.

The other services including the taxation consultancy services were exempted from payment of service tax on the ground that these services are not the monopoly of these professionals and specially in the matter of taxation consultancy which includes consultancy of VAT, income-tax and service tax the Chartered Accountants are facing stiff competition from the other professionals including the Advocates and all these professionals are out of the scope of service tax. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India had termed this levy as discriminatory hence the Government through Notification No. 59/98, dated 16th October, 1998 has exempted the service tax on services other than the Audit, Accounting and statutory certification services.

The situation remains the same and still the Advocates are providing these services but for the reasons best known to our law makers this exemption was abruptly withdrawn on 28th Feb., 2006 w.e.f 1st March, 2006 and the result is that all the services including the taxation consultancy services provided by Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost Accountants are now taxable.

Reactions to withdrawal of service tax exemption

2. When the notification was withdrawn on 28th Feb., 2006 there was stiff resistance and opposition from whole of the CA community and even the ICAI has reacted strongly on the matter. Let us see the initial reaction of the ICAI from the following Press Release of ICAI, dated Feb. 28, 2006 :

"1. The practising chartered accountants will be adversely affected due to the withdrawal of Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax, dated 16th October, 1998. This notification exempted the services other than accounting, auditing and statutory certification services provided by a practicing chartered accountant, company secretary or cost accountant from the levy of service tax. The implication of the withdrawal is that the legal and taxation services rendered by the chartered accountants will attract 10% service tax plus the applicable surcharge and educational cess on and from 1st March, 2006 and at 12% upon enactment of the Finance Bill, 2006.

Press note issued by the department

4. The Department’s Press Note explains the rationale for this exemption as under: "Representations have been received from the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, the Institute of Cost and Works Accountants of India and the Association of Company Secretaries of India requesting the Government to consider exemption from levy of service tax on certain specified services provided by them which are also provided by other professionals and those other professionals providing similar services are not taxable. It has been stated that such an exemption is required till such time other professionals providing similar services are also taxed.

Government has considered the representations. Taking into account the views expressed by the Institutes and the Association and the other material facts, Government has exempted from levy of service tax only representational services provided to a client by a practising Chartered Accountant/Cost Accountant/Company Secretary to appear before a statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice."

Thus, the Press Note accepts, in principle, the idea that exemption from levy of service tax is required in respect of certain specified services provided by practising CAs/CWAs/CSs which are also provided by other professionals and those other professionals providing similar services are not taxable. If it is so, then this rationale does not apply only to representational services and that to only in proceedings initiated by way of issue of notice but to other services such as filing of tax returns, appearing for a client in an appeal filed by him, tax consultancy etc. Giving such exemption is not only required for maintaining a level playing field for the CAs/CWAs/CSs but also in public interest. There is an apprehension that in services except statutory ones like audit etc. which only CAs/CWAs/CSs can statutorily render and representational services which are exempt, other work (such as filing of tax returns) will be done by these professionals but bills will be issued to the client in the name of an Advocate/Income-Tax practitioner/sales tax practitioner and these professionals will take their share in cash. This will be done to save the client from the service tax. This will cause more loss of revenue than Exemption Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax dated 16-10-1998. This will not only cause loss of service tax revenue but also of income tax. Therefore, it is desirable that the pre-1-3-2006 position is restored.

Conclusion

5. The exemption is only for representational services by way of appearing before any statutory authority in proceedings initiated by issue of notice. In the interest of a level playing field for CAs/CWAs/CSs and in the interest of the public exchequer, it is desirable that other professionals like Advocates/Income-Tax Practitioners also be taxed or the pre-1-3-2006 position in respect of CAs/CWAs/CSs be restored.

The exclusivity clause, other conditions of agency agreement and the commission paid to assessee gave the arrangement the complexion of a franchise. Some of the observation of the Apex Court in case of Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd. v. UOI [2005] 1 STT 41 are also relevant, which are quoted below :

In the case before us the discrimination is not, even according to the writ petitioners, by reason of the subject matter of tax. It is also not the writ petitioners’ case that within the separate classes of services covered by the different clauses in section 65(41), there is any discrimination or that the law operates unequally within the classes. According to them the discrimination lies in the method of collection of the tax followed. But as we have said this is not of the essence of the tax and the mere difference in the machinery provisions between the different classes of service cannot found a challenge of discrimination. If the Legislature thinks that it will facilitate the collection of the tax due from such specified traders on a rationally discernible basis, there is nothing in the said legislative measure to offend article 14 of the Constitution. It is therefore, outside the judicial ken to determine whether the Parliament should have specified a common mode for recovery of the tax as a convenient administrative measure in respect of particular class. [In this case, it was not the writ petitioners’ case that the law operates unequally within the classes, so the Apex Court upheld the constitutionality. But in the case of CA, now the law operates unequally within the classes of service, so the same may be hit by the article 14]

So the constitutional challenge to the levy of service tax was upheld by different Courts and the arguments and answer to those arguments were also almost similar. SERVICE TAX ON CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT’S SERVICES

This article is a comprehensive analysis of leviability of service tax on Chartered Accountant’s Services.

Introduction

1. Service tax has been imposed on practising chartered accountant’s services with effect from October 16, 1998 vide Notification No. 53/98-ST, dated October 7, 1998. The gross amount charged by a practising chartered accountant from the client, in professional capacity, is chargeable to service tax.

Meaning of-Practising Chartered Accountant

2. Section 65(83) defines ‘practising chartered accountant’ as under—

‘practising chartered accountant’ means a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and is holding a certificate of practice granted under the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 (38 of 1949) and includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy.

As per section 65(83), a practising chartered accountant is a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, New Delhi and holds a certificate of practice under the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and also includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy. Thus, both associate and fellow members of the Institute are covered. It would also cover individuals as well as firms and persons holding full-time as well as part-time certificate of practice.

According to Webster’s Dictionary, a professional means ‘calling requiring specialised knowledge and often long intensive academic preparation; calling, vocation or employment’. The services should be rendered in this capacity using this skill and knowledge.

‘In any manner’ would mean directly or indirectly, personally or otherwise or through his staff members or through computer aid or other device or manually.

To be treated as a practising chartered accountant, following basic tests must be satisfied—

(i)He must be a person;

(ii)He must be a member (whether associate or fellow) of the Institute to which he belongs (ICAI);

(iii)He must hold a certificate of practice granted by the Institute;

(iv)In case of a firm of the chartered accountants, it must be a concern engaged in rendering services in the field of the chartered accountancy.

Legal position

3. In All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. u As an economic concept, there is no distinction between the consumption of goods and service as both satisfy human needs and this economic concept is based on the legal principle of equivalence.

u Service tax is a VAT which, in turn, is a general tax which applies to all commercial activities involving production of goods and provision of services.

u VAT is a consumption tax as it is borne by the client.

u Applying the principle of equivalence, there is no difference between production or manufacture of saleable goods and production of marketable/saleable services in the form of an activity undertaken by the service provider for consideration, which correspondingly stands consumed by the service receiver. It is this principle of equivalence which is in-built into the concept of service tax, which has received legal support in the form of Finance Act, 1994.

u Service tax is VAT which, in turn, is both a general tax as well as destination based consumption tax leviable on services provided within the country.

u A new charge by way of service tax or tax on service came to be levied statutorily by the Finance Act, 1994, which has subsequently attained Constitutional status by virtue of the Constitution (Eighty-eighth Amendment) Act, 2003.

A Firm of chartered accountants has the gross billing for the year ending on 31-3-2006 as under:— Since the service provided by the firm with respect to audit was only 2.30 Lakh hence the firm is not collecting and paying service tax in the year 2006-07 on the assumption that it is eligible for the benefit of exemption available to the small service providers as per Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) up to the value of 4 Lakh of collection. Please advise properly.

The total taxable service rendered by this firm of Rs.4.30 Lakhs in the previous year ended on 31-3-2006 hence the firm is not eligible for the exemption scheme available to this firm.

For this purpose there is clear provision in the Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) in the form of conditions mentioned in clause 2 of the scheme. The exact wording of clause 2(viii) is as under:—

"(viii)The aggregate value of taxable services rendered by a provider of taxable service from one or more premises, does not exceed rupees four lakhs in the preceding financial year."

Here, to be eligible for exemption scheme available to small service providers, the aggregate value of taxable service should not be more than Rupees 4 Lakh in the preceding financial year and both the Audit services and taxation services were part of taxable service though the tax was exempt on the taxation services. Let us see the exact wordings of the Exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 in this respect:—

from whole of the service tax leviable thereon.

Here that the service is taxable but this taxable service is exempt from paying the whole of tax. The point here is that the taxable service is exempt from paying the tax and in that case its structure of taxable service remained intact but the tax payable on it is exempt.

History of service tax on chartered accountants

2.1 A brief legislative history is that service tax was, for the first time, imposed by the Finance Act, 1994. This tax was levied on three types of services. Later on the scope of this tax has been widened almost in every Budget. Service tax on practising chartered accountants was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998 by the Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998. But there were protests against this levy by the CA community all over India. One of the main causes of protest was that, while the service tax was levied on Chartered Accountants’ services, but the same was not levied on the similar services provided by an advocate. Also in case of Jodhpur Chartered Accountants Society v. CCE [1998] STT 33/(105) ELT 290 (Raj.) [dated 24th November, 1998], the operation and implementation of Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998, was stayed and kept in abeyance so far as its application was concerned to the practising chartered accountants practising in the State of Rajasthan. Also, in many of the other cases, the stay was granted. Thus, due to protest against the levy by chartered accountants and certain Court decisions, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998 only on auditing and accounting services. So, the services provided by CAs and Advocates, which can be of similar nature, remain out of service tax. But the later developments are of crucial and patently of discriminatory nature.

Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998, was superseded by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998. From this notification, the nature of services was made more explicit as compared to Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998. But this is not all which happens to these professionals. Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 was amended by Notification No. 15/2002-ST, dated 1-8-2002 w.e.f. 1-8-2002 by inserting an Explanation under this notification. This Explanation provides that, "Nothing contained in this notification shall apply to the services provided by a practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant which may fall in any other taxable services as defined in clause (105) of section 65 of the said Act". Also, the same was clarified by the following illustration:

"The service provided by a practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant in connection with the management of any organisation in any manner or recruitment of manpower in any manner shall be deemed to be the taxable service provided under the category of management consultant or manpower recruitment agency, as the case may be. Therefore, no exemption under this notification shall be applicable to such practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant."

Introduction

1. Responding to the various representations made, particularly the Joint Memorandum dated 8.3.2006 given by the three professional Institutes (i.e. ICAI, ICSI and ICWAI) both to the Minister for Company Affairs and the Finance Minister with respect to removal of discrimination and providing level playing field to practising chartered accountants, practising cost accountants and practising company secretaries, the Government has issued Exemption Notification No. 25/2006-Service Tax, dated 13-7-2006 which provides that the professional services provided or to be provided by the practising chartered accountants, practising cost accountants and practising company secretaries in relation to representing the client before any statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice, shall be exempt from whole of the service tax.

Extent of Relief

2. Exemption of representation services before any statutory authority has brought certain relief to the CAs, CWAs and CSs, for these services now can be provided on a level playing field. The statutory authorities may include Company Law Board (CLB), ITAT, CESTAT, National Tax Tribunal, National Company Law Tribunal and various other authorities and Tribunals under different laws. Withdrawal of Exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-19981 had resulted in making these services costlier by the amount of service tax if they were to be provided by CAs, CSs or CWAs as compared to the similar services rendered by other categories of professionals. At global level also when world is expecting our professionals to provide BPO/KPO services, CAs, CSs or CWAs may find themselves out of competition because their services, due to the levy of service tax, may be costlier in comparison to those of others.

Representation Services - When Exempt

3. Representation services are exempt only when these are provided in respect of a client who has been issued notice and he is to be represented before the statutory authority in the course of proceedings arising out of issuance of such notice. In a case where representation is to be made without or before issuance of notice to the client, the representation services provided by CAs, CSs or CWAs may not be tax free though in case of other professionals who are authorised to provide such services, they are tax free. This lacuna needs clarification from the department.

So far as statutory authorities are concerned, all are covered though no definition of ‘statutory authority’ as such has been provided. Thus, the CAs, CSs or CWAs may represent the case of their client before any statutory authority if they are authorised to do so.

It is akin to the services rendered by any professional including a medical practitioner and a lawyer and the relationship between a chartered accountant and his clients is like that of a lawyer and his client and it cannot be merely construed as a ‘service’ under the Finance Act 32 of 1990. The tone of the argument was that the Legislature has picked and chosen the chartered accountants or the cost accountants and left out the other professionals like doctors and lawyers. This argument was obviously incorrect because it is for the Legislature to select any particular service or any particular subject for taxing. The tests of the vice of discrimination in a taxing law are less rigorous. In examining the allegations of a hostile discriminatory treatment what is looked into is not its phraseology, but the real effect of its provisions. Therefore, there would be no question of finding any fault with the Legislature for picking up the chartered accountants or the cost accountants or the architects also for taxing their services. Introduction and brief history

1. A brief legislative history is that service tax was, for the first time, imposed by the Finance Act, 1994. This tax was levied on three types of services. Later on the scope of this tax has been widened almost in every Budget. Service tax on practising Chartered Accountants was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998 by the Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998. But there were protest against this levy by the CA community all over India. One of the main causes of protest was that, while the service tax was levied on Chartered Accountants’ services but the same was not levied on the similar services provided by an advocate. Also in case of Jodhpur Chartered Accountants Society v. CCE [1998] STT 33/(105) ELT 290 (Raj.) [dated 24th November, 1998], the operation and implementation of Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998, was stayed and kept in abeyance so far as its application was concerned to the practising Chartered Accountants practising in the State of Rajasthan. Also in many of the other cases, the stay was granted. Thus due to protest against the levy by Chartered Accountants and certain Court decisions, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998 only on auditing and accounting services. So the services provided by CA and Advocate, which can be of similar nature, remains out of service tax. But the later developments are of crucial and patently of discriminatory nature.

Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998, was superseded by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998. From this notification, the nature of services was made more explicit as compared to Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998. But this is not all which happens to these professionals. Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 was amended by Notification No. 15/2002-ST, dated 1-8-2002 w.e.f. 1-8-2002 by inserting an explanation under this notification. This explanation provide that, "Nothing contained in this notification shall apply to the services provided by a practising Chartered Accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant which may fall in any other taxable services as defined in clause (105) of section 65 of the said Act". Also the same was clarified by the following illustration:

"The service provided by a practising Chartered Accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant in connection with the management of any organisation in any manner or recruitment of manpower in any manner shall be deemed to be the taxable service provided under the category of management consultant or manpower recruitment agency, as the case may be. SERVICE TAX LEVY ON CHARTERED ACCOUNTANTS - UNCONSTITUTIONAL, ILLEGAL, INVALID AND UNWARRANTED

‘Service tax’ was first introduced in India by the Finance Act, 1994, on a few services and subsequently extended to several other services by the relevant Finance Acts. The Finance Act, 1998 brought the services rendered by a chartered accountant within the purview of service tax. In this article, the author attacks the levy of service tax at its very root by arguing that under the Constitution of India, the Parliament has no power to enact service tax legislation and, hence, the levy in question is lacking in constitutional validity. The author also specifically questions the extension of the levy to the profession of chartered accountancy, inter alia, on the ground that the exercise of profession by a chartered accountant does not amount to rendering of ‘service’ - EDITOR

Introduction

1. The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech for the year 1998-99 has observed in para 169 as hereunder:

"169. In the last budget, a number of services were added in the tax net. These included the service rendered on transportation of goods by road. The House is aware that it led to widespread resistance and protests. As a result, this service tax was virtually kept in abeyance and rightly so. I have decided to abolish the service tax on transportation of goods by road. I have also decided to abolish the service tax payable by outdoor caterers and pandal contractors. However, I have proposed service tax on some new services. With a view to effecting the aforesaid policy decision, the Finance Bill (No. 2) of 1998 by Chapter VI thereof and clause 129 has effected several ancillary and consequential amendments in the Finance Act, 1994, section 65, etc.

Section 116 of the Finance Act, 1998 has provided for a levy of service tax at 5 per cent on services rendered by practising chartered accountants, cost accountants and company secretaries. The said ‘service tax’ has been brought into effect with effect from October 16, 1998. A further notification issued by the Revenue Department provides that the taxable services rendered to a client by a practising Chartered Accountant or a company secretary or cost accountant which will attract service tax include: accounting and auditing or cost accounting or secretarial auditing or verification of declarations in prescribed forms under section 149 of the Companies Act, 1956 or signing of annual return of listed companies under section 161 of the Companies Act or certification requirements of Schedule XIII to the Companies Act, or certification of documents to be filed with Registrar of Companies or certification in Form No. 1 under the Companies Unpaid Dividend Rules, 1978 or certification of documents under Export and Import Policy (1997-2002) or Certification for exchange control purposes under FERA 1973 or certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets as per rule 8A(7) of the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957. Who can be appointed for conduct the audit envisaged under section 92E

Who is eligible to be the auditor u/s 92E?

According to section 92E, the report should be an 'accountant'. Section 92F(i) defines 'accountant' has having the same meaning as in Explanation below section 288(2). According to the above mentioned explanation, it covers a CA and Restricted State auditor.

According to ICAI's 'Guidance Note on Report on International Transactions under section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Transfer Pricing)' hereinafter referred to as "Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing" :

♦ Section 92E refers to "an accountant" which means a Chartered Accountant as defined in Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.

♦ However, audit under section 92E can be done by a firm of Chartered Accountants also.

Extending the above logic of the Guidance Note further, a view can be taken that w.e.f. 1-3-2011 [date on which Chartered Accountants (Amendment) Act, 2011 came into force] LLPs of CAs in practice/CAs in practice with other prescribed professionals can be appointed for transfer pricing audit u/s 92E. CBDT/ICAI needs to clarify this.

Can audit under section 92E be conducted by an employee of assessee-client?

In Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 169 Taxman 328 (SC), the Supreme Court held that "An auditor is a professional person". He has to function independently. He is not an employee of the assessee.

Is it necessary that tax audit under section 92E shall be a CA in full-time practice?

Yes. At its 242nd meeting, the Council of ICAI has decided that any member in part-time practice (i.e. a member who is holding certificate of practice and also engaged in any other business/occupation) shall not be entitled to perform attest functions. Therefore, a CA in part-time practice cannot be appointed as auditor under section 92E.

In case of companies, is it necessary that audit u/s 92E be conducted by statutory auditor?

No. In case of companies, it can be done by the statutory auditor of the company appointed under section 224 of the Companies Act, 1956 or by any other CA in practice or firm of CAs. This is because section 92E does not require that only the statutory auditor should perform the audit under section 92E.

Whether a CA or firm of CAs appointed as tax consultants can conduct audit u/s 92E?

A CA/firm of CAs who are appointed as tax consultants may be appointed as auditor under section 92E. [ICAI's Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing]

Can a CA or CA firm who is internal auditor of assessee can also be auditor u/s 92E?

No. Internal auditor cannot give audit report u/s 92E. [ICAI's Code of Ethics]

Is there any limit on the number of audits under section 92E which a CA/CA firm can accept?

No. There is no limit on number of audits u/s 92E which CA/CA firm can accept.

Is there any minimum fee to be charged by CA firms for Tax audits?

No. Chapter XII of the Council General Guidelines has been omitted with effect from 7-6-2011. Hence, no minimum fee stipulated for audits at the moment.

Scope of audit under section 92E

What are the matters covered by scope of the audit u/s 92E?

It covers the following:

♦ Examination of only those accounts and records of the assessee which relate to international transactions/SDTs entered into by him during the previous year under audit.

The main point raised by some service providers is that where they are carrying out any certification as required by any statute can it come under the purview of consultancy, advice or technical assistance. The Government clarified the same through the Circular F.No. 177/5/2001-CX. 4, dated 26-2-2002. It was clarified that the certificates given under authority of any statute/international protocol/code/convention, cannot be considered to be a consultancy job. It is then to be examined whether this activity can come under the purview of advice or technical assistance. An advice is generally understood to be optional in nature and has no statutory force. It is up to the client to accept the advice or not. The activity of certification will, therefore, not fall under the category of advice. As regards ‘technical assistance’, it is observed that an assistance is normally for the purpose of achieving a particular aim or result. A certificate given by, say, the Boiler Inspector under the Factories Act, 1948, about the safety of a boiler, cannot be considered to be ‘assistance’ to the person using the said boiler in his factory. To issue certificates under the authority of any statute, it will obviously be necessary for the certifying agency to conduct some survey/inspection. Thus, the survey/inspection by an agency for the purposes of issuing certificates by the same agency under an authority of law, will also not amount to consultancy advice or technical assistance. If however, the shipping company gets the ship surveyed or inspected by another agency, before taking it for certification by an authorised agency, only then can it be said that the first agency is providing some technical assistance or advice. It will, therefore, be essential to examine each activity of a service provider on the basis of facts, the terms of agreement between the assessee and the clients and the corresponding provision of Indian or International statute/convention/protocol, or code, to determine whether the certificate being given is under the authority of any such statute, convention protocol or code. If it is so, the payment received for that service will not be taxable under the head "Consulting engineer". Any other inspection, survey, assessment, technical assistance, consultancy, recommendation, advice, undertaken/provided directly or indirectly, by the assessee would be liable to service tax under the head ‘Consulting engineer’. Thus, the word ‘charity’ has narrow meaning in dictionary. However, the word has acquired a technical meaning in law, which is wide.

As per section 2 of Charitable Endowments Act, 1890, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief to poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general public utility, but does not include a purpose which relates exclusively to religious teaching or worship. Section 65(105)(j) - Clearing and Forwarding Agent’s Services - Whether service receiver can deduct amount of service tax from service provider’s bill

6.2 Facts The respondent, a transport contractor, entered into a contract with the appellant for handling of its materials. During the pendency of the said contract, section 65 was substituted by section 88 whereby 5 per cent service tax was introduced on various services including ‘clearing and forwarding (C&F) agent’. The appellant, consequently, deducted 5 per cent service tax from the respondent’s bills on the assumption that the respondent was a C&F agent from 31-10-1997 in spite of respondent’s objections. On reference, the sole arbitrator dismissed the respondent’s objection. On petition filed by the respondent, the Single Judge of the High Court allowed the same by setting aside the impugned award.

Decision of Bombay High Court:

u The High Court held that the constitutional validity with regard to the extension of service tax in view of the amendment to the Finance Act, 2000, section 116(a) and section 65(6) to treat the recipients of the services as an assessee in case of services rendered by goods transport operators and clearing and forwarding agents, was upheld by the Supreme Court in Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd. v. Union of India [2005] 1 STT 41.

u The High Court further held that Single Judge had set aside the award passed by the arbitrator by which the arbitrator held that the appellant was entitled to deduct the service tax amount from the amount payable to the respondent. Admittedly, the appellant was recipient of the service of the respondents as per the agreement-in-question. The appellant, pursuant to the provisions of service tax was registered and recognized as an ‘assessee’ and had also filed returns as contemplated accordingly. The appellant, therefore, was liable to pay the service tax being the recipient of the services from the respondent. Admittedly, there was no specific agreement with regard to payment of service tax-in-question by the respondent to the extent the appellant would be entitled to deduct the amount so paid or payable under the service tax, though the respondent was not an assessee and/or not liable to pay service tax under the law. There was no specific clause that such service tax liability would be deductible from the amount payable by the appellant to the respondent pursuant to the contract-in-question. The deduction as claimed and as directed by the award in absence of any agreement or clause, therefore, was not correct. The department, on application filed by the applicant, already rejected the specific claim of refund of that amount.

u The High Court further observed that there was nothing to show even from the plain reading of the agreement and the clauses thereof that, payment of service tax, though payable by the ‘assessee’, yet it would be the respondent, the service provider, to re-pay the same to the appellant and, therefore, the appellant was entitled to deduct service tax from the bills of the respondent in terms of the clauses of the agreement. The Single Judge, therefore, was right in reversing the award passed by the arbitrator. The agreement nowhere entitled the appellant to deduct and/or to recover such service tax from the respondent. Therefore, the High Court held, as rightly held by the Single Judge, that the award was, on the face of it, illegal and erroneous.

[Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. v. Dewan Chand Ram Saran [2008] 14 STT 328 (Bom.)]

Section 65(105)(s) - Chartered Accountant’s services - Scope of services

6.3 Service tax on practising chartered accountants was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998 by the Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998. But there were protests against this levy by the CA community all over India. One of the main causes of protest was that, while the service tax was levied on chartered accountants’ services, but the same was not levied on the similar services provided by an advocate. Thus, due to protest against the levy by chartered accountants and certain Court decisions, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998 only on auditing and accounting services. So, the services provided by CAs and advocates, which can be of similar nature, remain out of service tax. But the later developments are of crucial nature and patently of a discriminatory nature.

Section 92E does not stipulate that only the statutory auditor appointed under the Companies Act or other similar statute should perform the examination. The examination can, therefore, be conducted either by the statutory auditor or by any other Chartered Accountant in practice having certificate of practice.

The issue of a report u/s 92E, being a recurring assignment for expressing a professional opinion, the accountant accepting the assignment should communicate with the accountant who had done the examination in the earlier year, as provided in the Chartered Accountants Act. In the case of a person whose accounts of the business or profession have been audited under any other law (i.e., a company, a co-operative society, etc. which is required to get the accounts audited under a statute), it is not necessary to communicate with the statutory auditor if he had not done the examination in the earlier year.

The accountant should obtain from the assessee a letter of appointment for conducting the examination as mentioned in section 92E. It is advisable that such an appointment letter should be signed by the person competent to sign/verify the return of income in terms of the provisions of section 140 or by any person who has been authorized by the company to make such an appointment. The accountant should get the statement of particulars, as required in the annexure to the report, authenticated by the assessee before he proceeds to verify the same. The accountant is required to submit his report to the person appointing him, viz., the assessee.

The appointment of the accountant in the case of a company need not be made at the general meeting of the members. It can be made by the Board of Directors or even by any officer, if so authorised by the Board in this behalf. Court fees on documents presented before the income-tax authorities are chargeable according to the scales laid down in the Court Fees Act, 1870 and the amendments made in different States are not to be taken into consideration.—Circular : No. 50(XL-43) of 1956, dated 28-12-1956.

Special Audit of Cenvat Credit by Cost/Chartered Accountant

Section 72A of Finance Act, 1994 (as inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012) make provision for special audit by practicing Chartered/Cost Accountant [earlier, section 14AA of Central Excise Act was made applicable to service tax. This section provided only for special audit of Cenvat credit availed].

Special audit can be ordered by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Central Excise [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

Such audit can be ordered if the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of CE has reason to believe that any person liable to pay service tax—

(i)

has failed to declare or determine the value of a taxable service correctly; or

(ii)

has availed and utilised credit of duty or tax paid - (a) which is not within the normal limits having regard to the nature of taxable service provided, the extent of capital goods used or the type of inputs or input services used, or any other relevant factors as he may deem appropriate; or (b) by means of fraud, collusion, or any wilful misstatement or suppression of facts; or

(iii)

has operations spread out in multiple locations and it is not possible or practicable to obtain a true and complete picture of his accounts from the registered premises falling under the jurisdiction of the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner [section 72A(1) of Finance Act, 1994].

In such cases, the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner may direct such person to get his accounts audited by a chartered accountant or cost accountant nominated by him, to the extent and for the period as may be specified by the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner [section 72A(2) of Finance Act, 1994, inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012] [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

The provisions of special audit apply even if audit was conducted under some other law [section 72A(3) of Finance Act, 1994]

The auditee (person liable to pay service tax) shall be given opportunity of hearing in respect of any material gathered on the basis of such special audit and proposed to be utilised in any proceedings against him [section 72A(4) of Finance Act, 1994 inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012]

Section 14AA of Central Excise Act provides that the audit fees will be paid by Central Government (i.e. service tax department). However, section 72A of Finance Act, 1994 makes no provision of fees of the Chartered/Cost Accountant for such audit.

Reference to Transfer Pricing Officer [Section 92CA]

Section 92CA of the Income-tax Act provides that the Assessing Officer may refer the computation of arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or specified domestic transaction to a Transfer Pricing Officer. Such a reference can be made where:—

(a)

The Assessing Officer considers it is necessary or expedient to do so, and

(b)

The Assessing Officer has taken previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner to refer the computation to Transfer Pricing Officer.

This section specifies the entire process through which the arm's length price is determined by the Transfer Pricing Officer.

With effect from 1-11-2020, the Amendment Act, 2020 has inserted a new sub-section (8) in section 92CA to empower the Central Government to frame a scheme for the purpose of determination of arm's length price to impart greater efficiency, transparency and accountability by:—

(a)

Eliminating the interface between the Transfer Pricing Officer and the assessee or any other person to the extent technologically feasible;

(b)

Optimising utilisation of the resources through economies of scale and functional specialisation; and

(c)

Introducing a team-based determination of arm's length price (ALP) with dynamic jurisdiction.
Notified scheme - Tax Return Preparers Scheme - SO 2039(E), dated 28-11-2006.

The clause does not require the tax auditor to audit whether the assessee has complied with Chapter X provisions regarding the international transactions he entered into and whether suo motu made appropriate TP adjustments in his ITR. Nor is the tax auditor required to examine or report whether the assessee has maintained proper records as required by Rule 10D regarding international transactions. Nor is he required to examine whether the Arm's Length Price has been determined for international transactions in accordance with any of the recognised methods specified in Section 92F. That is the subject of the audit to be carried out under Section 92E, and the report is to be furnished in Form No. 3CEB.

The tax auditor must report in this clause only if a primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1). If no primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1), the tax auditor has no duty to report. The tax auditor is not even required to report if the primary TP adjustment has not been made as per the APA entered into by the assessee. If primary TP adjustment has been made according to the APA, then the reporting obligation under this Clause is triggered.

This clause also does not deal with Thin Cap adjustments under Section 94B. That is the subject matter of Clause 30B.

This Clause also does not deal with the issue of shares at a premium to non-resident investors by a closely held company that attracts Section 56(2)(vii). That is the subject matter of Clause 29A.

Although the tax auditor is not required to examine compliance with transfer pricing provisions under Chapter X of the Act except to the limited extent required by Clauses 30A, 30B and 43 of Form No. 3CD, it may be advisable for him to do so to identify impermissible avoidance arrangements for Clause 30C purposes as unacceptable circumvention of SAARs like Transfer Pricing provisions would attract GAAR. Indian Transfer Pricing law is essentially all about adjustments required if the pricing in international transactions is not at arm's length. There is no scope for adjustments for non-arm's length non-price terms and conditions as Chapter X has no treaty equivalent transfer pricing provisions along the lines of Article 9 of OECD Model Conventions. Nevertheless, the tax auditor may find it useful to examine if any of the non-price terms and conditions of international transactions are not at arm's length from the angle of Clause 30C.

4. Role of Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) 4.1 The role of the TPO begins after a reference is received from the AO. In terms of section 92CA, this role is limited to the determination of the ALP in relation to international transactions or specified domestic transactions referred to him by the AO. However, if any other international transaction comes to the notice of the TPO during the course of the proceedings before him, then he is empowered to determine the ALP of such other international transactions also by virtue of section 92CA(2A) and (2B). The transfer price has to be determined by the TPO in terms of section 92C. The price has to be determined by using any one of the methods stipulated in sub-section (1) of section 92C and by applying the most appropriate method referred to in sub-section (2) thereof. There may be occasions where application of the most appropriate method provides results which are different but equally reliable. In all such cases, further scrutiny may be necessary to evaluate the appropriateness of the method, the correctness of the data, weight given to various factors and so on. The selection of the most appropriate method will depend upon the facts of the case and the factors mentioned in Rule 10C. The TPO, after taking into account all relevant facts and data available to him, shall determine the ALP and pass a speaking order.

4.2 The TPO's order should contain details of the data used, reasons for arriving at a certain price and the applicability of methods. It may be emphasised that the application of method including the application of the most appropriate method, the data used, factors governing the applicability of respective methods, computation of price under a given method will all be subjected to judicial scrutiny. It is, therefore, necessary that the order of the TPO contains adequate reasons on all these counts. Copies of the documents or the relevant data used in arriving at the arm's length price should be made available to the AO for his records and the use at subsequent stages of appellate or penal proceedings.

4.3 The TPO, being an Additional/Joint CIT, shall obtain the approval of the jurisdictional CIT (Transfer Pricing) before passing the order. On the other hand, the TPO, being a Deputy/Assistant CIT, shall obtain the approval of the jurisdictional Additional/Joint CIT before passing the order. The jurisdictional CIT (TP) should assign a limited number of important and complex cases, not exceeding 50, to the Additional/Joint CsIT (TPOs) working in the same jurisdiction. For the selection of such important and complex cases by the CsIT (TP), the concerned CCsIT (International Taxation) shall frame appropriate guidelines.

4.4 In addition to the above, the TPO is required to carry out the Compliance Audit of the Advance Pricing Agreements (APAs) entered into by the Board and the taxpayers in accordance with Rule 10P of the Income-tax Rules.

4.5 The TPO is also required to play an important role in respect of Safe Harbour provisions. Whenever a reference is made to the TPO under sub-rule (4) or sub-rule (10) of Rule 10TE of the Income-tax Rules, the TPO has to carefully examine all the facts and circumstances of the taxpayer's exercise of an option for Safe Harbour and pass an order in writing as mandated in sub-rule (6) or sub-rule (11) of the said Rule, respectively.

5. Role of the AO after Determination of ALP by the TPO

Under sub-section (4) of section 92C (read with sub-section (4) of section 92CA), the AO has to compute the total income of the assessee in conformity with the ALP determined by the TPO under sub-section (3) of section 92CA.

6. Maintenance of Data Base

It is to be ensured by the CIT (TP) that the references received from the AOs by the TPOs in his jurisdiction are dealt with expeditiously and accurate record of all events connected with the whole process of determination of ALP is maintained. 6.2 It has been brought to the notice that the provision requiring payment of service tax after receipt of payment are used for tax avoidance especially when the transaction is between associated enterprises. There have been instances wherein service tax has not been paid on the ground of non-receipt of payment even though the transaction has been recognized as revenue/expenditure in the statement of profit and loss account for the purpose of determining corporate tax liability. 6.3 As an anti-avoidance measure, it is proposed to clarify that service tax is leviable on taxable services provided by the person liable to pay service tax even if the amount is not actually received, but the amount is credited or debited in the books of account of the service provider. In other words, service tax is required to be paid after receipt of payment or crediting/debiting of the amount in the books of accounts, whichever is earlier. However, this provision is restricted to transaction between associated enterprises. This provision shall also apply to service tax payable under reverse charge method (Section 66A) as taxable services received from associated enterprises. For this purpose section 67 and rule 6(1) are being amended.

6.4 The term 'associated enterprise' has the same meaning as assigned to it in section 92A of the Income Tax Act, 1961. It is a relative concept i.e. an enterprise is an associated enterprise when it is viewed in relation to other enterprises. This concept is used in the Income Tax Act for applying transfer pricing provisions. An enterprise which participates, directly or indirectly, or through one or more intermediaries, in the management or control or capital of the other enterprise is considered as associated enterprise. It also covers an enterprise in respect of which one or more persons who participate, directly or indirectly, or through one or more intermediaries, in the management or control or capital of the other enterprise.

6.5 Section 92A(2) of the Income Tax Act specifies various situations under which two enterprises shall be deemed to be associated enterprises. Enterprise means a person who is engaged in the provision of any services of any kind. For details, relevant provisions of Income Tax Act may be referred to.

"3.34 Transfer pricing adjustment

The adjustment to arrive at that price is known as a transfer pricing adjustment."

10.8

Reimbursement of expenses incurred on behalf of service receiver not includible

Often, a service provider incurs some expenditure on behalf of service receiver and then recovers the amount from him. Such expenditure is not part of service provided by him to service receiver, but is incurred by him as per business practice or convenience. Following illustrations may clarify the provisions -

Octroi/entry tax amount paid by Clearing & Forwarding Agent, CHA or Transporter on behalf of owner of goods/Principal.

Customs duty, dock dues, demurrage, transport charges etc. paid by Customs House Agent on behalf of client.

Advertisement charges paid by Advertising Agency to newspaper on behalf of clients.

Ticket charges paid by Travel Agent and recovered from his customer.

These are not part of service provided and hence are not includible. Rule 5(2) provides that the expenditure or costs that a service provider incurs, as a pure agent of the client, shall be excluded from the value if such service provider fulfils prescribed conditions.

The principle is also discernible from various exclusions as contained in rule 6(2).

Reimbursement of expenses incurred on behalf of client is not includible - Glaxo Smithkline Pharmaceuticals v. CCE (2005) 1 STT 37 (CESTAT).

In Bax Global India v. CST (2008) 13 STT 263 (CESTAT), it was held that activity of CHA relates to entry or departure of conveyances or import or export of goods any customs station. It cannot extend beyond it. Charges collected for freight, cartage, MSIL/JWG charges, examination charges, DO fees, Bill of Lading fee, CFS charges, storage and handling etc. do not pertain to CHA service. In case of charges collected by CHA for activities not related to CHA, he is not liable to pay service tax. Even if he earns profit on these activities, it is not includible in value of CHA services.

No service tax on registration fee and stamp duty of immovable property - Service tax is not payable on reimbursable expenses like registration charges and stamp duty, recovered by builder from the customer - LCS City Makers P Ltd. v. CST (2012) 36 STT 228 = 23 taxmann.com 169 (CESTAT).

No service tax on passenger service fee and airport tax collected by airlines - In Lufthansa German Airlines v. CST (2016) 56 GST 58 = 70 taxmann.com 60 (CESTAT), it has been held that passenger service fee and airport tax which is collected from passengers and paid over to airport/Government authorities is not includible in value of service as it is collected as pure agent - same view in Lufthansa German Airlines v. CST (2016) 56 GST 196 = 70 taxmann.com 169 (CESTAT).

No service tax on stamp duty and Security Transaction Tax (STT) - Stamp duty and Security Transaction Tax (STT) is liability of buyer and stock broker pays it acting as pure agent of the customer. These are not includible in taxable amount for service tax - CBE&C letter No. 187/107/2010-CX.4 dated 17-9-2010.

Reimbursement of expenses which is liability of service receiver as per agreement is not includible - In Scott Wilson Kirkpatrick India P Ltd. v. CCE (2007) 8 STT 58 (CESTAT), the customer (NHAI - National Highways Authority of India) was to provide some basic facilities as per agreement. NHAI agreed that service provider (assessee in this case) can procure the facilities and claim reimbursement from NHAI. It was held that such tax is not payable on reimbursement of such expenses.

Issue referred to large bench due to conflicting decisions - In view of conflicting views about reimbursement of expenses, the issue has been referred to large bench in Amit Sales v. CCE (Stay order Delhi CESTAT dated 1-10-2008) - quoted and stay granted in Kidstuff Promos v. CST (2010) 26 STT 127 (CESTAT).

6.2 Power to Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) to identify international transactions

Section 92CA(1) provides that the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) can determine the ALP only in relation to an international transaction, which has been referred to him by the Assessing Officer.

This was recognized by the CBDT vide its Instruction No. 3 of 28-3-2003 as follows: “In terms of section 92CA this role is limited to the determination of arm’s length price in relation to the international transaction(s) referred to him by the Assessing Officer. If during the course of proceedings before him it is found that there are certain other transactions, which have not been referred to him by the Assessing Officer, he will have to take up the matter with the Assessing Officer so that a fresh reference is received with regard to such transactions”.

Further, in Amadeus India Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 10 taxmann.com 88 (Delhi - Trib.) it was held that TPO has jurisdiction only in respect of international transactions referred to him by the Assessing Officer.

Section 92CA has now been amended with effect from 1-6-2011 so as to specifically provide that the jurisdiction of the TPO shall extend to the determination of the ALP in respect of other international transactions noticed by him subsequently, in the course of proceedings before him. Such international transactions would be in addition to the international transactions referred to the TPO by the Assessing Officer.

It is now well-settled that a procedural amendment is generally retrospective and applies even to pending proceedings [CWT v. Sharvan Kumar Swamp & Sons [1994] 210 ITR 886 (SC); CIT v. Synergy Financial Exchange Ltd. [2007] 288 ITR 366 (Mad.)]. Now, the amendment could be consi- dered as a procedural amendment and hence it could apply to all assessments including pending assessments in respect of years up to assessment year 2010-11, which are pending before the TPO.

6.3 Power to TPO under section 133A

Section 92CA(7) provides that for the purpose of determining the ALP, the TPO can exercise powers available to an Assessing Officer under section 131(1) and section 133(6). These are powers of summoning or calling for details for the purpose of inquiry or investigation into the matter. Section 92CA(7) has now been amended with effect from 1-6-2011 to enable the TPO to also exercise the power of survey conferred upon an income-tax authority under section 133A.

Section 133A provides for the power of an income-tax authority to enter a place of business or profession and inspect books of account and obtain such other information as he may require as to any matter which may be useful for, or relevant to, any proceeding under the Act.

3.4 For cases to be referred by the AO to the TPO in accordance with paragraphs 3.2 and 3.3 above, in respect of transactions having the following situations, the AO must, as a jurisdictional requirement, record his satisfaction that there is an income or a potential of an income arising and/or being affected on determination of the ALP of an international transaction or specified domestic transaction before seeking approval of the PCIT or CIT to refer the matter to the TPO for determination of the ALP:

where the taxpayer has not filed the Accountant's report under section 92E of the Act but the international transactions or specified domestic transactions undertaken by it come to the notice of the AO;

where the taxpayer has not declared one or more international transactions or specified domestic transactions in the Accountant's report filed under section 92E of the Act and the said transaction or transactions come to the notice of the AO; and

where the taxpayer has declared the international transactions or specified domestic transactions in the Accountant's report filed under section 92E of the Act but has made certain qualifying remarks to the effect that the said transactions are not international transactions or specified domestic transactions or they do not impact the income of the taxpayer.

In the above three situations, the AO must provide an opportunity of being heard to the taxpayer before recording his satisfaction or otherwise. In case no objection is raised by the taxpayer to the applicability of Chapter X [Sections 92 to 92F] of the Act to these three situations, then AO should refer the international transaction or specified domestic transaction to the TPO for determining the ALP after obtaining the approval of the PCIT or CIT. However, where the applicability of Chapter X [Sections 92 to 92F] to these three situations is objected to by the taxpayer, the AO must consider the taxpayer's objections and pass a speaking order so as to comply with the principles of natural justice. If the AO decides in the said order that the transaction in question needs to be referred to the TPO, he should make a reference after obtaining the approval of the PCIT or CIT.

3.5 In addition to the cases to be referred as per paragraphs 3.2 and 3.3, a case involving a transfer pricing adjustment in an earlier assessment year that has been fully or partially set-aside by the ITAT, High Court or Supreme Court on the issue of the said adjustment shall invariably be referred to the TPO for determination of the ALP.

3.6 Since the provisions of section 92CA of the Act, inter alia, refer to the computation of the ALP of the international transaction or specified domestic transaction, it is imperative for the AO to ensure that all international transactions or relevant specified domestic transactions or both, as the case may be, are explicitly mentioned in the letter through which the reference is made to the TPO. In this regard, guidelines as under may be followed :

(a)

If a case has been selected for scrutiny on a TP risk parameter pertaining to international transactions only, then the international transactions shall alone be referred to the TPO;

(b)

If a case has been selected for scrutiny on a TP risk parameter pertaining to specified domestic transactions only, then the specified domestic transactions shall alone be referred to the TPO; and

(c)

If a case has been selected for scrutiny on the basis of TP risk parameters pertaining to both international transactions and specified domestic transactions, then the international transactions and the specified domestic transactions shall together be referred to the TPO.

Since international transactions may be benchmarked together at the entity level due to the inter-linkages amongst them, if a case has been selected for scrutiny on a TP risk parameter pertaining to one or more international transactions, then all the international transactions entered into by the taxpayer - except those about which the AO has decided not to make a reference as per paragraph 3.4 - shall be referred to the TPO.

3.7 For administering the transfer pricing regime in an efficient manner, it is clarified that though AO has the power under section 92C to determine the ALP of international transactions or specified domestic transactions, determination of ALP should not be carried out at all by the AO in a case where reference is not made to the TPO. However, in such cases, the AO must record in the body of the assessment order that due to the Board's Instruction on this matter, the transfer pricing issue has not been examined at all.

6.3 Power to TPO under section 133A

Section 92CA(7) provides that for the purpose of determining the ALP, the TPO can exercise powers available to an Assessing Officer under section 131(1) and section 133(6). These are powers of summoning or calling for details for the purpose of inquiry or investigation into the matter. Section 92CA(7) has now been amended with effect from 1-6-2011 to enable the TPO to also exercise the power of survey conferred upon an income-tax authority under section 133A.

Section 133A provides for the power of an income-tax authority to enter a place of business or profession and inspect books of account and obtain such other information as he may require as to any matter which may be useful for, or relevant to, any proceeding under the Act.

6.2 Power to Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) to identify international transactions

Section 92CA(1) provides that the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) can determine the ALP only in relation to an international transaction, which has been referred to him by the Assessing Officer.

This was recognized by the CBDT vide its Instruction No. 3 of 28-3-2003 as follows:

"In terms of section 92CA this role is limited to the determination of arm's length price in relation to the international transaction(s) referred to him by the Assessing Officer. If during the course of proceedings before him it is found that there are certain other transactions, which have not been referred to him by the Assessing Officer, he will have to take up the matter with the Assessing Officer so that a fresh reference is received with regard to such transactions".

Further, in Amadeus India Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 10 taxmann.com 88 (Delhi - Trib.) it was held that TPO has jurisdiction only in respect of international transactions referred to him by the Assessing Officer.

Section 92CA has now been amended with effect from 1-6-2011 so as to specifically provide that the jurisdiction of the TPO shall extend to the determination of the ALP in respect of other international transactions noticed by him subsequently, in the course of proceedings before him. Such international transactions would be in addition to the international transactions referred to the TPO by the Assessing Officer.

It is now well-settled that a procedural amendment is generally retrospective and applies even to pending proceedings [CWT v. Sharvan Kumar Swamp & Sons [1994] 210 ITR 886 (SC); CIT v. Synergy Financial Exchange Ltd. [2007] 288 ITR 366 (Mad.)]. Now, the amendment could be consi- dered as a procedural amendment and hence it could apply to all assessments including pending assessments in respect of years up to assessment year 2010-11, which are pending before the TPO.

34.6-5 Charges for registration

A business entity is required to pay various types of registration charges e.g. motor vehicle registration, excise registration, service tax registration.

These charges are paid as the person paying these charges is given right to perform some acts. For example, RTO registration charges grant him right to run vehicle on roads. Hence, it cannot be said that there is no quid pro quo.

The motor vehicle registration charges are partly regulatory and partly compensatory. It is permission to run vehicle on road. It is activity for consideration. These can be subject to service tax.

However, all services of registration under any law have been exempted from GST.

34.6-6 Services of Inspection, testing, certification

A business entity is required to pay various types of inspection charges and fees e.g. PF administration charges, Motor Vehicles Inspection charges, Building inspection fee and what not.

These charges are paid as the person paying these charges is given right to enjoy various facilities.

When a person sets up a factory, purchases a vehicle, constructs a building or employs person, by necessary implication, he agrees to pay necessary fees.

It can be argued that these charges are not at the 'desire of promisor' - rather against the desire of promisor. However, the fact is that he is willing to pay those charges as he gets privileges and advantages after paying those charges.

These would be subject to GST.

However, services of testing, calibration, safety check or certification required under any law relating to (a) protection and safety of workmen (b) consumers (c) public at large, including fire license have been exempted from GST.

34.6-7 Filing fees with Registrar of Companies for registration of documents

The fees payable are of course statutory. However, the fees paid are to get privileges to run business as a 'company'. Hence, there is quid pro quo. Service tax should be payable.

However, if fees payable do not exceed Rs 5,000 are exempt and hence there is no reverse charge.

34.6-8 MOT charges payable to excise and customs authorities

A business entity is required to pay MOT (Merchant Overtime Charges) to excise and customs authorities for export and import clearances [These are in addition to the unofficial charges payable to them].

12.4 Change in the time limit to pass the order by the Transfer Pricing Officer [Section 166 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to section 92CA of ITA 1961)]

12.4-1 Position under the ITA 1961

Section 92CA of the ITA 1961 deals with the case where the assessee has entered into an international transaction or specified domestic transaction in any previous year, and the AO may refer the computation of the Arm's Length Price (ALP) in relation to the said international transaction or specified domestic transaction under section 92C to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO).

Sub-section (3A) to section 92CA states that TPO is required to pass an order before sixty days prior to the date on which the period of limitation under section 153, or as the case may be, in section 153B for making the order of assessment, reassessment or recomputation or fresh assessment, as the case may be, expires.

12.4-1a Exclusion of the last day of assessment limitation - The interpretation of the phrase 'before sixty days prior to the date' has been a consistent point of contention between taxpayers and the revenue, leading to significant litigation.

The Madras High Court, in the case of Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), which affirmed the Single Judge's decision in Jt. CIT v. Pfizer Healthcare India (P.) Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 536 (Madras), held that the word 'date' in section 92CA(3A) refers to the last date for the AO to pass the assessment order under section 153 (e.g., December 31st). The crucial words 'prior to' indicate that, for the purpose of calculating the 60 days, this last date must be excluded. Therefore, if the assessment limitation expires on December 31st, the TPO order ought to have been passed on or before October 31st.

This interpretation was consistently followed across numerous ITAT benches, including in the following cases:

Teleperformance Global Services (P.) Ltd. [2023] 155 taxmann.com 658 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Zydus Lifesciences Ltd. [2024] 163 taxmann.com 349 (Ahmedabad-Trib.)

Frost & Sullivan (India) (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 739 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Shell India Markets (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 366 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Siemens Technology and Services (P.) Ltd. [2024] 162 taxmann.com 357 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Huhtamaki India Ltd. [2024] 164 taxmann.com 194 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Atos India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 152 taxmann.com 217 (Mumbai-Trib.)
