12.4-1b Mandatory nature of the time limit - Another critical aspect clarified by the judiciary is whether the time limit prescribed in section 92CA(3A) is mandatory or merely directory. The revenue often argued that the use of the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) implies a directory nature.

However, the Madras High Court in Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), after a detailed analysis of the scheme of the Act and the consequences of non-compliance, unequivocally held that the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) has to be construed as 'shall' and the time period fixed therein has to be scrupulously followed.'

The court reasoned that the overall scheme of transfer pricing assessments, with various interlinked time limits (including extensions under the proviso to section 92CA(3A) and section 153), indicates a legislative intent to ensure timely completion. If the TPO's time limit were merely directory, it would undermine the entire assessment process. This principle has been reiterated in the case of Asstt. CIT v. CAE India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 691 (Bangalore - Trib.).

GENERAL

Application of Transfer Pricing Regulations - In order to reduce litigation, section 40A(2) and section 80-IA(10) need to be amended to empower Assessing Officer to make adjustments to income declared by assessee, having regard to fair market value of transactions between related parties by applying any of generally accepted methods of determination of arm's length price, including methods provided under Transfer Pricing Regulations. Law should also be amended to make it compulsory for taxpayers to maintain books of account and other documents on lines prescribed under rule 10D in respect of such domestic transactions and taxpayers should obtain an audit report from their chartered accountants so that taxpayers maintain proper documents and requisite books of account reflecting transactions between related entities at arm's length price, based on generally accepted methods specified under Transfer Pricing Regulations - CIT v. Glaxo Smithkline Asia (P.) Ltd. [2010] 195 Taxman 35 (SC).

APPLICABILITY

Expenditure must first be proved as excessive and unreasonable - Section 40A(2)(a) cannot have any application, unless it is first held that the expenditure was excessive and unreasonable - Upper India Publishing House (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 117 ITR 569 (SC).

'Services' must be commercial in character, having market value - The expression 'services' in section 40A(2)(a) is an expression of wider import. The goods, services and facilities referred to in section 40A(2)(a) are those which have a market value and which are commercial in character - T.T. (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [1980] 121 ITR 551 (Kar.).

Three requirements are independent of, and alternative to, each other - In relation to the disallowance under the provisions of section 40A(2), a plain reading of the provision reveals that where an assessee incurs any expenditure in respect of which payment is required to be made or has been made to any person referred to in clause (b) of section 40A(2) and the Assessing Officer is of the opinion that such expenditure is excessive or unreasonable having regard to (a) fair market value of the goods, services or facilities for which the payment is made; or (b) the legitimate needs of the business of the assessee; or (c) the benefits derived by or accruing to the assessee on receipt of such goods, services or facilities, then the Assessing Officer shall not allow as a deduction so much of the expenditure as is considered by the Assessing Officer to be excessive or unreasonable. Therefore, it becomes apparent that the Assessing Officer is required to record a finding as to whether the expenditure is excessive or unreasonable in relation to any one of the three requirements prescribed, which are independent and alternative to each other. All the three requirements need not exist simultaneously. In a given case, if any one condition is shown to be satisfied the provision can be invoked and applied, if the facts so warrant. - Coronation Flour Mills v. Asstt. CIT [2009] 314 ITR 1 (Guj.).

Quality and nature of services rendered must be considered - The question whether the expenditure is excessive or unreasonable in a given case has to be examined keeping in mind, the services for which payment is made. In the process, the legitimate needs of the business or profession of the assessee or the benefit derived by or accruing to the assessee from such services is also to be kept in mind. In the business of advertising and media, the role of a media consultant is much more important than the role of client management. In fact, considering the nature of business, media consultancy is the backbone of such business and plays much more pivotal role than the persons handling client management. For that reason, if the director in charge of media consultancy was paid higher remuneration than what was paid to director in charge of client management it could not be treated as excessive or unreasonable, more so, when the two cases were not at par and could not be treated as comparable by any standards. - Hive Communication (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 201 Taxman 99/12 taxmann.com 287 (Delhi).

CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETIES - Provisions of section 40A(2) are not applicable to a co-operative society - CIT v. Manjara Shetkari Sahakari Sakhar Karkhana Ltd. [2008] 166 Taxman 287 (Bom.).

RULE 10E*

Report from an accountant to be furnished under section 92E

Statutory background

10E.1 As per section 92E, every person who has entered into an international transaction or specified domestic transaction during a PY shall obtain a report from an accountant [as defined in Explanation below section 288(2)] and furnish such report on or before the specified date [i.e., date 1 month prior to the due date for furnishing the return of income u/s 139(1) for the relevant AY]. Further, such person has to furnish by that specified date the report of such accountant in the form prescribed under Rule 10E (see para 10E.2) duly signed and verified by such accountant.

10E.1-1 Furnishing of TP report is a basis for referring matter to TPO u/s 92CA - In terms of section 92CA, it is not every international transaction which is to be referred to TPO but only those transactions where the AO considers it necessary to do so u/s 92C. This satisfaction by the AO to refer the matter to the TPO could only be arrived at after a report from the accountant in terms of section 92E has been filed with the AO. It is on examination of the same the occasion would arise for the AO to refer the matter to the TPO u/s 92CA(1) to compute the ALP in relation to such transactions entered into by the assessee with its AEs. In the absence of such report being filed, it is impossible for the AO to form any opinion much less an opinion so as to conclude that the international transactions with related parties are not to be referred to the TPO—Sitara Diamond (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 39 taxmann.com 162/[2014] 225 Taxman 95 (Mag.)(Bom.).

The satisfaction to be arrived at by the AO regarding the existence of the international transaction or specified domestic transaction, even prima facie, is a sine qua non for making the reference to the TPO. Where such an accountant's report is submitted by the assessee in Form No. 3CEB, then there should be no difficulty for the AO to form an opinion, even a prima facie one, that it is necessary and expedient to make a reference to the TPO on the question of the determination of the ALP of such international transaction involving the assessee—Indorama Synthetics (India) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2016] 71 taxmann.com 349/241 Taxman 523 (Del.), SLP granted in Addl. CIT v. Indorama Synthetics (India) (P.) Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 588/269 Taxman 578 (SC).

Form of accountant's report [Rule 10E]

10E.2 The report of an accountant required to be furnished u/s 92E shall be in Form No. 3CEB and be verified in the manner indicated therein.

In view of proviso to Rule 12(2), the audit report shall have to be furnished electronically by the assessee.

The scope, as envisaged by section 92E, is restricted to examination of accounts and records of the assessee relating to the international transaction or specified domestic transaction entered into by the assessee during the previous year under examination. Further, the accountant has to give his opinion whether "proper information and documents as are prescribed" have been kept by the assessee in respect of the international transactions or specified domestic transaction entered into by him. The examination u/s 92E is not an audit requiring opinion of the accountant on the true and fair view of the financial statements of the enterprise.

The report consists of three (3) paragraphs dealing with distinct aspects as summarised hereunder:—

The first paragraph contains declaration about examination of the accounts and records of the assessee in order to review the international transaction(s) and the specified domestic transaction(s).

The second paragraph involves rendering of an opinion whether proper information and documents as are prescribed under Rule 10D are maintained by the assessee in respect of the identified international transactions and the specified domestic transaction(s), on the basis of the details furnished in Annexure to Form No. 3CEB.

The third and the last paragraph requires expression of the opinion whether the particulars given in the Annexure to Form No. 3CEB are true and correct.

Where payments were made by an Indian agent of foreign TV channels to Indian residents by way of AMP expenses, these payments were not required to be included in Form No. 3CEB—CIT v. N.G.C. Network (India) (P.) Ltd. [2014] 50 taxmann.com 240/[2015] 228 Taxman 176 (Bom.).

8.1 Amendment in time limit for making of order by transfer pricing officer [Section 92CA]

Section 92CA(3A) provides that a Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) may make an order anytime before 60 days prior to the date on which the period of limitation referred to in section 153 or section 153B for making an order of assessment etc. expires. A proviso has been inserted in the said section with effect from 1st June 2016 to provide that in the circumstances referred to in Explanation 1(ii)/(x) to section 153 if the period of limitation available to the TPO for making an order is less than 60 days, such remaining period shall be extended to 60 days and the aforesaid period of limitation shall be deemed to have been extended accordingly.

Explanation 1(ii) refers to the period during which the assessment proceedings is stayed by an order or injunction by any Court.

Explanation 1(x) refers to the period commencing from the date on which a reference or first of the references for exchange of information is made by an authority competent under an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A and ending with the date on which the information requested is last received by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner or a period of one year, whichever is less.

In Honda Trading Corpn. v. Dy. 44.2-3 Procedure for digital signature

Records of service tax and central excise can be preserved in electronic form and authenticate by digital signature. Similarly, invoices can be signed digitally.

Procedure for the same has been specified in Notification No. 18/2015-CE(NT) dated 6-7-2015.

The digital signature shall be class 2 or class 3 duly issued by Certifying Authority in India.

Specified details shall be informed to jurisdictional AC/DC of Central Excise at least 15 days in advance. Changes should also be informed.

Separate records shall be kept for each factory or service tax registration.

The specified records shall be produced to Central Excise Officer on demand. The records should be supplied by e-mail or electronically readable storage device.

During any enquiry, investigation or audit, if Central Excise Officer directs, the print outs of such records and invoices should be submitted. The electronic records should be preserved for five years. Its back up shall be kept.

Procedure for verifying digitally signed documents or invoices has been specified in CBEC Instruction F No. 224/44/2014-CX.6 dated 6-7-2015.

Once a digitally signed document is opened a pop up message will appear indicating the manner in which digitally signature can be verified. Once signature block is clicked, a window 'signature validation status' will appear. A tab bearing the title 'Signature Properties' shall also appear. Once you click 'show signer's certificate', information about signer, validity and authenticity of digital signature shall be displayed. After that, the Central Excise Officer may add the certificate to its list of trusted certificates by clicking the 'trust' tab on the menu. Then the signer gets added as a trusted source and process of verification is complete.

Digital signature as well as manual signature on same invoice permissible - Digital signature as well as manual signature on same invoice is permissible. Such invoices will be valid invoices for Cenvat credit - CBEC circular No. 1038/26/2016-CX dated 19-7-2016.

VALUE OF TAXABLE SERVICE

10.1

Background

Section 67 of Finance Act, 1994 (introduced w.e.f. 18-4-2006), makes provisions for valuation of service tax.

Chapter 8 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012 explains highlights of provisions of valuation for service tax.

10.1-1 Value and rate of exchange as on date when service provided or agreed to be provided

The rate of service tax, value of a taxable service and rate of exchange, if any, shall be the rate of service tax or value of a taxable service or rate of exchange, as the case may be, in force or as applicable at the time when the taxable service has been provided or agreed to be provided Explanation.—For the purposes of this section, "rate of exchange" means the rate of exchange referred to in the Explanation to section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 (52 of 1962) - section 67A(1) of Finance Act, 1994 as renumbered w.e.f. 14-5-2016. Earlier, it was only section 67A upto 14-5-2016.

As per section 67A(2) [introduced w.e.f. 14-5-2016], the time or the point in time with respect to the rate of service tax shall be such as may be prescribed.

The time or the point in time with respect to the rate of service tax has been prescribed vide Point of Taxation Rules, w.e.f. 14th May, 2016, Earlier, Point of Taxation Rules were not relevant to determine rate of service tax,

As discussed elsewhere, there is conflict between section 67A(1) and Point of Taxation Rules, at various places.

10.1-2 Foreign Exchange rate for valuation of import and export of service

Determination of rate of foreign exchange is relevant for determination of value of services in case of export of services and import of services. The rate is also relevant when place of provision of service is India and hence service tax is payable, but payment is received in foreign exchange.

Rate of exchange for valuation of export and import of service is the rate of exchange determined in accordance with rules as may be prescribed - Explanation to section 67A of Finance Act, 1994 as amended vide Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 w.e.f. 1-10-2014.

The rate of foreign exchange for determination of value of taxable service shall be the applicable rate of exchange as per Generally Accepted Accounting principles (GAAP) on the date when point of taxation arises in terms of Point of Taxation Rules - Rule 11 of Service Tax Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-10-2014.

This provision has been made, since, as per section 129(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, Financial Statements of companies must comply with Accounting Standards, and shall be in prescribed form.

Thus, it will be easy to reconcile value of service tax as per books of account and as per service tax returns.

10.1-2a GENERALLY ACCEPTED ACCOUNTING PRINCIPLES ON EFFECTS OF CHANGES IN FOREIGN EXCHANGE RATES - Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) are contained in AS-11 [Accounting Standard 11] in Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2006 issued Central Government in December 2006, on recommendation of NACAS [National Advisory Committee on Accounting Standards] under section 210A of Companies Act, 1956.

The AS-11 is on 'Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates'.

Section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013 envisages constitution of National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA). One of function of NFRA is to recommend Accounting Standards. However, this section is not yet notified.

Till constitution of NFRA under the 2013 Act, National Advisory Committee on Accounting Standards (NACAS) constituted under section 210A of the 1956 Act will continue to function.

Thus, presently accounting standards as notified in December 2006 are in force.

The highlights [only as relevant for service tax valuation] are as follows—

Initial recognition of foreign currency transactions - Initially, foreign currency transactions shall be recorded by applying an exchange rate at the time of transaction [In case of service tax, it should as on date of Point of Taxation as per POT Rules]. Alternatively, average for a week or month can be used if there is no significant fluctuation in exchange rate.

case_summary.text: TPO can’t ignore certificates issued by third-party vendors of AE confirming price charged from assessee: ITAT

TRANSFER PRICING : Where marketing support services costs, duly certified by Independent Accountant, had been allocated to assessee and same had been absorbed by making payment to AEs for services rendered by AEs, then action of lower authorities in determining ALP of such services at Rs. Nil is unwarranted

TRANSFER PRICING : Statutory Form 3CEB is a report of Chartered Accountant furnished under section 92E relating to international transactions and specific domestic transactions based on documents prescribed and maintained by assessee in respect of international transactions and Chartered Accountant report is based on Audited books of account maintained by assessee were international transaction have been incorporated and are authenticated therefore, report of CA cannot be ruled out and also factual position has to be considered to correct any mistake in calculating of ALP for valuation
TPO can’t question service provided to AE; his jurisdiction is limited only to benchmark transaction u/s 92C: ITAT

IT/ILT : In relation to a specified domestic transaction, TPO can under take transfer pricing study only in relation to those transactions which are referred to him under sub-section (1) of section 92C . Sub-section (2A) and (2B) of section 92C are confined to international transactions and with aid of any interpretive process, said provision cannot be applied to empower TPO to examine any specified domestic transaction not referred to him by Assessing Officer under sub-section (1).

TRANSFER PRICING : Where TP adjustment was made in hands of assessee on ad hoc basis without resorting to any prescribed method given under section 92C and rule 10B, it was not sustainable in eyes of law particularly when assessee had brought on record documents to prove availing of services viz. Inter-company invoices, cost allocation details, e-mail communication, training details, etc.

TRANSFER PRICING : When Assessing Officer makes reference to TPO for determining ALP of international transaction of services availed by assessee from its AE, job of TPO is to consider actual transaction of rendition of service and find out its ALP, however, TPO has no jurisdiction to examine whether service was needed or is duplicate in nature or stewardship or shareholder service because such an exercise falls in exclusive domain of Assessing Officer

TRANSFER PRICING: Where assessee-advertising agency availed different intra-group services from its foreign AEs, ALP cannot be determined by TPO in respect of said services on adhoc/estimation basis without applying any method prescribed under section 92C(1)

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee-company had imported raw materials from third party vendors under an agreed arrangement claiming that said transaction was at arm's length price by demonstrating that rate charged by assessee-company was lower than market price by providing certificate obtained from third party vendors but TPO rejected said certificates as same were signed by vendors which were also AEs of assessee, since certificates issued by third party vendors whereby, they confirmed that price they had charged to assessee-company was lower than original price, could not be ignored by holding that these certificates were issued by AEs, matter required remission to Assessing Officer/TPO to examine benchmarking analysis furnished by assessee

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee-company had imported raw materials from third party vendors under an agreed arrangement claiming that said transaction was at arm's length price by demonstrating that rate charged to assessee-company was lower than market price by providing certificate obtained from third party vendors, TPO could not have rejected said certificates on basis that same were signed by vendors which were also AEs of assessee

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had reimbursed expenses to its AE and in certificate given by AE had given details of services provided by AEs and also reimbursement expenses incurred by assessee and paid to AE, Assessing Officer was not justified in making TP adjustment

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had borne service tax component on royalty paid to its AE and TPO held that service tax payment was liability of AE and not that of assessee and, accordingly, made transfer pricing adjustment to extent of services tax component, since TPO had accepted service tax component as assessee's expenditure for subsequent assessment year and, consequently, did not make any transfer pricing adjustment, matter was to be restored to file of TPO for examining it afresh

TRANSFER PRICING : TPO is duty bound to follow one of method as mandated by provisions of section 92C and in absence of same addition made in respect of advance given to AEs and in respect of service fees for purchase of franchise should be deleted

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee-advertising agency entered into international transactions with its foreign AEs for availing certain intra-group services, TPO could not have determined ALP of said services on ad hoc basis, without applying any method prescribed under section 92C(1)

IT/ILT : Where assessee-company paid legal and professional charges to its AE, in view of fact that services rendered were supported by invoices and, moreover, assessee had achieved huge export turnover which demonstrated prima facie that services were infact rendered by AE, TPO was not justified in determining value of said services at nil

TRANSFER PRICING : Indian Transfer Pricing guidelines issued by Institute of Chartered Accountants of India vide guidance note on report under section 92E by ICAI and transfer pricing guidelines issued by OECD do not prohibit foreign AE to be a tested party

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee, providing supply chain and logistic services, extended a corporate guarantee to its Singapore AE without charging any fee but had charged a 1 per cent guarantee fee on similar guarantees to AEs in USA and UK, adoption of 1 per cent as arm's length price using internal CUP was justified and TP adjustment was correctly upheld

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee was availing specialized services which were provided by AEs from common pool and evidences in this regard had been filed by assessee, there was no merit in order of Assessing Officer in questioning availment of services and benefit derived by assessee

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee, Indian branch of US based company, paid fees for support services availed from its AEs and cost allocation key of ‘headcount’ was used by assessee for allocation of cost of support services, since cost allocation key on ‘headcount basis’ had been duly examined and accepted by TPO to be at ALP in transfer pricing proceedings under section 92CA(3), same could not be subjected to retest by AO under garb of examining same in context of allowability of deduction under section 37(1)

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee’s AE provided consultancy and technology services under Master Service Agreement, including onsite and 24/7 support to US clients duly evidenced by invoices and timesheets, determination of ALP at nil by TPO was unjustified and liable to be deleted

TRANSFER PRICING: TPO was directed to verify from annual report of selected companies whether they fulfil service income threshold being 75 per cent of revenue from technical consultancy services so that they can be taken as comparable

TRANSFER PRICING : Where TPO determined ALP of intra-group services being availed by assessee from its AEs on an ad-hoc basis , since all requirements to satisfy requisite tests had been elaborately demonstrated including allocation of cost and there was no shortcoming or defect in such allocations, there was no reason to reject benchmarking analysis done by assessee and matter was to be restored to file of TPO

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee paid technical support services fee to its AE, since there was an increase in turnover of 33 per cent and assessee had submitted Technical Services Agreement before TPO, TPO was not justified in disallowing said fee on basis that assessee did not provide any documentary evidence to prove said service

TRANSFER PRICING : Where TPO determined ALP of international transaction between assessee and AE at Nil value on ground that intra-group activities performed under aforesaid agreement were in nature of stewardship services, since TPO did apply any of six methods prescribed under section 92C and could not bring on record any comparable uncontrolled transaction for purpose of determining arm's length price of international transaction under consideration at Nil, action of TPO was without jurisdiction

TRANSFER PRICING : When documentary evidences submitted by assessee and claim of assessee that services provided in earlier Assessment years were akin to services provided in impugned Assessment year in which assessee was characterized as routine ITeS provider have not been examined either by TPO or by DRP while re-characterizing assessee as high-end ITeS/KPO service provider, then assessee should be accepted as low-end ITeS provider

TRANSFER PRICING : If assessee availed some of services listed out in composite agreement, it is suffice to prove consideration paid to AE and in case of intra group service payment, TPO does not have an authority to decide whether assessee has derived any benefit from these services or not and authority of TPO is restricted only to determine whether international transaction was at ALP

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee-company had availed intra group services from its AE for effective network development and high productivity service standards and had adduced documentary evidence supporting need, rendition of services and benefits derived therefrom, TPO’s conclusion that services were in nature of stewardship activity and no charges ought to have been paid by assessee was without any basis and TP adjustment made by TPO was to be deleted
Transfer pricing provisions couldn’t be applied if CA certificate of US co. verified that it wasn’t an AE of Indian Co.

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had entered into an agreement with its AE for rendering advisory services, and Tribunal found, on basis of documentary evidence on record that there was no considerable difference between services actually rendered by AE and those specified in agreement, such factual findings could not be attacked on ground of perversity
IT/ILT: Authority of TPO would be to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine arm's length price (ALP) and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits

TRANSFER PRICING: If assessee could demonstrate availment of services by furnishing proper documentary evidences, in that event, TPO was not justified in determining ALP at nil by applying benefit test

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had paid a certain sum to its AE towards Global information services, since assessee produced agreements showing services rendered, obligations of parties, fees to be charged, allocation of cost etc., assessee had reasonably satisfied various tests, i.e., need test, rendition test, benefit test, duplicate test and shareholder's activity and, thus, TPO was not correct in arriving at ALP as NIL
TRANSFER PRICING : After issue of notice under section 153C, Assessing Officer is required to make a fresh reference under section 92CA(1)

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee claimed to have availed certain services from its AE but TPO as well as DRP ignored documentary evidence filed by assessee and had proceeded on assumption that same were general in nature and did not prove rendering of services by AE, issue with regard to determination of ALP was to be set aside to Assessing Officer/TPO for fresh consideration

TRANSFER PRICING : As per provisions of section 92CA and as per CBDT instructions, reference to TPO under section 92CA is a must in case where such transaction as per Form 3CEB is more than Rs. 15 crores but there is no such provision in Act or in CBDT instruction that any such reference to TPO is bad in law in a case where international transaction as per Form 3CEB is less than Rs. 15 crores

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had paid a certain sum to its Associated Enterprise (AE) towards Global information services, since assessee produced agreements showing services rendered, obligations of parties, fees to be charged, allocation of cost etc., assessee had reasonably satisfied various tests i.e. need test, rendition test, benefit test, duplicate test and shareholder's activity and thus, TPO was not correct in arriving at ALP as NIL

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee company made payment towards marketing services fees expenses to its AE, however, TPO instead of benchmarking international transaction held that a payment made by assessee under another license agreement entered into by it with its AE already included such marketing fees, thus, there was duplication of services, TPO could not question whether service was duplicate in nature and its jurisdiction was only to benchmark transaction as per section 92C, thus,
TRANSFER PRICING : Order passed by TPO under section 92CA(3) even before issuance of notice under section 143(2) is without jurisdiction

TRANSFER PRICING : Authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits as that aspect of exercise is left to Assessing Officer therefore, TPO restoring matter to file of Assessing Officer to find out as to whether any service is rendered by AE to assessee and from which assessee has drawn any benefit from it is not correct

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee, engaged in recruitment services, made payments to AEs for Business Support and Business Technology Services, and furnished detailed documentation substantiating need, purpose, rendition, and benefits of such intra-group services along with benchmarking analysis, determination of ALP at nil on ground that assessee had failed to satisfy need, purpose, benefit and rendition test was unjustified

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee-company had availed intra group services from its AE for effective network development and high productivity service standards and had adduced documentary evidence supporting need, rendition of services and benefits derived therefrom, TPO’s conclusion that services were in nature of stewardship activity and no charges ought to have been paid by assessee was without any basis and thus, TP adjustment made by TPO was to be deleted

TRANSFER PRICING : Where TPO made ad-hoc transfer pricing adjustment on account of payment of royalty for central services by assessee, since assessee had benchmarked intra-group service payments by adopting CUP method and had furnished documentation substantiating rendition of services, ad-hoc transfer pricing adjustment made by TPO was legally unsustainable and same was to be deleted

TRANSFER PRICING : According to CBDT Instruction No. 3/2003, dated 20-5-2003, wherever aggregate value of international transaction exceeds Rs. 5 crores, reference to TPO under section 92CA is mandatory and in present case when Assessing Officer passed order in violation of CBDT Instruction then matter should be restored to file of Assessing Officer so that appropriate reference could be made to TPO in terms of section 92CA(1)

IT/ILT: Where assessee had availed intra group services from its AE and made payment for same, in view of fact that assessee had demonstrated and satisfied need test, evidence/rendition test and benefit test as envisaged under section 92(2) and services provided by AE were neither duplicative or shareholder's activity, TPO was to be directed to determine arm's length price of these services based on documents submitted by assessee
TPO couldn’t determine ALP of any service at nil without resorting to any transfer pricing exercise: ITAT

TRANSFER PRICING : Where software charges were paid by assessee for obtaining access to ERP software and for regular recurrent services, since charges had been paid pursuant to agreement and assessee had already placed on record audit certificate along with sample third party invoices raised by vendors on its AE, TPO should allow this expenditure to assessee
TRANSFER PRICING : AO should refer assessee's case to TPO for purposes of computing ALP of international transactions by following procedure laid down under section 92CA

TRANSFER PRICING : Where TPO determined ALP of intra-group services being availed by assessee from its AEs on an ad-hoc basis without applying any of prescribed methods as per section 92C(1), since TPO did not follow mandate of section 92C in determining ALP, matter was to be restored to file of Assessing Officer/TPO for determination of ALP of said international transactions by method prescribed under section 92C(1), read with Rule 10AB and 10B of Income-tax Rules, 1962

TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee claimed that transaction of import of raw materials from third parties was at arm's length price by demonstrating that rates charged to assessee-company were lower than market price by providing certificate obtained from third party vendors, since by certificate issued by third party vendors, they confirmed that discount of 10 per cent to 20 per cent had been given to assessee on raw materials and price they had charged to assessee-company was lower than original price, said certificates could not be ignored and matter required remission to Assessing Officer/TPO to examine above benchmarking analysis furnished by assessee

TRANSFER PRICING : Indian Transfer Pricing guidelines issued by Institute of Chartered Accountants of India vide guidance note on report under section 92E by ICAI and transfer pricing guidelines issued by OECD do not prohibit foreign AE to be a tested party, therefore, foreign AE could be taken as a tested party for purpose of establishing ALP of assessee

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 65, read with section 86 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Practising Chartered Accountants - Service tax was demanded from appellant, practising Chartered Accountant, for providing management consultancy service during period 16-10-1998 to 1-8-2002 - It was found that relevant Notifications did not include ‘management consultant’s service’ in list of taxable services of practising Chartered accountants - Whether for period of dispute, there was prima facie case for waiver of requirement of pre-deposit of tax and penalties demanded - Held, yes Circulars & Notifications : Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 and Notification No. 15/2000-ST, dated 1-8-2002

FACT: The lower authorities demanded service tax and imposed penalty on the appellant, practising Chartered Accountants (PCA), for providing management consultancy service during the period from 16-10-1998 to 1-8-2002.

On application :

HELD: Prima facie, the Explanation added in amended Notification No. 15/2000 ST, dated 1-8-2002 purported to add to the tax liability of a PCA, Practising Company Secretary and Practising Cost Accountant, by providing that the exemption under Notification No. 59/98-ST would not be applicable to services provided by these professionals, which may fall in any other taxable services defined in clause (90) of section 65. The legislative intent was amply clear. Prima facie, taxable services under clause (90) of section 65 were sought to be excluded from the scope of exemption. Notification No. 59 of 1998-ST, on its face, did not include ‘management consultancy service’ in the list of taxable services of PCAs. Hence, for the period of dispute, apparently, the appellants were not liable to pay service tax on management consultant’s service rendered by them. They had made out prima facie case for waiver of pre-deposit and stay of recovery. [Para 2]

HEADNOTE: Section 92B, read with section 92CA, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - International transaction (Reference to TPO) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether as per section 92CA(1) where Assessing Officer considers it 'necessary or expedient' to do so, he may with approval of Commissioner refer computation of arm's length price in relation to concerned international transaction to TPO - Held, yes - Whether said section does not contemplate that Assessing Officer has to first come to a definite finding that there is an international transaction within meaning of section 92B before he can exercise his power to refer matter to TPO - Held, yes - Whether thus, where Assessing Officer is of a prima facie view that an international transaction is involved and it is necessary or expedient to refer computation of arm's length price in relation thereto to TPO, he will be well within his powers to do so - Held, yes - Whether proceeding before TPO will be only upon notice to assessee who will have full opportunity of urging before TPO that no international transaction is involved - Held, yes [Para 41] [In favour of revenue/Matter remanded]IT/ILT: Assessing Officer can refer matter to TPO without recording finding as to whether international transaction exists; section 92CA(1) does not require Assessing Officer to first come to a definite finding that there is an 'international transaction' within meaning of section 92B before referring matter to TPO

FACT: Assessee PWH was an independent firm of Chartered Accountants managed and controlled by its partners who were individuals and residents of India.

It had entered into an agreement with Price Water HouseCoopers International Limited (PwCIL) a company incorporated in the United Kingdom to become member of PwCIL. The member firms of PwCIL were collectively known as PwC Network.

PWH had become a member firm of PwC Network, at the same time it was a separate independent legal entity whose affairs were managed and controlled only by its partners.

Price Water HouseCoopers Services BV, Netherlands(Services BV) was the central services entity of the PwC Network and operated exclusively for mutual benefit of all PwC Network member firms. Neither PWH nor any of its partners was a shareholder of Services BV. Services BV had not conferred on PWH any right regarding use of any brand name as Services BV itself did not own any brand name.

During relevant year PwC received a non-refundable loan to strengthen PWH's audit practices in India. Such loan was received under contractual arrangement existing between Services BV and PWH and PWH had shown it as business income in its return.

On scrutiny assessment, the Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax (R-3) issued notice requiring PWH to file its computation of income and tax for year, audit profit and loss account and balance sheet, tax and audit report issued under section 44AB. PWH filed all the necessary documents

Thereafter R-3 issued a letter to PWH informing it that a reference had been made to the TPO and called upon PWH to file details requested for in earlier notices.

PWH contended that TPO regulations did not apply to PWH as it did not have a relationship of being AE with any overseas network entity. It further contended that it had never entered into any international transaction envisaged under section 92B, and hence, it was unable to comprehend the reasons for which reference had been made under section 92CA(1) to the TPO. Further the fact that the transactions between PWH and Services BV were not international transactions had been accepted in the previous assessment year and hence there was no justification for R-3 to take a different view on same set of facts and law.

[Para 22]

Further the Supreme Court in T.D. Venkata Rao (supra) has accepted the fact that Chartered Accountants by the reason of their training have special aptitude in the matter of audit. The act of maintaining accounts is neither pleading, practice nor acting. For the reasons already discussed, the challenge to the Constitutional validity of the Legislation under articles 14 and 19 at the instance of the Bar Council will also have to be rejected. [Para 23] The Petitioners have not disputed that in the matter of enacting the law pertaining to recovery of sales tax, the same clearly fall within entry 54 of the State List. If in the process of making legislation, the legislature in its wisdom provides for the procedure in the manner in which tax has to be levied, maintenance of books, procedure for checking correctness or verification of books, it cannot be said that the same amounts to ancillary legislation or procedure not falling within the competence of the State Legislature under Entry 54. The Act requires that the dealer has to maintain books and the books have to be audited and required to be certified by a Chartered Accountant. That will not result in the legislation falling outside the competence of the State Legislature. The Legislation in pith and substance is relatable to imposition of sales tax which is within the competence of the State Legislature. The Courts examine and ascertain the pith and substance on scrutiny of the true character of the enactment. [Para 24]

It also cannot be said that in such a case audit by a Chartered Accountant would amount to outsourcing the statutory power to the third party. The Legislature can always delegate its powers as long as such delegation does not amount to abdication of its essential legislative functions. In the instant case, there is no abdication of the essential legislative functions. All that the section requires is that the accountant has to audit the accounts and to issue certificate that the dealer has maintained the books as required to be maintained under the Act and rules. The dealer has to file his accounts audited with the certificate. This neither amounts to abdication nor excessive delegation. Such an exercise also does not amount to conferring on the accountant a power to determine the correct tax liability of the dealer. The power to accept returns is of the Authorities under the Act. Even after the certificate is issued, that the dealer has maintained books, it is always open to the Commissioner under section 20 to ascertain whether the return is correct and complete or order an audit under section 22 to get the accounts audited by the officers of the department. A certificate, therefore, is not determinative but to enable the department to consider that the person having knowledge of audit and subject to the disciplinary control of its parent body has certified that the accounts are properly maintained. This is to aid the officers in discharging their statutory duties. This challenge, therefore, has to be rejected. [Para 25]

Further, it is for the dealer to decide whose services he seeks to obtain for appearance before the Sales Tax Authorities or for getting the accounts audited. Under section 82, there are a class of persons from whom a dealer can obtain services for being represented before the authorities under the Act. Under section 61, he is bound to select one of the class of accountants also. This is for a category of dealers whose turnover is more than 40 lakhs. The amount of fee which has to be paid is the amount to be decided between the dealer and that person, whom he selects from amongst the accountants that are available. This cannot be said to amount of compulsory levy amounting to tax. That being the case, the challenge under article 265 must also fail.

Similarly, the question of article 301 being attracted, does not arise. The challenge on that count also has to be rejected as the right claimed by the petitioners or their members or by the dealer is that Advocate and Sales Tax Practitioner cannot carry out audit in terms of section 61 in the State of Maharashtra. The enactment is pursuant to the power of the State Legislature to make law within its competence. This does not attract article 301. [Para 27]

HEADNOTE: I. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arms length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transactions/Allowability of expenditure) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee-company had entered into a multilateral service agreement with its Associated Enterprises for various intra-group services relating to strategic inputs such as product information, marketing field engineering services, scientific and laboratory services, logistic, administrative, etc. - TPO held that evidence submitted by assessee were only data excel sheets of cost allocation and further, these were duplicative in nature and a shareholders activity and therefore, he determined ALP of such services as nil - Assessee had submitted agreement showing description of services and benefit received therefrom and various e-mail correspondences were submitted which said that services had been rendered by AE and received by assessee and certificates of various AE were produced to show basis of allocation and exact cost allocation to assessee and employee wise cost sheet which showed distribution and allocation of such cost - Whether, on fact, assessee had reasonably sustantiated benefit test, need test and rendition test for said intra-group services and there was no justification in determining ALP at nil - Held, yes [Para 16] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where intra- group service received by assessee-company was supported by proper agreement and substantial evidences with respect to services rendered by Associated Enterprises also demonstrated benefits received therefrom, AO was not justified in determining of ALP of said service at nil  TRANSFER PRICING : Transfer Pricing Officer should restrict addition/TP adjustment only to International transactions

FACT: The assessee-company had entered into a multilateral service agreement with its Associated Enterprises for various intra-group services relating to strategic inputs such as product information, marketing field engineering services, scientific and laboratory services, logistic, administrative, etc.

The TPO held that evidence submitted by assessee were only data excel sheets of cost allocation and further, these were duplicative in nature and a shareholders activity and therefore, he determined ALP of such services as nil.

The DRP though held that the evidence submitted by the assessee were undisputed but it directed the Assessing Officer to verify the proper cost allocation as well as the rendition of the services and then determine the Arm's Length Price.

On appeal :

HELD: The intra-group services is supported by the proper agreement, substantial evidences with respect to services rendered by the Associated Enterprises and also demonstrated the benefits received therefrom. Letter dated 23rd January 2014 filed before the Transfer Pricing Officer in pursuance of the direction of Dispute Resolution Panel shows the cost allocation certificate of the Associated Enterprises, invoices received and the details of allocation of cost by the Associated Enterprises. This is rejected by the Transfer Pricing Officer stating that these are merely excel data sheet of cost allocation and no independent evidences have been submitted in respect of this cost sheet. Therefore, the Transfer Pricing Officer despite the direction of the Dispute Resolution Panel retained the Arm's Length Price adjustment of intra-group services of Rs. 6,54,10,826/- at Rs. nil. [Para 16]

HEADNOTE: Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Chartered accountant’s service - Period 16-10-1998 to 31-7-2002 - Assessee, a firm of practising chartered accountants, in terms of Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998, claimed exemption of service tax on management consultant’s service and man-power recruitment agent’s service provided by it during relevant period - Through Notification No. 15/2002, dated 1-8-2002, Explanation to Notification No. 59/98-ST (supra) was inserted and practising chartered accountants were made liable to discharge service tax liability on activities exigible to tax under any other head - Commissioner (Appeals) on finding that effective date of Notification No. 15/2002 (supra) was 16-10-1998, held assessee liable to service tax under categories of ‘Management consultant’ and ‘Manpower recruitment agent’ - Whether in absence of specific stipulation as regards date of effect, Explanation introduced under Notification No. 15/2002-ST, dated 1-8-2002, could be held to take effect from date of its issue - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, liability to tax of assessee as regards services of ‘Management consultant’ and ‘Manpower recruitment agent’ which it rendered during period 16-10-1998 to 31-7-2002, could not be sustained - Held, yes [Para 6] Circulars & Notifications : Notification No. 59/1998, dated 16-10-1998, No. 15/2002, dated 1-8-2002, CBEC Circular F. No. 178/1/2004-CX-4, dated 7-1-2003

FACT: The assessee was a firm of chartered accountants. The original authority confirmed demand of service tax on the assessee for the period 16-10-1998 to 31-7-2002 under the heads ‘Practising chartered accountant’, ‘Manpower recruitment service’, ‘Management consultant’ and ‘Business auxiliary service’. Modifying the findings of the original authority, the Commissioner (Appeals) found that the assessee was not liable to pay service tax under the head ‘Business auxiliary service’. He affirmed the demand on the assessee in respect of other categories of services. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that it had rendered services as management consultant and man-power recruitment agent which were exempt in terms of Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998. The assessee also contended that Commissioner (Appeals) had wrongly held that the Notification No. 15/2002, dated 1-8-2002 which inserted an Explanation to Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998, had come into effect from 16-10-1998.

HELD: The effect of the Notification No. 15/2002, dated 1-8-2002, was that individuals and firms assessed to tax on services under the head ‘Practising chartered accountant’ should discharge their liability to service tax in respect of activities exigible to tax under any other head. [Para 4]

[Para 22]

Further the Supreme Court in T.D. Venkatrao (supra ) has accepted the fact that Chartered Accountants by the reason of their training have special aptitude in the matter of audit. The act of maintaining accounts is neither pleading, practice nor acting. For the reasons already discussed, the challenge to the Constitutional validity of the Legislation under articles 14 and 19 at the instance of the Bar Council will also have to be rejected. [Para 23] The Petitioners have not disputed that in the matter of enacting the law pertaining to recovery of sales tax, the same clearly fall within entry 54 of the State List. If in the process of making legislation, the legislature in its wisdom provides for the procedure in the manner in which tax has to be levied, maintenance of books, procedure for checking correctness or verification of books, it cannot be said that the same amounts to ancillary legislation or procedure not falling within the competence of the State Legislature under Entry 54. The Act requires that the dealer has to maintain books and the books have to be audited and required to be certified by a Chartered Accountant. That will not result in the legislation falling outside the competence of the State Legislature. The Legislation in pith and substance is relatable to imposition of sales tax which is within the competence of the State Legislature. The Courts examine and ascertain the pith and substance on scrutiny of the true character of the enactment. [Para 24]

It also cannot be said that in such a case audit by a Chartered Accountant would amount to outsourcing the statutory power to the third party. The Legislature can always delegate its powers as long as such delegation does not amount to abdication of its essential legislative functions. In the instant case, there is no abdication of the essential legislative functions. All that the section requires is that the accountant has to audit the accounts and to issue certificate that the dealer has maintained the books as required to be maintained under the Act and rules. The dealer has to file his accounts audited with the certificate. This neither amounts to abdication nor excessive delegation. Such an exercise also does not amount to conferring on the accountant a power to determine the correct tax liability of the dealer. The power to accept returns is of the Authorities under the Act. Even after the certificate is issued, that the dealer has maintained books, it is always open to the Commissioner under section 20 to ascertain whether the return is correct and complete or order an audit under section 22 to get the accounts audited by the officers of the department. A certificate, therefore, is not determinative but to enable the department to consider that the person having knowledge of audit and subject to the disciplinary control of its parent body has certified that the accounts are properly maintained. This is to aid the officers in discharging their statutory duties. This challenge, therefore, has to be rejected. [Para 25]

Further, it is for the dealer to decide whose services he seeks to obtain for appearance before the Sales Tax Authorities or for getting the accounts audited. Under section 82, there are a class of persons from whom a dealer can obtain services for being represented before the authorities under the Act. Under section 61, he is bound to select one of the class of accountants also. This is for a category of dealers whose turnover is more than 40 lakhs. The amount of fee which has to be paid is the amount to be decided between the dealer and that person, whom he selects from amongst the accountants that are available. This cannot be said to amount of compulsory levy amounting to tax. That being the case, the challenge under article 265 must also fail.

Similarly, the question of article 301 being attracted, does not arise. The challenge on that count also has to be rejected as the right claimed by the petitioners or their members or by the dealer is that Advocate and Sales Tax Practitioner cannot carry out audit in terms of section 61 in the State of Maharashtra. The enactment is pursuant to the power of the State Legislature to make law within its competence. This does not attract article 301. [Para 27]

HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustments - General) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Whether TPO cannot sit in judgment of business module of assessee and its intention to avail or not to avail any services from its associated enterprises and role of TPO is to determine arm's length price of international transactions undertaken by assessee and whether same is at arm's length price when compared with similar transactions undertaken by external entities or internal comparables - Held, yes - Assessee had entered into international transactions of import of raw materials, trading goods and components, export of finished goods, income from services, information technology services availed and reimbursement of expenses with its associated enterprises - Five transactions were benchmarked together by using TNMM - However, transaction of information technology services had been segregated by TPO - TPO held that since assessee had failed to prove receipt of services and benefits derived from services with supporting evidence, arm's length price of transactions was to be treated as Nil and hence, adjustment was proposed to be made to arm's length price - It was found that information technology services availed by assessee also related to business carried on by assessee - Whether information technology services availed had to be aggregated with other transactions being intrinsically linked to other international transactions undertaken by assessee - Held, yes - Whether since various documents were filed by assessee which included certificate of AE evidencing not only availment of services but also basis of cost for such services and similar services were availed by other group entities from AE at same rates as charged to assessee, order of TPO/Assessing Officer was unjustified - Held, yes [Paras 18 to 39] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT/ILT: TPO cannot sit in judgment of business module of assessee and its intention to avail or not to avail any services from its associated enterprises and role of TPO is to determine arm's length price of international transactions undertaken by assessee and whether same is at arm's length price when compared with similar transactions undertaken by external entities or internal comparables

FACT: The assessee had entered into international transactions of import of raw materials, trading goods and components, export of finished goods, income from services, information technology services availed and reimbursement of expenses with its associated enterprises. The first five transactions were benchmarked together by using TNMM. The case of assessee that all these transactions need to be aggregated as they were interdependent on each other while benchmarking international transactions to be at arm's length price.

However, the transaction of information technology services availed had been segregated by the TPO.

The assessee claimed that the said information technologies services had been availed by it from its AE, namely, Eaton China for Information Technology (IT) and related support services. The assessee also during the course of assessment proceedings filed certificate issued by Eaton China certifying the factum of provision of services by it to the assessee. Eaton China also confirmed that other Eaton group companies availing same services were also charged on the same basis as the assessee.

The TPO was of the view that the assessee had to prove that the services were rendered and the second aspect of intra-group service was the quantification of such services in terms of actual expenditure incurred and commensurate benefit derived therefrom. The TPO thus, held that where the assessee had failed to prove the receipt of services and benefits derived from services with supporting evidence, the arm's length price of transactions was treated as Nil and hence, adjustment was proposed to be made to the arm's length price.

The assessee was aggrieved by the order of Assessing Officer / TPO in splitting up the assessee's operations into manufacturing and trading segment and benchmarking the same separately, despite the fact that both the activities were closely inter-linked.

HELD: In the first instance, TPO cannot sit in the judgment of business module of assessee and its intention to avail or not to avail any services from its associated enterprises the role of TPO is to determine the arm's length price of international transactions undertaken by the assessee and whether the same is at arm's length price when compared with similar transactions undertaken by external entities or internal comparables. [Para 29]

of an international transaction, the TPO would have an authority to examine any international transaction which comes to his notice during the proceedings, whether a reference in this respect was made by the Assessing Officer or not and whether the assessee had reported such transaction under section 92E or not. However, in view of specific non-inclusion of the specified domestic transaction under the said sub-sections, in so far as the domestic transactions are concerned, the situation would be vastly different.[Para 13] In plain terms, in absence of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, the TPO would get jurisdiction to examine a transaction whether it is international or specified domestic transaction, only upon reference being made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1) of section 92CA. Sub-section (2) of section 92CA provides that where a reference is made under sub-section (1), the TPO would serve a notice to the assessee requiring him to furnish details in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction referred to in sub-section (1). Thus, the jurisdiction of the TPO to issue a notice to the assessee would be in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction for which reference is made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). It is precisely for this reason that sub-sections (2A) and (2B) provide a deeming fiction where they provide that in case of an international transaction not referred to the TPO or an international transaction not reported by the assessee, which comes to his notice during the proceedings, the provision of the Chapter would apply as if such international transaction was one referred to in sub-section (1). In absence of this deeming fiction, it would not be open for the TPO to exercise the powers under the said chapter in relation to the transaction not referred to him. The reference to be made by the Assessing Officer is not an empty formality. Said reference has to be made only on approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. Legislature, requires the Assessing Officer to obtain an approval from senior Revenue Authority before a reference is made. Such requirement cannot be jettisoned by the TPO exercising suo motu jurisdiction over the transaction not reported to him.[Para 14]

Inescapable conclusion that is reached is that in relation to a specified domestic transaction, the TPO can under take transfer pricing study only in relation to those transactions which are referred to him under sub-section (1) of section 92C. Sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92C are confined to international transactions and with the aid of any interpretive process, the said provision cannot be applied to empower the TPO to examine any specified domestic transaction not referred to him by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). Any other view would be doing violence to the plain language of the statute.[Para 17]

The revenue is correct in pointing out that in the instant case, the assessee did not report such transaction at all and therefore, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to notice such transaction as specified domestic transaction. His reference, therefore, was necessarily confined to the reported transactions. The TPO noticed this anomaly, he proceeded to determine the arm's length price after full opportunity of hearing to the assessee.[Para 18]

Even in such a situation, the statute does not permit the TPO to assume the jurisdiction to determine the arm's length price of a specified domestic transaction not reported to him. There may be number of cases where the assessee may bona fide hold a belief that certain transaction is not a specified domestic transaction and therefore, would not report the same under section 92E. Whether bona fide or not, not making a report by the assessee of a specified domestic transaction would not leave the revenue without remedy. As clarified by CBDT in the instructions dated 20-5-2013, it is always open for the TPO who notices such transaction during the course of the proceedings before him to call for a reference by the Assessing Officer. If the Assessing Officer does make a report, only then TPO can undertake further steps as envisaged under sub-section (2) and other sub-sections of section 92CA. As noted, the statute is sufficiently clear. The legislature while expanding the scope of the transfer pricing study by the TPO to a transaction not referred him or not reported by the Assessing Officer, under sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, has confined the applicability thereof only to international transactions. The TPO exercising such powers suo motu in relation to a specified domestic transaction would be transgressing his jurisdiction and in the process would render the requirement of sub-section (1) of section 92CA redundant. As noted, the reference that the Assessing Officer can make to the TPO would have the approval of the Principal Commissioner or the Commissioner.[Para 19]

Under these circumstances, in relation to the transaction of payment to creditors in demerger process, the TPO had no jurisdiction to make any adjustments. Under these circumstances and even otherwise, the adjustment on merits cannot be examined, though it was argued by the assessee.[Para 20]

HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transaction/Allowability of expenditure) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Whether TPO cannot stand in judgment on what benefits assessee has derived from services and assessee's obligation lies to extent of demonstrating receipt of services; once assessee has been able to demonstrate receipt of services, transfer pricing adjustment without applying any prescribed benchmarking method is unsustainable - Held, yes - Assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing of plastic granules used in manufacturing plastics for varied industries - It availed services from its Global Head Office situated at Germany (GHO services) and from its Regional Head Office situated in Singapore (RHO services) - TPO analyzed nature of services provided under various sub-categories and noted that assessee did not submit proof of actual receipt of services, and, thus, he concluded that no India related services had been rendered and ALP of said transaction was taken as Nil - On perusal of summarized chart of services received, it was found that India specific support had been provided via GHO/RHO services to assessee and assessee submitted voluminous paper-books to show that services rendered were aimed at giving India specific benefit - Whether, on facts, TPO was not correct in computing ALP of services at Nil - Held, yes [Paras 9 to 11] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee-company availed services from its Global Head Office (GHO) and from its Regional Head Office situated outside India and TPO held that since assessee had failed to submit proof of actual receipt of services, no India related services had been rendered and computed ALP of this transaction to be NIL, since on perusal of summarized chart of services received by assessee, it was found that India specific support had been provided via GHO/RHO to assessee, and assessee submitted voluminous paper-books to show that services rendered were aimed at giving India specific benefit, TPO was not correct in computing ALP of said services at NIL

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transaction/Allowability of expenditure) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Whether TPO cannot stand in judgment on what benefits assessee has derived from services and assessee's obligation lies to extent of demonstrating receipt of services; once assessee has been able to demonstrate receipt of services, transfer pricing adjustment without applying any prescribed benchmarking method is unsustainable - Held, yes - Assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing of plastic granules used in manufacturing plastics for varied industries - It availed services from its Global Head Office situated at Germany (GHO services) and from its Regional Head Office situated in Singapore (RHO services) - TPO analyzed nature of services provided under various sub-categories and noted that assessee did not submit proof of actual receipt of services, and, thus, he concluded that no India related services had been rendered and ALP of said transaction was taken as Nil - On perusal of summarized chart of services received, it was found that India specific support had been provided via GHO/RHO services to assessee and assessee submitted voluminous paper-books to show that services rendered were aimed at giving India specific benefit - Whether, on facts, TPO was not correct in computing ALP of services at Nil - Held, yes [Paras 9 to 11] [In favour of assessee]

taxable at 9 per cent CGST under SI. No. 18 of Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended and 9 per cent SGST under SI. HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustment - Technical service fee) - Assessment years 2010-11 and 2011-12 - Assessee was in business of providing ground handling services in nature of ticketing, checking, load control, etc. - It entered into a technical service agreement with its Associated Enterprise to get technical advice and support in relation to its ground-handling business and paid technical service fee - Assessee benchmarked international transaction using TNMM - TPO rejected TNMM on ground that payment of technical service fee was in nature of intangibles and had to be analyzed under CUP method and compared amount of technical service fee paid with royalty percentage of 8 per cent as allowed to be repatriated by Press Note of Reserve Bank of India (RBI) prescribed under automatic route of remittance, resulting in TP adjustments - Press Note No. 8 (2009 series, dated 16-12-2009) pointed out that Government of India reviewed extant policy and decided to permit payments for royalty, lumpsum fee for transfer of technology and payments for use of trademark/brand name on automatic route, i.e., without any approval of Government of India and there is no cap for such payment as was there in earlier press note - Whether, on facts, Assessing Officer was not correct in referring to press notes to determine arm's length price - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 14] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where TPO compared amount of technical service fee paid with royalty percentage of 8 per cent as allowed to be repatriated by Press Note of RBI prescribed under automatic route of remittance, resulting in TP adjustments, since in view of Press Note No. 8, dated 16-12-2009, there was no cap for such payment, Assessing Officer was not correct in referring to press notes to determine arm's length price

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustment - Technical service fee) - Assessment years 2010-11 and 2011-12 - Assessee was in business of providing ground handling services in nature of ticketing, checking, load control, etc. - It entered into a technical service agreement with its Associated Enterprise to get technical advice and support in relation to its ground-handling business and paid technical service fee - Assessee benchmarked international transaction using TNMM - TPO rejected TNMM on ground that payment of technical service fee was in nature of intangibles and had to be analyzed under CUP method and compared amount of technical service fee paid with royalty percentage of 8 per cent as allowed to be repatriated by Press Note of Reserve Bank of India (RBI) prescribed under automatic route of remittance, resulting in TP adjustments - Press Note No. 8 (2009 series, dated 16-12-2009) pointed out that Government of India reviewed extant policy and decided to permit payments for royalty, lumpsum fee for transfer of technology and payments for use of trademark/brand name on automatic route, i.e., without any approval of Government of India and there is no cap for such payment as was there in earlier press note - Whether, on facts, Assessing Officer was not correct in referring to press notes to determine arm's length price - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 14] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : Press Note No. 8 (2009 series), dated 16-12-2009

FACT: The assessee was in the business of providing ground handling services in the nature of ticketing, checking, load control. etc.

It entered into a technical service agreement with its Associated Enterprise to get technical advice and support in relation to its ground-handling business and paid technical service fee.

The assessee, in its transfer pricing (TP) documentation, benchmarked the international transaction using Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM).

TPO rejected TNMM on the ground that payment of technical service fee was in the nature of intangibles and had to be analyzed under Comparable Uncontrolled Price (CUP) method and compared the amount of technical service fee paid with the royalty percentage of 8 per cent as allowed to be repatriated by the Press Note of Reserve Bank of India (RBI) prescribed under the automatic route of remittance, resulting in TP adjustments.

Commissioner (Appeals), however, rejected the appeal of the assessee.
