HEADNOTE: II. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with rule 10B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Others) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee-company made payment towards professional services to its AE ('Faurecia France') - TPO held that no benefit was derived by assessee-company from receipt of professional services and no services were received - Assessee had filed description of services received in several forms and evidence in respect of receipt of services in 2013-14, Tribunal in case of Dy. CIT v. India Kawasaki Motors (P.) Ltd. [ITA No. 88/PUN/2021, dated 19-5-2022], restored similar issue to file of Assessing Officer/TPO to examine evidence filed in support of receipt of services - Whether on parity of same reasoning, matter was to be remitted to file of Assessing Officer/TPO - Held, yes [Para 20] [Matter remanded]

FACT: The assessee-company made payment towards professional services to its AE (Faurecia France).

The TPO/DRP held that no benefit was derived by the assessee-company from the receipt of the professional services and no services were received.

On Appeal :

HELD: It is settled position of law that the onus of proving the receipt of services lies on the assessee claiming deduction on account of payment made towards professional charges. It is a condition precedent to prove the receipt of services for availing the deduction towards the payment. The assessee had filed description of the services received in several forms and also filed the copies of the descriptive evidence in respect of receipt of services. The Tribunal in the case of Dy. CIT v. India Kawasaki Motors (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 88/PUN/2021, dated 19-5-2022], restored this issue to the file of the Assessing Officer/TPO to examine the evidence filed in support of the receipt of the services. On the party of same reasoning, the matter was remitted to the file of the Assessing Officer/TPO to examine and reach a conclusion whether or not the assessee-company had received the services from its AEs.

HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transaction/allowability of expenditure) - Assessment years 2014-15 and 2017-18 – Assessee-company, engaged in advertising business, had paid GIS service charges to its AE and benchmarked said transactions adopting CUP method - Observing that assessee had failed to prove need test and benefit test, TPO considered ALP of said services at Nil - Whether since documentation of assessee clearly showed description of categories of services provided, resultant benefit arising therefrom, rational for provision of such services, reasonable description of benefits from services, reasonableness of adoption of allocation keys and reasons justifying that such allocation keys produce outcomes that would reasonably reflect benefit received, ALP of intra group services between assessee and its AE could not be considered at Nil - Held, yes [Paras 18 and 19] [Partly in favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee-company received Global Information Service (GIS) from its AE, since documentation submitted by assessee clearly showed description of categories of services provided, resultant benefit arising therefrom, rational for provision of such services, reasonable description of benefits from services, reasonableness of adoption of allocation keys etc., ALP of such intra group services between assessee and its AE could not be considered at Nil

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transaction/allowability of expenditure) - Assessment years 2014-15 and 2017-18 – Assessee-company, engaged in advertising business, had paid GIS service charges to its AE and benchmarked said transactions adopting CUP method - Observing that assessee had failed to prove need test and benefit test, TPO considered ALP of said services at Nil - Whether since documentation of assessee clearly showed description of categories of services provided, resultant benefit arising therefrom, rational for provision of such services, reasonable description of benefits from services, reasonableness of adoption of allocation keys and reasons justifying that such allocation keys produce outcomes that would reasonably reflect benefit received, ALP of intra group services between assessee and its AE could not be considered at Nil - Held, yes [Paras 18 and 19] [Partly in favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee company, engaged in advertising business, paid GIS service charges to its AE. Global information services were benchmarked adopting CUP method. It was the claim of assessee that AEs had charged only third-party cost incurred. The assessee stated that as markup of 5 per cent charged by AEs was lower than comparable margins, transaction was at arm's length.

The TPO refused to accept benchmarking of the assessee of GIS services because cost incurred by AE had not been proved and further according to him, assessee failed to produce need test of services. Accordingly, CUP method was also rejected. The TPO also analysed various information submitted by assessee and referring to OECD guidelines, questioned whether services had been rendered or not. Accordingly, he determined ALP of GIS Services at Nil.

On appeal:

HELD: The contention of the assessee that the Transfer Pricing Officer has not adopted any method could not be agreed. The TPO determined nil value of services adopting comparable uncontrolled price method. This is so because unless four basic specific tests are fulfilled, no independent party would have paid such sum to the Associated Enterprises. Accordingly, as nobody has paid for these services, the comparable uncontrolled price as per the TPO of these services is Nil. Therefore, there is definite method adopted by TPO which is one of the prescribed methods under Indian transfer pricing legislation. [Para 17]

However, for any payment for intra group services, the payer of such services maintained a robust documentation to show that those services are required for business of assessee and, therefore, they are requisitioned by the assessee from its Associated Enterprises. The AEs has rendered those services as agreed upon as per agreement between the parties. On rendition of such services, assessee has been benefitted. There is no standard requirement of providing manner of maintenance of documentation. The basic document will be the services agreement between the parties which would demonstrate the right and obligation of parties, nature of services, nature of reporting and the manner of billing along with documentary evidences. On appeal: HELD: The TPO has alleged that the assessee failed to furnish any evidence to substantiate its claim that the payment is made to the AE for availing Information System Services, however, the material on record reveal that the assessee has not only undertaken a benchmarking process for determining the arm's length price of the transaction in the transfer pricing study report which was filed before the TPO, but, other relevant and necessary documents like copy of the agreement, invoices raised, certificate from independent Chartered Accountant Firm, (KPMG), details of users were also furnished before the TPO. Therefore, the allegation of the TPO that the assessee has not furnished the necessary details is not totally correct. In any case of the matter, non-furnishing of certain documentary evidences, as alleged by the TPO does not empower him to embark upon determining the arm's length price of the international transaction on estimation basis. Further, a reading of the TPO's, order makes it clear that his finding on the issue is contradictory. On the one hand, he has observed that the assessee has failed all the three tests, including, whether the services have actually been provided, on the other hand, he has accepted that the AE has provided the software. Thus, ultimately, what the TPO disbelieves is the quantum of payment. Accordingly, he has proceeded to estimate the price of the services rendered by the AE at Rs. 1,62,05,000. Though, the TPO has observed that he has applied CUP method for determining the arm's length price, however, he has not brought on record even a single comparable to support the arm's length price determined by him even on estimate basis. The estimation of service charges on so-called man hour basis is without any supporting material. Similarly, the estimation of cost of software was without any basis. Thus, it is very much clear that the determination of arm's length price by the TPO is not as per any one of the methods prescribed under section 92C read with rule 10B. Such determination of arm's length price on ad hoc/estimation basis is not permissible under the scheme of the Act as the Transfer Pricing Officer is duty bound to determine the arm's length price by following any one of the most appropriate method prescribed under the statute. It is relevant to observe, that the DRP has approved the determination of the arm's length price by the TPO without properly appreciating the implication of the relevant statutory provisions. As regards the observations of the DRP regarding the report of the KPMG, it is necessary to observe that the KPMG report is not an audit report but was furnished by the assessee to support the attribution of cost. Therefore, it cannot be said that it is a qualified report. It is further relevant to observe, the material that submitted indicates that the cost of the software has been allocated to 40 group companies across the globe who are using the software and related services and assessee's share in cost allocation works out to 2.3 per cent. Moreover, when the TPO himself agrees that the AE has provided software and certain services, there is no reason for not accepting the payment made to the AE to be at arm's length in the absence of any contrary evidence brought on record and by simply applying the benefit test. If the TPO did not agree to the arm's length price shown by the assessee is it open for him to determine the arm's length price by applying one of the most appropriate methods being backed by supporting material. Without complying to the statutory provisions, the TPO certainly cannot determine the arm's length price on ad hoc/estimation basis. Accordingly, the adjustment made to the arm's length price of payment made towards availing information system services from AE was deleted. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: III. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Support services fee) - Assessment years 2003-04 and 2007-08 - Assessee had entered into transaction of payment of overseas support services charges which included training of employees, overseas research in respect of Indian capital market, overseas support services and FAO division etc. to its foreign AE - TPO determined Arm's Length Price (ALP) of this transaction at nil on ground that assessee had various employees and there was no requirement or need for such services - Whether since TPO determined ALP of aforesaid transaction at nil without asking assessee to demonstrate rendition of such services and whether there was any duplicative service, TPO could not substantiate disallowance of ALP at nil - Held, yes [Para 32] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee had made certain payment on account of overseas support services to its overseas AEs.

The TPO observed that assessee itself had employed so many employees for carrying out its business requirements and held that assessee had not received any extraordinary benefit in necessitating the payment of such a huge amount and, accordingly, he treated the ALP of the transaction at nil.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), in view of its earlier assessment year's order, held that no adjustment was required to be made.

On the revenue's appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: The assessee is required to prepare the documents to prima facie to prove the above tests depending upon the nature of services, the manner of allocation of the cost, functional analysis etc. It is required to be proved in the TP study report itself the detailed business overview and the industry analysis of the group and the associated enterprises as well as the assessee. The onus is on the assessee to show with documentation with regard to functions, performance with regard to rendition of the service and at least prima facie require to establish benefit test. There has to be some objective analysis of each and every service which are required by the assessee and rendered by the AE resulting into some qualitative and quantitative benefit if it can be measured. Another important factor is to examine whether the services have not been resulted into duplicative services. Further, assessee is also required to show it was for the business purpose and is not carried out by the shareholder as its own activity. [Para 29]

Not only that, the charging method, i.e., direct or indirect charge should also be based on proper allocation key which should be commensurate in the nature of services and the impurity of such services and utilization thereof by the assessee. Here in the instant case from the record, it is not discernable whether any such documentation was prepared by the assessee or was ever asked by the TPO. [Para 30]

The assessee submitted that in the subsequent year, the assessee had filed voluminous details before the Commissioner (Appeals) when asked by him. It has also been submitted that in the assessment year 2007-08, based on perusal of those documentation, the Commissioner (Appeals) has held that the payment for intra-group services is justified. [Para 31]

From the perusal of the TPO's order as noted above, it is seen that, he has merely noted that assessee had various employees and therefore, there was no requirement or need for such services. Nowhere he is questioned or asked about the rendition of the services or to demonstrate whether there was any duplicative service. Once assessee has given the details, then the TPO should have at least asked for the documentation of proving the aforesaid tests and cannot simply determine ALP at nil. Since the TPO has not brought anything on record, therefore, the earlier year orders even though none of the orders of the Tribunal have considered this aspect is to be followed. Accordingly, it is to be held that the TPO cannot substantiate the disallowance of ALP at nil. [Para 32]

Therefore, as held by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Kargill Food India Ltd. dated 24-10-2016, even applying the rule of consistency, the benchmarking done by the assessee under CUP method is to be accepted. [Para 8] Even otherwise also, if the Transfer Pricing Officer was not convinced with the benchmarking done by the assessee, he should have benchmarked the arm's length price of the services availed by following any one of the prescribed methods as provided under the statute. A perusal of the order passed by the Transfer Pricing Officer would reveal that while rejecting the benchmarking done by the assessee and determining the arm's length price at nil, he has not followed any prescribed method as provided under the statute. This view gets support from the decisions of jurisdictional High Court cited by the assessee. HEADNOTE: IV Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Others) - Assessment years 2017-18 and 2018-19 - During year, assessee had Regional Service Charges (RSC) as per RSC Agreement entered by assessee to its USA based AE - As per said RSC agreement, assessee received assistance and had access to centralized service of Goodyear group to deliver operational efficiencies and carry out its day to day operations - TPO held that payment of RSC charges was not for business purpose of assessee except IT services which was held at arm’s length - It was observed that assessee had not demonstrated impact of services obtained on business affairs of assessee in terms of turnover and profit - Cost incurred by recipient and mark-up charges had not been given in detail by assessee - Whether, in these circumstances, matter was to be restored to TPO with direction to assessee to demonstrate actual expenses incurred by AE and mark-up as well as rendition of service - Held, yes [Para 33] [Matter remanded]

FACT: ■

During the year under consideration, the assessee made payments of Regional Service Charges (RSC) as per RSC Agreement entered by the assessee with Goodyear USA. As per the said RSC agreement, the assessee received assistance and had access to the centralized service of the Goodyear group to deliver operational efficiencies and carry out its day to day operations.

■

The TPO held that payment of RSC charges was not for the business purpose of the assessee except in IT services which was held at arm’s length.

■

The DRP confirmed the adjustment.

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

It is opined that the comparable uncontrolled price (CUP) has been rightly taken up by the TPO. It is observed that the assessee has not demonstrated the impact of the services obtained on the business affairs of the assessee in terms of turnover and profit. The abstract words of greater operational efficiency have to be demonstrated in real terms in terms of benefit obtained by the assessee, the same has not been displayed by the assessee. The cost incurred by the recipient and mark-up charges have not been given in detail by the assessee. Hence, in the circumstances, it would be appropriate to refer the matter to the file of the TPO with direction to the assessee to demonstrate the actual expenses incurred by the AE and the mark-up as well as the rendition of the service by the assessee to the AE’s company with regard to the five international transactions of provision of services to the assessee (except Information & Technology Services). HEADNOTE: Section 92C, read with section 10A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Scope of provision) - Assessment years 2006-07 to 2008-09 - Whether there is no express provision under Act restricting application of section 92C for determining income at arm's length where such income is eligible for deduction under section 10A and, on contrary, there is a proviso to section 92C(4) which prohibits deduction under section 10A on income to extent enhanced as an effect of a determination of ALP - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where assessee was eligible for tax exemption at rate of hundred percent under section 10A/10B, arm's length price on its international transactions deserved to be determined under section 92C - Held, yes [Paras 9.10, 9.11 and 20] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRACING : Even when assessee was eligible for tax exemption at rate of hundred percent under section 10A/10B, then also arm's length price on its international transactions deserved to be determined under section 92C

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the activity of business process outsourcing (BPO) services in the field related to accounting & taxation such as book-keeping, VAT returns, payroll, management accounting, and audit. The assessee was providing these services to the firm, namely DC, which was an AE of the assessee. The assessee provided these services from the unit which was an STPI unit eligible for deduction/exemption under section 10A. The assessee benchmarked its transaction with AE by applying internal CUP method prescribed under section 92C and claimed that its transactions with the AE were at arm length price. However, the TPO opined that TNMM was the most appropriate method.

The assessee carried the matter to DRP and vehemently objected the rejection of CUP method and selection of TNM method as most appropriate method, comparable selected by the TPO and comparable rejected by the TPO as suggested by the assessee. The assessee also propositioned that it was enjoying the benefit of deduction under section 10A. Therefore, there was no reason to charge a lower price from the AE. Moreover, given the circumstances of the case, the effective tax rate in the UK would be higher than the effective tax rate in India, which as a result of section 10A was 0 per cent. As such, there was no motive and incentive in shifting the profits from India to the UK, where the rate of tax was comparatively higher. However, DRP rejected the contention of the assessee.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: It is cardinal rule of interpretation that where the language used by the legislature is clear and unambiguous then plain and natural meaning of those words should be applied to the language and resort to any rule of interpretation to unfold intentions is permissible where the language is ambiguous. [Para 9]

Now, the controversy in the instant case is disguised in the question as to whether the provisions of chapter X shall be invoked in a situation where the assessee is enjoying tax exemption under section 10A and/or where there is no motive to avoid tax. The purpose of enacting transfer pricing provisions was to put a stop to the avoidance of tax by shifting taxable income outside India. Similarly, extending the fundamental of intendment to section 10A it is comprehended that this particular section is purported to boost the business of those undertakings which are situated in free trade zones (FTZ) and engaged in export of article or things or computer software services etc. by exempting their income from levy of tax. Thus, here the question arises as to whether the transfer pricing provisions can be invoked concerning the international transaction carried out by the assessee with its AE where the former is enjoying exemption under section 10A. It is because, in such a situation, the assessee might not have any motive to shift the income from India to a foreign country as the same has already been exempted under section 10A [Para 9.8]

In this connection, section 92C has direct bearing on the controversy on hand. Therefore, it is imperative upon to take note of this section. On the perusal of the provision, of section 92C it is very clear that the purpose behind the provision of transfer pricing is to determine true profits/income as if such international transaction has been entered with an unrelated party or non-AE, irrespective of the fact that the income of the assessee was eligible for exemption. [Para 9.9]

TPO ought not to have disallowed 50 per cent of the said expenditure on an ad hoc basis. The TPO is duty bound to determine the ALP of an international transaction only by following any of the five prescribed methods provided in rule 10B of the Income-tax Rules and not otherwise. [Para 5.4]

The TPO was, therefore, directed to delete the transfer pricing adjustment made towards cost of allocation on an ad hoc basis. [Para 5.5] So far as central and regional support services are concerned, for providing the services, the AE had charged certain costs on the assessee based on appropriate cost allocation key. In these circumstances, it could not be said that assessee had not provided any documentary services to support its claim of payment of cost allocation charges to its AE for availing various services as detailed hereinabove. In any case, the TPO had merely determined the ALP of this international transaction at Rs. Nil without benchmarking the same by using any of the prescribed methods provided in section 92C read with rule 10B. Accordingly, the TPO was directed to delete the transfer pricing adjustment made in respect of cost allocation towards central and regional support services. [Para 5.8]

purchase & order handling services and sales services under the CCA and hence, the DRP confirmed the action of the TPO in determining the arm's length price of the said services at NIL value. It is pertinent to note that the aforesaid actions of the DRP and the TPO go against the basic tenet of the Indian Transfer Pricing Laws and violate the provision of sub-section (3) of section 92CA read with sub-section (3) of section 92C. In the assessee's case under consideration, the TPO/Assessing Officer has not selected any method (out of six methods), therefore, the arm's length price (ALP) computed by the Assessing Officer/TPO is not in accordance with the provisions of section 92C (1), hence the TPO/Assessing Officer should delete the addition. [Para 32]

Now, addressing the issue relating to 'benefit test'. The revenue alleged that the assessee had failed to satisfy the 'benefit test' in respect of payments made by the assessee under the CCA (Agreement) for receiving purchase services, order handling services and sales services. The assessee has submitted before the TPO, the detailed nature of the aforesaid services and copies of documentary evidences of receipt of services on sample basis. The assessee submitted, a brief chart to prove the benefit test. This chart explains the nature of services, main functions, and documentary evidences for receipt of services along with paper book reference. This chart also explains the relevant para of the Cost Contribution Agreement (CCA). The assessee received the purchase & order handling services and sales services and documented them properly. The assessee also submitted the certificate issued by PWC Austria, about the costs allocated to AT&S India Pvt. Ltd. The copies of 78 chains of e-mail, job description sheets of 10 individual employees of the CCA team, evaluation reports of 6 global customers and flow chart of quotation processing services prove that assessee has received benefit from these services. The revenue has not disputed that these services have not been received by the assessee, he disputed only the 'benefit test', that assessee did not get the benefit out of these services. Assessee has proved that he had received the benefit from these services, by way of submitting a brief chart containing the services obtained. Therefore, the assessee has satisfied the 'benefit test', and for that rendering of intra group services by AE and payment made thereon were in the nature of third party, which would willing to pay. [Para 33]

The Assessing Officer in the draft assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C(1), has not made any adverse comment under section 37 in respect of the services received under the CCA, for purchase services, order handling services and sales services. During the course of scrutiny assessment proceedings, the assessee submitted before the Assessing Officer the same evidences of receipt of purchase services, order handling services and sales services as those submitted to the TPO, as per the direction of the Assessing Officer. It is pertinent to note that the Assessing Officer, after examining the aforesaid details, did not make any adverse comment under section 37. As per the provision of sub-section (1) of section 37, the Assessing Officer is authorized to examine whether an expenditure (not being expenditure of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 and not being in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee) is incurred by an assessee wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business in the matter of computation of the income chargeable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'.

In the assessee's case under consideration, the Assessing Officer has not disallowed the benefit of services received by the assessee under the Cost Contribution Agreement. The authority of the TPO would be to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine the arm's length price ('ALP') and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which the assessee benefits. That exercise of actual verification would be left to the Assessing Officer under section 37. The Assessing Officer could, therefore, determine under section 37 that the expenditure claimed was not for the benefit of the business, and thus, disallow that amount, this does not restrict or in any way bypass the functions of the TPO. The jurisdiction of the TPO is specific and limited i.e. to determine the arm's length price of an international transaction in terms of Chapter X read with rules 10A to 10E of the Income-tax Rules. Therefore, the assessee has derived benefits from these services as per CCA agreement and hence the arguments advanced by the revenue is not acceptable. [Para 34]

HEADNOTE: Section 66 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with Entry 97 of List I and Entry 60 of List II of Schedule VII to the Constitution of India - Charge of service tax - By provisions of Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998 services offered by chartered accountants, real estate agents (property dealers) and architects had been brought under tax net - Whether where services are rendered by a professional as a chartered accountant or as an architect, inspite of there being a nexus between profession and service rendered, there is a distinct aspect of service which can be legitimately taxed by Parliament under Entry 97 of List I - Held, yes - Whether service tax levied on a practising chartered accountant, architect and property dealer does not relate to levy on profession under Entry 60 in List II but on service rendered by professionals and Parliament has acted perfectly within its jurisdiction to legislate an Act levying service tax on such services - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned provisions of Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998 are constitutionally valid - Held, yes

FACT: The Government of India notified service tax on 12 new services added in the service tax net by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998, vide notification dated 7-10-1998. In the instant writ petitions, the petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the provisions of the Act by which services offered by professionals like chartered accountants, architects and real estate agents had been brought under the tax net on ground of lack of legislative competence of the Parliament and discrimination inasmuch as the Legislature had picked and chosen some professions and left out the others.

HELD: A. Emergence of concept of service tax :

While on the manufacture of goods, tax is levied in the name of excise duty and on sale of goods tax is levied in the name of sales tax, there are number of activities, falling in the category of 'service sector' which constitute 40 per cent of National GDP, which are not subjected to tax. This has kept a number of activities, which in fact are an important part of the national economy, outside the tax net. It is of course true that the persons rendering such services are subjected to income-tax covered by Entry 83 in List I of Schedule VII of the Constitution, but that by itself is not sufficient as the persons manufacturing goods pay excise duty on the manufacture of goods and pay sales tax on sale of goods and are also liable to pay income-tax on the income earned by them. The professionals rendering services for remuneration and similarly other persons rendering service in a larger number of fields for remuneration can only be subjected to professional tax by the State Legislature by virtue of Entry 60 in List II but subject to the maximum limit of Rs. 2,500 per annum in view of the provisions of article 276(2) of the Constitution of India. Such tax is on profession/trade/calling/employment irrespective of the fact whether they were earning any income or not. In these circumstances, the Parliament decided to tax the services being rendered by the professionals and by other trades and callings. Thus, the service tax is absolutely distinct and separate from the tax on profession/trade/calling/employment. [Para 4]

B. Legislative history :

The Government of India has notified service tax on 12 new services added in the service tax net by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998, vide notification dated 7-10-1998. The liability has been made effective from 16-10-1998. Further, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 93, the Central Government had exempted in the public interest the taxable services other than that of auditing and accounting provided by a practising chartered accountant in his professional capacity to a client. Vide notification dated 16-10-1998 certain exemptions have been given to the Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost and Works Accountants. Thus, the net result was that the service tax was leviable on chartered accountants in relation to accounting, auditing and certification services provided by them, in their professional capacity. As section 12B of Central Excise Act, 1944 has been made applicable in relation to the impugned service tax, the direct legal consequence is that there is a presumption that service tax has been passed on to the customer, who is the beneficiary of the service, and that is the reason why the service tax is levied on the service provider himself. It is open to the service provider to pass on the tax to the beneficiary of the service and reimburse himself. Thus, it is evident that the service provider does not pay the tax and the tax falls on the service receiver. [Para 6]

C. Legislative competence :

HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustment - Nil) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether law does not require assessee to demonstrate need for availing services and revenue cannot step into shoes of businessman to decide what is necessary for businessman and what is not and, TPO is not empowered to question decision of assessee to avail support services from AE - Held, yes - Assessee, a 100 per cent subsidiary of US company, availed operational, strategic and advisory support services from its AE (EHK and ETH) - Assessee had furnished various documentary evidences before TPO, which were in form of e-mails/presentation, details of visit of personnel of associated enterprises in India, purposes of visit, etc. - TPO after considering submissions of assessee noted that though it was stated that operational, strategic and advisory supports were requested from Emerson HK and Emerson TH but no contemporaneous records were produced to indicate that such need was identified, which preceded entering into agreement with such services - TPO held that it was not possible to know what activities were carried on by AE and whether expenditure were in respect of services claimed to be provided - TPO concluded that in absence of any evidence available as to expertise of two concerns in respect of services claimed to be received from them, there was no basis for said claim - Perusal of various evidences filed by assessee, i.e., contemporaneous data available on record showed that services were highly technical and same had been used by assessee for carrying on its business activities - Whether TPO while benchmarking transactions need not determine whether price paid by assessee for services availed is what an independent enterprise would have paid for same services; analysis done by TPO of nature of services and benefits arising to assessee on availing such services was beyond scope of transfer pricing provisions - Held, yes - Whether TPO was justified - Held, no [Paras 20-27][In favour of assessee]IT/ILT: TPO while benchmarking transactions need not determine whether price paid by assessee for services availed is what an independent enterprise would have paid for same services

FACT: The assessee, a 100 per cent subsidiary of U.S. Company (Copeland), availed operational, strategic and advisory support services from its two AE Emerson HK and Emerson TH, for which the assessee entered into agreement/s with both the parties separately. The assessee had furnished various documentary evidences before the TPO, which were in the form of e-mails/presentation, details of visit of personnel of associated enterprises to India, purposes of visit, etc.

The TPO was of the view that no concrete evidence for receipt of such valuable services was provided by the assessee and even the calculation of payment made to the associated enterprises, related to any services received, or not had not been explained/furnished with any cogent evidence and there was no explicit cost allocation formula to link it to the actual services or value/volume of services received.

The TPO after considering the submissions of assessee noted that no contemporaneous records were produced to indicate that such need was identified. As per the TPO, it was not clear as to whether they were indeed capable of providing any valuable services. That allocation of cost on any basis was merely an allocation, but could not automatically imply that it was in respect of services provided or that it commensurate with the services provided.

The TPO held that no services were received and on CUP method, arm's length price of transaction was held to be at Nil. Thus, the TPO made an adjustment.

DRP found no valid reason to interfere with the draft proposed order of the Assessing Officer/TPO.

On appeal:

Investigation carried out by the SEBI revealed that certain directors and employees of SCSL had connived and collaborated in the overstatement, fabrication, falsification and misrepresentation in the books of account and financial statements of SCSL. The investigation also noted that the statutory auditors of SCSL had connived with the directors and employees of SCSL in falsifying the financial statements of SCSL. Show-cause notice was issued to PW Bangalore and its two partners who signed balance sheets of SCSL, seeking to take action for violation of sections 12A(a), 12A(b) and 12A(c) read with regulations 3(c), 3(d), 4(1), 4(2)(a), 4(2)(e), 4(2)(f), 4(2)(k) and 4(2)(r) of the SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations. The SCL inter alia alleged gross negligence and recklessness in conducting an audit in accordance with the accounting standards and repeatedly deviating from the mandated course of audit especially in relation to items of significant materiality; and failure to consider the direct confirmations received from banks with respect to the figures of fixed deposits while blindly relying on the indirect confirmations received from SCSL which showed higher balances. It was also mentioned in the SCN that PWC International Ltd. had approved 11 partnership firms consisting of Chartered Accountants as their partners to use the name 'Price Waterhouse' in India and that the 11 firms had common branch offices located in New Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurgaon, Bhuvneshwar & Ahmedabad and there were several common partners in these firms. These firms shared resources, manpower, offices, revenues, etc. amongst themselves and, for this purpose, the 11 firms had entered into an agreement in 2000 for resource sharing. It was further stated that the members of the "engagement team" which worked on the audit of SCSL was on the payroll of Price Waterhouse Kolkata and Lovelock & Lewes Kolkata.

Two writ petitions were filed before the Bombay High Court, first by PW Bangalore and second by ten other CA firms along with their partners who were using the brand name Price Waterhouse in India, for quashing of the SCNs on the ground that SEBI lacked jurisdiction as it was encroaching upon the jurisdiction of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI)

The Bombay High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that it could not be said that SEBI at that stage, had no jurisdiction to issue a SCN simply because the appellants were professional Chartered Accountants. The Bombay High Court, however, set out the scope and extent of SEBI's power under sections 11 and 11B, read with regulation 11 of the PFUTP Regulations to act against Chartered Accountants and the circumstances under which SEBI could issue direction to Chartered Accountants acting in their professional capacity. The Bombay High Court emphatically held that the jurisdiction of SEBI in the instant case would depend upon the evidence which was available during the investigation and that if there was only some omission without any mens rea or connivance with anyone, in any manner, then SEBI could not issue any further direction.

Thereafter, the WTM held that failure to seek external confirmation of the bank balances, fixed deposits, failure to detect fake invoices without adopting the rigorous procedure mandated by AAS drew an inference of gross negligence and inference of involvement of appellants in the fudging of the accounts. This gross negligence amounted to an act of commission of a fraud for the purposes of SEBI - Act and SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations for which mens rea was not required to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt but could be based on a preponderance of probability.

The WTM held that (i) entities/firms practising as Chartered Accountant (CA) in India under the brand and banner of Price Waterhouse (PW) would not directly or indirectly issue any certificate of audit of listed companies, compliance of obligations of listed companies and intermediaries registered with SEBI under the applicable laws for a period of two years, that, (ii) individual auditors, namely, 'SG' and 'ST', would not issue an audit certificate or any certificate of compliance with respect to a listed company for a period of three years; and that (iii) G, T and PW Bangalore would jointly and severally disgorge the wrongful gains of Rs. 13,09,01,664/- along with interest at the rate 12 per cent per annum from 7-1-2009, till the date of payment.

HEADNOTE: Section 73, read with section 86, of the Finance Act, 1994 - Recovery of service tax not levied or paid or short levied or short paid or erroneously refunded - Appellant, engaged in manufacture and sale of castings on specific rate of contract, paid service tax on account of services of goods transport operator - On basis of Chartered Accountant’s Certificate, said amount of service tax was refunded to it - However, Commissioner in exercise of its revisional power demanded back amount of refund sanctioned - It was case of appellant that it paid service tax which was not payable by it and said amount was not recovered from customers and so, doctrine of unjust enrichment did not arise in its case - It was found that said service tax amount had not vitiated contract price in any way - Commissioner in his order had not relied on any contradictory certificate of another professional - Whether certificate issued by a professional generally, should not be challenged without having contradictory certificate from another professional and in absence of such a contradictory certificate, it was to be held that appellant had a strong prima facie case in its favour for waiver of requirement of pre-deposit of service tax for hearing appeal - Held, yes

FACT: The appellant was sanctioned a refund by the adjudicating authority on basis of the factual situation prevailing and certificate given by the Chartered Accountant. However, the Commissioner reviewed the order of adjudicating authority and demanded the refund amount back on the ground that the certificate of the Chartered Accountant only stated that amount had been debited to expenses account in profit and loss statement. In appeal, the appellant contended that the amount had been paid as service tax which was not payable by the appellants and since they had not recovered the said amount from their customers. Therefore, the question of doctrine of unjust enrichment did not arise.

HELD: The Chartered Accountant’s Certificate was a detailed certificate which had been considered in depth by the adjudicating authority. The appellant was engaged in the manufacture and selling of casting on specific rate of contract. The amount of service tax paid by the appellant was on the goods transport operator. That had not vitiated the contract price in any way. Further, the certificate issued by the professional, generally should not be challenged without having contradictory certificate from another professional. The Commissioner in his order had not relied on any contradictory certificate of another professional. In the absence of which, it was to be held that the appellant had made out a prima facie case for waiver of pre-deposit of amount of service tax. [Para 5]

The bizarreness and whimsical nature of the allocation done by the TPO which has been supported by the DRP is not lost upon the revenue who has argued for a remand for proper appreciation by the TPO. However, it is opined that such an act of TPO and DRP cannot be set right by remitting the issue on this account. [Para 27] It is the claim of the assessee that the assessee has intra group AEs spread around the length and breadth of the globe. It has been claimed that the intra group services have been allocated on the basis of global agreement among the AEs. Proper allocation keys have been used and that the methodology adopted has the mandate of guiding of the OECD. In this regard, it is noted that in the OECD Guidelines in the Chapter VII relating to special consideration for intra group services has observed that mainly two issues were to be considered, one was whether intra group service have in fact been provided. The other issue is whether the intra group charge for such services for tax purpose should be in accordance with the arm's length principle. The OECD Guidelines inter alia also provide that the allocation of the group cost might be based upon the turnover or staff employed or some other basis. It mentioned that whether the allocation method is appropriate may depend upon the nature and use of the services. A reading of this OECD Guidelines makes it abundantly clear that contrary to the revenue's argument, the using of allocation keys for allocation of intra group services is not alien to international tax jurisprudence. Further, the allocation of concerned group expenses to different accounting units is a duly accepted accounting procedure. Furthermore, the assessee has used a CPA certificate for the allocation of intra group services from the AE. The authorities below have rejected the CPA certificate on the ground that underlying documents on the basis of which the CPA certificate has been issued has not been produced before them. In this regard, it is noted that the CPA certificate is quite specific and has been duly authenticated. It is found that in rule 10D, containing information and documents to be kept and maintained under section 92D it has been duly mentioned that the information's required under rule 10D(2)(A) shall be supported by authentic documents which may include inter alia public accounts and the financial statements relating to the business of the associated enterprises. Hence, the evidence for international transaction can be duly supported by public accounts and financial statements relating to business affairs of the AE. With such mandate of law, the action of the authorities below in rejecting the CPA certificate is not sustainable. The various other proposition mentioned by the assessee and case laws in support thereof are germane and duly support the case of the assessee. [Para 28]

HEADNOTE: II. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustment - Others) - Assessment years 2015-16 and 2016-17 - Assessee-company had made payment to its AE towards central service charge - TPO held that assessee-company had not explained exact nature of services which were categorized under central services and there was a vague description of services without any details being available and further assessee had not submitted any evidence in relation to actual receipt of services - It was found that assessee had given all detailed submission and analysis not only demonstrating rendition of central services but also commensurate benefits derived from such services to assessee - Whether, accordingly, TPO was not justified in holding that either there was no rendition or no benefit from said services and adjustment made by TPO was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 18] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee-company had made payment to its AE, viz., towards central service charge.

The AE had granted a non-exclusive license to assessee; firstly for using technical documentation, information, technical know-how and improvements; and secondly, for central services vide common-technology, trademark license and simple service agreement.

The assessee had benchmarked the transactions using CUP method.

The TPO held that assessee-company had not explained the exact nature of the services which were categorized under the central services and there was a vague description of the services without any details being available and further, assessee did not submit any evidence in relation to the actual receipt of services and made adjustment.

HELD: Before the authorities below, the assessee has given all the detailed submission and analysis not only demonstrating the rendition of central services but also commensurate benefits derived from such services to the assessee. Accordingly, it cannot be held that either there was no rendition or no benefit as observed by the TPO. Apart from that the CUP analysis done by the assessee by taking four comparables in both the assessment years in providing advisories, management advisory, strategic planning, business administration services, marketing plan, protocols, procedures, etc., wherein mean margin determined was 2.75 per cent in assessment year 2015-16 and 5.75 per cent in assessment year 2016-17; whereas the assessee has made payment at 0.50 per cent in assessment year 2015-16 and 0.75 per cent in 2016-17. Thus, the payment made by the assessee for central services are at ALP and the adjustments made by the TPO is deleted. [Para 18]

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

FACT: The assessee was engaged in manufacture of electric power steering for four wheelers and also had a non-exclusive right and license for the know-how and intellectual property rights in respect of designs, drawings, standards, specifications and all other technical data relating to various products.

The assessee had made payment of royalty for the technical know-how and documentation charges and testing charges and training charges and technical support charges to its AE's.

The TPO concluded that said transaction were not realty for benefit of assessee no independent party would have made such payment of technical fee and the TPO referred to OECD guidelines with regard to intragroup services and calculated the arm's length price.

DRP confirmed said order.

On appeal:

HELD: The principal activity of the assessee is to manufacture the automated product being power steering. On perusal of the Technical Collaboration Contract and Technical Personnel Dispatch Agreements dated 16-10-2006, it is observed that the assessee depends upon the technical support received from the technical personnel sent by the AE. It is also clear that, had the assessee not entered into a technical collaboration agreement with its AE, it would not have been able to make any sales whatsoever using the technology. These agreements are approved by the Ministry of Commerce, Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, including the payment of royalty and lump sum technical know-how fee. Article 5 of the Technical Collaboration Contract provides that, technical assistance would be provided by the AE, which shall include, dispatch and training of technical personnel. The very existence of the assessee's business depended upon the Technical Collaboration Contract and the technical Personnel Dispatch Agreements. [Para 6.1]

Further the transfer pricing study explains the nature and terms of the international transaction entered into by the assessee with its AE. The assessee was dependent upon its AE, even for carrying out research and development activities and providing manufacturing technology. Further the paper book narrates the details of the technical fees paid for the year under consideration. Whenever international transaction of such a nature is undertaken, it is a combination of technical know-how, royalty and technical assistance through deputation of employees. Merely by importing machinery or designs and drawings, it cannot be said that the assessee would be competent to make use of such machinery. No doubt that the technical know-how of the able personnel is needed under normal circumstances. [Para 6.2]

The evidence had been submitted before the authorities below showing rendering of certain services against the payments made to the AE. [Para 6.4]

So far as the segregation of international transaction is concerned, it is assumed that the various international transactions were entered into with respect to the final commercial venture undertaken by the assessee, be it the manufacture and the sale of the goods or provision of services by it. The assessee has priced the royalty and the technical services provided by the AE separately, and they were all provided under 2 different agreements which constitutes an International Transaction. TPO on one breath does not doubt the existence of services being rendered by the personnel sent by the AE, while on the next breath he has denied that technical support fees paid by the assessee to its AE, on the ground that no independent enterprise would pay such expenses under similar circumstances. [Para 6.6]

HEADNOTE: Section 92C, read with section 40A(2), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Section 92C v. Section 40A(2)) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether when assessee had chosen to use transfer pricing provisions to demonstrate its claim that expenditure for availing data service was at arm's length and that same was not excessive or unreasonable, revenue authorities were bound to rebut this claim of assessee and when transfer pricing reports submitted by assessee were not rejected, it was to be concluded that assessee had discharged burden of proof that lay on it as regards said payment - Held, yes - Assessee-company derived income from business of providing advisory and consulting services to companies engaged in business of general insurance and life assurance - It entered into an agreement with Amway, a foreign company and availed data processing services - However, Assessing Officer determined total income of assessee by making a disallowance under section 40A(2)(b) of data processing charges paid to Amway - It was found that assessee had filed Transfer Pricing Reports justifying price paid by it for services obtained, after conducting a Transfer Pricing Study and Amway as well as assessee were both assessed at maximum marginal rate and said transaction was tax neutral thus was not made with an intention to evade tax - Further no comparative data or instance was available and no exercise was made to arrive at a fair market price by Assessing Officer - Whether on facts ad hoc disallowance made was arbitrary - Held, yes [Para 14] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : When assessee had chosen to use transfer pricing provisions to demonstrate its claim that expenditure for availing data service was at arm's length and that same was not excessive or unreasonable, revenue authorities were bound to rebut this claim of assessee and when transfer pricing reports submitted by assessee were not rejected, it was to be concluded that assessee had proved that price paid for said services was at arm's length

FACT: The assessee-company derived income from the business of providing advisory and consulting services to companies engaged in the business of general insurance and life assurance. It entered into an agreement with Amway, a foreign company and availed data processing services. Assessee had filed Transfer Pricing Reports justifying price paid by it for services obtained, after conducting a Transfer Pricing Study.

However, the Assessing Officer determined total income of assessee inter alia making a disallowance under section 40A(2)(b) of data processing charges paid to Amway.

The FAA upheld the order passed by the Assessing Officer.

On appeal:

HELD: From Circular No. 6-B, dated 6-7-1968 of the CBDT, it is clear that the provision was made specifically to check tax avoidance. Thus when there is no tax avoidance, the applicability of this section would not be appropriate. [Para 12.4]

In the case the revenue does not dispute the fact that Amway as well as the assessee were both assessed at the maximum marginal rate and said transaction was tax neutral. Thus it was not made with an intention to evade tax. In fact the income of the Payee Company is much more than that of the assessee. Thus, Circular No. 6P dt. 6-7-1968, apply to the facts of this case. What is the amount that should have been paid for these services is to be decided by the Assessing Officer by keeping in view the requirements of business and the point of view of the businessman. [Para 12.9]

No basis or factual justification whatsoever is given by the revenue authorities in both these cases for this ad hoc disallowance. The factum of rendering of services is not in dispute. The requirement of payment of fees is also not in dispute. Only on the quantum of charges, the Assessing Officer is of the view that it is excessive and unreasonable. No comparative data or instance is available. No exercise is made to arrive at a fair market price by the Assessing Officer. Those ad hoc disallowances, are based on surmises and conjectures. [Para 13]

In the case on hand, there is not even an allegation that the assessee has evaded payment of tax.

In the case on hand the ad hoc disallowance made by the Assessing Officer is arbitrary and without any basis. The Assessing Officer had not given a finding as to what as per him, is the fair market value. Even if it is assumed that the payment made is excessive and unreasonable, such arbitrary and baseless, ad hoc disallowances cannot be upheld. On this ground also the assessee has to succeed. [Para 14.1]

HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act 1952 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transaction/allowability of expenditure ) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee-company had entered into agreements with its AEs - In terms of which, AEs would recharge on actual cost incurred towards rendering of services with 10 per cent mark-up and AEs would raise invoices on assessee towards support services rendered - TPO proceeded to compute ALP of transaction at Nil, for reason that evidences submitted were inadequate, need for availing services not substantiated break-up of cost was not submitted - Assessee had submitted substantial documents in form of agreements with AEs, details of cost recharged, employee wise cost details allocated to assessee, details of employee wise time sheet evidencing time spent by various employees towards rendering services to various countries including assessee in India, e-mail correspondence in support of nature and benefit of services rendered - Whether once availing of various services from AEs was duly substantiated by documentary evidence and cost allocation among group companies was also on basis of a well-accepted allocation key method, there was no basis in upholding transfer pricing adjustment made by TPO/Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether thus, TPO was to be directed to delete TP adjustment - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 12] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where availing of various services from AEs was duly substantiated by documentary evidence and cost allocation among group companies was also on basis of a well-accepted allocation key method, there was no basis in upholding transfer pricing adjustment made by TPO/Assessing Officer

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act 1952 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transaction/allowability of expenditure ) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee-company had entered into agreements with its AEs - In terms of which, AEs would recharge on actual cost incurred towards rendering of services with 10 per cent mark-up and AEs would raise invoices on assessee towards support services rendered - TPO proceeded to compute ALP of transaction at Nil, for reason that evidences submitted were inadequate, need for availing services not substantiated break-up of cost was not submitted - Assessee had submitted substantial documents in form of agreements with AEs, details of cost recharged, employee wise cost details allocated to assessee, details of employee wise time sheet evidencing time spent by various employees towards rendering services to various countries including assessee in India, e-mail correspondence in support of nature and benefit of services rendered - Whether once availing of various services from AEs was duly substantiated by documentary evidence and cost allocation among group companies was also on basis of a well-accepted allocation key method, there was no basis in upholding transfer pricing adjustment made by TPO/Assessing Officer - Held, yes - Whether thus, TPO was to be directed to delete TP adjustment - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 12] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of providing manpower recruitment and consultancy services to clients in India. It entered into various international transactions which included payment towards shared services availed from its AE and fees for such services was charged by AE at actual cost plus 10 per cent mark-up.

The TPO proceeded to compute the ALP of the transaction at Nil, for the reason that the evidences submitted were inadequate, the need for availing services was not substantiated and break-up of the cost was not submitted.

Before the Commissioner (Appeals) the assessee submitted additional evidences such as time sheet of employees, various documents to substantiate the benefits received, e-mail correspondences, marketing materials. etc. The Commissioner (Appeals) called for the remand report from the TPO. The Commissioner (Appeals) after perusing the remand report and the rebuttal of the assessee upheld the determination of ALP at Nil and confirmed the T.P. adjustment.

On appeal :

HELD: The assessee has submitted substantial documents in the form of agreements with AEs, details of cost recharged, employee wise cost details allocated to assessee, details of employee wise time sheet evidencing the time spent by various employees towards rendering services to various countries including assessee in India, email correspondence in support of nature and benefit of the services rendered. From the perusal of these records it is evident that the assessee before the lower authorities have submitted evidences in support of rendering of services, the benefits derived, basis of allocation of cost i.e. allocation key etc. and therefore, lower authorities were not justified in holding that no services were rendered by the AEs in respect of which payments were made by the assessee. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Methods for determination of - Most appropriate method, determination of) - Assessment years 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Assessee entered into service agreement with an entity to avail certain services in areas of business strategy, value based management, legal, marketing etc. - It paid consideration under said agreement - TPO computed TP adjustment by applying ad hoc estimation of salary cost and man hours - Whether while determining ALP of international transactions entered into by assessee, TPO cannot adopt any other method except methods prescribed in section 92C(1) and, therefore, impugned adjustment was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 17] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee has entered into service agreement with CEPT for availing certain services such as business strategy, financial planning and accounting supply chain, co-ordination and planning human resources legally and marketing, etc. It had made a payment towards availing these services where the AE has charged cost plus 5 per cent for providing the services.

The TPO computed TP adjustment by applying ad hoc estimation of salary cost and man hours.

The DRP confirmed the said TP adjustment.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: It is noticed that the TPO while arriving at the ALP has used the estimated salary and also used earlier year's man hours to determine the current year man hours spent. In the assessee's own case for assessment year 2009-10, the co-ordinate bench of the Tribunal has considered the issue of determination of ALP by the TPO and has held while determining ALP of international transactions entered into by assessee, TPO cannot adopt any other method except methods prescribed in section 92C(1) and, therefore, the TP adjustment made by the TPO is not tenable. Therefore, following the above decisions of the co-ordinate bench, impugned TP adjustment was to be deleted. [Para 17]

Nil - Whether since for these intra group services, assessee had demonstrated and satisfied need test, evidence/rendition test and benefit test as envisaged under section 92(2) and services provided by AE were neither duplicative or shareholder's activity, Assessing Officer/TPO was to be directed to determine arm's length price of these services based on documents submitted by assessee by determining tested party, determination of most appropriate method and comparability analysis - Held, yes [Para 38] [In favour of assessee/Matter remanded]IT/ILT: Where assessee had availed intra group services from its AE and made payment for same, in view of fact that assessee had demonstrated and satisfied need test, evidence/rendition test and benefit test as envisaged under section 92(2) and services provided by AE were neither duplicative or shareholder's activity, TPO was to be directed to determine arm's length price of these services based on documents submitted by assessee  IT/ILT: For determining arm's length price, tested party should be least complex of transacting parties for which data is available for comparability analysis

Section  92C , read with sections  92  and  92CA , of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section 165, read with sections 161 and 166 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 – Transfer Pricing - Computation of Arm’s length price (TP Adjustments -  Illustrations  - Support Services Fee) - Assessee paid its US AE for marketing, regulatory liaison and customer support services, reimbursed on cost plus 20 per cent basis, and benchmarked transactions under entity-level TNMM showing higher margins than comparables - TPO held entity-level TNMM inappropriate, proposed to treat AE as tested party, questioned necessity/benefit and documentation, and determined ALP of service charge/markup at Nil - CIT(A) recorded that assessee had substantial US exports and multiple ANDA filings, that services were actually rendered and costs were certified by an independent CPA, and that TPO had not brought comparables or disproved rendition; disallowance of mark-up was deleted - Whether ALP cannot be determined at Nil in absence of contrary evidence; services accepted and TNMM sustained; adjustment deleted - Held, yes [Paras 19.21 to 19.28] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Technical services fee) - Assessment year 2008-09 - DRP held that transaction relating to payments of intra group services and technical fees is treated as separate transactions and not aggregated with transaction of manufacturing activity - In light of above, it was held by TPO that assessee has failed to prove that it has actually received services and such services have benefitted assessee - Therefore TPO opined that it is appropriate to restore matter to file of Assessing Officer with direction to find out as to whether any service is rendered by AE to assessee and from which assessee has drawn any benefit from it - Whether authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits and that aspect of exercise is left to Assessing Officer therefore, TPO restoring matter to file of Assessing Officer to find out as to whether any service is rendered by AE to assessee and from which assessee has drawn any benefit from it is not correct - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits as that aspect of exercise is left to Assessing Officer therefore, TPO restoring matter to file of Assessing Officer to find out as to whether any service is rendered by AE to assessee and from which assessee has drawn any benefit from it is not correct

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments) - Assessment years 2007-08 and 2008-09 - Whether in transfer pricing proceedings, role of TPO is to determine arm's length price of a transaction but he cannot reject entire payment made to AE under provisions of section 92C - Held, yes - Whether in order to determine ALP of service fee paid by assessee to its AE, it is irrelevant as to what benefit assessee eventually derived from said services but in such a case, actual determinative factor is as to what assessee would have paid for those services if same had been rendered by a non-AE - Held, yes [Paras 96  102] [In favour of assessee]IT/ILT : In transfer pricing proceedings, role of TPO is to determine arm's length price of a transaction but he cannot reject entire payment made to AE under provisions of section 92C

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arms length price (Adjustments - Benefit from transactions/Allowability of expenditure) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee-company had entered into a multilateral service agreement with its Associated Enterprises for various intra-group services relating to strategic inputs such as product information, marketing field engineering services, scientific and laboratory services, logistic, administrative, etc. - TPO held that evidence submitted by assessee were only data excel sheets of cost allocation and further, these were duplicative in nature and a shareholders activity and therefore, he determined ALP of such services as nil - Assessee had submitted agreement showing description of services and benefit received therefrom and various e-mail correspondences were submitted which said that services had been rendered by AE and received by assessee and certificates of various AE were produced to show basis of allocation and exact cost allocation to assessee and employee wise cost sheet which showed distribution and allocation of such cost - Whether, on fact, assessee had reasonably sustantiated benefit test, need test and rendition test for said intra-group services and there was no justification in determining ALP at nil - Held, yes [Para 16] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where intra- group service received by assessee-company was supported by proper agreement and substantial evidences with respect to services rendered by Associated Enterprises also demonstrated benefits received therefrom, AO was not justified in determining of ALP of said service at nil  TRANSFER PRICING : Transfer Pricing Officer should restrict addition/TP adjustment only to International transactions
