Section  92C,  read with section  92CA,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer Pricing  -  Computation of Arm’s length price  (Adjustments - Segmentation) - Assessment year  2018-19  - Assessee, engaged in testing, inspection and certification (TIC) services to third-party customers in India and to AEs, also provided ITES support and shared services to AEs - For transfer pricing, it prepared segmental accounts showing AE margins of about 15% in ITES, shared services and certification segments, a 4% margin in non-AE certification services, an overall margin of about 6%, and ITES revenue of about Rs. 4.53 crores out of total revenue of about Rs. 124.81 crores (non-AE certification about Rs. 97.40 crores; AE certification about Rs. 15.09 crores; shared services about Rs. 7.79 crores) - In its TPSR, it benchmarked ITES transactions of about Rs. 4.5 crores under TNMM using OP/OC with a margin of 15% - On reference, TPO grouped TIC, shared services and ITES together as ITES, rejected assessee's segmental results stating that HR, finance, operations, legal and admin costs were not allocated to AEs, computed a consolidated margin of 4.44%, rejected TPSR and proposed a TP adjustment of about Rs. 26.18 crores - Whether since for earlier AYs TIC and ITES services were benchmarked separately, as TIC services and ITES services did not share same FAR, and TP Order did not explain why TIC and ITES services were being grouped together, combining TIC and ITES services for benchmarking was not justified - Held, yes [Para 24] [In favour of assessee]

V. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - High-end service providers) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether a company engaged in high-end services could not be compared with low end BPO service provider like assessee - Held, yes [Para 27] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - ITES services) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Whether Company which has an abnormally high RPT filter of 82.92 per cent could not be considered as comparable to ITES service provider - Held, yes (Para 26) [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Adjustments - Support service fee) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee company was engaged in business of developing, installation, commissioning and service of captive power plants - In course of transfer pricing proceedings, TPO found that assessee had rendered marketing support services to its AE in supplying gas turbines to Public Works Department (PWD) in carrying out construction for Common Wealth Games (CWG) - He thus made certain addition to assessee's ALP in respect of said services - Tribunal examined relevant clauses of contract and noted that eligibility condition for participating in tender was submission of registration under Delhi Value Added Tax Act, 2004, besides submission of certificate of being original equipment of gas turbines - Admittedly, assessee was not a manufacturer of gas turbines but AE was - However, AE did not have VAT registration certificate - Therefore, for participating in tender and for obtaining contract bid was submitted in assessee's name - However, Tribunal found that there was nothing on record to suggest that assessee had provided any other services to its AE for sales of its gas based turbines either to PWD or to other customers in India - Tribunal thus, deleted addition made by TPO - Whether since finding arrived by Tribunal was based on appreciation of evidence and materials on record, impugned order did not require any interference - Held, yes [Paras 24, 25 and 26] [In favour of assessee]TRANSFER PRICING : Where assessee had not rendered any marketing support services to its AE in supplying gas turbines to Public Works Department (PWD) in carrying out construction for CWG, impugned addition made to assessee's ALP in respect of said services was to be deleted

III. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Whether a company engaged in valuation of various assets which is highly technical involving huge expertise would not be comparable with assessee-company engaged in provision of business support services to its AE - Held, yes [Para 21] [In favour of assessee]

III. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Technical support service provider) Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether a company engaged as commercial testing house in running laboratory testing, chemical testing and services which are highly technical in nature who offers services like testing of products and also offers services in field of pollution control as allied activity cannot be compared with assessee company who were purely in nature of marketing support services and not engaged in providing technical services- Held, yes [Paras 21 to 23] [In favour of assessee]

III. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Whether where assessee was providing back office support services to its AE, a company which only earned 0.14 per cent income from export and, thus, failed to satisfy export filter of 25 per cent as applied by TPO, was not acceptable as comparable - Held, yes [Para 2.4.2] [In favour of assessee]

VI. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Business support services) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether where assessee was providing back office support services to its Associated Enterprise, a company providing full range of geospatial services was not comparable to assessee - Held, yes [Para 14] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustration) - Assessment years 2007-08 and 2008-09 - Assessee rendered marketing support services to its AE - Whether a company engaged in providing testing services for various products and also offering services in field of pollution control, was incomparable - Held, yes [Para 13] [In favour of assessee]

II.Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee was rendering Call Centre services to its associated enterprises - Whether company operating as an IT enabled, knowledge based Back Office Processing Centre which served needs of financial content sector, was not comparable to Call Centre services - Held, yes - Whether RPT being more that 25 per cent, said company be excluded from comparability analysis - Held, yes - Whether when export revenue of a company was 74.45 per cent as against TPO's filter of 75 per cent, said company could not be excluded for such a minuscule difference if it was otherwise comparable - Held, yes [Para 14-15] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparability functional similarity - Consultancy service providers) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether in case of assessee engaged in rendering business support services to AE, a company providing financial consultancy services, was not acceptable as comparable - Held, yes [Para 24] [In favour of assessee]

IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparability factors - Related party transactions) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Whether a company having RPT filter of more than 15 per cent cannot be compared with captive service provider like assessee - Held, yes [Para 12D] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section  92C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer pricing  -  Computation of arm's length price  (Adjustments - Others) - Assessment year  2021-22  - Assessee was involved in main business of advertising agent for its various clients as well as providing media planning services to its clients - Assessee-company had paid a certain sum to its Associated Enterprise (AE) towards intra group services, namely, Global information services (GIS) - TPO determined ALP of intra-group services at nil on ground that need and benefit test was not satisfied by assessee and made adjustment - It was noted that assessee had submitted relevant agreements showing services rendered, obligations of parties, fees to be charged, allocation of cost, etc.- Whether since assessee had reasonably satisfied various tests, i.e., need test, rendition test, benefit test, duplicate test and shareholder's activity, TPO was not correct in arriving at ALP as NIL without giving any contrary findings with regard to various documents including TP study submitted by assessee - Held, yes [Para 12.2] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Advisory services) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Whether in case of assessee providing marketing support services to AE, a company, which basically aimed at providing advisory services on procurement and also carrying out procurement audit, was not acceptable as comparable - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables-Illustration) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee-company provided marketing support services to its AE - Whether where a company was providing end to end solution and was into commercial testing and analysis laboratory engaged in analyzing food and agricultural products etc., it was not a valid comparable - Held, yes [Para 17] [In favour of assessee]

Section  92C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Transfer pricing  -  Computation of arm's length price  (Adjustments - Benefit for transaction/allowability of expenditure)) - Assessment year  2021-22  - Assessee-company, engaged in recruitment services, had made payments to its AEs towards Business Support Services and Business Technology Services (Intra group services) - TPO noted that assessee had not been able to substantiate need for such services, benefits derived from same and quantification of service payments in relation to same and, thus, determined ALP of such services as nil and made transfer pricing additions - It was noted that assessee had submitted detailed description of various services availed, copy of relevant agreements, inter-company invoices, cost allocation workings as well as a description of each category of services along with need and benefit derived from each of said services - Further, assessee had furnished details of employees on its payroll and it was noted that assessee did not have any personnel on its payroll to perform support functions - Moreover, assessee had carried out primary benchmarking analysis taking foreign AEs as tested party and secondary benchmarking analysis taking assessee as tested party - Whether since assessee had discharged burden to satisfy that need, purpose, rendition and benefit test for relevant previous year by furnishing relevant documents and details during proceedings before TPO, transfer pricing addition was to be set aside with directions to TPO to compute ALP as per corroborative benchmarking analysis after verifying computation of PLI - Held, yes [Paras 15, 16 and 19][In favour of assessee]

Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm's length price - (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustment - Whether where Payment was made by assessee for services rendered by its at but - TPO had not carried out exercise for computing arm's length price on plea that assessee did not provide agreement with ANCR, whereas assessee claimed to have provided a copy - Since to determined arms length price of benefit, service etc. as per most appropriate method as envisaged in section 92C(1) matter be remanded back - Held, yes [Para 7] [Matter remanded]

IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustments - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether a company providing consultancy services to financial institutions in and out of India couldn't be compared to company providing market support services - Held, yes [Para 22][In favour of assessee]

Section 92CA, read with section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Reference to TPO (Section 37(1) v. section 92CA) - Whether jurisdiction of Assessing Officer under section 37 and TPO under section 92CA is distinct and, therefore, a referral made by Assessing Officer to TPO for limited purpose of determining ALP does not take away power of Assessing Officer to determine as to whether payment made by assessee to its AE for services rendered was basically an expenditure incurred for purpose of business so as to allow same under section 37(1) - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]IT/ILT : Jurisdiction of Assessing Officer under section 37(1) and TPO under section 92CA is distinct and, therefore, a referral made by Assessing Officer to TPO for limited purpose of determining ALP does not take away power of Assessing Officer to determine as to whether payment made by assessee to its AE for services rendered was basically an expenditure incurred for purpose of business so as to allow same under section 37(1)  IT/ILT : Authority of TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine ALP and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which assessee benefits; therefore, TPO cannot determine ALP of payments made by assessee to its AE at nil taking a view that assessee did not derive any benefit from services rendered by AE

IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricingComputation of arm’s length price (Comparables, functional similarity - Marketing/sales support services)- Assessment Year 2010-11 - Whether a company providing advisory services can be no match with a company providing actual marketing support services - Held, yes [Para 11.29] [In favour of assessee]

IV. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer Pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparability factors - Export turnover) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee was a BPO service provider - It was also providing services to customers of its holding company abroad - It had selected a comparable in its TP documentation - However, TPO had excluded comparable on ground that it had failed export filter - Whether since entire turnover of said company was attributed to exports, there was no reason for exclusion of this comparable and, thus, it was to be included in set of comparables - Held, yes [Para 25] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Comparables - Illustrations) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Whether where assessee provided services related to accounts payable management, payroll, processing invoice processing and handling of related queries to its AEs as a captive service provider, a KPO engaged in providing high-end services such as data analytics, data solutions services etc. was not acceptable as comparable - Held, yes [Para 58] [In favour of assessee]

facts.text:
The assessee was a practising chartered accountant. The revenue levied tax on certification service holding that it was an auditing service and, therefore, not entitled to exemption in terms of Notification No. 59/89-ST, dated 16-10-1998.

On appeal :

The assessee was a firm of chartered accountants. The original authority confirmed demand of service tax on the assessee for the period 16-10-1998 to 31-7-2002 under the heads ‘Practising chartered accountant’, ‘Manpower recruitment service’, ‘Management consultant’ and ‘Business auxiliary service’. Modifying the findings of the original authority, the Commissioner (Appeals) found that the assessee was not liable to pay service tax under the head ‘Business auxiliary service’. He affirmed the demand on the assessee in respect of other categories of services. In the instant appeal, the assessee contended that it had rendered services as management consultant and man-power recruitment agent which were exempt in terms of Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998. The assessee also contended that Commissioner (Appeals) had wrongly held that the Notification No. 15/2002, dated 1-8-2002 which inserted an Explanation to Notification No. 59/1998-ST, dated 16-10-1998, had come into effect from 16-10-1998.

The Income-tax Department’s case was that when a Chartered Accountant is authorised in terms of section 288, the authorisation, if in the form of power of attorney, is required to bear stamp duty of Rs. 50. It was further contended that an authorisation of a Chartered Accountant or an income-tax practitioner by a person to represent his case in income-tax proceedings is not an instrument subject to payment of court fees under the Court Fees Act. That being so, such an authorisation could only be considered as a ‘Power of Attorney’ as defined in section 2(p) of the Kerala Stamp Act, 1959 in respect of which stamp duty is payable as specified in article 44 of the Schedule thereof. Accordingly, while a Vakalatnama signed by an advocate is chargeable to court fee under the Court Fees Act, an authorisation in the case of a Chartered Accountant or an income-tax practitioner is only a ‘Power of Attorney’ which is subject to stamp duty under the Stamp Act.

On writ :

Assessee PWH was an independent firm of Chartered Accountants managed and controlled by its partners who were individuals and residents of India.

It had entered into an agreement with Price Water HouseCoopers International Limited (PwCIL) a company incorporated in the United Kingdom to become member of PwCIL. The member firms of PwCIL were collectively known as PwC Network.

PWH had become a member firm of PwC Network, at the same time it was a separate independent legal entity whose affairs were managed and controlled only by its partners.

Price Water HouseCoopers Services BV, Netherlands(Services BV) was the central services entity of the PwC Network and operated exclusively for mutual benefit of all PwC Network member firms. Neither PWH nor any of its partners was a shareholder of Services BV. Services BV had not conferred on PWH any right regarding use of any brand name as Services BV itself did not own any brand name.

During relevant year PwC received a non-refundable loan to strengthen PWH's audit practices in India. Such loan was received under contractual arrangement existing between Services BV and PWH and PWH had shown it as business income in its return.

On scrutiny assessment, the Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax (R-3) issued notice requiring PWH to file its computation of income and tax for year, audit profit and loss account and balance sheet, tax and audit report issued under section 44AB. PWH filed all the necessary documents

Thereafter R-3 issued a letter to PWH informing it that a reference had been made to the TPO and called upon PWH to file details requested for in earlier notices.

PWH contended that TPO regulations did not apply to PWH as it did not have a relationship of being AE with any overseas network entity. It further contended that it had never entered into any international transaction envisaged under section 92B, and hence, it was unable to comprehend the reasons for which reference had been made under section 92CA(1) to the TPO. Further the fact that the transactions between PWH and Services BV were not international transactions had been accepted in the previous assessment year and hence there was no justification for R-3 to take a different view on same set of facts and law.

Facts

The assessees had provided chartered accountant's services prior to 1-4-2012 and raised the bills therefor prior to that date, levying service tax at the rate of 10 per cent.

Up to 1-4-2012, Chartered Accountants services were governed by rule 7 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011 wherein point of taxation was determined based on date of receipt of payment.

With effect from 1-4-2012, rate of service tax was increased to 12 per cent and services of chartered accountants were excluded from Rule 7 ibid.

Circular No. 158/9/2012-ST dated 8-05-2012 and Circular No.154/5/2012-ST dated 28-03-2012 had provided that since, prior to 1-4-2012, services of Chartered Accountants were covered by rule 7 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011, hence, point of taxation of services provided prior to that date will continue to be governed by said Rule 7, as it stood before that date. Accordingly, in case of services provided and invoices raised before 1-4-2012, the point of taxation would be date of payment and if payment was received on or after 1-4-2012, revised rate of service tax viz. 12 per cent would apply.

The assessees argued that point of taxation, in their case, was determinable as per Rule 4 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011.

Therefore, the assessees challenged the said circulars as ultra vires the Constitution and the provisions of the Finance Act, 1994 and rules.

Issue Involved

Whether Circular was ultra vires the Act ?

The applicant, a tax resident of Hong Kong, belongs to X group of companies. The group entities are engaged in the business of inspection, verification, testing and certification (IVTC) services to various customers. The X trademark is owned by ABC (Parent Company), who had entered into a trademark license and Support Services Agreement (Support Services Agreement) with all its group entities, separately, including the applicant. The support service agreement is stated to bring uniform standards, procedures and policies described therein to IVTC services. It is stated that the inspection services are generally performed either at the load port or discharge port of a product or activity and are based on scientific and internationally accepted techniques and as per the clients' requirements. Verification services are used to evaluate whether the product services are system complaint with given regulation, specifications or condition. Testing services are used to determine the quality of the product or services as per the customer's requirements and are carried out in laboratories owned by respective X entities which are accredited to international bodies. Certification services refers to the confirmation of regulations, standards or contractual specifications of a product or organization or training. The applicant provided IVTC services to Indian Customers either directly or through X India. The applicant states that the IVTC Services are provided to the Indian Customer outside India if there is a direct arrangement between the customer and the applicant and the payment is made on the invoice raised by the applicant. But when the arrangement is not direct and is through the X India, then the invoice is raised either on X India or the Indian customer. Explaining it by an example, the applicant states that where a customer approaches X India to have its goods inspected in India and outside India, then X India sub-contracts the inspection to its applicant and the applicant raises invoice on X India for services provided by it and a consolidated invoice is raised on the customer. The applicant sought advance ruling on the question as to (i) whether the payments received/receivable the applicant in connection with transactions under taken/proposed to be undertaken in relation to the (a) inspection and verification services (b) testing/analysis services; and (c) certification services are chargeable to tax in India as 'fees for technical services' (FTS) under section 9(1)(vii)( b) and (ii ) whether payments received/receivable in connection with procurement of goods/services and reimbursement of other expenses proposed to be incurred for and on behalf of X India are chargeable to tax in India. The applicant also raised issue relation to withholding of taxes under section 195 and filing of return under section 139.

The assessee has entered into service agreement with CEPT for availing certain services such as business strategy, financial planning and accounting supply chain, co-ordination and planning human resources legally and marketing, etc. It had made a payment towards availing these services where the AE has charged cost plus 5 per cent for providing the services.

The TPO computed TP adjustment by applying ad hoc estimation of salary cost and man hours.

The DRP confirmed the said TP adjustment.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The AO had made a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) under section 92CA. Pursuant to this reference, the TPO passed an order under section 92CA(3) accepting that the international transactions entered into by the assessee with its Associated Enterprises were at an Arms Length Price. In other words, the TPO made no variation.

■

The Assessing Officer passed a draft assessment order under section 144C(1) and thereafter passed a final assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C(3) and section 144B.

■

On writ:

■

The assessee, engaged in providing basic market research and testing services to its associated enterprises (AEs), reported international transactions in Form 3CEB. The matter was referred to the TPO for determination of the arm's length price (ALP).

■

The TPO, by order passed under section 92CA(3), proposed a transfer pricing adjustment of Rs. 16.13 crore. While benchmarking the international transaction, the TPO applied export-income and employee-cost filters, rejected certain comparables selected by the assessee and included fresh comparables in the final set. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer passed a draft assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C.

■

Pursuant to the directions of the DRP, the TPO passed an order giving effect and revised the transfer pricing adjustment to Rs. 17.99 crore, which was incorporated by the Assessing Officer in the final assessment order. Subsequently, pursuant to rectification proceedings under section 154 on account of working capital adjustment, the transfer pricing adjustment was recomputed at Rs. 7.90 crore.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of providing design and engineering services to its Associated Enterprise (AE). It entered into various international transactions with its AE and hence a reference was made under section 92CA to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) to determine the Arm's Length Price (ALP) of the international transactions with its AEs.

The TPO was of the view that said services were in the nature of knowledge process outsourcing within ITES/BPO services.

On appeal, the (DRP) Dispute Resolution Panel observed that the reasoning given by the TPO was correct.

The assessee-company was engaged in the activity of business process outsourcing (BPO) services in the field related to accounting & taxation such as book-keeping, VAT returns, payroll, management accounting, and audit. The assessee was providing these services to the firm, namely DC, which was an AE of the assessee. The assessee provided these services from the unit which was an STPI unit eligible for deduction/exemption under section 10A. The assessee benchmarked its transaction with AE by applying internal CUP method prescribed under section 92C and claimed that its transactions with the AE were at arm length price. However, the TPO opined that TNMM was the most appropriate method.

The assessee carried the matter to DRP and vehemently objected the rejection of CUP method and selection of TNM method as most appropriate method, comparable selected by the TPO and comparable rejected by the TPO as suggested by the assessee. The assessee also propositioned that it was enjoying the benefit of deduction under section 10A. Therefore, there was no reason to charge a lower price from the AE. Moreover, given the circumstances of the case, the effective tax rate in the UK would be higher than the effective tax rate in India, which as a result of section 10A was 0 per cent. As such, there was no motive and incentive in shifting the profits from India to the UK, where the rate of tax was comparatively higher. However, DRP rejected the contention of the assessee.

On the assessee's appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of chemicals and chemical intermediates and providing marketing and technical support services, entered into international transactions with its AEs for availing PTSE services, IT support services (including SAP charges) and centralized support services.

■

The TPO determined the ALP of the aforesaid intra-group services at nil and proposed a transfer pricing adjustment of Rs. 61.22 crore.

■

The DRP upheld the TPO’s determination of ALP at nil and sustained the proposed adjustment.

■

Pursuant to the DRP’s directions under section 144C(5), the Assessing Officer passed the final assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C(13) and 144B making the addition on account of the transfer pricing adjustment.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

•

The assessee paid consultancy charges of Rs. 17,62,68,906 to REL, its associated enterprise. In response to TPO calling for information on the resources available with REL, assessee explained that the services rendered by REL were examined by two leading management consultancy firms who were rendering similar services. These quotations were bench marked against the consultancy charges paid to the A.E. and 'CUP' method was applied.

•

TPO rejected assessee's contentions stating that a quotation given by third party did not constitute 'comparable uncontrolled transactions' and held that the estimation on valuation of services attempted by the assessee through third parties did not fall within any of the prescribed methods for determination of ALP. TPO accordingly applied 'Cost Plus' method with 5 per cent mark-up and made certain adjustments.

•

The Commissioner (Appeals) held that in the absence of comparable instances, an estimate of reasonable mark-up could only be made after taking into account all material factors and indices. He held that the consideration paid by the assessee to REL towards consultancy services was reasonable having regard to the net profit disclosed by REL and also the fact that said net profit included income from time charter of Relchem Isha vessel where a transfer pricing adjustment had been made.

•

On appeal by revenue :

Based on the observations made by the Supreme Court in Associated Cement Co. Ltd. 's case (supra) , the CBDT issued Circular No. 681 dated 8-3-1994 according to which persons rendering services as lawyers, chartered accountants, physicians, surgeons, etc., were made liable to pay tax at the rate of 2 per cent of remuneration payable to them by the party engaging them for professional services under section 194C, after with- drawing the earlier circulars.

On writ:

■

The assessee-company was primarily engaged in the business of freight forwarding services.

■

The transfer pricing reference under section 92CA(1) was made by the Assessing Officer Technical Unit in the case of the assessee on account of availing intra group services and making payment of group fee for determination of arm's length price (ALP).

■

The assessee submitted the details from time to time on ITBA portal which was duly considered by the TPO who determined the arm's length price (ALP) and made adjustment.

■

The Assessing Officer passed a draft assessment order under section 143(3) and the assessee referred the matter to the Dispute Resolution Panel.

■

Finally, on the recommendation of the DRP, the Assessing Officer passed impugned assessment order and determined the income of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

made an adjustment of Rs. 1,24,03,828, on account of technical services and also retained the transfer pricing adjustment of Rs. 55,25,877 with regard to back office support service. He held that the assessee would not get the benefit of +/-5 per cent range as the amount of Rs. 4,21,23,805, shown by the assessee for back office support service was beyond the limit of the ALP of such service determined at Rs . 4,76,49,682.

■

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of providing Information technology services specific to the payments industry to customers such as banks, financial institutions, third party processors and to its AEs. The assessee filed its return of income. The case was selected for complete scrutiny and notice under section 143(2) was issued to the assessee.

■

Subsequently, a reference under section 92CA(1) was made by the Jurisdictional Assessing Officer ('AO') to the Transfer Pricing Officer ('TPO') after obtaining the approval of the Pr. CIT for determination of Arm's length price. The TPO proposed to reject comparables identified by the assessee for SWD segment and made adjustment for outstanding receivables from the AEs and adjustment for corporate cost allocation paid to AEs on account of Intra Group Services(IGS). The TPO proposed an aggregate transfer pricing adjustment.

■

The Assessing Officer passed a draft assessment order incorporating the above TP adjustments. On appeal, the Dispute Resolution Panel upheld the TPO's approach for computation of arm's length price with respect to the SWD segment. Based on the directions of the DRP, the TPO affirmed the original TP adjustment.

■

The final assessment order was passed in the assessee's case. On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee filed its return of income. Further, the assessee received notices under section 148 and under section 92CA from the Transfer Pricing Officer seeking details about the international transactions entered into by the assessee with the group companies on a reference made by the Assessing Authority. In reply to the notice issued, the assessee filed a letter requesting the Assessing Authority to treat the return filed as return in compliance with the notice under section 148. In fact, the Transfer Pricing Officer passed an order under section 92CA accepting the pricing of the Assessing Authority.

However, the Commissioner invoked section 263 and set aside the order of the Assessing Authority.

On appeal, the Tribunal held that when two views were possible and when the Transfer Pricing Authority accepted valuation by the Assessing Authority determining the arm's length price, the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to interfere with the said order under section 263. Accordingly, the Tribunal set aside the order of the Commissioner.

On revenue's appeal to the High Court :

■

The assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing of brakes and braking systems. A reference under section 92CA(1) was made for determination of arm’s length price of specified domestic transactions of its Brakes Division. In its transfer pricing study, assessee benchmarked transactions under TNMM and claimed them to be at arm’s length.

■

The TPO rejected assessee’s comparables, adopted his own set of comparables, applied three-year weighted average margins of comparables, and proposed a transfer pricing adjustment by order under section 92CA(3).

■

The draft assessment order was confirmed by the DRP, inter alia, relying on Notification dated 19-10-2015 introducing multiple-year data and range concept.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

During the relevant previous year, the assessee availed intra-group services from its AEs and paid charges aggregating to Rs. 17.55 crores.

■

The TPO determined the arm's length price of the intra-group services at nil and proposed a transfer pricing adjustment of Rs. 17.55 crores.

■

The DRP confirmed the adjustment and further concluded that the expenditure incurred on intra-group services was not allowable under section 37(1). Accordingly, the adjustment was sustained in the final assessment order.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal.

Price Waterhouse (PW) Bangalore, a CA firm, was given the audit for auditing the books of account 'SCSL', which was regarded as one of top IT outsourcing firms in the world.

In the year 2009, the SEBI received an email from the then Chairman of SCSL stating that the statements of accounts of SCSL were not true and fair. The e-mail basically revealed that there was large scale financial manipulation in the books of account of SCSL, namely, that the balance sheet of SCSL as of 30-9-2008 carried inflated/non-existent cash and bank balances.

Investigation carried out by the SEBI revealed that certain directors and employees of SCSL had connived and collaborated in the overstatement, fabrication, falsification and misrepresentation in the books of account and financial statements of SCSL. The investigation also noted that the statutory auditors of SCSL had connived with the directors and employees of SCSL in falsifying the financial statements of SCSL.

Show-cause notice was issued to PW Bangalore and its two partners who signed balance sheets of SCSL, seeking to take action for violation of sections 12A(a), 12A(b) and 12A(c) read with regulations 3(c), 3(d), 4(1), 4(2)(a), 4(2)(e), 4(2)(f), 4(2)(k) and 4(2)(r) of the SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations. The SCL inter alia alleged gross negligence and recklessness in conducting an audit in accordance with the accounting standards and repeatedly deviating from the mandated course of audit especially in relation to items of significant materiality; and failure to consider the direct confirmations received from banks with respect to the figures of fixed deposits while blindly relying on the indirect confirmations received from SCSL which showed higher balances. It was also mentioned in the SCN that PWC International Ltd. had approved 11 partnership firms consisting of Chartered Accountants as their partners to use the name 'Price Waterhouse' in India and that the 11 firms had common branch offices located in New Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurgaon, Bhuvneshwar & Ahmedabad and there were several common partners in these firms. These firms shared resources, manpower, offices, revenues, etc. amongst themselves and, for this purpose, the 11 firms had entered into an agreement in 2000 for resource sharing. It was further stated that the members of the "engagement team" which worked on the audit of SCSL was on the payroll of Price Waterhouse Kolkata and Lovelock & Lewes Kolkata.

Two writ petitions were filed before the Bombay High Court, first by PW Bangalore and second by ten other CA firms along with their partners who were using the brand name Price Waterhouse in India, for quashing of the SCNs on the ground that SEBI lacked jurisdiction as it was encroaching upon the jurisdiction of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI)

The Bombay High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that it could not be said that SEBI at that stage, had no jurisdiction to issue a SCN simply because the appellants were professional Chartered Accountants. The Bombay High Court, however, set out the scope and extent of SEBI's power under sections 11 and 11B, read with regulation 11 of the PFUTP Regulations to act against Chartered Accountants and the circumstances under which SEBI could issue direction to Chartered Accountants acting in their professional capacity. The Bombay High Court emphatically held that the jurisdiction of SEBI in the instant case would depend upon the evidence which was available during the investigation and that if there was only some omission without any mens rea or connivance with anyone, in any manner, then SEBI could not issue any further direction.

Thereafter, the WTM held that failure to seek external confirmation of the bank balances, fixed deposits, failure to detect fake invoices without adopting the rigorous procedure mandated by AAS drew an inference of gross negligence and inference of involvement of appellants in the fudging of the accounts. This gross negligence amounted to an act of commission of a fraud for the purposes of SEBI - Act and SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations for which mens rea was not required to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt but could be based on a preponderance of probability.

The Chartered Accountant’s Certificate was a detailed certificate which had been considered in depth by the adjudicating authority. The appellant was engaged in the manufacture and selling of casting on specific rate of contract. The amount of service tax paid by the appellant was on the goods transport operator. That had not vitiated the contract price in any way. Further, the certificate issued by the professional, generally should not be challenged without having contradictory certificate from another professional. The Commissioner in his order had not relied on any contradictory certificate of another professional. In the absence of which, it was to be held that the appellant had made out a prima facie case for waiver of pre-deposit of amount of service tax. [Para 5]

K.K. Banerjee for the Appellant. A. Hore for the Respondent.

Management consultant’s service was a taxable service under section 65(48) during the relevant time and, therefore, the appellants were entitled to exemption under Notification No. 2/99-ST. As regards non-repatriation of foreign exchange, chartered accountant’s certificate had since been produced before the Tribunal, and since the same was not available before the adjudicating authority, the matter was to be remanded back to the adjudicating authority to look into the chartered accountant’s certificate and if nothing contrary was found the exemption should be extended to them. [Para 6(3)]

Prima facie, the Explanation added in amended Notification No. 15/2000 ST, dated 1-8-2002 purported to add to the tax liability of a PCA, Practising Company Secretary and Practising Cost Accountant, by providing that the exemption under Notification No. 59/98-ST would not be applicable to services provided by these professionals, which may fall in any other taxable services defined in clause (90) of section 65. The legislative intent was amply clear. Prima facie, taxable services under clause (90) of section 65 were sought to be excluded from the scope of exemption. Notification No. 59 of 1998-ST, on its face, did not include ‘management consultancy service’ in the list of taxable services of PCAs. Hence, for the period of dispute, apparently, the appellants were not liable to pay service tax on management consultant’s service rendered by them. They had made out prima facie case for waiver of pre-deposit and stay of recovery. [Para 2]

It is well settled through series of judgments of the High Courts and Supreme Court that writ jurisdiction of the High Courts in exercise of powers under article 226 of Constitution of India is extremely wide. If a jurisdictional error is pointed out or it is shown that an authority has acted wholly without jurisdiction, the Court can, without relegating the petitioner/assessee to the departmental or even statutory remedies, strike down exercise of such powers. Therefore, if it is found that the action of the TPO or a part of it which can be severed from the rest is wholly without jurisdiction, such order or part thereof is to be struck down even though statute provides certain appeal remedies to the aggrieved assessee.[Para 4]

It is indisputable that by virtue of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, in case of an international transaction, the TPO would have an authority to examine any international transaction which comes to his notice during the proceedings, whether a reference in this respect was made by the Assessing Officer or not and whether the assessee had reported such transaction under section 92E or not. However, in view of specific non-inclusion of the specified domestic transaction under the said sub-sections, in so far as the domestic transactions are concerned, the situation would be vastly different.[Para 13]

In plain terms, in absence of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, the TPO would get jurisdiction to examine a transaction whether it is international or specified domestic transaction, only upon reference being made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1) of section 92CA. Sub-section (2) of section 92CA provides that where a reference is made under sub-section (1), the TPO would serve a notice to the assessee requiring him to furnish details in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction referred to in sub-section (1). Thus, the jurisdiction of the TPO to issue a notice to the assessee would be in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction for which reference is made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). It is precisely for this reason that sub-sections (2A) and (2B) provide a deeming fiction where they provide that in case of an international transaction not referred to the TPO or an international transaction not reported by the assessee, which comes to his notice during the proceedings, the provision of the Chapter would apply as if such international transaction was one referred to in sub-section (1). In absence of this deeming fiction, it would not be open for the TPO to exercise the powers under the said chapter in relation to the transaction not referred to him. The reference to be made by the Assessing Officer is not an empty formality. Said reference has to be made only on approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. Legislature, requires the Assessing Officer to obtain an approval from senior Revenue Authority before a reference is made. Such requirement cannot be jettisoned by the TPO exercising suo motu jurisdiction over the transaction not reported to him.[Para 14]

Inescapable conclusion that is reached is that in relation to a specified domestic transaction, the TPO can under take transfer pricing study only in relation to those transactions which are referred to him under sub-section (1) of section 92C. Sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92C are confined to international transactions and with the aid of any interpretive process, the said provision cannot be applied to empower the TPO to examine any specified domestic transaction not referred to him by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). Any other view would be doing violence to the plain language of the statute.[Para 17]

The revenue is correct in pointing out that in the instant case, the assessee did not report such transaction at all and therefore, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to notice such transaction as specified domestic transaction. His reference, therefore, was necessarily confined to the reported transactions. The TPO noticed this anomaly, he proceeded to determine the arm's length price after full opportunity of hearing to the assessee.[Para 18]

. [Para 20.10]

The assessee submitted that under the provisions of section 92CA, the TPO has the authority to determine the arm's length price of the transactions undertaken by the assessee. The jurisdiction of the TPO cannot extend to decide the basis of charge/allocation of expenses. In the instant case, the TPO ought to have confined his jurisdiction in determining whether the cost allocated by AE is at arm's length or not. [Para 20.11] For the purposes of benchmarking the profits, the assessee considered TNMM as the most appropriate method and the PLI of the assessee is higher than that of the comparable companies. Recently, in the case of Durr India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2017] 78 taxmann.com 50 (Chennai - Trib.), the co-ordinate Bench of Tribunal held that allocation of cost partly on the basis of turnover and net profit cannot be considered as a factor to propose transfer pricing adjustment. Further, it was held that where the PLI of the Appellant under TNMM is at arm's length and it is not possible on the part of the department to identify a comparable, which is rendering similar services, the question of considering CUP method would not arise at all. [Para 20.12]

The assessee remitted service tax under reverse charge mechanism in respect of the said management fee. Further, the assessee has obtained a certificate under section 197 of the Act from the Deputy Director of Income Tax, International Taxation, Chennai in relation to the management fee. Recently, in the case of Aban Offshore Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2016] 76 taxmann.com 147 (Chennai - Trib.), the Co-ordinate bench has held that any payment which is systematically subject to deduction of tax at source cannot be said to be non-genuine. [Para 20.13]

However, for the Assessment year 2012-13, though the assessee was asked to explain as to how the cost of allocation for the management fee was done. The assessee had submitted vide letter dated 20-3-2017 a copy of application filed with Centre for Wind Energy Technology which was rejected by the DRP stating that no cognizance is required to be taken of these documents submitted after the hearing were completed. Regarding copy of correspondence with the AE for allocation of cost, it was observed by the DRP that no such document was furnished by the assessee. However, in instant proceedings the assessee filed additional evidences for the Assessment year 2012-13 and in-principle the contention of the assessee is correct regarding the allowability of management fees and there is no requirement of transfer pricing adjustment on this issue, subject to verification of availing of actual services and allocation of its cost to the assessee.

For the Assessment year 2011-12, it was stated that all the relevant evidences were already available with the Assessing Officer /TPO and on that basis, it is required to be verified with regard to availing actual services and its allocation of cost to the assessee. Accordingly, this ground relating to Management fees is remitted to the file of Assessing Officer for fresh consideration for both the assessment years and the Assessing Officer after going through the evidences filed by the assessee decide the issue fresh as indicated above. This ground is partly allowed for statistical purposes for both the assessment years. [Para 21]

■

Section 92CA(1) empowers the Assessing Officer to make reference to TPO for the computation of arm's length price of international transactions. Further, the TPO as defined in Explanation to section 92CA to be the person authorized by board to perform functions of Assessing Officer specified in section 92C. In sub-section (3) of section 144B, roles of Technical unit is clearly spelt out according to which, functions of technical unit includes assistance or advice on transfer pricing issues. During the course of performing such function, the technical unit can obtain advice from the TPO on the issue of determination of arm's length price of international transaction as they are expert in this field. Thus, the reference by technical unit to TPO is in accordance with the provisions of the Act and therefore, consequent orders passed are not barred by limitations. [Para 10]

AEs or VARs. The taxpayer shall ensure that it is made available to the TPO. All the relevant evidences including the specific document on the basis of which the services have been called upon for rendering and the basis on which the invoices have been raised needs to be made available to the revenue. The evidence placed on record in the absence of any explanation as to how the figures have been arrived at in the invoice cannot be said to be sufficient and cogent evidence. [Para 8] Needless to say that the TPO after a FAR analysis characterizing the assessee shall carry out the exercise of search for comparables in order to decide whether the transaction is at arms length or not. [Para 8]

In view of the above conclusion, appeal of the assessee is allowed for statistical purposes. [Para 9]

The Transfer Pricing Officer has failed to apply any method while determining the Arm's Length Price (ALP) at nil for Global Information System (GIS) services; for determining the ALP of payment made towards Management Service Fee (MSF) services by accepting 20 per cent thereon on adhoc basis and accepting 50 per cent for Multinational Client Co-ordination (MNC) services on adhoc basis thereon. The provisions of section 92C(1) mandates adoption of one of the prescribed method mentioned therein for determining the Arm's Length Price of the international transactions. [Para 8]

It is to be held that once a reference is received by the Transfer Pricing Officer under section 92CA(1) from the Assessing Officer, the Transfer Pricing Officer is required to determine the Arm's Length Price of the international transaction as per the provisions contained in sections 92C and 92CA read with relevant rules thereon. From the conjoint reading of the relevant sections and the relevant rules, it is observed that the duty of the Transfer Pricing Officer is restricted only to the determination of the Arm's Length Price of an international transaction between two related parties by applying any of the methods prescribed under section 92C read with Rule 10B of the Income-tax Rules. Thus, there is no provision made in the statute empowering the Transfer Pricing Officer for determining the Arm's Length Price on a particular international transaction on an estimation basis/adhoc basis. [Para 8.1]

Hence, the Transfer Pricing Officer is directed to delete the adjustment made to Arm's Length Price in respect of the aforesaid three services, viz., GIS services, MSF services and MNC services. [Para 8.3]

The statute has primarily conferred certain functions of Assessing Officer on TPO but that does not imply that jurisdiction of Assessing Officer to determine ALP gets excluded on reference being made by him to TPO for determining ALP. The substantive power of determining ALP vests in Assessing Officer as per section 92C. The reference to TPO as per section 92CA is only to facilitate proper determination of ALP. TPO has to simply pass an order determining the ALP and send the same to Assessing Officer who is ultimately authorized to pass the assessment order though in conformity with ALP determined by TPO. Thus, primarily section 92CA has been incorporated in order to ensure proper determination of ALP. The TPO primarily performs the functions which are to be performed by the Assessing Officer only. As per CBDT Instruction No. 3 of 2003, the Assessing Officer can make a valid reference to the TPO only if the correct value of international transaction exceeds Rs. 5 crores. Thus, the services of office of TPO can be utilized by Assessing Officer in such cases where revenue effect is likely to be considerable. This is primarily a legislative in-built check on the quasi judicial functions to be performed by Assessing Officer. For the purposes of performance of all or any of the functions of an Assessing Officer, the TPO is considered at par with an Assessing Officer. But essentially it is the function of Assessing Officer only to determine the ALP. Therefore, there is no infirmity in the ALP being determined by the Assessing Officer as per section 92C(3) even after making a reference to TPO under section 92CA which was returned by TPO without determining the ALP. [Para 15]

■

As per the provisions of section 92CA, once a matter is falling in the jurisdiction of the TPO {apparently only for determining the arm’s length price (ALP) by applying appropriate method}, there is no authority vested with the TPO for examining the matter with reference to section 37. [Para 6]

■

Once a matter is referred to the TPO by the Assessing Officer ("AO") to determine the ALP of an international transaction or specified domestic transaction ("SDT") (collectively referred to as "covered transactions") entered into by the taxpayer during the given financial year under review, he would then examine the facts and circumstances surrounding the covered transactions. Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) is an integral part of the whole assessment proceedings where international transaction or specified domestic transaction (“SDT”) is involved. Although role of the TPO is, certainly limited upto the “Covered Transactions” only. [Para 7]

■

The intention of the legislature is examination of covered transaction by a specific authority established solely for those transactions. On this view is further fortified by the fact that, report of the TPO on specific transactions are binding in nature on jurisdictional AO and he can’t have any deviation from the same. In that case, once report of TPO is limited upto determination of ALP only, a challenge by the assessee can be there that the report of TPO is meant for determination of ALP only and not beyond. [Para 8]

■

No exercise relating to determination of ALP with reference to method adopted by the assessee along with records submitted by him has been carried out. Rather, his questionnaire is there on record which he issued keeping in view the provisions of section 37 of the Act, which certainly is not in his domain. The whole order is silent on the working of ALP and rather determined the benchmarking value at Rs. NIL. This is not possible from any angle of accounting or the intention of the statute. [Para 9]

■

In view of the above, there is force in the grounds taken by the assessee. In these terms Grounds raised by the assessee are allowed and matter is restored back to the file of TPO for determination of ALP as per the scheme of law after giving a reasonable opportunity to the assessee to present its transfer pricing study report. [Para 10]

It is primarily the duty of the Assessing Officer to compute the arm's length price in relation to an international transaction in accordance with the most appropriate method specified in section 92C(1). However, where the Assessing Officer, requires, the arm's length price to be computed by a specialist, a reference may be made to the Transfer Pricing Officer. [Para 16]

A plain reading of section 92CA makes it clear that the Assessing Officer, if he considers it necessary or expedient so to do, may, with the previous approval of the Commissioner, refer the computation of the arm's length price in relation to an international transaction under section 92C to the Transfer Pricing Officer. At this juncture, it is primarily the duty of the Assessing Officer to compute any income arising from an international transaction having regard to the arm's length price. He may determine the arm's length price of an international transaction himself or, if he feels that it is necessary or expedient so to do, he may seek the approval of the Commissioner and, thereafter, refer the computation of the arm's length price in respect of an international transaction to the Transfer Pricing Officer. This makes it clear that it is the Assessing Officer who has to determine, first of all, whether a transaction is an international transaction under section 92B. Secondly, if it is an international transaction in his view, he has to proceed to determine the arm's length price in terms of section 92C. However, if, for any reason, he feels that it is necessary or expedient so to do, he may seek the approval of the Commissioner and then refer the computation of the arm's length price in relation to the said international transaction to the Transfer Pricing Officer. The role of the Transfer Pricing Officer, as indicated in section 92CA, is restricted to determine the arm's length price in relation to the international transaction which has been referred to him by the Assessing Officer and such computation of the arm's length price in relation to the said international transaction has to be done in terms of section 92C. It is not within the domain of the Transfer Pricing Officer to determine whether a particular transaction, which has come to his notice, but which has not been referred to him, is or is not an international transaction and then to go on and determine the arm's length price thereof. This is in the exclusive jurisdiction of the Assessing Officer. It ought to be pointed out that these views are on the basis of the provisions of section 92CA, as applicable to the assessment year 2006-07, that is, prior to the introduction of sub-section (2A) of section 92CA by virtue of the Finance Act, 2011 with effect from 01.06.2011. Insofar as the present appeal is concerned, section 92CA would have to be read without sub-section (2A). Sub-section (2A) cannot have retrospective effect inasmuch as it deals with the jurisdiction of the Transfer Pricing Officer and, therefore, sub-section (2A) cannot be regarded as being a mere procedural provision. [Para 17]

In the instant case there is nothing in the statute to indicate that sub-section (2A) was introduced in a manner so as to operate with retrospective effect. Sub-section (2A) expands the jurisdiction of the Transfer Pricing Officer by empowering him to determine the arm's length price of any international transaction other than an international transaction referred to him by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1) of section 92CA. This is clearly an expansion of the jurisdiction of the Transfer Pricing Officer and, therefore, sub-section (2A) can only have prospective effect from 01.06.2011 and would have no application to the present appeal which is in respect of the assessment year 2006-07. [Para 20]

A. Emergence of concept of service tax :

While on the manufacture of goods, tax is levied in the name of excise duty and on sale of goods tax is levied in the name of sales tax, there are number of activities, falling in the category of 'service sector' which constitute 40 per cent of National GDP, which are not subjected to tax. This has kept a number of activities, which in fact are an important part of the national economy, outside the tax net. It is of course true that the persons rendering such services are subjected to income-tax covered by Entry 83 in List I of Schedule VII of the Constitution, but that by itself is not sufficient as the persons manufacturing goods pay excise duty on the manufacture of goods and pay sales tax on sale of goods and are also liable to pay income-tax on the income earned by them. The professionals rendering services for remuneration and similarly other persons rendering service in a larger number of fields for remuneration can only be subjected to professional tax by the State Legislature by virtue of Entry 60 in List II but subject to the maximum limit of Rs. 2,500 per annum in view of the provisions of article 276(2) of the Constitution of India. Such tax is on profession/trade/calling/employment irrespective of the fact whether they were earning any income or not. In these circumstances, the Parliament decided to tax the services being rendered by the professionals and by other trades and callings. Thus, the service tax is absolutely distinct and separate from the tax on profession/trade/calling/employment. [Para 4]

B. Legislative history :

The Government of India has notified service tax on 12 new services added in the service tax net by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998, vide notification dated 7-10-1998. The liability has been made effective from 16-10-1998. Further, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 93, the Central Government had exempted in the public interest the taxable services other than that of auditing and accounting provided by a practising chartered accountant in his professional capacity to a client. Vide notification dated 16-10-1998 certain exemptions have been given to the Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost and Works Accountants. Thus, the net result was that the service tax was leviable on chartered accountants in relation to accounting, auditing and certification services provided by them, in their professional capacity. As section 12B of Central Excise Act, 1944 has been made applicable in relation to the impugned service tax, the direct legal consequence is that there is a presumption that service tax has been passed on to the customer, who is the beneficiary of the service, and that is the reason why the service tax is levied on the service provider himself. It is open to the service provider to pass on the tax to the beneficiary of the service and reimburse himself. Thus, it is evident that the service provider does not pay the tax and the tax falls on the service receiver. [Para 6]

C. Legislative competence :

The subject-matter of taxation available to the Parliament is enumerated in Entries 80 to 97 of List I. Entries 45 to 66 of List II are available to the State Legislature. Under article 246(1), the Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters and that includes the power to impose tax enumerated in List I. Where the case does not fall either in the State List or the Concurrent List, the Parliament has residuary power under Entry 97 of List I. [Para 7]

The Parliament has power to levy tax on the manufacture of goods as per Entry 84 in the Union List, and also to levy tax on the services being rendered by a professional. Thus, if the tax on a trade or calling would also include the power to tax the transactions being entered into by a person carrying on any trade or calling, there would not have been a separate entry to confer the power to levy tax on sale of goods. A trader carrying on his business of buying and selling goods and subjected to tax under Entry 60 in the State List is also liable to pay taxes on the sale or purchase of goods under Entry 54 in the State List. Thus, it is evident that the two taxes are separate and distinct and they cannot be merged merely because a person liable to pay tax under Entry 60 in the State List and also liable to collect and pay tax on sale of goods under entry 54 in the said list is one and the same person in both the cases. [Para 8]

A chartered accountant or an architect who is paying professional tax but not providing any service though he chooses to be on the roll of Architects or the chartered accountants, would not be required to pay the service tax. [Para 11]

The TPO has alleged that the assessee failed to furnish any evidence to substantiate its claim that the payment is made to the AE for availing Information System Services, however, the material on record reveal that the assessee has not only undertaken a benchmarking process for determining the arm's length price of the transaction in the transfer pricing study report which was filed before the TPO, but, other relevant and necessary documents like copy of the agreement, invoices raised, certificate from independent Chartered Accountant Firm, (KPMG), details of users were also furnished before the TPO. Therefore, the allegation of the TPO that the assessee has not furnished the necessary details is not totally correct. In any case of the matter, non-furnishing of certain documentary evidences, as alleged by the TPO does not empower him to embark upon determining the arm's length price of the international transaction on estimation basis. Further, a reading of the TPO's, order makes it clear that his finding on the issue is contradictory. On the one hand, he has observed that the assessee has failed all the three tests, including, whether the services have actually been provided, on the other hand, he has accepted that the AE has provided the software. Thus, ultimately, what the TPO disbelieves is the quantum of payment. Accordingly, he has proceeded to estimate the price of the services rendered by the AE at Rs. 1,62,05,000. Though, the TPO has observed that he has applied CUP method for determining the arm's length price, however, he has not brought on record even a single comparable to support the arm's length price determined by him even on estimate basis. The estimation of service charges on so-called man hour basis is without any supporting material. Similarly, the estimation of cost of software was without any basis. Thus, it is very much clear that the determination of arm's length price by the TPO is not as per any one of the methods prescribed under section 92C read with rule 10B. Such determination of arm's length price on ad hoc/estimation basis is not permissible under the scheme of the Act as the Transfer Pricing Officer is duty bound to determine the arm's length price by following any one of the most appropriate method prescribed under the statute. It is relevant to observe, that the DRP has approved the determination of the arm's length price by the TPO without properly appreciating the implication of the relevant statutory provisions. As regards the observations of the DRP regarding the report of the KPMG, it is necessary to observe that the KPMG report is not an audit report but was furnished by the assessee to support the attribution of cost. Therefore, it cannot be said that it is a qualified report. It is further relevant to observe, the material that submitted indicates that the cost of the software has been allocated to 40 group companies across the globe who are using the software and related services and assessee's share in cost allocation works out to 2.3 per cent. Moreover, when the TPO himself agrees that the AE has provided software and certain services, there is no reason for not accepting the payment made to the AE to be at arm's length in the absence of any contrary evidence brought on record and by simply applying the benefit test. If the TPO did not agree to the arm's length price shown by the assessee is it open for him to determine the arm's length price by applying one of the most appropriate methods being backed by supporting material. Without complying to the statutory provisions, the TPO certainly cannot determine the arm's length price on ad hoc/estimation basis. Accordingly, the adjustment made to the arm's length price of payment made towards availing information system services from AE was deleted. [Para 21]

Under section 92CA(1) where any person being the assessee has entered into an international transaction in any previous year, and the Assessing Officer considers it necessary or expedient to do so, he may, with the previous approval of the Commissioner refer the computation of arm's length price in relation to the said international transaction under section 92C to the Transfer Pricing Officer. Under section 92CA(2) where a reference is made under sub-section (1) of section 92CA, the Transfer Pricing Officer shall serve a notice on the assessee requiring him to produce or cause to be produced on a date to be specified therein, any evidence on which the assessee may rely in support of computation made by him of the arm's length price in relation to international transactions referred to in sub-section (1). On plain reading of provisions of sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of section 92CA it is clear that the TPO has to compute the arm's length price in relation to the international transactions referred to him by the Assessing Officer. Sub-section (2A) to section 92CA was inserted by Finance Act, 2011 with effect from 1-6-2011, according to which where any other international transaction [other than an international transaction referred under sub-section (1)] comes to the notice of TPO during the course of the proceedings before him, the provisions of this chapter shall apply as if such international transaction is an international transaction referred to him under sub-section (1). Therefore, prior to 1-6-2011 the TPO could not have selected any transaction suo motu for computation of arm's length price. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer made reference under section 92CA(1) in respect of three international transactions and the TPO in his order dated 17-3-2005 had found those international transactions at arm's length. However he had recommended addition of Rs. 1,55,52,470 in respect of advertising expenses incurred by the assessee which was not referred to him by the Assessing Officer. Therefore, the computation of arm's length price in respect of advertising expenses is not in accordance with the provisions of section 92CA(1). The TPO can suggest adjustment in international transaction entered into by an assessee with its associate enterprises, which were sent to him for computation of arm's length price by the Assessing Officer. Suo motu, he cannot take cognizance of any international transaction for suggesting adjustment in arm's length price. [Para 7]

Thus, TPO cannot take cognizance suo motu of any international transaction for computation of arm's length price under section 92C. The provisions of section 92CA(2A) are prospective in nature and will not apply for the assessment year under consideration i.e. , assessment year 2002-03. The Assessing Officer is directed to delete the addition of Rs. 1,55,52,470, made on the basis of the report of the TPO. [Para 10]

The jurisdiction High Court in the case of CIT v. Cushman & Wakefield (India) (P.) Ltd. [2014] 367 ITR 730/46 taxmann.com 317 (Delhi) held that TPO cannot determine arm's length price of the payments made by the assessee to its AE at 'NIL' for the reason that assessee did not derive any benefit from services rendered by AE. [Para 11]

The High Court categorically held that the TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine the arm's length price (ALP) and not to determine whether there is a service from which assessee has derived benefit or not. The Court held that the exercise to determine whether assessee had derived any benefit or not from payment of such management fee is to be examined by the Assessing Officer and appropriate disallowance under section 37 is called for.

In the instant case, the TPO had determined the ALP of payment of management fees at 'NIL' by holding that the assessee did not derive any benefit from services rendered by the AE. Therefore, keeping in view the dictum laid down by the judgment of the jurisdictional High Court, necessarily Assessing Officer has to determine whether the assessee has derived any benefit from payment of professional fees and if any benefit had derived, whether such payment is commensurate to comparable transaction has to be examined by the TPO.

For the above said purpose, the Transfer Pricing issue is restored to Assessing Officer/TPO for de novo consideration. [Para 12]

It could be noticed from the certificate of the chartered accountant that the chartered accountant before issuing certificate had verified the entire books of account and had come to a categorical conclusion that neither the assessee had passed on burden of service tax to the customers nor had it recovered the amount from the transporters. The certificate also categorically stated that the assessee had borne the incidence of service tax. The Commissioner (Appeals) after checking the records was satisfied with the evidences produced before him as regards the non-passing of the incidence of service tax by the assessee to its customers. The revenue in its appeal had not produced any contrary evidence to the said findings nor there was any challenge to the chartered accountants Certificate. [Para 2]

Accordingly, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the impugned order was correct and legal and did not require any interference. The appeal filed by the revenue was to be dismissed. [Para 3]

The TPO himself mentioned in his order that the assessee performed arm's length analysis in respect of all the international transactions entered into by it with its associated enterprises under section 92C read with rules 10B and 10C and nothing was found in the TPO's order which was indicative of the existence of any of the circumstances prescribed under clauses (a) to (d) of section 92C (3) which necessitate intervention of the Assessing Officer/TPO for determination of arm's length price. But the TPO determined the arm's length price of the international transactions under review at 'NIL' value, based on his main allegation that the benefits claimed to have been received by the assessee from NP under the agreement would not be ones for which an independent enterprise would be willing to pay. [Para 19]

In the case of McCann Erickson India (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2012] 24 taxmann.com 21 (Delhi) the Delhi Tribunal has held that it is only a particular business expert who can evaluate the true intrinsic and creative value of intra-group services and in any case, the value of these services cannot be taken at nil. However, in the instant case, the TPO judged the reasonableness of the aforesaid intra-group service charge and computed the arm's length price of the international transactions under review at 'NIL' value based on his main allegation that the benefits claimed to have been received by the assessee from NP under the aforesaid agreement would not be ones for which an independent enterprise would be willing to pay. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the valuation of the intra-group services made by the TPO at 'NIL' value. [Para 22]

In the instant case, TPO computed the arm's length price of intra-group services received by assessee from NP under the aforesaid agreements at 'nil' value without applying any of the transfer pricing methodologies prescribed under section 92C read with rules 10B and 10C of the Rules. Accordingly, the action of the TPO in arriving at the arm's length price of the relevant international transactions at 'nil' value without application of any transfer pricing methodology, was without any basis and, hence, was not sustainable. In the instant case, TPO was authorised to determine, by order in writing, the arm's length price of an international transaction in accordance with section 92C(3). As per the provision of sub-section (1) of section 37, the Assessing Officer is authorized to examine whether an expenditure (not being expenditure of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 and not being in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee) is incurred by an assessee wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business in the matter of computation of the income chargeable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'.

The Assessing Officer could, therefore, determine under section 37 that the expenditure claimed was not for the benefit of the business, and thus, disallow that amount, this does not restrict or in any way bypass the functions of the TPO. The aforesaid conclusion is also in line with latest change made in section 92CA by the Legislature through the Finance Act, 2007. [Para 52] Now words ‘having regard to’ have been replaced by words ‘in conformity with’. So now the Assessing Officer after introduction of section 92CA(4) with effect from 1-6-2007 is required to pass assessment order in conformity with the order of the TPO determining ALP .
