Service tax is a tax on services and not on a tax on the service provider or on the professionals providing the services. This fact was also pronounced by various Courts while deciding the constitutional validity of the service tax on various services.

The exemption notification was also issued on the same consideration because the field of providing this service is open for various other professionals and if getting same type of services from a particular professional, say chartered accountants, attracts service tax then this has two side effects. One is that the other professional will have the upper hand compared to the chartered accountants only because they need not to pay service tax. Introduction

Recent Exemption to Chartered Accountants : One More Reconsideration Needed

The withdrawal of exemption Notification No.59/ 98-Service Tax, dated 16-10-1998 w.e.f. 1-3-2006 resulted in bringing all services rendered by practicing CAs, CWAs and CSs into the service tax net. The idea behind the exemption was to tax these professionals only on the services in which they have monopoly (accounting, auditing, cost audit, secretarial audit) and to exempt other services rendered by them (filing of returns, tax consultancy, representation services) till other professionals (e.g. Advocates) rendering these services were brought under the net. The withdrawal of exemption Notification 59/98 attracted strong reactions and representations were made to the Central Government. The Central Government, in principle, has accepted the representations of ICAI, ICWAI and ICSI that certain specified services rendered by these professionals should be exempted from service tax till the other professionals (e.g. Advocates) rendering these services are also brought into the service tax net. This can be seen from the Government’s Press Note. Therefore, based on these considerations (i.e., to maintain a level playing field), the Central Government has by Notification No.25/2006, dated 13-7-2006 exempted representation services (i.e. services relating to representation before statutory authorities) rendered by these professionals from service tax. The author argues that the logic for exempting representation services applies equally to tax consultancy services, filing of tax returns which constitute the main source of income for many CAs in non-metros and small cities and makes a passionate plea for exempting tax consultancy services and filing of tax returns also from service tax.

SERVICE TAX ON CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT’S SERVICES

This article is a comprehensive analysis of leviability of service tax on Chartered Accountant’s Services.

Introduction

1. Service tax has been imposed on practising chartered accountant’s services with effect from October 16, 1998 vide Notification No. 53/98-ST, dated October 7, 1998. The gross amount charged by a practising chartered accountant from the client, in professional capacity, is chargeable to service tax.

Meaning of-Practising Chartered Accountant

2. Section 65(83) defines ‘practising chartered accountant’ as under—

‘practising chartered accountant’ means a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and is holding a certificate of practice granted under the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 (38 of 1949) and includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy.

As per section 65(83), a practising chartered accountant is a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, New Delhi and holds a certificate of practice under the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and also includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy. Thus, both associate and fellow members of the Institute are covered. It would also cover individuals as well as firms and persons holding full-time as well as part-time certificate of practice.

According to Webster’s Dictionary, a professional means ‘calling requiring specialised knowledge and often long intensive academic preparation; calling, vocation or employment’. The services should be rendered in this capacity using this skill and knowledge.

‘In any manner’ would mean directly or indirectly, personally or otherwise or through his staff members or through computer aid or other device or manually.

To be treated as a practising chartered accountant, following basic tests must be satisfied—

(i)He must be a person;

(ii)He must be a member (whether associate or fellow) of the Institute to which he belongs (ICAI);

(iii)He must hold a certificate of practice granted by the Institute;

(iv)In case of a firm of the chartered accountants, it must be a concern engaged in rendering services in the field of the chartered accountancy.

Legal position

3. In All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [2007] 10 STT 166 (SC), the Apex Court has settled the levy of service tax on the chartered accountants, cost accountants, and architects, by holding that the Parliament of India has the legislative competence to levy service tax on the professional services rendered by the chartered accountants, the cost accountants, and architects and that professional tax and service tax operate on different spheres.

The Apex Court dealt with the constitutional status of levy of service tax and the legislative competence of the Parliament to impose service tax under article 246(1) and Entry 97 of List-I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India having regard to Entry 60 in List-II of Seventh Schedule (i.e., professional tax). The major findings of the Apex Court in the instant case are as follows—

u As an economic concept, there is no distinction between the consumption of goods and service as both satisfy human needs and this economic concept is based on the legal principle of equivalence.

u Service tax is a VAT which, in turn, is a general tax which applies to all commercial activities involving production of goods and provision of services.

u VAT is a consumption tax as it is borne by the client.

u Applying the principle of equivalence, there is no difference between production or manufacture of saleable goods and production of marketable/saleable services in the form of an activity undertaken by the service provider for consideration, which correspondingly stands consumed by the service receiver. It is this principle of equivalence which is in-built into the concept of service tax, which has received legal support in the form of Finance Act, 1994.

u Service tax is VAT which, in turn, is both a general tax as well as destination based consumption tax leviable on services provided within the country.

u A new charge by way of service tax or tax on service came to be levied statutorily by the Finance Act, 1994, which has subsequently attained Constitutional status by virtue of the Constitution (Eighty-eighth Amendment) Act, 2003.

SERVICE TAX LEVY ON CHARTERED ACCOUNTANTS - UNCONSTITUTIONAL, ILLEGAL, INVALID AND UNWARRANTED

‘Service tax’ was first introduced in India by the Finance Act, 1994, on a few services and subsequently extended to several other services by the relevant Finance Acts. The Finance Act, 1998 brought the services rendered by a chartered accountant within the purview of service tax. In this article, the author attacks the levy of service tax at its very root by arguing that under the Constitution of India, the Parliament has no power to enact service tax legislation and, hence, the levy in question is lacking in constitutional validity. The author also specifically questions the extension of the levy to the profession of chartered accountancy, inter alia, on the ground that the exercise of profession by a chartered accountant does not amount to rendering of ‘service’ - EDITOR

Introduction

1. The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech for the year 1998-99 has observed in para 169 as hereunder:

"169. In the last budget, a number of services were added in the tax net. These included the service rendered on transportation of goods by road. The House is aware that it led to widespread resistance and protests. As a result, this service tax was virtually kept in abeyance and rightly so. I have decided to abolish the service tax on transportation of goods by road. I have also decided to abolish the service tax payable by outdoor caterers and pandal contractors. However, I have proposed service tax on some new services. These are services provided by: Architects, Interior decorators, Management Consultants, Chartered Accountants, Cost Accountants, Company Secretaries, Private security services, Real estate agents and real estate consultants, Market research agencies, Credit rating agencies, Underwriting agencies, Slaughter houses using mechanised means for the large animals.

We will examine how in respect of certain segments liable to Service Tax, the manner and mode of payment could be further simplified to improve compliance. These new service taxes will yield Rs. 220 crore in a full year."

With a view to effecting the aforesaid policy decision, the Finance Bill (No. 2) of 1998 by Chapter VI thereof and clause 129 has effected several ancillary and consequential amendments in the Finance Act, 1994, section 65, etc.

Section 116 of the Finance Act, 1998 has provided for a levy of service tax at 5 per cent on services rendered by practising chartered accountants, cost accountants and company secretaries. The said ‘service tax’ has been brought into effect with effect from October 16, 1998. A further notification issued by the Revenue Department provides that the taxable services rendered to a client by a practising Chartered Accountant or a company secretary or cost accountant which will attract service tax include: accounting and auditing or cost accounting or secretarial auditing or verification of declarations in prescribed forms under section 149 of the Companies Act, 1956 or signing of annual return of listed companies under section 161 of the Companies Act or certification requirements of Schedule XIII to the Companies Act, or certification of documents to be filed with Registrar of Companies or certification in Form No. 1 under the Companies Unpaid Dividend Rules, 1978 or certification of documents under Export and Import Policy (1997-2002) or Certification for exchange control purposes under FERA 1973 or certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets as per rule 8A(7) of the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957. ♦ Section 92E refers to "an accountant" which means a Chartered Accountant as defined in Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.

♦ However, audit under section 92E can be done by a firm of Chartered Accountants also.

Extending the above logic of the Guidance Note further, a view can be taken that w.e.f. 1-3-2011 [date on which Chartered Accountants (Amendment) Act, 2011 came into force] LLPs of CAs in practice/CAs in practice with other prescribed professionals can be appointed for transfer pricing audit u/s 92E. CBDT/ICAI needs to clarify this.

Can audit under section 92E be conducted by an employee of assessee-client?

In Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 169 Taxman 328 (SC), the Supreme Court held that "An auditor is a professional person". He has to function independently. He is not an employee of the assessee.

Is it necessary that tax audit under section 92E shall be a CA in full-time practice?

Yes. At its 242nd meeting, the Council of ICAI has decided that any member in part-time practice (i.e. a member who is holding certificate of practice and also engaged in any other business/occupation) shall not be entitled to perform attest functions. Therefore, a CA in part-time practice cannot be appointed as auditor under section 92E.

In case of companies, is it necessary that audit u/s 92E be conducted by statutory auditor?

No. In case of companies, it can be done by the statutory auditor of the company appointed under section 224 of the Companies Act, 1956 or by any other CA in practice or firm of CAs. This is because section 92E does not require that only the statutory auditor should perform the audit under section 92E.

Whether a CA or firm of CAs appointed as tax consultants can conduct audit u/s 92E?

A CA/firm of CAs who are appointed as tax consultants may be appointed as auditor under section 92E. [ICAI's Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing]

Can a CA or CA firm who is internal auditor of assessee can also be auditor u/s 92E?

No. Internal auditor cannot give audit report u/s 92E. [ICAI's Code of Ethics]

Is there any limit on the number of audits under section 92E which a CA/CA firm can accept?

No. There is no limit on number of audits u/s 92E which CA/CA firm can accept.

Is there any minimum fee to be charged by CA firms for Tax audits?

No. Chapter XII of the Council General Guidelines has been omitted with effect from 7-6-2011. Hence, no minimum fee stipulated for audits at the moment.

Scope of audit under section 92E

What are the matters covered by scope of the audit u/s 92E?

It covers the following:

♦ Examination of only those accounts and records of the assessee which relate to international transactions/SDTs entered into by him during the previous year under audit.

♦ Ascertaining and reporting whether the assessee has maintained proper information and documentations prescribed in respect of international transactions entered into by him.

The Government clarified the same through the Circular F.No. 177/5/2001-CX. 4, dated 26-2-2002. It was clarified that the certificates given under authority of any statute/international protocol/code/convention, cannot be considered to be a consultancy job. It is then to be examined whether this activity can come under the purview of advice or technical assistance. An advice is generally understood to be optional in nature and has no statutory force. It is up to the client to accept the advice or not. The activity of certification will, therefore, not fall under the category of advice. As regards ‘technical assistance’, it is observed that an assistance is normally for the purpose of achieving a particular aim or result. A certificate given by, say, the Boiler Inspector under the Factories Act, 1948, about the safety of a boiler, cannot be considered to be ‘assistance’ to the person using the said boiler in his factory. To issue certificates under the authority of any statute, it will obviously be necessary for the certifying agency to conduct some survey/inspection. Thus, the survey/inspection by an agency for the purposes of issuing certificates by the same agency under an authority of law, will also not amount to consultancy advice or technical assistance. If however, the shipping company gets the ship surveyed or inspected by another agency, before taking it for certification by an authorised agency, only then can it be said that the first agency is providing some technical assistance or advice. It will, therefore, be essential to examine each activity of a service provider on the basis of facts, the terms of agreement between the assessee and the clients and the corresponding provision of Indian or International statute/convention/protocol, or code, to determine whether the certificate being given is under the authority of any such statute, convention protocol or code. CBE&C not charitable about ‘Charitable’

11. As per section 65(25a ),definition of "club or association" does not include— (iii) any person or body of persons engaged in any activity having objectives which are in the nature of public service and are of a charitable, religious or political nature.

‘Charitable’ means ‘generous in giving to those in need’ or ‘of, or relating to, or connected with a charity or charities’. ‘Charity’ means giving voluntarily to those in need, alms-giving’ – Concise Oxford Dictionary.

Thus, the word ‘charity’ has narrow meaning in dictionary. However, the word has acquired a technical meaning in law, which is wide.

As per section 2 of Charitable Endowments Act, 1890, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief to poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general public utility, but does not include a purpose which relates exclusively to religious teaching or worship. As per section 2(15) of Income-tax Act, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief of the poor, education, medical relief, and the advancement of any other object of general public utility.

Thus, any object of ‘general public utility’ will be a ‘charitable purpose’. Hence, the wide meaning should apply and not narrow dictionary meaning. However, department is of the view that narrow meaning should apply – CBE&C, vide Circular No. 84/2/2006-ST dated 19-9-2006.

The Bench thus held that the liability to pay service tax to the Government in such a case is on the prime consultant, who was IRCON in the instant case and not on the sub-consultant, who was the appellant.

In this case, the Bangalore Asstt. Commissioner did not follow Trade Notice No. 53-C.E. (Service Tax)/97, dated 4-7-1997, issued by the Commissioner of Central Excise, New Delhi, uttering that services should be rendered to a client directly and not in the capacity of a sub-consultant/associate consultant to the prime consultant.

2.4 Mandap keeper Service- third party receipts - The Mumbai CESTAT in C.K.P. Mandal v. CCE [2006] 5 STT 1, in relation to service provided by mandap keeper to the client, held that the valuation of taxable service shall be gross amount charged by such mandap keeper from the client for the use of mandap including the facilities provided to the client. In the instant case, the mandap keeper received some consideration from caterers for giving them monopoly rights for rendering services of catering and decoration to the hirer of the mandap. The Bench held that such amount would not be chargeable to service tax since there was no relationship of ‘mandap keeper’ and the ‘client’ between the appellant and Saideep Caterer, which was a third party.

The Bench thus held that the hirer is the person who hires the mandap for organizing any official, social or business function. More particularly, in the context of use of the phrase ‘in relation to’ in sub-clause (m) of 65(90), the Bench commented that howsoever, the expansive, wide and comprehensive meaning one may give to the expression ‘in relation to’ in sub-clause (m), the consideration received by the appellant from Saideep Caterers for giving them exclusive and monopoly rights for rendering the services of catering and decoration to the hirer of the appellant’ would not be covered by ‘taxable service’ as defined in section.

2.5 Chartered Accountant Services - professional service or professional capacity - In K. Surendra Nayak, In re 2006 (4) STR 170 (Commr. Appl.), the chartered accountant had been engaged to render certain services, namely, opening ledger accounts, preparation of monthly bills, preparation of skeleton bills, accounting of demands and recoveries, maintenance of daily abstracts and tallying, preparation and issue of disconnection lists to field staff and preparation of union MIS and consolidated DCB statements. The appellant claimed that the services provided were not provided by him in his professional capacity as a practising chartered accountant and that the service actually done was limited to maintaining ledger accounts of billing related activity, which did not amount to professional accounting service of a practising chartered accountant. The appellant claimed alternative classification under Business Support Services, which came into existence only in 2006.

The method chosen by the assessee to justify his declared price to be arm’s length price should be ‘the Most Appropriate Method (MAP) under section 92C(2)’, since proviso to section 92C recognises that there may be circumstances, where there can be more than one appropriate method in which case arithmetical means of the arm’s length price so arrived at can be taken, subject to variation of 5 per cent at the option of the assessee. Section 92E requires certification by way of a report from a chartered accountant in the prescribed Form 3CEB. It is understood that chartered accountant is not responsible for the choice of the method but only for the working on the basis of which the choice is made by the assessee. In the result, the choice is left to the assessee with no requirement on the part of the chartered accountant to certify that the method chosen is the MAP. This is a glaring defect, since the assessee is not likely to have the necessary expertise. Again, column 13 of the Form requires certification of the arm’s length price as computed by the assessee on the single method chosen by him and does not provide for arithmetical means of more than one method, so as to require certification of application of two methods, where more than one arm’s length price is available with option of the assessee to vary the same by 5 per cent. The result is that, the Assessing Officer, it can be said, does not get all the assistance that may be expected from such a certificate.

Not surprisingly, the choice of the method is a disputed issue in almost every case. In the decision of the Special Bench in Aztec Software Technology Services Ltd.’s case (supra ), it was pointed out that the selection of the MAP depends on the nature of transactions or availability of relevant data and the possibility of making the appropriate adjustment from the available data to arrive at arm’s length price on a reasonable basis.

COST PLUS v . TNMM METHOD - AZTEC SOFTWARE TECHNOLOGY SERVICES LTD.’S CASE

6. In the case before the Special Bench in Aztec Software & Technology Services Ltd. (supra), the assessee had chosen CPM and TNMM with a mark-up of 5 per cent for on-site software development services and 10 per cent for marketing services as provided in the agreement. The TPO, however, considered CUP method as the most suitable one. But then, the problem was in selecting comparable cases for application of this method.

There is considerable discussion as to the computation with reference to each of the methods by the Special Bench. Adoption of Nasscom average hourly rate, it was found, does not meet the requirement of CUP method to justify the mark-up rate over the assessee’s cost. The Special Bench pointed out OECD Guidelines on International Transfer Pricing, 2006, which required adjustments for

-Differences in the quality of the products;

-Differences in the geographic markets;

-Differences in the level of the market; and

-Differences in the amount and type of intangible property involved.

The Special Bench had set out the guidelines and set aside the assessment, while pointing out, that the burden of proof vested on the assessee to prove the declared price to be the arm’s length price. The Special Bench after referring to OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines would not consider TNMM as the most appropriate method. For purposes of Bench marking under this method, it was pointed out that it is necessary to arrive at net margin earned by comparable uncontrolled transaction, so as to require the data necessary for CUP method. The manner in which net margin was worked out was also faulted as it took into consideration only the net margin earned by the associated enterprise on its entire business activities. The cases chosen by the Assessing Officer for comparability was also found to be not completely reliable. Incidentally, it was found that the RPM was not applicable, since the assessee was not a reseller of goods or services. The CPM requires verification of cost. PSM was rejected, because it was not a case of ‘unique intangibles or multiple inseparable transactions’ apart from the fact that this method is rarely used. TNM method, on the other hand, requires consideration of the specified transactions and not overall business. It is under these circumstances, that the matter was restored to the Assessing Officer on the basis of the guidance thus offered.

But then, these two cases could probably be reconciled in the light of the nature of the payments and the data available, which are equally relevant. The Supreme Court in Morgan Stanley & Co. Section 65(105)(j) - Clearing and Forwarding Agent’s Services - Whether service receiver can deduct amount of service tax from service provider’s bill

6.2 Facts The respondent, a transport contractor, entered into a contract with the appellant for handling of its materials. During the pendency of the said contract, section 65 was substituted by section 88 whereby 5 per cent service tax was introduced on various services including ‘clearing and forwarding (C&F) agent’. The appellant, consequently, deducted 5 per cent service tax from the respondent’s bills on the assumption that the respondent was a C&F agent from 31-10-1997 in spite of respondent’s objections. On reference, the sole arbitrator dismissed the respondent’s objection. On petition filed by the respondent, the Single Judge of the High Court allowed the same by setting aside the impugned award.

Decision of Bombay High Court:

u The High Court held that the constitutional validity with regard to the extension of service tax in view of the amendment to the Finance Act, 2000, section 116(a) and section 65(6) to treat the recipients of the services as an assessee in case of services rendered by goods transport operators and clearing and forwarding agents, was upheld by the Supreme Court in Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd. v. Union of India [2005] 1 STT 41.

u The High Court further held that Single Judge had set aside the award passed by the arbitrator by which the arbitrator held that the appellant was entitled to deduct the service tax amount from the amount payable to the respondent. Admittedly, the appellant was recipient of the service of the respondents as per the agreement-in-question. The appellant, pursuant to the provisions of service tax was registered and recognized as an ‘assessee’ and had also filed returns as contemplated accordingly. The appellant, therefore, was liable to pay the service tax being the recipient of the services from the respondent. Admittedly, there was no specific agreement with regard to payment of service tax-in-question by the respondent to the extent the appellant would be entitled to deduct the amount so paid or payable under the service tax, though the respondent was not an assessee and/or not liable to pay service tax under the law. There was no specific clause that such service tax liability would be deductible from the amount payable by the appellant to the respondent pursuant to the contract-in-question. The deduction as claimed and as directed by the award in absence of any agreement or clause, therefore, was not correct. The department, on application filed by the applicant, already rejected the specific claim of refund of that amount.

u The High Court further observed that there was nothing to show even from the plain reading of the agreement and the clauses thereof that, payment of service tax, though payable by the ‘assessee’, yet it would be the respondent, the service provider, to re-pay the same to the appellant and, therefore, the appellant was entitled to deduct service tax from the bills of the respondent in terms of the clauses of the agreement. The Single Judge, therefore, was right in reversing the award passed by the arbitrator. The agreement nowhere entitled the appellant to deduct and/or to recover such service tax from the respondent. Therefore, the High Court held, as rightly held by the Single Judge, that the award was, on the face of it, illegal and erroneous.

[Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. v. Dewan Chand Ram Saran [2008] 14 STT 328 (Bom.)]

Section 65(105)(s) - Chartered Accountant’s services - Scope of services

6.3 Service tax on practising chartered accountants was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998 by the Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998. But there were protests against this levy by the CA community all over India. One of the main causes of protest was that, while the service tax was levied on chartered accountants’ services, but the same was not levied on the similar services provided by an advocate. Thus, due to protest against the levy by chartered accountants and certain Court decisions, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998 only on auditing and accounting services. So, the services provided by CAs and advocates, which can be of similar nature, remain out of service tax. But the later developments are of crucial nature and patently of a discriminatory nature.

10E.3 The meaning of "accountant" now applies for the definition of an "authorised representative" u/s 288(2). As a result, in order to be appointed as an authorised representative for an assessee for any proceedings under the Act, a Chartered Accountant must have a certificate of practice. However, a Chartered Accountant having any other qualification specified in section 288 may be appointed as an authorised representative. Therefore, after this amendment, a Chartered Accountant who does not satisfy both the following conditions cannot be appointed as an authorised representative for an assessee:—

(i)

Though the section refers to the accounts being examined by an accountant, which means a Chartered Accountant, the examination can also be done by a firm of chartered accountants. This has been a recognised practice under the Act. In such a case, it would be necessary to state the name of the partner who has signed the report on behalf of the firm. The accountant signing the report as a partner of a firm or in his individual capacity should give his membership number below his name.

As per the decision taken by the Council of the ICAI, all attest functions undertaken by the members have to bear a UDIN issued by the ICAI. The same needs to be mentioned on the document being signed/attested by the member.

Section 92E does not stipulate that only the statutory auditor appointed under the Companies Act or other similar statute should perform the examination. The examination can, therefore, be conducted either by the statutory auditor or by any other Chartered Accountant in practice having certificate of practice.

The issue of a report u/s 92E, being a recurring assignment for expressing a professional opinion, the accountant accepting the assignment should communicate with the accountant who had done the examination in the earlier year, as provided in the Chartered Accountants Act. In the case of a person whose accounts of the business or profession have been audited under any other law (i.e., a company, a co-operative society, etc. which is required to get the accounts audited under a statute), it is not necessary to communicate with the statutory auditor if he had not done the examination in the earlier year.

The accountant should obtain from the assessee a letter of appointment for conducting the examination as mentioned in section 92E. It is advisable that such an appointment letter should be signed by the person competent to sign/verify the return of income in terms of the provisions of section 140 or by any person who has been authorized by the company to make such an appointment. The accountant should get the statement of particulars, as required in the annexure to the report, authenticated by the assessee before he proceeds to verify the same. The accountant is required to submit his report to the person appointing him, viz., the assessee.

The appointment of the accountant in the case of a company need not be made at the general meeting of the members. It can be made by the Board of Directors or even by any officer, if so authorised by the Board in this behalf. The appointment in the case of a firm or a proprietary concern can be made by a partner or the proprietor or a person authorised by the assessee. It is possible for the assessee to appoint two or more Chartered Accountants for carrying out the examination, in which case, the report will have to be signed by all the chartered accountants. In case of disagreement, they can give their reports separately.

The Act prohibits a relative or an employee of the assessee being appointed as an accountant under section 92E. Also, as per a decision of the Council (reported in the Code of Ethics under clause (4) of Part I of Second Schedule), a Chartered Accountant who is in employment of a concern or in any other concern under the same management cannot be appointed as an auditor of that concern. Therefore, an employee of an assessee or an employee of a concern under the same management cannot examine the accounts and records of an assessee u/s 92E.

An accountant responsible for writing or the maintenance of the books of account of the assessee should not examine such accounts. This principle will apply to the partner of such an accountant as well as to the firm in which he is a partner. In view of this, an accountant who is responsible for writing or the maintenance of the books of account, his partner or the firm in which he is a partner should not accept the examination assignment u/s 92E in the case of such an assessee.

Section 72A of Finance Act, 1994 (as inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012) make provision for special audit by practicing Chartered/Cost Accountant [earlier, section 14AA of Central Excise Act was made applicable to service tax. This section provided only for special audit of Cenvat credit availed].

(iii)

These are not includible in taxable amount for service tax - CBE&C letter No. 187/107/2010-CX.4, dated 17-9-2010 - view reiterated in FAQ No. 77 issued by CBI&C on banking sector on 27-12-2018.

Reimbursement of expenses which is liability of service receiver as per agreement is not includible - In Scott Wilson Kirkpatrick India P. Ltd. v. CCE (2007) 8 STT 58 (CESTAT), the customer (NHAI - National Highways Authority of India) was to provide some basic facilities as per agreement. NHAI agreed that service provider (assessee in this case) can procure the facilities and claim reimbursement from NHAI. It was held that such tax is not payable on reimbursement of such expenses.

Salary paid on behalf of Principal as his pure agent - In DRS Marine Services (P.) Ltd., In re [2018] 100 taxmann.com 323 (AAR - MAHARASHTRA), applicant, a Crew Recruitment and Placement Agency, was involved in selecting and recruiting shipping personnel on behalf of their principal/client (RMS) who is a Foreign Ship Owner . They were disbursing salary to crew members on behalf of Principal, for which Principal was sending amount to them. It was held that applicant will be acting as a pure agent of RMS. Applicant will not be liable to pay GST on salary amount received from RMS and disbursed to crew.

Additional discount for early payment given by principal passed on to final customer as pure agent - In K.K. Polymers (Prop. Advantage Agency (P.) Ltd.), In re [2018] 100 taxmann.com 17 (AAR - Rajasthan), applicant was working as del credere agent (DCA) of Principal. The Principal supplier was giving additional discount to del credere agent for early payment, which was passed on by del credere agent (DCA) to final customer. It was held that such passing on of additional discount is as pure agent of Principal and no GST is payable. However, any amount retained by the DCA on account of early payment is in the nature of supply made to the principal as business support services on which the DCA is already paying GST.

Collecting examination fees from students and remitting to Government - Collecting examination fees from students and remitting to Government is service as 'pure agent' and is not taxable - Arivu Educational Consultants P Ltd. In re (2020) 77 GST 28 = 110 taxmann.com 426 (AAR - Karn).

Valuation of services of C&F Agent - The C&F Agent gets his commission or remuneration for the services provided to Principal. In addition, he claims reimbursement of expenses incurred by him for providing the service e.g. transport, godown charges, office expenses etc. Issue is whether service tax is payable on these expenses also.

Reference to Transfer Pricing Officer [Section 92CA]

Section 92CA of the Income-tax Act provides that the Assessing Officer may refer the computation of arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or specified domestic transaction to a Transfer Pricing Officer. Such a reference can be made where:—

(a)

The Assessing Officer considers it is necessary or expedient to do so, and

(b)

The Assessing Officer has taken previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner to refer the computation to Transfer Pricing Officer.

This section specifies the entire process through which the arm's length price is determined by the Transfer Pricing Officer.

With effect from 1-11-2020, the Amendment Act, 2020 has inserted a new sub-section (8) in section 92CA to empower the Central Government to frame a scheme for the purpose of determination of arm's length price to impart greater efficiency, transparency and accountability by:—

(a)

Eliminating the interface between the Transfer Pricing Officer and the assessee or any other person to the extent technologically feasible;

(b)

Optimising utilisation of the resources through economies of scale and functional specialisation; and

(c)

Introducing a team-based determination of arm's length price (ALP) with dynamic jurisdiction.
Notified scheme - Tax Return Preparers Scheme - SO 2039(E), dated 28-11-2006.

The clause does not require the tax auditor to audit whether the assessee has complied with Chapter X provisions regarding the international transactions he entered into and whether suo motu made appropriate TP adjustments in his ITR. Nor is the tax auditor required to examine or report whether the assessee has maintained proper records as required by Rule 10D regarding international transactions. Nor is he required to examine whether the Arm's Length Price has been determined for international transactions in accordance with any of the recognised methods specified in Section 92F. That is the subject of the audit to be carried out under Section 92E, and the report is to be furnished in Form No. 3CEB.

The tax auditor must report in this clause only if a primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1). If no primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1), the tax auditor has no duty to report. The tax auditor is not even required to report if the primary TP adjustment has not been made as per the APA entered into by the assessee. If primary TP adjustment has been made according to the APA, then the reporting obligation under this Clause is triggered.

This clause also does not deal with Thin Cap adjustments under Section 94B. That is the subject matter of Clause 30B.

This Clause also does not deal with the issue of shares at a premium to non-resident investors by a closely held company that attracts Section 56(2)(vii). That is the subject matter of Clause 29A.

Although the tax auditor is not required to examine compliance with transfer pricing provisions under Chapter X of the Act except to the limited extent required by Clauses 30A, 30B and 43 of Form No. 3CD, it may be advisable for him to do so to identify impermissible avoidance arrangements for Clause 30C purposes as unacceptable circumvention of SAARs like Transfer Pricing provisions would attract GAAR. Indian Transfer Pricing law is essentially all about adjustments required if the pricing in international transactions is not at arm's length. There is no scope for adjustments for non-arm's length non-price terms and conditions as Chapter X has no treaty equivalent transfer pricing provisions along the lines of Article 9 of OECD Model Conventions. Nevertheless, the tax auditor may find it useful to examine if any of the non-price terms and conditions of international transactions are not at arm's length from the angle of Clause 30C.

4. Role of Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) 4.1 The role of the TPO begins after a reference is received from the AO. In terms of section 92CA, this role is limited to the determination of the ALP in relation to international transactions or specified domestic transactions referred to him by the AO. However, if any other international transaction comes to the notice of the TPO during the course of the proceedings before him, then he is empowered to determine the ALP of such other international transactions also by virtue of section 92CA(2A) and (2B). The transfer price has to be determined by the TPO in terms of section 92C. The price has to be determined by using any one of the methods stipulated in sub-section (1) of section 92C and by applying the most appropriate method referred to in sub-section (2) thereof. There may be occasions where application of the most appropriate method provides results which are different but equally reliable. In all such cases, further scrutiny may be necessary to evaluate the appropriateness of the method, the correctness of the data, weight given to various factors and so on. The selection of the most appropriate method will depend upon the facts of the case and the factors mentioned in Rule 10C. The TPO, after taking into account all relevant facts and data available to him, shall determine the ALP and pass a speaking order.

4.2 The TPO's order should contain details of the data used, reasons for arriving at a certain price and the applicability of methods. It may be emphasised that the application of method including the application of the most appropriate method, the data used, factors governing the applicability of respective methods, computation of price under a given method will all be subjected to judicial scrutiny. It is, therefore, necessary that the order of the TPO contains adequate reasons on all these counts. Copies of the documents or the relevant data used in arriving at the arm's length price should be made available to the AO for his records and the use at subsequent stages of appellate or penal proceedings.

4.3 The TPO, being an Additional/Joint CIT, shall obtain the approval of the jurisdictional CIT (Transfer Pricing) before passing the order. On the other hand, the TPO, being a Deputy/Assistant CIT, shall obtain the approval of the jurisdictional Additional/Joint CIT before passing the order. The jurisdictional CIT (TP) should assign a limited number of important and complex cases, not exceeding 50, to the Additional/Joint CsIT (TPOs) working in the same jurisdiction. For the selection of such important and complex cases by the CsIT (TP), the concerned CCsIT (International Taxation) shall frame appropriate guidelines.

4.4 In addition to the above, the TPO is required to carry out the Compliance Audit of the Advance Pricing Agreements (APAs) entered into by the Board and the taxpayers in accordance with Rule 10P of the Income-tax Rules.

4.5 The TPO is also required to play an important role in respect of Safe Harbour provisions. Whenever a reference is made to the TPO under sub-rule (4) or sub-rule (10) of Rule 10TE of the Income-tax Rules, the TPO has to carefully examine all the facts and circumstances of the taxpayer's exercise of an option for Safe Harbour and pass an order in writing as mandated in sub-rule (6) or sub-rule (11) of the said Rule, respectively.

5. Role of the AO after Determination of ALP by the TPO

Under sub-section (4) of section 92C (read with sub-section (4) of section 92CA), the AO has to compute the total income of the assessee in conformity with the ALP determined by the TPO under sub-section (3) of section 92CA.

6. Maintenance of Data Base

It is to be ensured by the CIT (TP) that the references received from the AOs by the TPOs in his jurisdiction are dealt with expeditiously and accurate record of all events connected with the whole process of determination of ALP is maintained. This record is to be maintained by each TPO, separately for international transactions and specified domestic transactions, in the formats enclosed as Annexure I and Annexure II to this Instruction and the same shall be maintained electronically on the Department's ITBA system as and when the same becomes fully functional. These formats will serve as an important database for future action and also help in bringing about uniformity in the determination of the ALP in identical or substantially identical cases. The CsIT (TP) must ensure that a consolidated report for the entire Charge is generated and stored after the completion of each transfer pricing audit cycle.

There have been instances wherein service tax has not been paid on the ground of non-receipt of payment even though the transaction has been recognized as revenue/expenditure in the statement of profit and loss account for the purpose of determining corporate tax liability. 6.3 As an anti-avoidance measure, it is proposed to clarify that service tax is leviable on taxable services provided by the person liable to pay service tax even if the amount is not actually received, but the amount is credited or debited in the books of account of the service provider. In other words, service tax is required to be paid after receipt of payment or crediting/debiting of the amount in the books of accounts, whichever is earlier. 6.4 The term 'associated enterprise' has the same meaning as assigned to it in section 92A of the Income Tax Act, 1961. It is a relative concept i.e. an enterprise is an associated enterprise when it is viewed in relation to other enterprises. This concept is used in the Income Tax Act for applying transfer pricing provisions. An enterprise which participates, directly or indirectly, or through one or more intermediaries, in the management or control or capital of the other enterprise is considered as associated enterprise. It also covers an enterprise in respect of which one or more persons who participate, directly or indirectly, or through one or more intermediaries, in the management or control or capital of the other enterprise.

6.5 Section 92A(2) of the Income Tax Act specifies various situations under which two enterprises shall be deemed to be associated enterprises. Primary Transfer Pricing Adjustments are what are known in popular parlance as "transfer pricing adjustments" or TP Adjustments."Primary adjustment" to a transfer price means the determination of transfer price in accordance with the arm's length principle resulting in an increase in the total income or reduction in the loss, as the case may be, of the assessee.

The e-tax Guide-Transfer Pricing Guidelines (2016 edition) of the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore defines "transfer pricing adjustment" or what is referred to as "primary transfer pricing adjustment" in section 92CE(1) as under:

"3.34 Transfer pricing adjustment

In the event the related parties do not transact with each other at arm's length prices, tax authorities may for tax purposes, substitute the price of the transaction with one that could have been charged if the parties were unrelated. The adjustment to arrive at that price is known as a transfer pricing adjustment."

A primary TP adjustment covers the following TP adjustments,—

(i)

a TP adjustment to transfer price made suo motu by the assessee in his return of income;

(ii)

a TP adjustment to the transfer price made by the Assessing Officer has been accepted by the assessee;

(iii)

a TP adjustment determined by an advance pricing agreement (APA) entered into by the assessee under section 92CC;

(iv)

a TP adjustment made as per the safe harbour rules framed under section 92CB; or

(v)

a TP adjustment arising from the resolution of an assessment by way of the mutual agreement procedure (MAP under an agreement (DTAA) entered into under section 90 or section 90A to avoid double taxa-tion.

10.8

Reimbursement of expenses incurred on behalf of service receiver not includible

Often, a service provider incurs some expenditure on behalf of service receiver and then recovers the amount from him. Such expenditure is not part of service provided by him to service receiver, but is incurred by him as per business practice or convenience. Following illustrations may clarify the provisions -

Octroi/entry tax amount paid by Clearing & Forwarding Agent, CHA or Transporter on behalf of owner of goods/Principal.

Customs duty, dock dues, demurrage, transport charges etc. paid by Customs House Agent on behalf of client.

Advertisement charges paid by Advertising Agency to newspaper on behalf of clients.

Ticket charges paid by Travel Agent and recovered from his customer.

These are not part of service provided and hence are not includible. Rule 5(2) provides that the expenditure or costs that a service provider incurs, as a pure agent of the client, shall be excluded from the value if such service provider fulfils prescribed conditions.

The principle is also discernible from various exclusions as contained in rule 6(2).

Reimbursement of expenses incurred on behalf of client is not includible - Glaxo Smithkline Pharmaceuticals v. CCE (2005) 1 STT 37 (CESTAT).

In Bax Global India v. CST (2008) 13 STT 263 (CESTAT), it was held that activity of CHA relates to entry or departure of conveyances or import or export of goods any customs station. It cannot extend beyond it. Charges collected for freight, cartage, MSIL/JWG charges, examination charges, DO fees, Bill of Lading fee, CFS charges, storage and handling etc. do not pertain to CHA service. In case of charges collected by CHA for activities not related to CHA, he is not liable to pay service tax. Even if he earns profit on these activities, it is not includible in value of CHA services.

No service tax on registration fee and stamp duty of immovable property - Service tax is not payable on reimbursable expenses like registration charges and stamp duty, recovered by builder from the customer - LCS City Makers P Ltd. v. CST (2012) 36 STT 228 = 23 taxmann.com 169 (CESTAT).

No service tax on passenger service fee and airport tax collected by airlines - In Lufthansa German Airlines v. CST (2016) 56 GST 58 = 70 taxmann.com 60 (CESTAT), it has been held that passenger service fee and airport tax which is collected from passengers and paid over to airport/Government authorities is not includible in value of service as it is collected as pure agent - same view in Lufthansa German Airlines v. CST (2016) 56 GST 196 = 70 taxmann.com 169 (CESTAT).

No service tax on stamp duty and Security Transaction Tax (STT) - Stamp duty and Security Transaction Tax (STT) is liability of buyer and stock broker pays it acting as pure agent of the customer. These are not includible in taxable amount for service tax - CBE&C letter No. 187/107/2010-CX.4 dated 17-9-2010.

Reimbursement of expenses which is liability of service receiver as per agreement is not includible - In Scott Wilson Kirkpatrick India P Ltd. v. CCE (2007) 8 STT 58 (CESTAT), the customer (NHAI - National Highways Authority of India) was to provide some basic facilities as per agreement. NHAI agreed that service provider (assessee in this case) can procure the facilities and claim reimbursement from NHAI. It was held that such tax is not payable on reimbursement of such expenses.

Issue referred to large bench due to conflicting decisions - In view of conflicting views about reimbursement of expenses, the issue has been referred to large bench in Amit Sales v. CCE (Stay order Delhi CESTAT dated 1-10-2008) - quoted and stay granted in Kidstuff Promos v. CST (2010) 26 STT 127 (CESTAT).

6.2 Power to Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) to identify international transactions

Section 92CA(1) provides that the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) can determine the ALP only in relation to an international transaction, which has been referred to him by the Assessing Officer.

This was recognized by the CBDT vide its Instruction No. 3 of 28-3-2003 as follows: “In terms of section 92CA this role is limited to the determination of arm’s length price in relation to the international transaction(s) referred to him by the Assessing Officer. If during the course of proceedings before him it is found that there are certain other transactions, which have not been referred to him by the Assessing Officer, he will have to take up the matter with the Assessing Officer so that a fresh reference is received with regard to such transactions”.

Further, in Amadeus India Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 10 taxmann.com 88 (Delhi - Trib.) it was held that TPO has jurisdiction only in respect of international transactions referred to him by the Assessing Officer.

Section 92CA has now been amended with effect from 1-6-2011 so as to specifically provide that the jurisdiction of the TPO shall extend to the determination of the ALP in respect of other international transactions noticed by him subsequently, in the course of proceedings before him. Such international transactions would be in addition to the international transactions referred to the TPO by the Assessing Officer.

It is now well-settled that a procedural amendment is generally retrospective and applies even to pending proceedings [CWT v. Sharvan Kumar Swamp & Sons [1994] 210 ITR 886 (SC); CIT v. Synergy Financial Exchange Ltd. [2007] 288 ITR 366 (Mad.)]. Now, the amendment could be consi- dered as a procedural amendment and hence it could apply to all assessments including pending assessments in respect of years up to assessment year 2010-11, which are pending before the TPO.

6.3 Power to TPO under section 133A

Section 92CA(7) provides that for the purpose of determining the ALP, the TPO can exercise powers available to an Assessing Officer under section 131(1) and section 133(6). These are powers of summoning or calling for details for the purpose of inquiry or investigation into the matter. Section 92CA(7) has now been amended with effect from 1-6-2011 to enable the TPO to also exercise the power of survey conferred upon an income-tax authority under section 133A.

Section 133A provides for the power of an income-tax authority to enter a place of business or profession and inspect books of account and obtain such other information as he may require as to any matter which may be useful for, or relevant to, any proceeding under the Act.

3.4 For cases to be referred by the AO to the TPO in accordance with paragraphs 3.2 and 3.3 above, in respect of transactions having the following situations, the AO must, as a jurisdictional requirement, record his satisfaction that there is an income or a potential of an income arising and/or being affected on determination of the ALP of an international transaction or specified domestic transaction before seeking approval of the PCIT or CIT to refer the matter to the TPO for determination of the ALP:

where the taxpayer has not filed the Accountant's report under section 92E of the Act but the international transactions or specified domestic transactions undertaken by it come to the notice of the AO;

where the taxpayer has not declared one or more international transactions or specified domestic transactions in the Accountant's report filed under section 92E of the Act and the said transaction or transactions come to the notice of the AO; and

where the taxpayer has declared the international transactions or specified domestic transactions in the Accountant's report filed under section 92E of the Act but has made certain qualifying remarks to the effect that the said transactions are not international transactions or specified domestic transactions or they do not impact the income of the taxpayer.

In the above three situations, the AO must provide an opportunity of being heard to the taxpayer before recording his satisfaction or otherwise. In case no objection is raised by the taxpayer to the applicability of Chapter X [Sections 92 to 92F] of the Act to these three situations, then AO should refer the international transaction or specified domestic transaction to the TPO for determining the ALP after obtaining the approval of the PCIT or CIT. However, where the applicability of Chapter X [Sections 92 to 92F] to these three situations is objected to by the taxpayer, the AO must consider the taxpayer's objections and pass a speaking order so as to comply with the principles of natural justice. If the AO decides in the said order that the transaction in question needs to be referred to the TPO, he should make a reference after obtaining the approval of the PCIT or CIT.

3.5 In addition to the cases to be referred as per paragraphs 3.2 and 3.3, a case involving a transfer pricing adjustment in an earlier assessment year that has been fully or partially set-aside by the ITAT, High Court or Supreme Court on the issue of the said adjustment shall invariably be referred to the TPO for determination of the ALP.

3.6 Since the provisions of section 92CA of the Act, inter alia, refer to the computation of the ALP of the international transaction or specified domestic transaction, it is imperative for the AO to ensure that all international transactions or relevant specified domestic transactions or both, as the case may be, are explicitly mentioned in the letter through which the reference is made to the TPO. In this regard, guidelines as under may be followed :

(a)

If a case has been selected for scrutiny on a TP risk parameter pertaining to international transactions only, then the international transactions shall alone be referred to the TPO;

(b)

If a case has been selected for scrutiny on a TP risk parameter pertaining to specified domestic transactions only, then the specified domestic transactions shall alone be referred to the TPO; and

(c)

If a case has been selected for scrutiny on the basis of TP risk parameters pertaining to both international transactions and specified domestic transactions, then the international transactions and the specified domestic transactions shall together be referred to the TPO.

Since international transactions may be benchmarked together at the entity level due to the inter-linkages amongst them, if a case has been selected for scrutiny on a TP risk parameter pertaining to one or more international transactions, then all the international transactions entered into by the taxpayer - except those about which the AO has decided not to make a reference as per paragraph 3.4 - shall be referred to the TPO.

3.7 For administering the transfer pricing regime in an efficient manner, it is clarified that though AO has the power under section 92C to determine the ALP of international transactions or specified domestic transactions, determination of ALP should not be carried out at all by the AO in a case where reference is not made to the TPO. However, in such cases, the AO must record in the body of the assessment order that due to the Board's Instruction on this matter, the transfer pricing issue has not been examined at all.

34.6-5 Charges for registration

A business entity is required to pay various types of registration charges e.g. motor vehicle registration, excise registration, service tax registration.

These charges are paid as the person paying these charges is given right to perform some acts. For example, RTO registration charges grant him right to run vehicle on roads. Hence, it cannot be said that there is no quid pro quo.

The motor vehicle registration charges are partly regulatory and partly compensatory. It is permission to run vehicle on road. It is activity for consideration. These can be subject to service tax.

However, all services of registration under any law have been exempted from GST.

34.6-6 Services of Inspection, testing, certification

A business entity is required to pay various types of inspection charges and fees e.g. PF administration charges, Motor Vehicles Inspection charges, Building inspection fee and what not.

These charges are paid as the person paying these charges is given right to enjoy various facilities.

When a person sets up a factory, purchases a vehicle, constructs a building or employs person, by necessary implication, he agrees to pay necessary fees.

It can be argued that these charges are not at the 'desire of promisor' - rather against the desire of promisor. However, the fact is that he is willing to pay those charges as he gets privileges and advantages after paying those charges.

These would be subject to GST.

However, services of testing, calibration, safety check or certification required under any law relating to (a) protection and safety of workmen (b) consumers (c) public at large, including fire license have been exempted from GST.

34.6-7 Filing fees with Registrar of Companies for registration of documents

The fees payable are of course statutory. However, the fees paid are to get privileges to run business as a 'company'. Hence, there is quid pro quo. Service tax should be payable.

However, if fees payable do not exceed Rs 5,000 are exempt and hence there is no reverse charge.

34.6-8 MOT charges payable to excise and customs authorities

A business entity is required to pay MOT (Merchant Overtime Charges) to excise and customs authorities for export and import clearances [These are in addition to the unofficial charges payable to them].

12.4 Change in the time limit to pass the order by the Transfer Pricing Officer [Section 166 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to section 92CA of ITA 1961)]

12.4-1 Position under the ITA 1961

Section 92CA of the ITA 1961 deals with the case where the assessee has entered into an international transaction or specified domestic transaction in any previous year, and the AO may refer the computation of the Arm's Length Price (ALP) in relation to the said international transaction or specified domestic transaction under section 92C to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO).

Sub-section (3A) to section 92CA states that TPO is required to pass an order before sixty days prior to the date on which the period of limitation under section 153, or as the case may be, in section 153B for making the order of assessment, reassessment or recomputation or fresh assessment, as the case may be, expires.

12.4-1a Exclusion of the last day of assessment limitation - The interpretation of the phrase 'before sixty days prior to the date' has been a consistent point of contention between taxpayers and the revenue, leading to significant litigation.

The Madras High Court, in the case of Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), which affirmed the Single Judge's decision in Jt. CIT v. Pfizer Healthcare India (P.) Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 536 (Madras), held that the word 'date' in section 92CA(3A) refers to the last date for the AO to pass the assessment order under section 153 (e.g., December 31st). The crucial words 'prior to' indicate that, for the purpose of calculating the 60 days, this last date must be excluded. Therefore, if the assessment limitation expires on December 31st, the TPO order ought to have been passed on or before October 31st.

This interpretation was consistently followed across numerous ITAT benches, including in the following cases:

Teleperformance Global Services (P.) Ltd. [2023] 155 taxmann.com 658 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Zydus Lifesciences Ltd. [2024] 163 taxmann.com 349 (Ahmedabad-Trib.)

Frost & Sullivan (India) (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 739 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Shell India Markets (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 366 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Siemens Technology and Services (P.) Ltd. [2024] 162 taxmann.com 357 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Huhtamaki India Ltd. [2024] 164 taxmann.com 194 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Atos India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 152 taxmann.com 217 (Mumbai-Trib.)

CAE India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 691 (Bangalore-Trib.)

Pioneer India Electronics (P.) Ltd. [2025] 178 taxmann.com 553 (Delhi-Trib.)

Sigma Aldrich Chemicals (P.) Ltd. [2022] 141 taxmann.com 431 (Bangalore-Trib.)

12.4-1b Mandatory nature of the time limit - Another critical aspect clarified by the judiciary is whether the time limit prescribed in section 92CA(3A) is mandatory or merely directory. The revenue often argued that the use of the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) implies a directory nature.

However, the Madras High Court in Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), after a detailed analysis of the scheme of the Act and the consequences of non-compliance, unequivocally held that the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) has to be construed as 'shall' and the time period fixed therein has to be scrupulously followed.'

The court reasoned that the overall scheme of transfer pricing assessments, with various interlinked time limits (including extensions under the proviso to section 92CA(3A) and section 153), indicates a legislative intent to ensure timely completion. If the TPO's time limit were merely directory, it would undermine the entire assessment process. This principle has been reiterated in the case of Asstt. CIT v. CAE India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 691 (Bangalore - Trib.).

GENERAL

Application of Transfer Pricing Regulations - In order to reduce litigation, section 40A(2) and section 80-IA(10) need to be amended to empower Assessing Officer to make adjustments to income declared by assessee, having regard to fair market value of transactions between related parties by applying any of generally accepted methods of determination of arm's length price, including methods provided under Transfer Pricing Regulations. Law should also be amended to make it compulsory for taxpayers to maintain books of account and other documents on lines prescribed under rule 10D in respect of such domestic transactions and taxpayers should obtain an audit report from their chartered accountants so that taxpayers maintain proper documents and requisite books of account reflecting transactions between related entities at arm's length price, based on generally accepted methods specified under Transfer Pricing Regulations - CIT v. Glaxo Smithkline Asia (P.) Ltd. [2010] 195 Taxman 35 (SC).

APPLICABILITY

Expenditure must first be proved as excessive and unreasonable - Section 40A(2)(a) cannot have any application, unless it is first held that the expenditure was excessive and unreasonable - Upper India Publishing House (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 117 ITR 569 (SC).

'Services' must be commercial in character, having market value - The expression 'services' in section 40A(2)(a) is an expression of wider import. The goods, services and facilities referred to in section 40A(2)(a) are those which have a market value and which are commercial in character - T.T. (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [1980] 121 ITR 551 (Kar.).

Three requirements are independent of, and alternative to, each other - In relation to the disallowance under the provisions of section 40A(2), a plain reading of the provision reveals that where an assessee incurs any expenditure in respect of which payment is required to be made or has been made to any person referred to in clause (b) of section 40A(2) and the Assessing Officer is of the opinion that such expenditure is excessive or unreasonable having regard to (a) fair market value of the goods, services or facilities for which the payment is made; or (b) the legitimate needs of the business of the assessee; or (c) the benefits derived by or accruing to the assessee on receipt of such goods, services or facilities, then the Assessing Officer shall not allow as a deduction so much of the expenditure as is considered by the Assessing Officer to be excessive or unreasonable. Therefore, it becomes apparent that the Assessing Officer is required to record a finding as to whether the expenditure is excessive or unreasonable in relation to any one of the three requirements prescribed, which are independent and alternative to each other. All the three requirements need not exist simultaneously. In a given case, if any one condition is shown to be satisfied the provision can be invoked and applied, if the facts so warrant. - Coronation Flour Mills v. Asstt. CIT [2009] 314 ITR 1 (Guj.).

Quality and nature of services rendered must be considered - The question whether the expenditure is excessive or unreasonable in a given case has to be examined keeping in mind, the services for which payment is made. In the process, the legitimate needs of the business or profession of the assessee or the benefit derived by or accruing to the assessee from such services is also to be kept in mind. In the business of advertising and media, the role of a media consultant is much more important than the role of client management. In fact, considering the nature of business, media consultancy is the backbone of such business and plays much more pivotal role than the persons handling client management. For that reason, if the director in charge of media consultancy was paid higher remuneration than what was paid to director in charge of client management it could not be treated as excessive or unreasonable, more so, when the two cases were not at par and could not be treated as comparable by any standards. - Hive Communication (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 201 Taxman 99/12 taxmann.com 287 (Delhi).

CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETIES - Provisions of section 40A(2) are not applicable to a co-operative society - CIT v. Manjara Shetkari Sahakari Sakhar Karkhana Ltd. [2008] 166 Taxman 287 (Bom.).

RULE 10E*

Report from an accountant to be furnished under section 92E

Statutory background

10E.1 As per section 92E, every person who has entered into an international transaction or specified domestic transaction during a PY shall obtain a report from an accountant [as defined in Explanation below section 288(2)] and furnish such report on or before the specified date [i.e., date 1 month prior to the due date for furnishing the return of income u/s 139(1) for the relevant AY]. Further, such person has to furnish by that specified date the report of such accountant in the form prescribed under Rule 10E (see para 10E.2) duly signed and verified by such accountant.

10E.1-1 Furnishing of TP report is a basis for referring matter to TPO u/s 92CA - In terms of section 92CA, it is not every international transaction which is to be referred to TPO but only those transactions where the AO considers it necessary to do so u/s 92C. This satisfaction by the AO to refer the matter to the TPO could only be arrived at after a report from the accountant in terms of section 92E has been filed with the AO. It is on examination of the same the occasion would arise for the AO to refer the matter to the TPO u/s 92CA(1) to compute the ALP in relation to such transactions entered into by the assessee with its AEs. In the absence of such report being filed, it is impossible for the AO to form any opinion much less an opinion so as to conclude that the international transactions with related parties are not to be referred to the TPO—Sitara Diamond (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 39 taxmann.com 162/[2014] 225 Taxman 95 (Mag.)(Bom.).

The satisfaction to be arrived at by the AO regarding the existence of the international transaction or specified domestic transaction, even prima facie, is a sine qua non for making the reference to the TPO. Where such an accountant's report is submitted by the assessee in Form No. 3CEB, then there should be no difficulty for the AO to form an opinion, even a prima facie one, that it is necessary and expedient to make a reference to the TPO on the question of the determination of the ALP of such international transaction involving the assessee—Indorama Synthetics (India) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2016] 71 taxmann.com 349/241 Taxman 523 (Del.), SLP granted in Addl. CIT v. Indorama Synthetics (India) (P.) Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 588/269 Taxman 578 (SC).

Form of accountant's report [Rule 10E]

10E.2 The report of an accountant required to be furnished u/s 92E shall be in Form No. 3CEB and be verified in the manner indicated therein.

In view of proviso to Rule 12(2), the audit report shall have to be furnished electronically by the assessee.

The scope, as envisaged by section 92E, is restricted to examination of accounts and records of the assessee relating to the international transaction or specified domestic transaction entered into by the assessee during the previous year under examination. Further, the accountant has to give his opinion whether "proper information and documents as are prescribed" have been kept by the assessee in respect of the international transactions or specified domestic transaction entered into by him. The examination u/s 92E is not an audit requiring opinion of the accountant on the true and fair view of the financial statements of the enterprise.

The report consists of three (3) paragraphs dealing with distinct aspects as summarised hereunder:—

The first paragraph contains declaration about examination of the accounts and records of the assessee in order to review the international transaction(s) and the specified domestic transaction(s).

The second paragraph involves rendering of an opinion whether proper information and documents as are prescribed under Rule 10D are maintained by the assessee in respect of the identified international transactions and the specified domestic transaction(s), on the basis of the details furnished in Annexure to Form No. 3CEB.

The third and the last paragraph requires expression of the opinion whether the particulars given in the Annexure to Form No. 3CEB are true and correct.

Where payments were made by an Indian agent of foreign TV channels to Indian residents by way of AMP expenses, these payments were not required to be included in Form No. 3CEB—CIT v. N.G.C. Network (India) (P.) Ltd. [2014] 50 taxmann.com 240/[2015] 228 Taxman 176 (Bom.).

8.1 Amendment in time limit for making of order by transfer pricing officer [Section 92CA]

Service provider is liable to pay service tax even if the service receiver did not pay service tax amount to him - Avtar and Co. v. CCE (2015) 51 GST 491 = 58 taxmann.com 97 (CESTAT). In Delhi Transport Corporation v. CST (2015) 51 GST 511 = 59 taxmann.com 51 (Del HC DB). It was rightly held that assessee cannot ask revenue (a) to recover tax from third party or (b) to wait till he has recovered service tax amount from its customers. Claim of assessee from customers has no bearing in so far as claim of revenue against assessee for recovery of tax dues is concerned. Thus, service provider is liable to pay service tax even if service receiver does not pay service tax.
