44.2-3 Procedure for digital signature

Records of service tax and central excise can be preserved in electronic form and authenticate by digital signature. Similarly, invoices can be signed digitally.

Procedure for the same has been specified in Notification No. 18/2015-CE(NT) dated 6-7-2015.

The digital signature shall be class 2 or class 3 duly issued by Certifying Authority in India.

Specified details shall be informed to jurisdictional AC/DC of Central Excise at least 15 days in advance. Changes should also be informed.

Separate records shall be kept for each factory or service tax registration.

The specified records shall be produced to Central Excise Officer on demand. The records should be supplied by e-mail or electronically readable storage device.

During any enquiry, investigation or audit, if Central Excise Officer directs, the print outs of such records and invoices should be submitted. The electronic records should be preserved for five years. Its back up shall be kept.

Procedure for verifying digitally signed documents or invoices has been specified in CBEC Instruction F No. 224/44/2014-CX.6 dated 6-7-2015.

Once a digitally signed document is opened a pop up message will appear indicating the manner in which digitally signature can be verified. Once signature block is clicked, a window 'signature validation status' will appear. A tab bearing the title 'Signature Properties' shall also appear. Once you click 'show signer's certificate', information about signer, validity and authenticity of digital signature shall be displayed. After that, the Central Excise Officer may add the certificate to its list of trusted certificates by clicking the 'trust' tab on the menu. Then the signer gets added as a trusted source and process of verification is complete.

Digital signature as well as manual signature on same invoice permissible - Digital signature as well as manual signature on same invoice is permissible. Such invoices will be valid invoices for Cenvat credit - CBEC circular No. 1038/26/2016-CX dated 19-7-2016.

VALUE OF TAXABLE SERVICE

10.1

Background

Section 67 of Finance Act, 1994 (introduced w.e.f. 18-4-2006), makes provisions for valuation of service tax.

Chapter 8 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012 explains highlights of provisions of valuation for service tax.

10.1-1 Value and rate of exchange as on date when service provided or agreed to be provided

The rate of service tax, value of a taxable service and rate of exchange, if any, shall be the rate of service tax or value of a taxable service or rate of exchange, as the case may be, in force or as applicable at the time when the taxable service has been provided or agreed to be provided Explanation.—For the purposes of this section, "rate of exchange" means the rate of exchange referred to in the Explanation to section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 (52 of 1962) - section 67A(1) of Finance Act, 1994 as renumbered w.e.f. 14-5-2016. Earlier, it was only section 67A upto 14-5-2016.

As per section 67A(2) [introduced w.e.f. 14-5-2016], the time or the point in time with respect to the rate of service tax shall be such as may be prescribed.

The time or the point in time with respect to the rate of service tax has been prescribed vide Point of Taxation Rules, w.e.f. 14th May, 2016, Earlier, Point of Taxation Rules were not relevant to determine rate of service tax,

As discussed elsewhere, there is conflict between section 67A(1) and Point of Taxation Rules, at various places.

10.1-2 Foreign Exchange rate for valuation of import and export of service

Determination of rate of foreign exchange is relevant for determination of value of services in case of export of services and import of services. The rate is also relevant when place of provision of service is India and hence service tax is payable, but payment is received in foreign exchange.

Rate of exchange for valuation of export and import of service is the rate of exchange determined in accordance with rules as may be prescribed - Explanation to section 67A of Finance Act, 1994 as amended vide Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 w.e.f. 1-10-2014.

The rate of foreign exchange for determination of value of taxable service shall be the applicable rate of exchange as per Generally Accepted Accounting principles (GAAP) on the date when point of taxation arises in terms of Point of Taxation Rules - Rule 11 of Service Tax Rules, inserted w.e.f. 1-10-2014.

This provision has been made, since, as per section 129(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, Financial Statements of companies must comply with Accounting Standards, and shall be in prescribed form.

Thus, it will be easy to reconcile value of service tax as per books of account and as per service tax returns.

10.1-2a GENERALLY ACCEPTED ACCOUNTING PRINCIPLES ON EFFECTS OF CHANGES IN FOREIGN EXCHANGE RATES - Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) are contained in AS-11 [Accounting Standard 11] in Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2006 issued Central Government in December 2006, on recommendation of NACAS [National Advisory Committee on Accounting Standards] under section 210A of Companies Act, 1956.

The AS-11 is on 'Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates'.

Section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013 envisages constitution of National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA). One of function of NFRA is to recommend Accounting Standards. However, this section is not yet notified.

Till constitution of NFRA under the 2013 Act, National Advisory Committee on Accounting Standards (NACAS) constituted under section 210A of the 1956 Act will continue to function.

Thus, presently accounting standards as notified in December 2006 are in force.

The highlights [only as relevant for service tax valuation] are as follows—

Initial recognition of foreign currency transactions - Initially, foreign currency transactions shall be recorded by applying an exchange rate at the time of transaction [In case of service tax, it should as on date of Point of Taxation as per POT Rules]. Alternatively, average for a week or month can be used if there is no significant fluctuation in exchange rate.

tax exemption Notification No. 59/98, dated October 16, 1998, which provided full exemption from service tax to services (except the ones specified in that notification) provided by the practising chartered accountants, has been rescinded by the Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006 (a budget notification) and, consequently, all services provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity, have become taxable. Before going into the impact of the rescission of the exemption notification, one should first understand the statutory charge of service tax on the practising chartered accountants, as given in Chapter V of the Finance Act, 1994,—

(a) Meaning of practising chartered accountant [Section 65(83)] : Practising chartered accountant means a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and is holding a certificate of practice granted under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy.

(b) Taxable service [Section 65(105 )(s)] : Taxable service means any service provided or to be provided to a client, by a practising chartered accountant in his professional capacity, in any manner.

Position before withdrawal of exemption notification

2. Before rescission of the service tax exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998, i.e., upto February 28, 2006, all services, except those mentioned below, provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA were exempt from service tax—

(a)accounting and auditing; or

(b)cost accounting and cost auditing; or

(c)secretarial auditing; or

(d)verification of declarations in prescribed forms of compliances for obtaining a certificate of commencement of business or commencement of other business under section 149 of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(e)signing of the annual return of listed companies under section 161 of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(f)certification that requirements of Schedule XIII to the Companies Act, 1956 have been complied with as regards statutory guidelines for appointment of managerial personnel and payment of managerial remuneration to them without the approval of the Central Government under section 269 and Schedule XIII, of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(g)certification of documents to be filed by companies with the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act, 1956; or

(h)certification in Form No. 1 that the whole of the amount remaining unpaid or unclaimed for a period of three years from the date of transfer to the special account under section 205(1)/(2) of the Companies Act, 1956 has been transferred to the General Revenue Account of the Central Government under the Companies Unpaid Dividend (Transfer to General Revenue Account of the Central Government) Rules, 1978; or

(i)certification of documents under the Exports and Imports Policy of the Government of India; or

(j)certification for exchange control purposes which a practising chartered accountant can issue as documentary evidence in support of certain applications under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973; or

(k)certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets as per rule 8A(7) of the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957.

Thus, in case any practising CA/CS/ICWA was rendering any service other than (a) to (k ) enumerated above, like legal or taxation consultancy service, etc., he wasn’t liable for service tax.

However, any service provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, which fell under the ambit of any other taxable service, was liable to service tax under the category of that other taxable service. For example, if a chartered accountant also provided manpower recruitment services to his clients, then he was liable to service tax on such services under the category of manpower recruitment service.

Reasons behind issuance of earlier exemption notification

3. The said exemption notification was issued on the principles of equity. The then Government had recognized the fact that the—

(i)practising CA/CS/ICWAs were providing services like legal consultancy, etc., which were equally being provided by other professionals like advocates and legal practitioners and, therefore,

(ii)levy of service tax on such services provided by practising CA/CS/ICWAs and non-levy of service tax on the same services provided by advocates and legal practitioners would be inequitable levy.

Having recognized the abovesaid facts the aforesaid exemption notification was issued to prevent the levy of service tax from being unjust and inequitable.

Position after withdrawal of exemption notification

4. After the withdrawal of the aforesaid exemption notification by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006, i.e., with effect from March 1, 2006 all the services provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, in his professional capacity, are chargeable to service tax.

1. A brief legislative history is that service tax was, for the first time, imposed by the Finance Act, 1994. This tax was levied on three types of services. So, the services provided by CAs and advocates, which can be of similar nature, remain out of purview of service tax. But the later developments are of crucial nature and patently of discriminatory nature. Perhaps in democracy, you can get no better example of favouritism. Our beloved Finance Minister, who himself is an advocate by profession, can do no better than to spare their fraternity from the ambit of this tax. The position now is that, while the services of lawyers are still out of service tax net, all the services provided by chartered accountants are now under the net of service tax. Service tax is a tax on services and not on a tax on the service provider or on the professionals providing the services. This fact was also pronounced by various Courts while deciding the constitutional validity of the service tax on various services.

The exemption notification was also issued on the same consideration because the field of providing this service is open for various other professionals and if getting same type of services from a particular professional, say chartered accountants, attracts service tax then this has two side effects. One is that the other professional will have the upper hand compared to the chartered accountants only because they need not to pay service tax. Secondly, it will snatch the level playing field from a professional. Hence, in this particular case this is a tax on a professional or on a particular profession and not on a particular service because the others providing the same service need not to pay the tax.

On both these grounds the withdrawal of this exemption notification is totally discriminatory, unwarranted and unjustified and as a remedial action the exemption notification should be restored in the same spirit in which it was initially provided.

Withdrawal of Service Tax Exemption to Practising Chartered Accountants - An unjust move by Government!

Exemption granted to certain services provided by CAs, CSs and ICWAs, by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998 stands withdrawn by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006. Is this withdrawal unjust and unjustifiable? Is it discriminatory? How damaging is it to the practice of CAs, etc.? The author here examines the issues from legal as well as moral angle. The abrupt move on the part of the Government is going to create a feeling of insecurity among the professional affected and cause harm to the healthy growth of their profession. Applying the logic of the Kerala High Court decision in Malappuram District Parallel College Association v. Union of India [2006] 150 Taxman 624, wherein levy of service tax on parallel colleges was held to be discriminatory, the author feels that the withdrawal of exemption to CAs/CSs/ICWAs may not pass the test of constitutionality.

Introduction

1. Chartered accountants, being professionally qualified and proficiently trained, are providing most valuable services to the people of this nation and abroad in the matters pertaining to accountancy, audit, management and technical consultancy and consultancy in the matters pertaining to various State as well Central laws. Their professional attitude and devotion are earning name and fame for the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and also for other fellow chartered accountants. Now, the chartered accountants are equally competing with the legal practitioners in the field of State and Central legislations as well as with the advocates and owing to varied experience and vast potential of the chartered accountants, the people are preferring to avail the services of the chartered accountants in place of other practitioners engaged in the similar fields. The facts aforesaid are widely accepted ones, which need no evidence.

Is it wrong for a person providing valuable services to the society and the Government to expect equitable treatment from the Government? If the answer to this question is ‘Yes’, then, what the Government has done by issuing Notification No. 2/2006, dated March 1, 2006 for withdrawing service tax exemption to practising chartered accountants is just and all right. But if the readers answer this question as ‘No’, then, one should read the succeeding paras of this article to know how the move of the Government in issuance of Notification No. 2/2006, dated March 1, 2006 for withdrawing service tax exemption to practising chartered accountants has turned out to be unjust and devastating for the practising chartered accountants.

The same is the case with the professionals engaged in practice in the field of company secretaryship and cost accountancy. The exemption from service tax provided to practicing company secretaries and practising cost accountants has also been withdrawn by the aforesaid notification.

The service tax exemption Notification No. 59/98, dated October 16, 1998, which provided full exemption from service tax to services (except the ones specified in that notification) provided by the practising chartered accountants, has been rescinded by the Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006 (a budget notification) and, consequently, all services provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity, have become taxable.

Recent Exemption to Chartered Accountants : One More Reconsideration Needed

The withdrawal of exemption Notification No.59/ 98-Service Tax, dated 16-10-1998 w.e.f. 1-3-2006 resulted in bringing all services rendered by practicing CAs, CWAs and CSs into the service tax net. The idea behind the exemption was to tax these professionals only on the services in which they have monopoly (accounting, auditing, cost audit, secretarial audit) and to exempt other services rendered by them (filing of returns, tax consultancy, representation services) till other professionals (e.g. Advocates) rendering these services were brought under the net. The withdrawal of exemption Notification 59/98 attracted strong reactions and representations were made to the Central Government. The Central Government, in principle, has accepted the representations of ICAI, ICWAI and ICSI that certain specified services rendered by these professionals should be exempted from service tax till the other professionals (e.g. Advocates) rendering these services are also brought into the service tax net. This can be seen from the Government’s Press Note. Therefore, based on these considerations (i.e., to maintain a level playing field), the Central Government has by Notification No.25/2006, dated 13-7-2006 exempted representation services (i.e. services relating to representation before statutory authorities) rendered by these professionals from service tax. The author argues that the logic for exempting representation services applies equally to tax consultancy services, filing of tax returns which constitute the main source of income for many CAs in non-metros and small cities and makes a passionate plea for exempting tax consultancy services and filing of tax returns also from service tax.

Backdrop

1. The Finance Act, 2006 has removed the exemption notification issued with respect to exemption to the Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost Accountants from the services other than audit, accounting and statutory certification services. The above exemption was given through Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax, dated the 16th October, 1998. This Notification was withdrawn w.e.f. 1st March, 2006 and from this date all the services including taxation services rendered by a practicing CA/ICWA/CS in his professional capacity are now covered by service tax. Auditing, accounting and statutory services of the Chartered Accountants were under the scope of service tax since initial stage of imposition of service tax on these professionals.

The other services including the taxation consultancy services were exempted from payment of service tax on the ground that these services are not the monopoly of these professionals and specially in the matter of taxation consultancy which includes consultancy of VAT, income-tax and service tax the Chartered Accountants are facing stiff competition from the other professionals including the Advocates and all these professionals are out of the scope of service tax. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India had termed this levy as discriminatory hence the Government through Notification No. 59/98, dated 16th October, 1998 has exempted the service tax on services other than the Audit, Accounting and statutory certification services.

The situation remains the same and still the Advocates are providing these services but for the reasons best known to our law makers this exemption was abruptly withdrawn on 28th Feb., 2006 w.e.f 1st March, 2006 and the result is that all the services including the taxation consultancy services provided by Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost Accountants are now taxable.

SERVICE TAX ON CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT’S SERVICES

This article is a comprehensive analysis of leviability of service tax on Chartered Accountant’s Services.

Introduction

1. Service tax has been imposed on practising chartered accountant’s services with effect from October 16, 1998 vide Notification No. 53/98-ST, dated October 7, 1998. The gross amount charged by a practising chartered accountant from the client, in professional capacity, is chargeable to service tax.

Meaning of-Practising Chartered Accountant

2. Section 65(83) defines ‘practising chartered accountant’ as under—

‘practising chartered accountant’ means a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and is holding a certificate of practice granted under the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 (38 of 1949) and includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy.

As per section 65(83), a practising chartered accountant is a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, New Delhi and holds a certificate of practice under the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and also includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy. Thus, both associate and fellow members of the Institute are covered. It would also cover individuals as well as firms and persons holding full-time as well as part-time certificate of practice.

According to Webster’s Dictionary, a professional means ‘calling requiring specialised knowledge and often long intensive academic preparation; calling, vocation or employment’. The services should be rendered in this capacity using this skill and knowledge.

‘In any manner’ would mean directly or indirectly, personally or otherwise or through his staff members or through computer aid or other device or manually.

To be treated as a practising chartered accountant, following basic tests must be satisfied—

(i)He must be a person;

(ii)He must be a member (whether associate or fellow) of the Institute to which he belongs (ICAI);

(iii)He must hold a certificate of practice granted by the Institute;

(iv)In case of a firm of the chartered accountants, it must be a concern engaged in rendering services in the field of the chartered accountancy.

Legal position

3. In All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [2007] 10 STT 166 (SC), the Apex Court has settled the levy of service tax on the chartered accountants, cost accountants, and architects, by holding that the Parliament of India has the legislative competence to levy service tax on the professional services rendered by the chartered accountants, the cost accountants, and architects and that professional tax and service tax operate on different spheres.

The Apex Court dealt with the constitutional status of levy of service tax and the legislative competence of the Parliament to impose service tax under article 246(1) and Entry 97 of List-I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India having regard to Entry 60 in List-II of Seventh Schedule (i.e., professional tax). The major findings of the Apex Court in the instant case are as follows—

u As an economic concept, there is no distinction between the consumption of goods and service as both satisfy human needs and this economic concept is based on the legal principle of equivalence.

u Service tax is a VAT which, in turn, is a general tax which applies to all commercial activities involving production of goods and provision of services.

u VAT is a consumption tax as it is borne by the client.

u Applying the principle of equivalence, there is no difference between production or manufacture of saleable goods and production of marketable/saleable services in the form of an activity undertaken by the service provider for consideration, which correspondingly stands consumed by the service receiver. It is this principle of equivalence which is in-built into the concept of service tax, which has received legal support in the form of Finance Act, 1994.

u Service tax is VAT which, in turn, is both a general tax as well as destination based consumption tax leviable on services provided within the country.

u A new charge by way of service tax or tax on service came to be levied statutorily by the Finance Act, 1994, which has subsequently attained Constitutional status by virtue of the Constitution (Eighty-eighth Amendment) Act, 2003.

2.1 A brief legislative history is that service tax was, for the first time, imposed by the Finance Act, 1994. This tax was levied on three types of services. Later on the scope of this tax has been widened almost in every Budget. Service tax on practising chartered accountants was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998 by the Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998. But there were protests against this levy by the CA community all over India. One of the main causes of protest was that, while the service tax was levied on Chartered Accountants’ services, but the same was not levied on the similar services provided by an advocate. Thus, due to protest against the levy by chartered accountants and certain Court decisions, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998 only on auditing and accounting services. The author has analysed the new exemption Notification No. 25/2006-Service Tax, dated 13-7-2006 which exempts representational services provided by a practising CA/CWA/CS, i.e., representing a client before statutory authority in any proceeding initiated by issue of notice. The author points out that there is no definition of ‘statutory authority’ in the notification. Therefore, the term covers any statutory authority before whom CA/CWA/CS is permitted by law to represent his client’s case. Further, the author notes that the new notification gives only partial relief to these professionals from the situation arising out of the withdrawal of Notification No. 59/98 w.e.f. 1-3-2006. The new Notification No.25/2006-Service Tax does not cover services such as taxation services rendered by these professionals which came into the service tax net because of withdrawal of Notification No. 59/98 w.e.f. 1-3-2006. In case of these services, the services provided by these professionals will become costlier as compared to the services provided by other professionals (advocates) who are not in the service tax net.

Introduction

1. Responding to the various representations made, particularly the Joint Memorandum dated 8.3.2006 given by the three professional Institutes (i.e. ICAI, ICSI and ICWAI) both to the Minister for Company Affairs and the Finance Minister with respect to removal of discrimination and providing level playing field to practising chartered accountants, practising cost accountants and practising company secretaries, the Government has issued Exemption Notification No. 25/2006-Service Tax, dated 13-7-2006 which provides that the professional services provided or to be provided by the practising chartered accountants, practising cost accountants and practising company secretaries in relation to representing the client before any statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice, shall be exempt from whole of the service tax.

Extent of Relief

2. Exemption of representation services before any statutory authority has brought certain relief to the CAs, CWAs and CSs, for these services now can be provided on a level playing field. The statutory authorities may include Company Law Board (CLB), ITAT, CESTAT, National Tax Tribunal, National Company Law Tribunal and various other authorities and Tribunals under different laws. Withdrawal of Exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-19981 had resulted in making these services costlier by the amount of service tax if they were to be provided by CAs, CSs or CWAs as compared to the similar services rendered by other categories of professionals. At global level also when world is expecting our professionals to provide BPO/KPO services, CAs, CSs or CWAs may find themselves out of competition because their services, due to the levy of service tax, may be costlier in comparison to those of others.

Representation Services - When Exempt

3. Representation services are exempt only when these are provided in respect of a client who has been issued notice and he is to be represented before the statutory authority in the course of proceedings arising out of issuance of such notice. In a case where representation is to be made without or before issuance of notice to the client, the representation services provided by CAs, CSs or CWAs may not be tax free though in case of other professionals who are authorised to provide such services, they are tax free. This lacuna needs clarification from the department.

So far as statutory authorities are concerned, all are covered though no definition of ‘statutory authority’ as such has been provided. Thus, the CAs, CSs or CWAs may represent the case of their client before any statutory authority if they are authorised to do so.

It is important to note that now the benefit of Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 will not be therefor the defence and the classification may be hit by article 14. Some of the previous case laws on the same are discussed herewith to know the stand of the judiciary. In case of Chartered Accountants Association v. UOI [2000] STT 64/[2001] 115 Taxman 543 (Guj.) [dated 27-12-2000] also, the Chartered Accountants/Consulting Engineers/Architect challenged constitutional validity of provisions levying service tax on consulting engineers, architects and practising chartered accountants on different grounds, but with no success. The relevant part of this decision, which is important for the purpose of understanding, is mentioned below:

"Nature of services provided by a qualified Chartered Accountant, consulting engineer or a qualified architect, is bound to be qualitatively higher than services rendered by non-qualified persons in same or similar fields, and, hence, when Legislature has made a classification between services rendered by a qualified professional and those rendered by a non-qualified person in same or similar field, it would be wrong to say that classification is hit by article 14. [Now by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated 1-3-2006, Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax, dated 16-10-1998 is withdrawn. Though some exemption is provided now, but still the classification may be hit by article 14]"

Thus, what the Gujarat High Court has upheld as reasonable classification is classification between services rendered by a qualified professional and services rendered by a non-qualified person in same or similar field. It has not upheld classification between equally qualified professionals (CAs and Advocates) in same or similar fields.

In other case of Indian Institute of Architects v. UOI [2001] STT 143/[2002] 121 Taxman 821 (Mad.) [dated 30.4.2001] also, the result was same. But the Hon’ble Madras High Court held that:

n The petitioners also argued that the provisions of section 65(48) and section 67(r) and (s) were confusing and arbitrary. The contention in short was that the services which the chartered accountants give is a bundle of service. It is akin to the services rendered by any professional including a medical practitioner and a lawyer and the relationship between a chartered accountant and his clients is like that of a lawyer and his client and it cannot be merely construed as a ‘service’ under the Finance Act 32 of 1990. The tone of the argument was that the Legislature has picked and chosen the chartered accountants or the cost accountants and left out the other professionals like doctors and lawyers. This argument was obviously incorrect because it is for the Legislature to select any particular service or any particular subject for taxing. The tests of the vice of discrimination in a taxing law are less rigorous. In examining the allegations of a hostile discriminatory treatment what is looked into is not its phraseology, but the real effect of its provisions. Therefore, there would be no question of finding any fault with the Legislature for picking up the chartered accountants or the cost accountants or the architects also for taxing their services. But it was not held that on the same services some professionals can be taxed and the others remain out of tax net even if both are of the same standing requiring same professional competence]

Introduction and brief history

1. A brief legislative history is that service tax was, for the first time, imposed by the Finance Act, 1994. This tax was levied on three types of services. Later on the scope of this tax has been widened almost in every Budget. Service tax on practising Chartered Accountants was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998 by the Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998. But there were protest against this levy by the CA community all over India. One of the main causes of protest was that, while the service tax was levied on Chartered Accountants’ services but the same was not levied on the similar services provided by an advocate. Also in case of Jodhpur Chartered Accountants Society v. CCE [1998] STT 33/(105) ELT 290 (Raj.) [dated 24th November, 1998], the operation and implementation of Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998, was stayed and kept in abeyance so far as its application was concerned to the practising Chartered Accountants practising in the State of Rajasthan. Also in many of the other cases, the stay was granted. Thus due to protest against the levy by Chartered Accountants and certain Court decisions, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998 only on auditing and accounting services. So the services provided by CA and Advocate, which can be of similar nature, remains out of service tax. But the later developments are of crucial and patently of discriminatory nature.

Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998, was superseded by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998. From this notification, the nature of services was made more explicit as compared to Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998. But this is not all which happens to these professionals. Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 was amended by Notification No. 15/2002-ST, dated 1-8-2002 w.e.f. 1-8-2002 by inserting an explanation under this notification. This explanation provide that, "Nothing contained in this notification shall apply to the services provided by a practising Chartered Accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant which may fall in any other taxable services as defined in clause (105) of section 65 of the said Act". Also the same was clarified by the following illustration:

"The service provided by a practising Chartered Accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant in connection with the management of any organisation in any manner or recruitment of manpower in any manner shall be deemed to be the taxable service provided under the category of management consultant or manpower recruitment agency, as the case may be. Therefore, no exemption under this notification shall be applicable to such practising Chartered Accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant."

‘Service tax’ was first introduced in India by the Finance Act, 1994, on a few services and subsequently extended to several other services by the relevant Finance Acts. The Finance Act, 1998 brought the services rendered by a chartered accountant within the purview of service tax. In this article, the author attacks the levy of service tax at its very root by arguing that under the Constitution of India, the Parliament has no power to enact service tax legislation and, hence, the levy in question is lacking in constitutional validity. The author also specifically questions the extension of the levy to the profession of chartered accountancy, inter alia, on the ground that the exercise of profession by a chartered accountant does not amount to rendering of ‘service’ - EDITOR

Introduction

1. The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech for the year 1998-99 has observed in para 169 as hereunder:

"169. In the last budget, a number of services were added in the tax net. These included the service rendered on transportation of goods by road. The House is aware that it led to widespread resistance and protests. As a result, this service tax was virtually kept in abeyance and rightly so. I have decided to abolish the service tax on transportation of goods by road. I have also decided to abolish the service tax payable by outdoor caterers and pandal contractors. However, I have proposed service tax on some new services. These are services provided by: Architects, Interior decorators, Management Consultants, Chartered Accountants, Cost Accountants, Company Secretaries, Private security services, Real estate agents and real estate consultants, Market research agencies, Credit rating agencies, Underwriting agencies, Slaughter houses using mechanised means for the large animals.

We will examine how in respect of certain segments liable to Service Tax, the manner and mode of payment could be further simplified to improve compliance. These new service taxes will yield Rs. 220 crore in a full year."

With a view to effecting the aforesaid policy decision, the Finance Bill (No. 2) of 1998 by Chapter VI thereof and clause 129 has effected several ancillary and consequential amendments in the Finance Act, 1994, section 65, etc.

Section 116 of the Finance Act, 1998 has provided for a levy of service tax at 5 per cent on services rendered by practising chartered accountants, cost accountants and company secretaries. The said ‘service tax’ has been brought into effect with effect from October 16, 1998. A further notification issued by the Revenue Department provides that the taxable services rendered to a client by a practising Chartered Accountant or a company secretary or cost accountant which will attract service tax include: accounting and auditing or cost accounting or secretarial auditing or verification of declarations in prescribed forms under section 149 of the Companies Act, 1956 or signing of annual return of listed companies under section 161 of the Companies Act or certification requirements of Schedule XIII to the Companies Act, or certification of documents to be filed with Registrar of Companies or certification in Form No. 1 under the Companies Unpaid Dividend Rules, 1978 or certification of documents under Export and Import Policy (1997-2002) or Certification for exchange control purposes under FERA 1973 or certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets as per rule 8A(7) of the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957. SRINIVASAN ANAND G.

Who is primarily responsible to furnish information in Form No. 3CEB - Taxpayer or the auditor?

The Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill,2012 clarifies that "If the assessee does not report such a transaction in the report furnished under section 92E then the Assessing Officer would normally not be aware of such an International Transaction so as to make a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer." Thus, from the Explanatory Memorandum, it is clear that it is the primary responsibility of an asssessee to furnish correct and complete details of all international transactions/SDTs undertaken by him during the year.

Who can be appointed for conduct the audit envisaged under section 92E

Who is eligible to be the auditor u/s 92E?

According to section 92E, the report should be an 'accountant'. Section 92F(i) defines 'accountant' has having the same meaning as in Explanation below section 288(2). According to the above mentioned explanation, it covers a CA and Restricted State auditor.

According to ICAI's 'Guidance Note on Report on International Transactions under section 92E of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Transfer Pricing)' hereinafter referred to as "Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing" :

♦ Section 92E refers to "an accountant" which means a Chartered Accountant as defined in Chartered Accountants Act, 1949.

♦ However, audit under section 92E can be done by a firm of Chartered Accountants also.

Extending the above logic of the Guidance Note further, a view can be taken that w.e.f. 1-3-2011 [date on which Chartered Accountants (Amendment) Act, 2011 came into force] LLPs of CAs in practice/CAs in practice with other prescribed professionals can be appointed for transfer pricing audit u/s 92E. CBDT/ICAI needs to clarify this.

Can audit under section 92E be conducted by an employee of assessee-client?

In Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 169 Taxman 328 (SC), the Supreme Court held that "An auditor is a professional person". He has to function independently. He is not an employee of the assessee.

Is it necessary that tax audit under section 92E shall be a CA in full-time practice?

Yes. At its 242nd meeting, the Council of ICAI has decided that any member in part-time practice (i.e. a member who is holding certificate of practice and also engaged in any other business/occupation) shall not be entitled to perform attest functions. Therefore, a CA in part-time practice cannot be appointed as auditor under section 92E.

In case of companies, is it necessary that audit u/s 92E be conducted by statutory auditor?

No. In case of companies, it can be done by the statutory auditor of the company appointed under section 224 of the Companies Act, 1956 or by any other CA in practice or firm of CAs. This is because section 92E does not require that only the statutory auditor should perform the audit under section 92E.

Whether a CA or firm of CAs appointed as tax consultants can conduct audit u/s 92E?

A CA/firm of CAs who are appointed as tax consultants may be appointed as auditor under section 92E. [ICAI's Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing]

Can a CA or CA firm who is internal auditor of assessee can also be auditor u/s 92E?

No. Internal auditor cannot give audit report u/s 92E. [ICAI's Code of Ethics]

Is there any limit on the number of audits under section 92E which a CA/CA firm can accept?

No. There is no limit on number of audits u/s 92E which CA/CA firm can accept.

Is there any minimum fee to be charged by CA firms for Tax audits?

No. Chapter XII of the Council General Guidelines has been omitted with effect from 7-6-2011. Hence, no minimum fee stipulated for audits at the moment.

Scope of audit under section 92E

What are the matters covered by scope of the audit u/s 92E?

It covers the following:

♦ Examination of only those accounts and records of the assessee which relate to international transactions/SDTs entered into by him during the previous year under audit.

♦ Ascertaining and reporting whether the assessee has maintained proper information and documentations prescribed in respect of international transactions entered into by him.

Extended scope of service tax on practising Chartered Accountants - Unjustified withdrawal of exemption

The earlier exemption for services other than accounting, auditing, and statutory certification services provided by practising CA, company secretary, or cost accountant in his professional capacity, stands withdrawn from March 1, 2006. Taking exception to this withdrawal, the author points out that this is discriminatory as for the same type of service the other professionals including the legal and tax practitioners are not liable to pay service tax. The author also points out that the move goes against the basic tenet of service tax levy, i.e. , service tax is a tax on services and not on the service provider or the professionals providing the services. It will snatch the level playing field from a professional. In this particular case, this is a tax on a professional or on a particular profession and not on a particular service because the others providing the same service are not required to pay the tax. The author submits that the withdrawal of exemption notification is totally discriminatory, unwarranted and unjustified and as a remedial action the exemption notification should be restored in the same spirit in which it was initially provided.

The main point raised by some service providers is that where they are carrying out any certification as required by any statute can it come under the purview of consultancy, advice or technical assistance. The Government clarified the same through the Circular F.No. 177/5/2001-CX. 4, dated 26-2-2002. It was clarified that the certificates given under authority of any statute/international protocol/code/convention, cannot be considered to be a consultancy job. It is then to be examined whether this activity can come under the purview of advice or technical assistance. An advice is generally understood to be optional in nature and has no statutory force. It is up to the client to accept the advice or not. The activity of certification will, therefore, not fall under the category of advice. As regards ‘technical assistance’, it is observed that an assistance is normally for the purpose of achieving a particular aim or result. A certificate given by, say, the Boiler Inspector under the Factories Act, 1948, about the safety of a boiler, cannot be considered to be ‘assistance’ to the person using the said boiler in his factory. To issue certificates under the authority of any statute, it will obviously be necessary for the certifying agency to conduct some survey/inspection. Thus, the survey/inspection by an agency for the purposes of issuing certificates by the same agency under an authority of law, will also not amount to consultancy advice or technical assistance. If however, the shipping company gets the ship surveyed or inspected by another agency, before taking it for certification by an authorised agency, only then can it be said that the first agency is providing some technical assistance or advice. It will, therefore, be essential to examine each activity of a service provider on the basis of facts, the terms of agreement between the assessee and the clients and the corresponding provision of Indian or International statute/convention/protocol, or code, to determine whether the certificate being given is under the authority of any such statute, convention protocol or code. If it is so, the payment received for that service will not be taxable under the head "Consulting engineer". Any other inspection, survey, assessment, technical assistance, consultancy, recommendation, advice, undertaken/provided directly or indirectly, by the assessee would be liable to service tax under the head ‘Consulting engineer’. CBE&C not charitable about ‘Charitable’

11. As per section 65(25a ),definition of "club or association" does not include— (iii) any person or body of persons engaged in any activity having objectives which are in the nature of public service and are of a charitable, religious or political nature.

‘Charitable’ means ‘generous in giving to those in need’ or ‘of, or relating to, or connected with a charity or charities’. ‘Charity’ means giving voluntarily to those in need, alms-giving’ – Concise Oxford Dictionary.

Thus, the word ‘charity’ has narrow meaning in dictionary. However, the word has acquired a technical meaning in law, which is wide.

As per section 2 of Charitable Endowments Act, 1890, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief to poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general public utility, but does not include a purpose which relates exclusively to religious teaching or worship. As per section 2(15) of Income-tax Act, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief of the poor, education, medical relief, and the advancement of any other object of general public utility.

Thus, any object of ‘general public utility’ will be a ‘charitable purpose’. Hence, the wide meaning should apply and not narrow dictionary meaning. However, department is of the view that narrow meaning should apply – CBE&C, vide Circular No. 84/2/2006-ST dated 19-9-2006.

(supra), the assessee had chosen CPM and TNMM with a mark-up of 5 per cent for on-site software development services and 10 per cent for marketing services as provided in the agreement. The TPO, however, considered CUP method as the most suitable one. But then, the problem was in selecting comparable cases for application of this method.

There is considerable discussion as to the computation with reference to each of the methods by the Special Bench. Adoption of Nasscom average hourly rate, it was found, does not meet the requirement of CUP method to justify the mark-up rate over the assessee’s cost. The Special Bench pointed out OECD Guidelines on International Transfer Pricing, 2006, which required adjustments for

-Differences in the quality of the products;

-Differences in the geographic markets;

-Differences in the level of the market; and

-Differences in the amount and type of intangible property involved.

The Special Bench had set out the guidelines and set aside the assessment, while pointing out, that the burden of proof vested on the assessee to prove the declared price to be the arm’s length price. The Special Bench after referring to OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines would not consider TNMM as the most appropriate method. For purposes of Bench marking under this method, it was pointed out that it is necessary to arrive at net margin earned by comparable uncontrolled transaction, so as to require the data necessary for CUP method. The manner in which net margin was worked out was also faulted as it took into consideration only the net margin earned by the associated enterprise on its entire business activities. The cases chosen by the Assessing Officer for comparability was also found to be not completely reliable. Incidentally, it was found that the RPM was not applicable, since the assessee was not a reseller of goods or services. The CPM requires verification of cost. PSM was rejected, because it was not a case of ‘unique intangibles or multiple inseparable transactions’ apart from the fact that this method is rarely used. TNM method, on the other hand, requires consideration of the specified transactions and not overall business. It is under these circumstances, that the matter was restored to the Assessing Officer on the basis of the guidance thus offered.

Section 65(105)(j) - Clearing and Forwarding Agent’s Services - Whether service receiver can deduct amount of service tax from service provider’s bill

6.2 Facts The respondent, a transport contractor, entered into a contract with the appellant for handling of its materials. During the pendency of the said contract, section 65 was substituted by section 88 whereby 5 per cent service tax was introduced on various services including ‘clearing and forwarding (C&F) agent’. The appellant, consequently, deducted 5 per cent service tax from the respondent’s bills on the assumption that the respondent was a C&F agent from 31-10-1997 in spite of respondent’s objections. On reference, the sole arbitrator dismissed the respondent’s objection. On petition filed by the respondent, the Single Judge of the High Court allowed the same by setting aside the impugned award.

Decision of Bombay High Court:

u The High Court held that the constitutional validity with regard to the extension of service tax in view of the amendment to the Finance Act, 2000, section 116(a) and section 65(6) to treat the recipients of the services as an assessee in case of services rendered by goods transport operators and clearing and forwarding agents, was upheld by the Supreme Court in Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd. v. Union of India [2005] 1 STT 41.

u The High Court further held that Single Judge had set aside the award passed by the arbitrator by which the arbitrator held that the appellant was entitled to deduct the service tax amount from the amount payable to the respondent. Admittedly, the appellant was recipient of the service of the respondents as per the agreement-in-question. The appellant, pursuant to the provisions of service tax was registered and recognized as an ‘assessee’ and had also filed returns as contemplated accordingly. The appellant, therefore, was liable to pay the service tax being the recipient of the services from the respondent. Admittedly, there was no specific agreement with regard to payment of service tax-in-question by the respondent to the extent the appellant would be entitled to deduct the amount so paid or payable under the service tax, though the respondent was not an assessee and/or not liable to pay service tax under the law. There was no specific clause that such service tax liability would be deductible from the amount payable by the appellant to the respondent pursuant to the contract-in-question. The deduction as claimed and as directed by the award in absence of any agreement or clause, therefore, was not correct. The department, on application filed by the applicant, already rejected the specific claim of refund of that amount.

u The High Court further observed that there was nothing to show even from the plain reading of the agreement and the clauses thereof that, payment of service tax, though payable by the ‘assessee’, yet it would be the respondent, the service provider, to re-pay the same to the appellant and, therefore, the appellant was entitled to deduct service tax from the bills of the respondent in terms of the clauses of the agreement. The Single Judge, therefore, was right in reversing the award passed by the arbitrator. The agreement nowhere entitled the appellant to deduct and/or to recover such service tax from the respondent. Therefore, the High Court held, as rightly held by the Single Judge, that the award was, on the face of it, illegal and erroneous.

[Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. v. Dewan Chand Ram Saran [2008] 14 STT 328 (Bom.)]

10E.3 The meaning of "accountant" now applies for the definition of an "authorised representative" u/s 288(2). As a result, in order to be appointed as an authorised representative for an assessee for any proceedings under the Act, a Chartered Accountant must have a certificate of practice. However, a Chartered Accountant having any other qualification specified in section 288 may be appointed as an authorised representative. Therefore, after this amendment, a Chartered Accountant who does not satisfy both the following conditions cannot be appointed as an authorised representative for an assessee:—

(i)

He/she does not have a certificate of practice; and

(ii)

He/she does not have any other specified qualification.

Though the section refers to the accounts being examined by an accountant, which means a Chartered Accountant, the examination can also be done by a firm of chartered accountants. This has been a recognised practice under the Act. In such a case, it would be necessary to state the name of the partner who has signed the report on behalf of the firm. The accountant signing the report as a partner of a firm or in his individual capacity should give his membership number below his name.

As per the decision taken by the Council of the ICAI, all attest functions undertaken by the members have to bear a UDIN issued by the ICAI. The same needs to be mentioned on the document being signed/attested by the member.

Section 92E does not stipulate that only the statutory auditor appointed under the Companies Act or other similar statute should perform the examination. The examination can, therefore, be conducted either by the statutory auditor or by any other Chartered Accountant in practice having certificate of practice.

The issue of a report u/s 92E, being a recurring assignment for expressing a professional opinion, the accountant accepting the assignment should communicate with the accountant who had done the examination in the earlier year, as provided in the Chartered Accountants Act. In the case of a person whose accounts of the business or profession have been audited under any other law (i.e., a company, a co-operative society, etc. which is required to get the accounts audited under a statute), it is not necessary to communicate with the statutory auditor if he had not done the examination in the earlier year.

The accountant should obtain from the assessee a letter of appointment for conducting the examination as mentioned in section 92E. It is advisable that such an appointment letter should be signed by the person competent to sign/verify the return of income in terms of the provisions of section 140 or by any person who has been authorized by the company to make such an appointment. The accountant should get the statement of particulars, as required in the annexure to the report, authenticated by the assessee before he proceeds to verify the same. The accountant is required to submit his report to the person appointing him, viz., the assessee.

The appointment of the accountant in the case of a company need not be made at the general meeting of the members. It can be made by the Board of Directors or even by any officer, if so authorised by the Board in this behalf. The appointment in the case of a firm or a proprietary concern can be made by a partner or the proprietor or a person authorised by the assessee. It is possible for the assessee to appoint two or more Chartered Accountants for carrying out the examination, in which case, the report will have to be signed by all the chartered accountants. In case of disagreement, they can give their reports separately.

The Act prohibits a relative or an employee of the assessee being appointed as an accountant under section 92E. Also, as per a decision of the Council (reported in the Code of Ethics under clause (4) of Part I of Second Schedule), a Chartered Accountant who is in employment of a concern or in any other concern under the same management cannot be appointed as an auditor of that concern. Therefore, an employee of an assessee or an employee of a concern under the same management cannot examine the accounts and records of an assessee u/s 92E.

An accountant responsible for writing or the maintenance of the books of account of the assessee should not examine such accounts. On scrutiny assessment, the Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax (R-3) issued notice requiring PWH to file its computation of income and tax for year, audit profit and loss account and balance sheet, tax and audit report issued under section 44AB. PWH filed all the necessary documents

Thereafter R-3 issued a letter to PWH informing it that a reference had been made to the TPO and called upon PWH to file details requested for in earlier notices.

PWH contended that TPO regulations did not apply to PWH as it did not have a relationship of being AE with any overseas network entity. It further contended that it had never entered into any international transaction envisaged under section 92B, and hence, it was unable to comprehend the reasons for which reference had been made under section 92CA(1) to the TPO. It is well settled through series of judgments of the High Courts and Supreme Court that writ jurisdiction of the High Courts in exercise of powers under article 226 of Constitution of India is extremely wide. If a jurisdictional error is pointed out or it is shown that an authority has acted wholly without jurisdiction, the Court can, without relegating the petitioner/assessee to the departmental or even statutory remedies, strike down exercise of such powers. Therefore, if it is found that the action of the TPO or a part of it which can be severed from the rest is wholly without jurisdiction, such order or part thereof is to be struck down even though statute provides certain appeal remedies to the aggrieved assessee.[Para 4]

It is indisputable that by virtue of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, in case of an international transaction, the TPO would have an authority to examine any international transaction which comes to his notice during the proceedings, whether a reference in this respect was made by the Assessing Officer or not and whether the assessee had reported such transaction under section 92E or not. However, in view of specific non-inclusion of the specified domestic transaction under the said sub-sections, in so far as the domestic transactions are concerned, the situation would be vastly different.[Para 13]

In plain terms, in absence of sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92CA, the TPO would get jurisdiction to examine a transaction whether it is international or specified domestic transaction, only upon reference being made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1) of section 92CA. Sub-section (2) of section 92CA provides that where a reference is made under sub-section (1), the TPO would serve a notice to the assessee requiring him to furnish details in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction referred to in sub-section (1). Thus, the jurisdiction of the TPO to issue a notice to the assessee would be in relation to international transaction or specified domestic transaction for which reference is made by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). It is precisely for this reason that sub-sections (2A) and (2B) provide a deeming fiction where they provide that in case of an international transaction not referred to the TPO or an international transaction not reported by the assessee, which comes to his notice during the proceedings, the provision of the Chapter would apply as if such international transaction was one referred to in sub-section (1). In absence of this deeming fiction, it would not be open for the TPO to exercise the powers under the said chapter in relation to the transaction not referred to him. The reference to be made by the Assessing Officer is not an empty formality. Said reference has to be made only on approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. Legislature, requires the Assessing Officer to obtain an approval from senior Revenue Authority before a reference is made. Such requirement cannot be jettisoned by the TPO exercising suo motu jurisdiction over the transaction not reported to him.[Para 14]

Inescapable conclusion that is reached is that in relation to a specified domestic transaction, the TPO can under take transfer pricing study only in relation to those transactions which are referred to him under sub-section (1) of section 92C. Sub-sections (2A) and (2B) of section 92C are confined to international transactions and with the aid of any interpretive process, the said provision cannot be applied to empower the TPO to examine any specified domestic transaction not referred to him by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (1). Any other view would be doing violence to the plain language of the statute.[Para 17]

The revenue is correct in pointing out that in the instant case, the assessee did not report such transaction at all and therefore, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to notice such transaction as specified domestic transaction. His reference, therefore, was necessarily confined to the reported transactions. The TPO noticed this anomaly, he proceeded to determine the arm's length price after full opportunity of hearing to the assessee.[Para 18]

Further the Supreme Court in T.D. Venkata Rao (supra) has accepted the fact that Chartered Accountants by the reason of their training have special aptitude in the matter of audit. The act of maintaining accounts is neither pleading, practice nor acting. For the reasons already discussed, the challenge to the Constitutional validity of the Legislation under articles 14 and 19 at the instance of the Bar Council will also have to be rejected. [Para 23] The Petitioners have not disputed that in the matter of enacting the law pertaining to recovery of sales tax, the same clearly fall within entry 54 of the State List. If in the process of making legislation, the legislature in its wisdom provides for the procedure in the manner in which tax has to be levied, maintenance of books, procedure for checking correctness or verification of books, it cannot be said that the same amounts to ancillary legislation or procedure not falling within the competence of the State Legislature under Entry 54. The Act requires that the dealer has to maintain books and the books have to be audited and required to be certified by a Chartered Accountant. That will not result in the legislation falling outside the competence of the State Legislature. The Legislation in pith and substance is relatable to imposition of sales tax which is within the competence of the State Legislature. The Courts examine and ascertain the pith and substance on scrutiny of the true character of the enactment. [Para 24]

It also cannot be said that in such a case audit by a Chartered Accountant would amount to outsourcing the statutory power to the third party. The Legislature can always delegate its powers as long as such delegation does not amount to abdication of its essential legislative functions. In the instant case, there is no abdication of the essential legislative functions. All that the section requires is that the accountant has to audit the accounts and to issue certificate that the dealer has maintained the books as required to be maintained under the Act and rules. The dealer has to file his accounts audited with the certificate. This neither amounts to abdication nor excessive delegation. Such an exercise also does not amount to conferring on the accountant a power to determine the correct tax liability of the dealer. The power to accept returns is of the Authorities under the Act. Even after the certificate is issued, that the dealer has maintained books, it is always open to the Commissioner under section 20 to ascertain whether the return is correct and complete or order an audit under section 22 to get the accounts audited by the officers of the department. A certificate, therefore, is not determinative but to enable the department to consider that the person having knowledge of audit and subject to the disciplinary control of its parent body has certified that the accounts are properly maintained. This is to aid the officers in discharging their statutory duties. This challenge, therefore, has to be rejected. [Para 25]

Further, it is for the dealer to decide whose services he seeks to obtain for appearance before the Sales Tax Authorities or for getting the accounts audited. Under section 82, there are a class of persons from whom a dealer can obtain services for being represented before the authorities under the Act. Section 72A of Finance Act, 1994 (as inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012) make provision for special audit by practicing Chartered/Cost Accountant [earlier, section 14AA of Central Excise Act was made applicable to service tax. This section provided only for special audit of Cenvat credit availed].

Special audit can be ordered by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Central Excise [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

Such audit can be ordered if the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of CE has reason to believe that any person liable to pay service tax—

(i)

has failed to declare or determine the value of a taxable service correctly; or

(ii)

has availed and utilised credit of duty or tax paid - (a) which is not within the normal limits having regard to the nature of taxable service provided, the extent of capital goods used or the type of inputs or input services used, or any other relevant factors as he may deem appropriate; or (b) by means of fraud, collusion, or any wilful misstatement or suppression of facts; or

(iii)

has operations spread out in multiple locations and it is not possible or practicable to obtain a true and complete picture of his accounts from the registered premises falling under the jurisdiction of the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner [section 72A(1) of Finance Act, 1994].

In such cases, the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner may direct such person to get his accounts audited by a chartered accountant or cost accountant nominated by him, to the extent and for the period as may be specified by the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner [section 72A(2) of Finance Act, 1994, inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012] [Reference to 'Principal Commissioner' has been added w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

The provisions of special audit apply even if audit was conducted under some other law [section 72A(3) of Finance Act, 1994]

The auditee (person liable to pay service tax) shall be given opportunity of hearing in respect of any material gathered on the basis of such special audit and proposed to be utilised in any proceedings against him [section 72A(4) of Finance Act, 1994 inserted w.e.f. 28-5-2012]

Section 14AA of Central Excise Act provides that the audit fees will be paid by Central Government (i.e. service tax department). However, section 72A of Finance Act, 1994 makes no provision of fees of the Chartered/Cost Accountant for such audit.

As per rule 5A(2) of Service Tax Rules (as amended w.e.f. 5-12-2014), assessee is required to produce records maintained by him to cost/chartered accountant nominated under section 72A of Finance Act, 1994.

Further, the TPO as defined in Explanation to section 92CA to be the person authorized by board to perform functions of Assessing Officer specified in section 92C. In sub-section (3) of section 144B, roles of Technical unit is clearly spelt out according to which, functions of technical unit includes assistance or advice on transfer pricing issues. During the course of performing such function, the technical unit can obtain advice from the TPO on the issue of determination of arm's length price of international transaction as they are expert in this field. Thus, the reference by technical unit to TPO is in accordance with the provisions of the Act and therefore, consequent orders passed are not barred by limitations. [Para 10]

HEADNOTE: Section 92C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Transfer pricing - Computation of arm’s length price (Comparables and adjustments/Adjustments - General) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Whether TPO cannot sit in judgment of business module of assessee and its intention to avail or not to avail any services from its associated enterprises and role of TPO is to determine arm's length price of international transactions undertaken by assessee and whether same is at arm's length price when compared with similar transactions undertaken by external entities or internal comparables - Held, yes - Assessee had entered into international transactions of import of raw materials, trading goods and components, export of finished goods, income from services, information technology services availed and reimbursement of expenses with its associated enterprises - Five transactions were benchmarked together by using TNMM - However, transaction of information technology services had been segregated by TPO - TPO held that since assessee had failed to prove receipt of services and benefits derived from services with supporting evidence, arm's length price of transactions was to be treated as Nil and hence, adjustment was proposed to be made to arm's length price - It was found that information technology services availed by assessee also related to business carried on by assessee - Whether information technology services availed had to be aggregated with other transactions being intrinsically linked to other international transactions undertaken by assessee - Held, yes - Whether since various documents were filed by assessee which included certificate of AE evidencing not only availment of services but also basis of cost for such services and similar services were availed by other group entities from AE at same rates as charged to assessee, order of TPO/Assessing Officer was unjustified - Held, yes [Paras 18 to 39] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT/ILT: TPO cannot sit in judgment of business module of assessee and its intention to avail or not to avail any services from its associated enterprises and role of TPO is to determine arm's length price of international transactions undertaken by assessee and whether same is at arm's length price when compared with similar transactions undertaken by external entities or internal comparables

FACT: The assessee had entered into international transactions of import of raw materials, trading goods and components, export of finished goods, income from services, information technology services availed and reimbursement of expenses with its associated enterprises. The first five transactions were benchmarked together by using TNMM. The case of assessee that all these transactions need to be aggregated as they were interdependent on each other while benchmarking international transactions to be at arm's length price.

However, the transaction of information technology services availed had been segregated by the TPO.

The assessee claimed that the said information technologies services had been availed by it from its AE, namely, Eaton China for Information Technology (IT) and related support services. The assessee also during the course of assessment proceedings filed certificate issued by Eaton China certifying the factum of provision of services by it to the assessee. Eaton China also confirmed that other Eaton group companies availing same services were also charged on the same basis as the assessee.

The TPO was of the view that the assessee had to prove that the services were rendered and the second aspect of intra-group service was the quantification of such services in terms of actual expenditure incurred and commensurate benefit derived therefrom. The TPO thus, held that where the assessee had failed to prove the receipt of services and benefits derived from services with supporting evidence, the arm's length price of transactions was treated as Nil and hence, adjustment was proposed to be made to the arm's length price.

The assessee was aggrieved by the order of Assessing Officer / TPO in splitting up the assessee's operations into manufacturing and trading segment and benchmarking the same separately, despite the fact that both the activities were closely inter-linked.

HELD: In the first instance, TPO cannot sit in the judgment of business module of assessee and its intention to avail or not to avail any services from its associated enterprises the role of TPO is to determine the arm's length price of international transactions undertaken by the assessee and whether the same is at arm's length price when compared with similar transactions undertaken by external entities or internal comparables. [Para 29]

The clause does not require the tax auditor to audit whether the assessee has complied with Chapter X provisions regarding the international transactions he entered into and whether suo motu made appropriate TP adjustments in his ITR. Nor is the tax auditor required to examine or report whether the assessee has maintained proper records as required by Rule 10D regarding international transactions. Nor is he required to examine whether the Arm's Length Price has been determined for international transactions in accordance with any of the recognised methods specified in Section 92F. That is the subject of the audit to be carried out under Section 92E, and the report is to be furnished in Form No. 3CEB.

The tax auditor must report in this clause only if a primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1). If no primary transfer pricing adjustment has been made under any of the Clauses in Section 92CE(1), the tax auditor has no duty to report. The tax auditor is not even required to report if the primary TP adjustment has not been made as per the APA entered into by the assessee. If primary TP adjustment has been made according to the APA, then the reporting obligation under this Clause is triggered.

This clause also does not deal with Thin Cap adjustments under Section 94B. That is the subject matter of Clause 30B.

This Clause also does not deal with the issue of shares at a premium to non-resident investors by a closely held company that attracts Section 56(2)(vii). That is the subject matter of Clause 29A.

Although the tax auditor is not required to examine compliance with transfer pricing provisions under Chapter X of the Act except to the limited extent required by Clauses 30A, 30B and 43 of Form No. 3CD, it may be advisable for him to do so to identify impermissible avoidance arrangements for Clause 30C purposes as unacceptable circumvention of SAARs like Transfer Pricing provisions would attract GAAR. Indian Transfer Pricing law is essentially all about adjustments required if the pricing in international transactions is not at arm's length. There is no scope for adjustments for non-arm's length non-price terms and conditions as Chapter X has no treaty equivalent transfer pricing provisions along the lines of Article 9 of OECD Model Conventions. Nevertheless, the tax auditor may find it useful to examine if any of the non-price terms and conditions of international transactions are not at arm's length from the angle of Clause 30C.
