[Para 26] Coming to the second issue by which the TPO determined Nil ALP of the international transaction without applying any specific method. In this regard, section 92(1) of the Act provides that 'Any income arising from an international transaction shall be computed having regard to the arm's length price'. Section 92C of the Act deals with the computation of ALP. Sub-section (1) of 92C, at the material time, provides that: 'The arm's length price in relation to an international transaction shall be determined by any of the following methods, being the most appropriate method, having regard to the nature of transaction or class of transaction or class of associated persons or functions performed by such persons or such other relevant factors as the Board may prescribe, namely:-

(a)

Comparable uncontrolled price method;

(b)

resale price method;

(c)

cost plus method;

(d)

profit split method;

(e)

transactional net margin method;

(f)

such other method as may be prescribed by the Board.' [Para 27]

A perusal of the provision divulges that the ALP in relation to an international transaction 'shall' be determined by any one of the prescribed methods, which is most appropriate method for the transaction under consideration. The term 'shall' used in the provision gives it a status of mandatory character and it cannot be construed here as directory so as to empower the TPO to determine the ALP of an international transaction in an arbitrary manner. He has to confine himself to one of the prescribed methods for determination of the ALP of international transaction, for which mechanism has been prescribed in Rule 10B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962. Thus, it is evident that the ALP of an international transaction can be determined only by applying one of the prescribed methods given under section 92C(1). If the ALP is determined by TPO by not applying any method at all or by choosing a method which is not prescribed under section 92C(1), then such a determination of ALP frustrates the transfer pricing addition. Since the methods prescribed for determining the ALP are statutory prescription, it is absolutely essential for the TPO to compute the ALP by adhering strictly to one of such methods. [Para 28]

Notwithstanding the above, it is necessary to examine if the ALP of the international transaction of payment of 'Management support services fees', is at ALP. [Para 30]

Price Waterhouse (PW) Bangalore, a CA firm, was given the audit for auditing the books of account 'SCSL', which was regarded as one of top IT outsourcing firms in the world.

In the year 2009, the SEBI received an email from the then Chairman of SCSL stating that the statements of accounts of SCSL were not true and fair. The e-mail basically revealed that there was large scale financial manipulation in the books of account of SCSL, namely, that the balance sheet of SCSL as of 30-9-2008 carried inflated/non-existent cash and bank balances.

Investigation carried out by the SEBI revealed that certain directors and employees of SCSL had connived and collaborated in the overstatement, fabrication, falsification and misrepresentation in the books of account and financial statements of SCSL. The investigation also noted that the statutory auditors of SCSL had connived with the directors and employees of SCSL in falsifying the financial statements of SCSL.

Show-cause notice was issued to PW Bangalore and its two partners who signed balance sheets of SCSL, seeking to take action for violation of sections 12A(a), 12A(b) and 12A(c) read with regulations 3(c), 3(d), 4(1), 4(2)(a), 4(2)(e), 4(2)(f), 4(2)(k) and 4(2)(r) of the SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations. The SCL inter alia alleged gross negligence and recklessness in conducting an audit in accordance with the accounting standards and repeatedly deviating from the mandated course of audit especially in relation to items of significant materiality; and failure to consider the direct confirmations received from banks with respect to the figures of fixed deposits while blindly relying on the indirect confirmations received from SCSL which showed higher balances. It was also mentioned in the SCN that PWC International Ltd. had approved 11 partnership firms consisting of Chartered Accountants as their partners to use the name 'Price Waterhouse' in India and that the 11 firms had common branch offices located in New Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurgaon, Bhuvneshwar & Ahmedabad and there were several common partners in these firms. These firms shared resources, manpower, offices, revenues, etc. amongst themselves and, for this purpose, the 11 firms had entered into an agreement in 2000 for resource sharing. It was further stated that the members of the "engagement team" which worked on the audit of SCSL was on the payroll of Price Waterhouse Kolkata and Lovelock & Lewes Kolkata.

Two writ petitions were filed before the Bombay High Court, first by PW Bangalore and second by ten other CA firms along with their partners who were using the brand name Price Waterhouse in India, for quashing of the SCNs on the ground that SEBI lacked jurisdiction as it was encroaching upon the jurisdiction of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI)

The Bombay High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that it could not be said that SEBI at that stage, had no jurisdiction to issue a SCN simply because the appellants were professional Chartered Accountants. The Bombay High Court, however, set out the scope and extent of SEBI's power under sections 11 and 11B, read with regulation 11 of the PFUTP Regulations to act against Chartered Accountants and the circumstances under which SEBI could issue direction to Chartered Accountants acting in their professional capacity. The Bombay High Court emphatically held that the jurisdiction of SEBI in the instant case would depend upon the evidence which was available during the investigation and that if there was only some omission without any mens rea or connivance with anyone, in any manner, then SEBI could not issue any further direction.

Thereafter, the WTM held that failure to seek external confirmation of the bank balances, fixed deposits, failure to detect fake invoices without adopting the rigorous procedure mandated by AAS drew an inference of gross negligence and inference of involvement of appellants in the fudging of the accounts. This gross negligence amounted to an act of commission of a fraud for the purposes of SEBI - Act and SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations for which mens rea was not required to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt but could be based on a preponderance of probability.

Therefore, the argument that the service tax could have been legitimately charged by the State Government under a State enactment was incorrect and it had to be held that while the profession tax deals with the privilege to practice a particular profession, the service tax deals with the 'services' provided by the professionals and, therefore, the two are distinct and separate and the service tax cannot be viewed or confused as a tax on profession. [Paras 14, 15, 17, 22, 24] As regards the argument regarding linking of the measure of tax with income, article 276(2) itself creates a fiction that though a tax on profession relates to an income therefrom, it would not be so and the creation of a limit to the professional tax in article 276(2) itself suggests that income from the profession is irrelevant in the matter of tax on profession. It is only with that idea that clause (2) creates a limit. The creation of the limit itself gives a distinct character to the tax on profession and, therefore, a tax which is not fettered by a limit like the one created by article 276(2) and which relates to the professional income, cannot be viewed as a professional tax. Even if service tax is linked with the professional income or the professional services, it has a 'distinct aspect' of services. The tax is not on the basis that a professional is carrying on his profession like a chartered accountant or a cost accountant. The tax is, on the other hand, on the professional services offered by him to the clients and the service aspect is a distinct aspect and cannot be confused with the aspect of a tax which arises only on account of the fact that a professional is having the privilege of carrying on his profession. A tax which the professional has to pay because he has had the privilege to carry on the profession or because he is carrying on the profession in a particular State is totally distinct and separate from the tax which he has to pay on services and which tax he would be able to pass on to the customer who has the advantage of his professional services. A professional tax covered under Entry 60 cannot be transferred in sharp contradistinction with the service tax, which is capable of being transferred to the customer. Again, professional tax has to be paid whether a professional actually has given the professional service or not whereas, the service tax would not be payable if a professional like a chartered accountant or a cost accountant has in reality not rendered any professional services to a customer. These aspects are distinct aspects and, therefore, an aspect which entirely depends upon the services offered by the professional though may have a nexus with profession, yet the service becomes a distinct aspect in itself and can be legitimately taxed by the Parliament under Entry 97 of List I as had been done in the instant case. [Paras 25, 27]

Therefore, the aspect of service is entirely a distinct aspect from the aspect of the profession though there can be some latent overlapping but there is no overlapping in law. The criticism against the judgments of the Gujarat High Court and Bombay High Court in Chartered Accountants' Association v. Union of India [2001] 252 ITR 53/ 115 Taxman 543 and All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [2002] 256 ITR 401 could not be upheld. [Paras 28, 29]

As regards the argument that provisions of sections 65(48) and 67(r) and 67(s) are confusing and contrary, the tone of the argument was that the Legislature had picked and chosen chartered accountants or cost accountants and left out other professionals like doctors and lawyers. That argument was incorrect because it is for the Legislature to select any particular service or any particular subject for taxing. The celebrated judgment in Federation of Hotel & Restaurant Association of India v. Union of India [1989] 178 ITR 97/46 Taxman 47 (SC) aptly covers the subject. [Paras 32, 33]

Therefore, there would be no question of finding any fault with the Legislature for picking up chartered accountants or cost accountants or architects also for taxing their services. [Para 34]

Payment towards 'Headquarter Common Expenses' and 'Allocation of Regional Management Assistance'

This issue is with regard to the adjustment made on account of charges for intra-group services paid by assessee to its associated enterprises. The assessee claims that it was only having manufacturing facility in India and all the other services were provided by associated enterprises, for which assessee had entered into separate agreements with two entities i.e., Nalco Singapore and Nalco US. The services which were received under the Regional Management and Assistance Services were as per agreement entered into by the assessee with Nalco Singapore. The said services were availed in the field of marketing, sales, business and market development, information systems services, logistic support, human resources services, regional finance services, regional procurement services, research and development services, etc. The appropriation was made under the Asia Pacific Procurement Policy. Further, the assessee had also received support services from the Asia Pacific IT team in setting up of IT facility of new office at Pune and evidence in this regard is also provided. Further, support was also received from global team in errors faced in accounting in Vendor account in SAP and tracking payments and the evidences are also provided. Further, the assessee has also received HR support by way of e-mails between Global HR and Indian HR on account of increments, salary hikes and also technical training conducted in Dubai, evidences in this regard are also provided. The associated enterprise was providing such support services to all entities in the Asia Pacific Region and methodology was adopted for allocating the cost entity-wise and allocation of costs were further certified by an independent accountant. In respect of services availed from Nalco Singapore, the assessee had paid sum of Rs. 25.70 crores to Nalco Singapore and had claimed that the said intra-group services provided to it along with other group companies of Nalco in Asia Pacific Region were at arm's length. The assessee has filed evidences in support of services which in turn, were filed before the Assessing Officer/TPO/DRP. The TPO on the other hand, had determined the arm's length price of intra-group fees at Nil on the ground of lack of evidences. There is no merit in the plea of authorities below in this behalf especially where the assessee had demonstrated the availment of intra-group services and in support filed copy of agreement, under which it had availed the said services and had further furnished e-mails exchanged and other documents to establish its case of availment of services from its associated enterprises and also the benefits arising therefrom. In support the allocation key adopted has been consistently followed. It is not the case that such services were provided by Nalco Singapore only to the assessee but similar services were provided to group entities of Nalco group and in such circumstances, it could not be said that the assessee had not availed any services and benchmark the arm's length price of international transactions at Nil. The Assessing Officer is not to sit in the armchair of businessman in order to determine the nature of services availed. Where the assessee has filed voluminous evidence of services received, then the same cannot be brushed aside on the ground that no evidences have been filed as to how the assessee asked for the said services. The need is of the businessman and the same cannot be questioned on filmsy grounds. [Para 27]

The Pune Bench of Tribunal in Emerson Climate Technologies (India) P. Ltd. v. Dy.CIT [2018] 100 taxmann.com 478 (Pune - Trib.) has deliberated on similar issue of availment of services from the associated enterprises and held that there is no merit in the order of TPO in holding that as to whether the said concerns have given services or whether they are qualified to give the services and the cost incurred by AEs. First of all, this is outside the domain of TPO. Under the Transfer Pricing Regulations what the TPO has to determine is whether the services which have been provided by associated enterprises are at arm's length price. [Para 28]

The Tribunal also adjudicated the arguments of the Assessing Officer as to what benefits had been received by the assessee against said support services and also the value of services given by associated enterprise. The Tribunal held that the said aspect was not linked to the issue of whether there was any need for services and in the absence of establishing the same, whether the Assessing Officer/TPO was correct in determining the arm's length price of transactions at Nil and in this regard the Tribunal held that the TPO while benchmarking the transactions has to determine whether the price paid by the assessee for the services availed is what an independent enterprise would have paid for the same services. The analysis done by the TPO of the nature of services and benefits arising to the assessee on availing such services was beyond the scope of transfer pricing provisions. [Para 29]

Facts

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacture and trading of pneumatic equipment. The assessee entered into international transactions with its Associated Enterprise ('AE').

In one of the international transactions the assessee paid certain amount to 'F', Germany, an Associated Enterprise, for SAP service charges.

In its TP study, the assessee explained the nature of this payment. According to assessee, 'F' Group had implemented a standard DRP software namely SAP R/3. In this regard, the cost incurred to implement the software and the ongoing cost towards user license and maintenance was allocated to each of the group companies on the basis of use. For the financial year 2006-08, 'F' Germany had allocated the actual cost incurred in relation to use of such software amounting to Rs. 22,865,807 to assessee.

The Assessing Officer referred the determination of ALP in respect of the aforesaid transaction to the TPO under section 92CA.

The TPO proceeded on the assumption that no services were rendered by 'F', Germany for which SAP charges were paid by the assessee. For this reason and also for the reason that no comparable instances had been provided by the assessee, the TPO treated the entire payment as not at arm's length.

The DRP confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer rejecting the stand of the assessee that the TPO had no jurisdiction to go into the question as to whether the tax payer received services for which a payment had been made by the taxpayer.

[Para 29] Further, the Tribunal in Eaton Fluid Power Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2018] 92 taxmann.com 158 (Pune - Trib.) on similar issue had held that the TPO cannot sit in the judgment of business module of assessee and its intention to avail or not to avail any services from its associated enterprises. The role of the TPO is to determine the arm's length price of international transactions undertaken by the assessee and whether the same is at arm's length price when compared with similar transactions undertaken by external entities or internal comparables. [Para 31]

In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, which are similar to the facts and circumstances in the case of Emerson Climate Technologies (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra) and Eaton Fluid Power Ltd. (supra), it is to be held that there is no merit in the observations of the TPO in holding that the assessee had not availed any services, hence the arm's length price of transactions was to be adopted at Nil. The findings of authorities below in this regard is to be reversed. [Para 32]

Now, coming to second part of intra-group fees paid by assessee to Nalco US for providing services such as information technology, engineering support services, business development services, supply chain services. The assessee had grouped the said services under the head 'headquarter common expenses'. As in the case of Nalco Singapore, similarly, in the case of Nalco US also, the services were provided by associated enterprises not only to the assessee but also to all other entities in Asia Pacific Group of Nalco group. The assessee has placed the evidences of availment of services both before the TPO and DRP and also before the Tribunal. The assessee has filed the details of experts visited India for providing various services. Further communication via e-mails containing details of Nalco US employees assisting Nalco India are also provided which were by way of engineering supports services. [Para 34]

Coming to the next limb of services i.e. business development, the assessee had furnished various documents. In the IT support segment, the assessee had received presentations on how to use Microsoft, which are furnished. All these services were availed not only by the assessee but other entities of Nalco group and the cost was allocated entity-wise by following particular methodology. In support, the assessee has also furnished certificate from an independent accountant vis-a-vis allocation of cost. The TPO in assessee's case has doubted not only the availment of services but also the evidences filed in this regard. First of all, the availment of services was consequent to agreement between the parties, copy of which is furnished. As per terms of said agreement, the cost of services were allocated without any markup. In other words, it is case of pure reimbursement of expenses, which were incurred by US entity to its group companies and the question which arises is whether arm's length price of such allocation of costs and its recovery could be taken at Nil in the hands of assessee. In this regard, the TPO, in case of Nalco US wherein he has treated the receipts from the assessee and other entities as fees for included services and assessment order had been passed after the order passed under section 263, wherein it was held that the said fees for included services were taxable in the hands of US entity. The said US entity is in appeal before the authorities but the question which arises is that whether in such circumstances also can the payment made by assessee for availing intra-group services, while benchmarking the international transactions can be taken at Nil. The answer to the same is 'No'. Following the ratio laid down by the Pune Bench of Tribunal in the case of Emerson Climate Technologies (India) P. Ltd. (supra) and Eaton Fluid Power Ltd. (supra) it is to be held that the TPO cannot benchmark the said transaction of availment of intra-group services at Nil on the ground of doubting whether any services were availed or not. In the instant case, the aforesaid services were availed, payment for which was made at cost without any markup and such cost was attributed to the assessee on the basis of particular methodology adopted by US company for recovering the expenditure from all entities under Nalco group and the same cannot be disturbed in the hands of assessee. The payment made by assessee was thus, at arm's length price and no adjustment needs to be made on this account. Further, in any case, where when in the hands of Nalco US the services have been taxed as fees for included services, then corollary which follows is that the arm's length price of payment made for such services cannot be determined at Nil. Accordingly, the order of Assessing Officer /TPO/DRP is to be reversed. [Para 35]

The DRP itself has categorically admitted that the issue involved in the present year is identical to the issue decided in earlier years in assessee's own case. [Para 19]

■

Thus, the DRP itself accepted that the issue stood covered by the earlier orders of the Tribunal and sustained the addition merely for the purpose of keeping the issue alive in further appeal. However, it is found that subsequently the Gujarat High Court has affirmed the decisions of the Tribunal and dismissed the appeals filed by the Revenue. Therefore, the very foundation on which the DRP sustained the adjustment no longer survives. [Para 21]

■

While adjudicating identical controversy in assessee’s own case for assessment years 2017-18 and 2018-19, the Coordinate Bench of the Tribunal deleted similar transfer pricing adjustments. The relevant observations of the Tribunal are reproduced hereunder:

"The assessee has furnished detailed documentary evidences in support of actual rendition of services including agreements, emails, presentations, reports, cost allocation workings and operational support records. The TPO has proceeded merely on presumptions that the services are duplicative or shareholder activities without bringing any cogent material on record." [Para 22]

■

The Gujarat High Court while affirming the aforesaid findings of the Tribunal in Tax Appeal No.470 of 2023 and Tax Appeal No.683 of 2023 specifically approved the deletion of transfer pricing adjustment relating to intra-group services. The High Court observed as under:

"18. As per the provisions of Rule 10AB, price which has been or would have been charged or paid for same or similar uncontrolled transaction between non-associated enterprises under similar circumstances is to be considered as per the other method. However, TPO has not made any effort for searching similar uncontrolled transaction between non associated enterprises by treating the value of international transaction to be at Nil. TPO did not conduct any search to find out independent entity in a comparable transaction and arm's length price of international transaction was treated to be Nil in absence of such inquiry. Tribunal has also arrived at finding of fact that assessee has been able to demonstrate with substantial supporting material that it availed India specific services from its head office/regional office and in view of such findings, Tribunal has rightly held that view taken by the TPO is a restrictive view in coming to the conclusion that no services were rendered for which any independent party would be paid resulting into impossibility to determine the arm's length price in facts of the case.

19. Tribunal has therefore, rightly held that once the assessee has been able to demonstrate the receipt of services Transfer Pricing adjustment without applying any prescribed bench-marking method is not tenable and TPO cannot determine ALP at Nil and ALP has to be determined as per one of the methods prescribed under the Act read with Rules." [Para 25]

■

Respectfully following the binding decisions of the Coordinate Bench in assessee's own case for assessment Years 2017-18 and 2018-19, which stand affirmed by the Gujarat High Court vide judgment dated 05.03.2024, it is held that the transfer pricing adjustment made in respect of GHO non-IT services, GHO IT services and RHO services is unsustainable in law. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer/TPO is directed to delete the entire transfer pricing adjustment. [Para 26]

As could be seen from the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as other materials brought on record, not only before the Transfer Pricing Officer but before the Commissioner (Appeals), the assessee has made elaborate submissions with regard to the services availed and cost allocation relating to Lotus Note and other evidences to justify the payment made to the AE. It is also a fact on record that the assessee has benchmarked the arm's length price of the payment made towards services availed from the AE by applying CUP method. Except making some general observations, the Transfer Pricing Officer has not provided any valid reason why the benchmarking done by the assessee is not acceptable. Further, the Transfer Pricing Officer while determining the arm's length price of the services availed from the AE at nil has apparently not followed any of the methods prescribed under the statute. It is also relevant to observe, the agreement under which the assessee is making payment for availing such services has continued from the preceding assessment years and is also continuing in the subsequent assessment years. It is worth mentioning, in the subsequent assessment years i.e., assessment years 2009-10, 2010-11, 2011-12 and 2012-13, the Transfer Pricing Officer has accepted similar benchmarking of arm's length price of the services availed by the assessee from the AE on account of Lotus Note. Therefore, as held by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Kargill Food India Ltd. dated 24-10-2016, even applying the rule of consistency, the benchmarking done by the assessee under CUP method is to be accepted. [Para 8]

Even otherwise also, if the Transfer Pricing Officer was not convinced with the benchmarking done by the assessee, he should have benchmarked the arm's length price of the services availed by following any one of the prescribed methods as provided under the statute. A perusal of the order passed by the Transfer Pricing Officer would reveal that while rejecting the benchmarking done by the assessee and determining the arm's length price at nil, he has not followed any prescribed method as provided under the statute. That being the case, the determination of arm's length price at nil by the Transfer Pricing Officer being contrary to the provisions of the Act is not acceptable. This view gets support from the decisions of jurisdictional High Court cited by the assessee. Moreover, the Transfer Pricing Officer having failed to point out any specific defect or invalidity in benchmarking done by the assessee, the price paid by the assessee to the AE for the services availed has to be held to be at arm's length. In view of the aforesaid, the Assessing Officer is directed to delete the addition of Rs. 24,54,556. [Para 9]

The assessee had summarized about 100 e-mails justifying the receipt and benefit of services from associated enterprises and filed the same separately. In addition to the same, the assessee had enlisted certain key benefits, which were derived by it on account of payment of fees for advisory and other services in support of which documentary evidence was filed.

The assessee, thus, filed documentary evidence to demonstrate that it had availed services in the field of Human Resources, Marking and Product, Finance, Business Development and Management and other services, i.e., support for new product, marketing material, training material and technical support. The assessee has also explained the need for services being in field of operational, strategic and advisory support services. The first aspect which arises in the present appeal is whether the TPO while ascertaining whether price paid for the services is at arm's length price or not, can enter the field of businessman, who is the best judge as to whether it needs to avail the said services. The answer to the same is 'No'. Each businessman is the best judge to come to decision as to whether it needs the said support services or not. Secondly, once such a decision has been taken by the businessman and it provides the evidence of services received by it from its associated enterprises, then the TPO cannot question the same by commenting upon the nature of services provided, where in any case, information is hyper technical. First of all, where the TPO has referred to the services provided and pointed out defects in the services provided, the first step that services have been provided stands established. Once the same is established by way of assessee producing several evidences before the TPO, which were in the form of contemporaneous data, then the TPO is precluded from commenting upon the same and holding that the assessee had not received any services and also there was no need for making any payments for such services, as the services provided were not upto the mark. In any case, the perusal of various evidences filed by the assessee, i.e., contemporaneous data available on record shows that it is highly technical and the same has been used by the assessee for carrying on its business activities, such evidence cannot be brushed aside being not upto the mark. The TPO had referred to part of the data and drew conclusion, which is not warranted in any case. [Para 19]

Another aspect of the issue which needs to be kept in mind is the developing scenario of carrying on the business in the country. The said business is carried on by the entities which have presence outside India and have certain standards, which are attached to its brand name. In order to maintain its brand value, arrangements are made with different entities across the globe by holding companies, so that different entities operating in different parts of the world adhere to specific rules and regulations while carrying on business under the said brand. The assessee is 100 per cent subsidiary of Copeland Corporation, which admittedly, has presence in various Countries. The assessee has placed on record that besides the assessee entering into agreement with Emerson HK, Emerson TH, various entities of other countries had entered into such agreements. The terms of the agreement are similar for providing services, wherein a particular formula is designed by the person providing the services, i.e., the basis for remuneration is the cost incurred by way of man hours charged to the entity with mark up of 5.8 per cent. Such method of charging and remunerating was identical in the case of all the entities which were availing the services from Copeland Corporation through Emerson HK and Emerson TH. The assessee had also furnished on record the basis for charging cost by the two entities from the assessee. No doubt, the complete details of operations of the said concerns worldwide had not been filed, but that had no relevance to the activities or services availed by the assessee. There is no merit in the order of TPO in rejecting the segmental details of AEs filed by the assessee vis-à-vis services availed by it. What is to be considered in the hands of assessee is the services it had availed from Emerson HK and Emerson TH and not the whole activities undertaken by the said two concerns worldwide. The assessee had put on record that not only the assessee but many other concerns were availing same services from the two entities and even the basis for remuneration to the said concerns was the same in respect of all the countries. In such circumstances, there is no merit in the order of TPO in holding that as to whether the said concerns have given services or whether they are qualified to give the services and the cost incurred by AEs. First of all, this is outside the domain of TPO. Under the Transfer Pricing Regulations what the TPO has to determine is whether the services which have been provided by associated enterprises are at arm's length price. Accordingly, there is no merit in this part of the order of TPO. [Para 20]

It is noted that the assessee has made submissions on the validity of passing of TP order stating that the TPO has passed the transfer pricing order on 30-1-2014. As per section 92CA(3A) read with section 153, the TP order has to be passed 60 days prior to due date of completion of assessment as per section 153(1). As per provisions of section 153, the time limit to pass the assessment order is 24 months from end of relevant assessment year. Further as per provisions of section 153(4), if reference is made under section 92CA, then time limit to pass order under section 153 is extended by 12 months. Accordingly, for assessment year 2010-11, time limit for completion of the period of limitation for passing the assessment order would expire on 31-3-2014. Consequently, the time limit to pass the TP order under section 92CA(3A) for assessment year 2010-11 would expire before 60 days prior to 31-3-2014 i.e. 29-1-2014. Since, the TP order has been passed on 30-1-2014, the said order is time barred as per provisions of section 92CA(3A) read with section 153, and ought to be quashed. [Para 8]

It is found that on the identical disputed issue, the assessee has relied on the judicial decisions on the validity of TPO order in the case of Accenture Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2022] 141 taxmann.com 426 (Mum. - Trib.) wherein it was held that under section 92CA(3A) read with section 153, TPO is required to pass order within period of 60 days prior to date on which period of limitation referred to in section 153 expires i.e., 21 months. [Para 9]

Considering the facts, circumstances and the ratio of the judicial decisions discussed above it is found that the order passed by the TPO is barred by the limitation is illegal and void ab initio and is to be quashed. Consequently assessment order passed after transfer pricing adjustment is without jurisdiction. [Para 10]

As far as the determination of ALP is concerned, the TP study done by the assessee does not give out any comparable instances of similar transactions between the unrelated parties. As far as the determination of ALP under the Act is concerned, the provisions lay down that the assessee has to adopt one of the methods laid down in section 92C(1). The assessee has to substantiate the price that is paid to its AE as at Arm's Length within one of the methods so prescribed. As already noticed, the TP study of the assessee is not in tune with the provisions of section 92C. [Para 55]

In the present case, voluminous evidence was filed by the assessee before the TPO. The TPO as well as DRP proceeded on wrong facts regarding the nature of services rendered and also made reference to entities which were not in any way connected with the assessee or the payment of management fee. Clearly there has been lack of proper application of mind by the TPO as well as the DRP. However, for this reason, that the addition made should be deleted on this ground alone cannot be accepted.

The evidence on record exists regarding allocation of cost and the basis of such allocation. The invoices regarding nature of services rendered, however, are in the form of invoices supported by e-mails exchanged between the assessee and the AE. These invoices per se, do not demonstrate the nature of services rendered. The invoices have to be linked to the e-mails in support of the invoices. The assessee has not made any attempts to demonstrate the ALP of the transaction with the AE.

As already stated, the evidence in the present case has to be linked with the invoices to show the nature of services rendered. The assessee has to choose a method in accordance with the Act and the Rules. On production of such evidence, the TPO will have to give the basis of his price, if he disputes the assessee's claim with comparable cases. In such circumstances, it would be just and proper to set aside the order of the Assessing Officer and remand the question of determination of ALP to the TPO for fresh consideration. [Para 57]

Comparables – Segment-wise Benchmarking (AMC and Agency/Marketing Support)

■

From examination of record in light of rival contention, it is crystal clear that the issue of TP adjustment on impugned services is settled through findings for previous years 2007-08 to assessment year 2009-10 vide orders dated 07.03.2024, 17.12.2025 and 07.01.2026 of Co-ordinate Bench. [Para 9]

■

The findings given in assessment year 2008-09 are as under: "Since the Tribunal had accepted that the assessee is into two different business segments i.e. AMC service provider and agency market and support services provider the transfer pricing adjustment made by the TPO by considering both the segments as a single segment for the year under consideration is to be revisited. Counsel for the Assessee, in principle we agree that the assessee is having two segments as observed by the Tribunal in assessee's own case for the immediately preceding assessment year and, therefore, since the assessee is having segmental account the benchmarking has to be done segment wise separately and thus we direct the TPO to analyze the submissions of the assessee viz-a-viz the segmental accounts and the comparables and pass appropriate order after providing opportunities to the Assessee. In case the PLI of the assessee as tested party as per the segmental accounts is % and average result of comparable companies is 19.63% and is within permissible tolerance range as per proviso to 92C(2), then no transfer pricing adjustment is called for by the TPO. With these observations we restore this issue to TPO for limited purpose of verification in the light of our above observations." [Para 9.1]

■

The findings given in assessment year 2009-10 are as under: "We have considered the rival submissions and have gone through the documents before us. Following this finding, we direct the Ld. AO/TPO to consider the two segments of the business as presented by the assessee. Thereafter, the Bench marking has to be done with respect to the two segments of business. The TPO would analyze and consider the submissions of the assessee, including the details of comparables provided by him, and thereafter pass an appropriate order on the segmental aspects of the assessee's business. Secondly, the TPO would also test his conclusions on the parameters and conclusions arrived at by the assessee and see if the same are within the tolerance level provided in the proviso to section 92C(2) of the Act. It is settled law that the Commissioner cannot grant approval in a mechanical manner, and this provision is clearly understood to provide some check on arbitrary exercise of power by the Assessing Officer. Therefore, the Assessing Officer must have some material with him which would enable him to get approval of the Commissioner for making a reference to the TPO. [Para 41]

IV. LEGALITY OF CBDT INSTRUCTION NO.3 OF 2003, DATED 20-5-2003 As per the impugned I nstruction, the CBDT has directed all the officers of the department to refer the matter of determination of ALP to the TPO where the aggregate value of international transaction and transactions exceed Rs. 5 crores. As is clear from the circular, the idea of issuing instructions under reference is to avoid selection of small cases with international transaction less than Rs. 5 crores for scrutiny of transfer price and to avoid arbitrariness in the application of the provision. All cases where aggregate value of international transactions exceed Rs. 5 crores, are required to be referred to the TPO by the Assessing Officer. The limit has now been increased to Rs. 15 crores. Having regard to the object stated in the Circular, no fault can be found nor any illegality seen in the instructions.

When the provisions of section 92CA(i) are read with Circular of the CBDT (Instruction No.3) dated 20-5-2003, it becomes ‘necessary’ for the Assessing Officer to refer the question of determination of transfer pricing of international transactions to the TPO. He has no discretion in the matter in the light of limit fixed by the CBDT. The Assessing Officer has only to look at the aggregate value of international transactions disclosed by the assessee in the audit report and then follows directions of the CBDT The Assessing Officer, therefore, is left with a very limited role under section 92CA(1). Likewise, while granting approval to the action of the Assessing Officer, the Commissioner has only to see whether aggregate value of international transaction is more than Rs. 5 crores or not. If it is more than Rs. 5 crores, he has to grant approval in the light of directions of the CBDT. These directions are mandatory and binding on the Assessing Officer and the Commissioner. The fact that directions are not binding on the assessee or the C ourts is immaterial. The relevant question to be answered is whether circulars are binding on the departmental authorities. The question has an obvious answer. [Para 44]

Therefore, there is no illegality in the directions issued by the CBDT.[Para 45]

V. ALP DETERMINED BY TPO - HOW MUCH BINDING ON ASSESSING OFFICER FOR MAKING ASSESSMENT

Section 92CA(6) would come into operation only in the cases where the Assessing Officer in the assessment order has adopted the order of the TPO. Now if subsequently, the TPO rectified his order in terms of section 92CA(5), the Assessing Officer is duty-bound to pass an order in conformity with order of the TPO. Otherwise it can lead to anomaly and, therefore, it is provided that where the TPO’s order is amended to rectify a mistake apparent from record, the Assessing Officer must also rectify assessment order in conformity with above order. The TPO’s order under sub-section (3) of section 92CA cannot be treated as final and binding on the Assessing Officer. It does not mean that the order of the TPO is of no value or consequence. The words ‘having regard to’ convey definite meaning and are strong enough to enjoin upon the Assessing Officer a duty to pass order and adopt transfer pricing as determined by the TPO, unless there are very good grounds to modify or alter the transfer pricing ordered by the TPO. Only after recording reasons, the Assessing Officer can take transfer pricing other than one determined by the TPO. There may be cases in which the assessee after ALP is determined by the TPO and before his order is made the basis of assessment, may get such authentic material to show that transfer pricing determined by the TPO is not correct or should not be blindly adopted without modifying it. However, where the Assessing Officer has adopted the orders of the TPO and computed assessments accordingly, there is no illegality in the procedure followed by the Assessing Officer. [Para 51]

There is nothing to suggest that the TPO’s report on transfer pricing is conclusive and debars the Assessing Officer from looking at any other material. The aforesaid conclusion is also in line with latest change made in section 92CA by the Legislature through the Finance Act, 2007. [Para 52]

Thus, due to protest against the levy by chartered accountants and certain Court decisions, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998 only on auditing and accounting services. So, the services provided by CAs and advocates, which can be of similar nature, remain out of service tax. But the later developments are of crucial nature and patently of a discriminatory nature. Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998, was superseded by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998. From this notification, the nature of services was made more explicit as compared to Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998. But this is not all that happened to these professionals. Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 was amended by Notification No. 15/2002-ST, dated 1-8-2002 w.e.f. 1-8-2002 by inserting an Explanation under this notification. This Explanation provides that, "Nothing contained in this notification shall apply to the services provided by a practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant which may fall in any other taxable services as defined in clause (105) of section 65 of the said Act". Also, the same was clarified by the following illustration:

"The service provided by a practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant in connection with the management of any organisation in any manner or recruitment of manpower in any manner shall be deemed to be the taxable service provided under the category of management consultant or manpower recruitment agency, as the case may be. Therefore, no exemption under this notification shall be applicable to such practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant."

So, w.e.f. 1-8-2002, it was clarified that only those services are taxable under service tax which are either covered under Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 or covered under any of the other categories of services. And not all services, which are not covered under Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998, are exempt in case of these professionals, as was the thinking of these professionals. In case of S.B. Billimoria & Co. v. CCE [2006] 4 STT 148 (Chennai - CESTAT), based on this Notification, service tax was demanded for providing management consultancy service during the period 16-10-1998 to 1-8-2002. It was held that as per Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998, management consultancy services are not included in the list of taxable services of a practising chartered accountant. Hence, for the period of dispute, apparently, the appellants were not liable to pay service tax on management consultant’s service rendered by them and they had made out a prima facie case of waiver of pre-deposit and stay of recovery. Simply, this notification apparently seems to be prospective and not retrospective in nature, though this notification seems to be against the mandate of section 65A of the Finance Act, 1994 even for the later period also. If one accepts this logic, then many of the services provided by an advocate can also be made taxable, which is not the case.

But this was not the end. By Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated 1-3-2006, Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax, dated 16-10-1998 was withdrawn. So, all the services provided by these professionals became liable for service tax. But by Notification No. 25/2006-ST, dated 13-7-2006, certain services provided or to be provided by chartered accountants are made non-taxable. According to this notification, the following services are made non-taxable [relevant to CAs only]:

"In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (1) of section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994 (32 of 1994), the Central Government, on being satisfied that it is necessary in the public interest so to do, hereby exempts taxable service falling under sub-clause(s) of clause (105) of section 65 of the Finance Act, provided or to be provided by a practising Chartered Accountant, in his professional capacity to a client relating to representing the client before any statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice from the whole of service tax leviable thereon under section 666 of the Finance Act."

HELD: Prima facie, the Explanation added in amended Notification No. 15/2000 ST, dated 1-8-2002 purported to add to the tax liability of a PCA, Practising Company Secretary and Practising Cost Accountant, by providing that the exemption under Notification No. 59/98-ST would not be applicable to services provided by these professionals, which may fall in any other taxable services defined in clause (90) of section 65. The legislative intent was amply clear. Prima facie, taxable services under clause (90) of section 65 were sought to be excluded from the scope of exemption. Notification No. 59 of 1998-ST, on its face, did not include ‘management consultancy service’ in the list of taxable services of PCAs. Position before withdrawal of exemption notification

2. Before rescission of the service tax exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998, i.e., upto February 28, 2006, all services, except those mentioned below, provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA were exempt from service tax—

(a)accounting and auditing; or

(b)cost accounting and cost auditing; or

(c)secretarial auditing; or

(d)verification of declarations in prescribed forms of compliances for obtaining a certificate of commencement of business or commencement of other business under section 149 of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(e)signing of the annual return of listed companies under section 161 of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(f)certification that requirements of Schedule XIII to the Companies Act, 1956 have been complied with as regards statutory guidelines for appointment of managerial personnel and payment of managerial remuneration to them without the approval of the Central Government under section 269 and Schedule XIII, of the Companies Act, 1956; or

(g)certification of documents to be filed by companies with the Registrar of Companies under the Companies Act, 1956; or

(h)certification in Form No. 1 that the whole of the amount remaining unpaid or unclaimed for a period of three years from the date of transfer to the special account under section 205(1)/(2) of the Companies Act, 1956 has been transferred to the General Revenue Account of the Central Government under the Companies Unpaid Dividend (Transfer to General Revenue Account of the Central Government) Rules, 1978; or

(i)certification of documents under the Exports and Imports Policy of the Government of India; or

(j)certification for exchange control purposes which a practising chartered accountant can issue as documentary evidence in support of certain applications under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973; or

(k)certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets as per rule 8A(7) of the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957.

Thus, in case any practising CA/CS/ICWA was rendering any service other than (a) to (k ) enumerated above, like legal or taxation consultancy service, etc., he wasn’t liable for service tax.

However, any service provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, which fell under the ambit of any other taxable service, was liable to service tax under the category of that other taxable service. For example, if a chartered accountant also provided manpower recruitment services to his clients, then he was liable to service tax on such services under the category of manpower recruitment service.

Reasons behind issuance of earlier exemption notification

3. The said exemption notification was issued on the principles of equity. The then Government had recognized the fact that the—

(i)practising CA/CS/ICWAs were providing services like legal consultancy, etc., which were equally being provided by other professionals like advocates and legal practitioners and, therefore,

(ii)levy of service tax on such services provided by practising CA/CS/ICWAs and non-levy of service tax on the same services provided by advocates and legal practitioners would be inequitable levy.

Having recognized the abovesaid facts the aforesaid exemption notification was issued to prevent the levy of service tax from being unjust and inequitable.

Position after withdrawal of exemption notification

4. After the withdrawal of the aforesaid exemption notification by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006, i.e., with effect from March 1, 2006 all the services provided by a practising CA/CS/ICWA, in his professional capacity, are chargeable to service tax.

Exemption granted to certain services provided by CAs, CSs and ICWAs, by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1998 stands withdrawn by Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006. Is this withdrawal unjust and unjustifiable? Is it discriminatory? How damaging is it to the practice of CAs, etc.? The author here examines the issues from legal as well as moral angle. The abrupt move on the part of the Government is going to create a feeling of insecurity among the professional affected and cause harm to the healthy growth of their profession. Applying the logic of the Kerala High Court decision in Malappuram District Parallel College Association v. Union of India [2006] 150 Taxman 624, wherein levy of service tax on parallel colleges was held to be discriminatory, the author feels that the withdrawal of exemption to CAs/CSs/ICWAs may not pass the test of constitutionality.

Introduction

1. Chartered accountants, being professionally qualified and proficiently trained, are providing most valuable services to the people of this nation and abroad in the matters pertaining to accountancy, audit, management and technical consultancy and consultancy in the matters pertaining to various State as well Central laws. Their professional attitude and devotion are earning name and fame for the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and also for other fellow chartered accountants. Now, the chartered accountants are equally competing with the legal practitioners in the field of State and Central legislations as well as with the advocates and owing to varied experience and vast potential of the chartered accountants, the people are preferring to avail the services of the chartered accountants in place of other practitioners engaged in the similar fields. The facts aforesaid are widely accepted ones, which need no evidence.

Is it wrong for a person providing valuable services to the society and the Government to expect equitable treatment from the Government? If the answer to this question is ‘Yes’, then, what the Government has done by issuing Notification No. 2/2006, dated March 1, 2006 for withdrawing service tax exemption to practising chartered accountants is just and all right. But if the readers answer this question as ‘No’, then, one should read the succeeding paras of this article to know how the move of the Government in issuance of Notification No. 2/2006, dated March 1, 2006 for withdrawing service tax exemption to practising chartered accountants has turned out to be unjust and devastating for the practising chartered accountants.

The same is the case with the professionals engaged in practice in the field of company secretaryship and cost accountancy. The exemption from service tax provided to practicing company secretaries and practising cost accountants has also been withdrawn by the aforesaid notification.

The service tax exemption Notification No. 59/98, dated October 16, 1998, which provided full exemption from service tax to services (except the ones specified in that notification) provided by the practising chartered accountants, has been rescinded by the Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated March 1, 2006 (a budget notification) and, consequently, all services provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity, have become taxable.

This article is a comprehensive analysis of leviability of service tax on Chartered Accountant’s Services.

Introduction

1. Service tax has been imposed on practising chartered accountant’s services with effect from October 16, 1998 vide Notification No. 53/98-ST, dated October 7, 1998. The gross amount charged by a practising chartered accountant from the client, in professional capacity, is chargeable to service tax.

Meaning of-Practising Chartered Accountant

2. Section 65(83) defines ‘practising chartered accountant’ as under—

‘practising chartered accountant’ means a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and is holding a certificate of practice granted under the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 (38 of 1949) and includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy.

As per section 65(83), a practising chartered accountant is a person who is a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, New Delhi and holds a certificate of practice under the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and also includes any concern engaged in rendering services in the field of chartered accountancy. Thus, both associate and fellow members of the Institute are covered. It would also cover individuals as well as firms and persons holding full-time as well as part-time certificate of practice.

According to Webster’s Dictionary, a professional means ‘calling requiring specialised knowledge and often long intensive academic preparation; calling, vocation or employment’. The services should be rendered in this capacity using this skill and knowledge.

‘In any manner’ would mean directly or indirectly, personally or otherwise or through his staff members or through computer aid or other device or manually.

To be treated as a practising chartered accountant, following basic tests must be satisfied—

(i)He must be a person;

(ii)He must be a member (whether associate or fellow) of the Institute to which he belongs (ICAI);

(iii)He must hold a certificate of practice granted by the Institute;

(iv)In case of a firm of the chartered accountants, it must be a concern engaged in rendering services in the field of the chartered accountancy.

Legal position

3. In All India Federation of Tax Practitioners v. Union of India [2007] 10 STT 166 (SC), the Apex Court has settled the levy of service tax on the chartered accountants, cost accountants, and architects, by holding that the Parliament of India has the legislative competence to levy service tax on the professional services rendered by the chartered accountants, the cost accountants, and architects and that professional tax and service tax operate on different spheres.

The Apex Court dealt with the constitutional status of levy of service tax and the legislative competence of the Parliament to impose service tax under article 246(1) and Entry 97 of List-I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India having regard to Entry 60 in List-II of Seventh Schedule (i.e., professional tax). The major findings of the Apex Court in the instant case are as follows—

u As an economic concept, there is no distinction between the consumption of goods and service as both satisfy human needs and this economic concept is based on the legal principle of equivalence.

u Service tax is a VAT which, in turn, is a general tax which applies to all commercial activities involving production of goods and provision of services.

u VAT is a consumption tax as it is borne by the client.

u Applying the principle of equivalence, there is no difference between production or manufacture of saleable goods and production of marketable/saleable services in the form of an activity undertaken by the service provider for consideration, which correspondingly stands consumed by the service receiver. It is this principle of equivalence which is in-built into the concept of service tax, which has received legal support in the form of Finance Act, 1994.

u Service tax is VAT which, in turn, is both a general tax as well as destination based consumption tax leviable on services provided within the country.

u A new charge by way of service tax or tax on service came to be levied statutorily by the Finance Act, 1994, which has subsequently attained Constitutional status by virtue of the Constitution (Eighty-eighth Amendment) Act, 2003.

So, all the services provided by these professionals became liable for service tax. A writ filed by some of chartered accountants has been admitted in the Delhi High Court. But by Notification No. 25/2006-ST, dated 13-7-2006, certain services provided or to be provided by chartered accountants are made non-taxable. According to this notification, the following services are made non-taxable [relevant to CAs only]:

"In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (1) of section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994 (32 of 1994), the Central Government, on being satisfied that it is necessary in the public interest so to do, hereby exempts taxable service falling under sub-clause (s) of clause (105) of section 65 of the Finance Act, provided or to be provided by a practising Chartered Accountant, in his professional capacity to a client relating to representing the client before any statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice from the whole of service tax leviable thereon under section 666 of the Finance Act."

Hence, the scope of this notification can be analyzed as below:

n Service should be provided ‘in his professional capacity’ and if the same is provided in non-professional capacity, then the same will not be taxable under this service, which hardly needs exemption. But what is professional capacity and what is non-professional, are highly controversial.

n Proceedings should be initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice. If the proceeding is not by way of issue of notice, then the same will not be covered under this exemption.

n Service should be relating to representing the client before any statutory authority, i.e., authority created under or by some statute. CORPORATE LITERATURE/SERVICE TAX

SERVICE TAX LEVY ON CHARTERED ACCOUNTANTS - UNCONSTITUTIONAL, ILLEGAL, INVALID AND UNWARRANTED

N. Vijia Kumar*

‘Service tax’ was first introduced in India by the Finance Act, 1994, on a few services and subsequently extended to several other services by the relevant Finance Acts. The Finance Act, 1998 brought the services rendered by a chartered accountant within the purview of service tax. In this article, the author attacks the levy of service tax at its very root by arguing that under the Constitution of India, the Parliament has no power to enact service tax legislation and, hence, the levy in question is lacking in constitutional validity. The author also specifically questions the extension of the levy to the profession of chartered accountancy, inter alia, on the ground that the exercise of profession by a chartered accountant does not amount to rendering of ‘service’ - EDITOR

Introduction

1. The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech for the year 1998-99 has observed in para 169 as hereunder:

"169. In the last budget, a number of services were added in the tax net. These included the service rendered on transportation of goods by road. The House is aware that it led to widespread resistance and protests. As a result, this service tax was virtually kept in abeyance and rightly so. I have decided to abolish the service tax on transportation of goods by road. I have also decided to abolish the service tax payable by outdoor caterers and pandal contractors. However, I have proposed service tax on some new services. These are services provided by: Architects, Interior decorators, Management Consultants, Chartered Accountants, Cost Accountants, Company Secretaries, Private security services, Real estate agents and real estate consultants, Market research agencies, Credit rating agencies, Underwriting agencies, Slaughter houses using mechanised means for the large animals.

We will examine how in respect of certain segments liable to Service Tax, the manner and mode of payment could be further simplified to improve compliance. These new service taxes will yield Rs. 220 crore in a full year."

With a view to effecting the aforesaid policy decision, the Finance Bill (No. 2) of 1998 by Chapter VI thereof and clause 129 has effected several ancillary and consequential amendments in the Finance Act, 1994, section 65, etc.

Section 116 of the Finance Act, 1998 has provided for a levy of service tax at 5 per cent on services rendered by practising chartered accountants, cost accountants and company secretaries. The said ‘service tax’ has been brought into effect with effect from October 16, 1998. A further notification issued by the Revenue Department provides that the taxable services rendered to a client by a practising Chartered Accountant or a company secretary or cost accountant which will attract service tax include: accounting and auditing or cost accounting or secretarial auditing or verification of declarations in prescribed forms under section 149 of the Companies Act, 1956 or signing of annual return of listed companies under section 161 of the Companies Act or certification requirements of Schedule XIII to the Companies Act, or certification of documents to be filed with Registrar of Companies or certification in Form No. 1 under the Companies Unpaid Dividend Rules, 1978 or certification of documents under Export and Import Policy (1997-2002) or Certification for exchange control purposes under FERA 1973 or certification in respect of valuation of instruments or assets as per rule 8A(7) of the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957. Vide GSR 597E, Notification Nos. 53, 54, 57 of 1998 Service Tax, issued by the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) vide F. No. B11/3/93 TRU dated October 7, 1998.

Revival of Exemption to Practising Chartered Accountants, Cost Accountants and Company Secretaries

The author has analysed the new exemption Notification No. 25/2006-Service Tax, dated 13-7-2006 which exempts representational services provided by a practising CA/CWA/CS, i.e., representing a client before statutory authority in any proceeding initiated by issue of notice. The author points out that there is no definition of ‘statutory authority’ in the notification. Therefore, the term covers any statutory authority before whom CA/CWA/CS is permitted by law to represent his client’s case. Further, the author notes that the new notification gives only partial relief to these professionals from the situation arising out of the withdrawal of Notification No. 59/98 w.e.f. 1-3-2006. The new Notification No.25/2006-Service Tax does not cover services such as taxation services rendered by these professionals which came into the service tax net because of withdrawal of Notification No. 59/98 w.e.f. 1-3-2006. In case of these services, the services provided by these professionals will become costlier as compared to the services provided by other professionals (advocates) who are not in the service tax net.

Introduction

1. Responding to the various representations made, particularly the Joint Memorandum dated 8.3.2006 given by the three professional Institutes (i.e. ICAI, ICSI and ICWAI) both to the Minister for Company Affairs and the Finance Minister with respect to removal of discrimination and providing level playing field to practising chartered accountants, practising cost accountants and practising company secretaries, the Government has issued Exemption Notification No. 25/2006-Service Tax, dated 13-7-2006 which provides that the professional services provided or to be provided by the practising chartered accountants, practising cost accountants and practising company secretaries in relation to representing the client before any statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice, shall be exempt from whole of the service tax.

Extent of Relief

2. Exemption of representation services before any statutory authority has brought certain relief to the CAs, CWAs and CSs, for these services now can be provided on a level playing field. The statutory authorities may include Company Law Board (CLB), ITAT, CESTAT, National Tax Tribunal, National Company Law Tribunal and various other authorities and Tribunals under different laws. Withdrawal of Exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-19981 had resulted in making these services costlier by the amount of service tax if they were to be provided by CAs, CSs or CWAs as compared to the similar services rendered by other categories of professionals. At global level also when world is expecting our professionals to provide BPO/KPO services, CAs, CSs or CWAs may find themselves out of competition because their services, due to the levy of service tax, may be costlier in comparison to those of others.

Representation Services - When Exempt

3. Representation services are exempt only when these are provided in respect of a client who has been issued notice and he is to be represented before the statutory authority in the course of proceedings arising out of issuance of such notice. In a case where representation is to be made without or before issuance of notice to the client, the representation services provided by CAs, CSs or CWAs may not be tax free though in case of other professionals who are authorised to provide such services, they are tax free. This lacuna needs clarification from the department.

So far as statutory authorities are concerned, all are covered though no definition of ‘statutory authority’ as such has been provided. Thus, the CAs, CSs or CWAs may represent the case of their client before any statutory authority if they are authorised to do so.

Discrimination/Distortion created by withdrawal of Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 - Whether fully removed

Consequently, all services provided by such persons in their professional capacity become taxable. This implies that any service or all services provided by these professionals in their professional capacity to the client would be charged to service tax irrespective of whether such services are covered under any other taxable service category or not. For example, if a person is rendering manpower recruitment service, or say, business auxiliary service or business support services, all such services will be covered under service tax. The only condition is that such service should be rendered in professional capacity. The recession of Notification No. 59 of 1998 and consequent withdrawal of exemption would bring in the following situations/implications —

(a)There is wider scope of service tax covering both taxable as well as non-taxable services.

(b)There will be no need to get the registration certificate endorsed for other services, as is presently required.

(c)All services rendered for only one month, i.e., March 1 to March 31, will be taxable in the financial year 2005-06 and for full period thereafter.

(d)Payment received for other services rendered earlier but received in March 2006 will not be subject to service tax.

(e)The services rendered not in any professional capacity would not be liable to service tax.

(f)From March 1, 2006 onwards, service providers will get full benefit of CENVAT Credit as all services would be taxable services.

(g)Certain services which are also provided by other persons (not professionals covered) will not be liable to service tax, whereas similar services provided by the chartered accountants, etc., would be subject to levy of service tax (except representational matters before statutory authority with effect from July 13, 2006).

(h)Services rendered by the chartered accountants, company secretaries and cost accountants are bound to be costlier by 12 per cent when compared to similar services rendered by non-CA/CS/CWA.

The earlier exemption for services other than accounting, auditing, and statutory certification services provided by practising CA, company secretary, or cost accountant in his professional capacity, stands withdrawn from March 1, 2006. Taking exception to this withdrawal, the author points out that this is discriminatory as for the same type of service the other professionals including the legal and tax practitioners are not liable to pay service tax. The author also points out that the move goes against the basic tenet of service tax levy, i.e. , service tax is a tax on services and not on the service provider or the professionals providing the services. It will snatch the level playing field from a professional. In this particular case, this is a tax on a professional or on a particular profession and not on a particular service because the others providing the same service are not required to pay the tax. The author submits that the withdrawal of exemption notification is totally discriminatory, unwarranted and unjustified and as a remedial action the exemption notification should be restored in the same spirit in which it was initially provided.

Recent Exemption to Chartered Accountants : One More Reconsideration Needed

The withdrawal of exemption Notification No.59/ 98-Service Tax, dated 16-10-1998 w.e.f. 1-3-2006 resulted in bringing all services rendered by practicing CAs, CWAs and CSs into the service tax net. The idea behind the exemption was to tax these professionals only on the services in which they have monopoly (accounting, auditing, cost audit, secretarial audit) and to exempt other services rendered by them (filing of returns, tax consultancy, representation services) till other professionals (e.g. Advocates) rendering these services were brought under the net. The withdrawal of exemption Notification 59/98 attracted strong reactions and representations were made to the Central Government. The Central Government, in principle, has accepted the representations of ICAI, ICWAI and ICSI that certain specified services rendered by these professionals should be exempted from service tax till the other professionals (e.g. Advocates) rendering these services are also brought into the service tax net. This can be seen from the Government’s Press Note. Therefore, based on these considerations (i.e., to maintain a level playing field), the Central Government has by Notification No.25/2006, dated 13-7-2006 exempted representation services (i.e. services relating to representation before statutory authorities) rendered by these professionals from service tax. The author argues that the logic for exempting representation services applies equally to tax consultancy services, filing of tax returns which constitute the main source of income for many CAs in non-metros and small cities and makes a passionate plea for exempting tax consultancy services and filing of tax returns also from service tax.

Backdrop

1. The Finance Act, 2006 has removed the exemption notification issued with respect to exemption to the Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost Accountants from the services other than audit, accounting and statutory certification services. The above exemption was given through Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax, dated the 16th October, 1998. This Notification was withdrawn w.e.f. 1st March, 2006 and from this date all the services including taxation services rendered by a practicing CA/ICWA/CS in his professional capacity are now covered by service tax. Auditing, accounting and statutory services of the Chartered Accountants were under the scope of service tax since initial stage of imposition of service tax on these professionals.

The other services including the taxation consultancy services were exempted from payment of service tax on the ground that these services are not the monopoly of these professionals and specially in the matter of taxation consultancy which includes consultancy of VAT, income-tax and service tax the Chartered Accountants are facing stiff competition from the other professionals including the Advocates and all these professionals are out of the scope of service tax. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India had termed this levy as discriminatory hence the Government through Notification No. 59/98, dated 16th October, 1998 has exempted the service tax on services other than the Audit, Accounting and statutory certification services.

The situation remains the same and still the Advocates are providing these services but for the reasons best known to our law makers this exemption was abruptly withdrawn on 28th Feb., 2006 w.e.f 1st March, 2006 and the result is that all the services including the taxation consultancy services provided by Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost Accountants are now taxable.

Service tax is a tax on services and not on a tax on the service provider or on the professionals providing the services. This fact was also pronounced by various Courts while deciding the constitutional validity of the service tax on various services.

The exemption notification was also issued on the same consideration because the field of providing this service is open for various other professionals and if getting same type of services from a particular professional, say chartered accountants, attracts service tax then this has two side effects. One is that the other professional will have the upper hand compared to the chartered accountants only because they need not to pay service tax.
