HEADNOTE: Section 66 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with Entry 97 of List I and Entry 60 of List II of Schedule VII to the Constitution of India - Charge of service tax - By provisions of Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998 services offered by chartered accountants, real estate agents (property dealers) and architects had been brought under tax net - Whether where services are rendered by a professional as a chartered accountant or as an architect, inspite of there being a nexus between profession and service rendered, there is a distinct aspect of service which can be legitimately taxed by Parliament under Entry 97 of List I - Held, yes - Whether service tax levied on a practising chartered accountant, architect and property dealer does not relate to levy on profession under Entry 60 in List II but on service rendered by professionals and Parliament has acted perfectly within its jurisdiction to legislate an Act levying service tax on such services - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned provisions of Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998 are constitutionally valid - Held, yes

FACT: The Government of India notified service tax on 12 new services added in the service tax net by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998, vide notification dated 7-10-1998. In the instant writ petitions, the petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the provisions of the Act by which services offered by professionals like chartered accountants, architects and real estate agents had been brought under the tax net on ground of lack of legislative competence of the Parliament and discrimination inasmuch as the Legislature had picked and chosen some professions and left out the others.

HELD: A. Emergence of concept of service tax :

While on the manufacture of goods, tax is levied in the name of excise duty and on sale of goods tax is levied in the name of sales tax, there are number of activities, falling in the category of 'service sector' which constitute 40 per cent of National GDP, which are not subjected to tax. This has kept a number of activities, which in fact are an important part of the national economy, outside the tax net. It is of course true that the persons rendering such services are subjected to income-tax covered by Entry 83 in List I of Schedule VII of the Constitution, but that by itself is not sufficient as the persons manufacturing goods pay excise duty on the manufacture of goods and pay sales tax on sale of goods and are also liable to pay income-tax on the income earned by them. The professionals rendering services for remuneration and similarly other persons rendering service in a larger number of fields for remuneration can only be subjected to professional tax by the State Legislature by virtue of Entry 60 in List II but subject to the maximum limit of Rs. 2,500 per annum in view of the provisions of article 276(2) of the Constitution of India. Such tax is on profession/trade/calling/employment irrespective of the fact whether they were earning any income or not. In these circumstances, the Parliament decided to tax the services being rendered by the professionals and by other trades and callings. Thus, the service tax is absolutely distinct and separate from the tax on profession/trade/calling/employment. [Para 4]

B. Legislative history :

The Government of India has notified service tax on 12 new services added in the service tax net by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998, vide notification dated 7-10-1998. The liability has been made effective from 16-10-1998. Further, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 93, the Central Government had exempted in the public interest the taxable services other than that of auditing and accounting provided by a practising chartered accountant in his professional capacity to a client. Vide notification dated 16-10-1998 certain exemptions have been given to the Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost and Works Accountants. Thus, the net result was that the service tax was leviable on chartered accountants in relation to accounting, auditing and certification services provided by them, in their professional capacity. As section 12B of Central Excise Act, 1944 has been made applicable in relation to the impugned service tax, the direct legal consequence is that there is a presumption that service tax has been passed on to the customer, who is the beneficiary of the service, and that is the reason why the service tax is levied on the service provider himself. It is open to the service provider to pass on the tax to the beneficiary of the service and reimburse himself. Thus, it is evident that the service provider does not pay the tax and the tax falls on the service receiver. [Para 6]

Simply this notification apparently, seems to be prospective and not retrospective. Though according to me this notification seems to be against the mandate of section 65A of the Finance Act, 1994 even for the later period also [explain later]. If we accept this logic, than many of the services provided by an Advocate can also be taxable, which is not the case [explain later].

But this was not the end. By Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated 1-3-2006, Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax, dated 16-10-1998 is withdrawn. New lollipop to CAs

2. What is this lollipop? By Notification No. 25/2006 - ST, dated 13-7-2006, certain services provided or to be provided by Chartered Accountants are made non taxable. According to this notification the following services are made non taxable [relevant to CA only];

"In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (1) of section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994 (32 of 1994), the Central Government, on being satisfied that it is necessary in the public interest so to do, hereby exempts taxable service falling under sub-clause (s) of clause (105) of section 65 of the Finance Act, provided or to be provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity to a client relating to representing the client before any statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice from the whole of service tax leviable thereon under section 666 of the Finance Act." So the scope of this notification can be analyzed as below :

uService should be provided ‘in his professional capacity’ and if the same is provided in non professional capacity, then even the same will not be taxable under this service, so hardly need exemption. But what is professional capacity and what is non professional, are highly controversial.

uProceedings should be initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice. So if the proceeding is not by way of issue of notice i.e. then the same will not be covered under this exemption.

uService should be relating to representing the client before any statutory authority i.e. authority created under or by some statute. So the fee received for representing will be exempt but in case some ancillary work have also to be done then whether it will be covered under this exemption can be controversial. If the assessee does not file return and receive notice for the same from the department, then also the question arises that if the Chartered Accountant prepare and file return, then whether the same will be exempt from service tax? So if the work is of dual type then also the problem may arise for classification.

The assessees had provided chartered accountant's services prior to 1-4-2012 and raised the bills therefor prior to that date, levying service tax at the rate of 10 per cent.

Up to 1-4-2012, Chartered Accountants services were governed by rule 7 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011 wherein point of taxation was determined based on date of receipt of payment.

With effect from 1-4-2012, rate of service tax was increased to 12 per cent and services of chartered accountants were excluded from Rule 7 ibid.

Circular No. 158/9/2012-ST dated 8-05-2012 and Circular No.154/5/2012-ST dated 28-03-2012 had provided that since, prior to 1-4-2012, services of Chartered Accountants were covered by rule 7 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011, hence, point of taxation of services provided prior to that date will continue to be governed by said Rule 7, as it stood before that date. Accordingly, in case of services provided and invoices raised before 1-4-2012, the point of taxation would be date of payment and if payment was received on or after 1-4-2012, revised rate of service tax viz. 12 per cent would apply.

The assessees argued that point of taxation, in their case, was determinable as per Rule 4 of the Point of Taxation Rules, 2011.

1998. This notification exempted the services other than accounting, auditing and statutory certification services provided by a practicing chartered accountant, company secretary or cost accountant from the levy of service tax. The implication of the withdrawal is that the legal and taxation services rendered by the chartered accountants will attract 10% service tax plus the applicable surcharge and educational cess on and from 1st March, 2006 and at 12% upon enactment of the Finance Bill, 2006. 2. Shri T.N. Manohran, President, ICAI said that this step is retrograde and discriminatory in nature. It will affect the level playing field as the advocates, the income-tax and the sales tax practitioners are not required to pay any service tax on the legal and taxation services rendered by them. The aforesaid notification exempting such services rendered by chartered accountants was issued after much deliberation and following the principle of equity, and there appears to be no reason for withdrawal of the same. Further, in the era of the opening up of the economy, such a discriminatory step will weaken accounting profession in India, which in the recent times has been able to make inroads into global markets. The President of the ICAI, Shri T.N. Manohran, further stated that the Institute would vigorously take up the matter with the Finance Ministry, Government of India to reconsider the decision to withdraw this notification. - As displayed on the Official Website of the ICAI www.icai.org"

Is withdrawal deliberate or unintentional ?

3. The withdrawal of this notification is not unintentional and it is very clear from the initial Government reaction issued through a letter written by the Joint Secretary, TRU, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue to all the Commissioners, Chief Commissioners immediately after release of the Notification withdrawing the exemption. Let us see the relevant portion related to the Notification under consideration in this article which we can term as first departmental clarification in this respect: -

"2. Exemption for services, other than accounting, auditing, and statutory certification services, provided by a practicing chartered accountant, company secretary or cost accountant in his professional capacity. Consequently all services provided by such persons in their professional capacity become taxable."

Hence the exemption which was provided due to certain prevailing circumstances and specially due to the fact that these services were also provided by other non-service tax paying professionals and still there is no change in those circumstances but the notification was withdrawn.

Partial Restoration of exemption w.e.f. 13-7-2006

4. Now on 13-07-2006, i.e. today (This article is being written on the same day) an exemption notification has been issued by the Government in response to the demand of Chartered Accountants and also in response to the representation from the ICAI and two other professional bodies governing the profession of Company Secretaries and Cost Accountants. Let us see the exemption Notification No. 25/2006-Service Tax, dated July 13, 2006:—

"In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (1) of section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994 (32 of 1994) (hereinafter referred to as the Finance Act), the Central Government, on being satisfied that it is necessary in the public interest so to do, hereby exempts the taxable services falling under sub-clauses (s), (t) and (u ) of clause (105) of section 65 of the Finance Act, provided or to be provided by a practicing chartered accountant, a practicing cost accountant and a practicing company secretary respectively, in his professional capacity, to a client, relating to representing the client before any statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice, from the whole of service tax leviable thereon under section 66 of the said Finance Act."

Now if we study this notification the following will be highlighted from it that the exemption is applicable only in the following circumstances and services :—

1.The representation services under any law are exempted.

2.The representation must be before any statutory authority.

3.The representation must be part of any proceedings initiated under any law.

4.The proceedings must be started by issue of a notice.

Here only statutory representation service provided by the Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost Accountants are made exempt from payment of whole of service tax.

Still the basis of exemption is that these services are not the monopoly of these professionals hence the exemption is granted till all the professionals providing these service specially the advocates are covered by the service tax. Let us see the Press Release issued by the Government in this respect in which it is clearly mentioned that why this exemption notification is being issued :—

PRESS NOTE

Central Government issued Notification No.25/2006-Service Tax, dated 13-7-2006 exempting from levy of service tax services provided by a practising Chartered Accountant/Cost Accountant/Company Secretary, in his professional capacity, to a client, relating to representing the client before any statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice.

Service tax is leviable on all the services provided by a practising Chartered Accountant/Cost Accountant/Company Secretary to a client with effect from 1-3-2006.

6. Considered the submissions made at length and perused the records.

7. It is undisputed that the respondents herein had paid the service tax for receipt of the services from the Goods Transport Agencies. This service tax was paid by the respondent on 16-12-2002, subsequent to the retrospective amendment, which made the recipient of the goods transport services liable to pay the service tax. It is also undisputed that the respondent is eligible for exemption of the service tax as per the Notification No. 43/97-CE, dated 5-11-1997. On this background, in the remand proceedings, the Commissioner (Appeals) held as under:—

"I find that as per section 12B of the Central Excise Act, 1944, this is the parameter to measure whether the incidence of duty has been paid or not. Here, I find that the invoices issued for sale during the year 2003 not show the recovery of service tax of Rs. 29,441 as it was for the period 16-11-1997 to 1-6-1998 and was paid in 2003-04. The adjudicating authority himself has admitted the same in his findings. Profit and loss account and balance sheet are the documents, which indicate the true financial position of the unit and whether the business is in profit or in loss. They have nothing to do with the working out of the cost of final product. The Cost Accountant after taking into consideration all related expenditure does costing of the product. It has on being presumed that the expenses of past period must have been considered cost of goods. The Tribunal decision in the case of Sunbeam Auto Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (185) ELT 297 is applicable wherein it is held that merely because the amount is mentioned as sales expenses the bar of unjust enrichment is not applicable, that even if the assessee is keeping such amount in their account sales expenses and deducted the same out of their profits, the refund claim not deniable. SERVICE TAX NOTIFICATION NO. 25/2006 - DATED JULY 13, 2006: DOES IT SERVE THE PURPOSE ?

Previously professional services rendered by CA, CWA and CS in connection with representation before statutory authorities, appearance on behalf of the clients in quasi-judicial proceedings before statutory authorities and appellate forums like CESTAT, ITAT, etc., were exempt. However, vide otification No. 25/2006-ST, dated July 13, 2006 such services are not taxable, provided these professionals represent their clients before such authorities in a proceeding initiated by issue of notice. This particular pre-condition appears to be unwarranted as it may usher in some practical difficulties. The author, in this article, examines the exemption provided under otification No. 25/2006-ST, dated July 13, 2006 which exempts taxable service provided by a chartered accountant, cost accountant and company secretary who represent clients before statutory authority in a proceeding initiated by issue of notice, and opines that the pre-condition imposed under the said notification vis-a-vis issue of a ‘notice’ has to be withdrawn immediately, preferably with retrospective effect, as it takes away the intended benefit and deprives of exemption on several occasions enumerated in this article.

Introduction

1. Readers may be aware that earlier under Notification No.59/98-ST, dated October 16, 1996, as amended certain services rendered by the CA, CWAs and CS (other than those specified services ) were exempt. However, by virtue of an Explanation inserted with effect from August 1, 2002, distinct taxable services provided such as management consultant, manpower recruitment, etc., and classifiable elsewhere as other distinct services were liable for service tax. The major relief which was available to such professionals was exemption of such of those services rendered in their professional capacity like representation before statutory authorities, appearance on behalf of the clients in quasi-judicial proceedings before statutory authorities and appellate forums like CESTAT, ITAT, etc. For the reasons best known, the exemption was withdrawn in the 2006 budget with effect from March 1, 2006. Everyone felt that this step was discriminatory in nature as it affected the level playing field, inasmuch as the advocates, income-tax and sales tax practitioners are not required to pay any service tax on similar services rendered by them.

2. Finally, the institutional bodies had to step-in to safeguard the interest of their members, and sought for restoration of exemption. ICAI represented to the Finance Minister that this resulted in discrimination, as similar services provided by legal and tax practitioners were not liable to service tax. Besides, it was also pointed out that the cost of services to the various business enterprises including small and medium entities increased by 12.24 per cent on engaging the services of chartered accountants - (ICAI Press Release July 14, 2006)

"The exemption comes after the ICAI, the ICWAI and ICSI represented to the Government not to levy service tax for certain specified services provided by them which are also provided by other professionals. In particular a case was made that while these professionals appearing before statutory authorities on behalf of clients had to pay service tax, lawyers providing similar services paid no such tax". (Business Line, New Delhi, dated July 7, 2006)

In the erstwhile Notification No. 59/98, the services rendered in connection with representation of a client before various statutory bodies and authorities to a catena of proceedings were exempt unconditionally, whereas the present notification places an embargo that such proceedings shall be initiated by issue of notice.

‘Notice’ means information, the result of observation, knowledge of the existence of a fact or state of affairs (Black’s Law Dictionary)

A person has notice of fact when (a) he has actual knowledge of it or (b) he has received a notice of it or (c) from all the facts and circumstances known to him at the time in question he has reason to know that it exists.

Types of notice (a ) express notice (b) implied notice, (c) personal notice and (d) public notice.

Statutory authorities would mean to include both the quasi-judicial authorities performing various functions under a statute and the appellate authorities who are created by virtue of provisions of the statute.

Press note issued by the department

4. The Department’s Press Note explains the rationale for this exemption as under: "Representations have been received from the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, the Institute of Cost and Works Accountants of India and the Association of Company Secretaries of India requesting the Government to consider exemption from levy of service tax on certain specified services provided by them which are also provided by other professionals and those other professionals providing similar services are not taxable. It has been stated that such an exemption is required till such time other professionals providing similar services are also taxed.

Government has considered the representations. Taking into account the views expressed by the Institutes and the Association and the other material facts, Government has exempted from levy of service tax only representational services provided to a client by a practising Chartered Accountant/Cost Accountant/Company Secretary to appear before a statutory authority in the course of proceedings initiated under any law for the time being in force, by way of issue of notice."

Thus, the Press Note accepts, in principle, the idea that exemption from levy of service tax is required in respect of certain specified services provided by practising CAs/CWAs/CSs which are also provided by other professionals and those other professionals providing similar services are not taxable. If it is so, then this rationale does not apply only to representational services and that to only in proceedings initiated by way of issue of notice but to other services such as filing of tax returns, appearing for a client in an appeal filed by him, tax consultancy etc. Giving such exemption is not only required for maintaining a level playing field for the CAs/CWAs/CSs but also in public interest. There is an apprehension that in services except statutory ones like audit etc. which only CAs/CWAs/CSs can statutorily render and representational services which are exempt, other work (such as filing of tax returns) will be done by these professionals but bills will be issued to the client in the name of an Advocate/Income-Tax practitioner/sales tax practitioner and these professionals will take their share in cash. This will be done to save the client from the service tax. This will cause more loss of revenue than Exemption Notification No. 59/98-Service Tax dated 16-10-1998. This will not only cause loss of service tax revenue but also of income tax. Therefore, it is desirable that the pre-1-3-2006 position is restored.

Conclusion

5. The exemption is only for representational services by way of appearing before any statutory authority in proceedings initiated by issue of notice. In the interest of a level playing field for CAs/CWAs/CSs and in the interest of the public exchequer, it is desirable that other professionals like Advocates/Income-Tax Practitioners also be taxed or the pre-1-3-2006 position in respect of CAs/CWAs/CSs be restored.

2 SECTION 65(105)(s ) - CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT SERVICES - CONSTITUTIONALITY

History of service tax on chartered accountants

2.1 A brief legislative history is that service tax was, for the first time, imposed by the Finance Act, 1994. This tax was levied on three types of services. Later on the scope of this tax has been widened almost in every Budget. Service tax on practising chartered accountants was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998 by the Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998. But there were protests against this levy by the CA community all over India. One of the main causes of protest was that, while the service tax was levied on Chartered Accountants’ services, but the same was not levied on the similar services provided by an advocate. Also in case of Jodhpur Chartered Accountants Society v. CCE [1998] STT 33/(105) ELT 290 (Raj.) [dated 24th November, 1998], the operation and implementation of Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998, was stayed and kept in abeyance so far as its application was concerned to the practising chartered accountants practising in the State of Rajasthan. Also, in many of the other cases, the stay was granted. Thus, due to protest against the levy by chartered accountants and certain Court decisions, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998 only on auditing and accounting services. So, the services provided by CAs and Advocates, which can be of similar nature, remain out of service tax. But the later developments are of crucial and patently of discriminatory nature.

Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998, was superseded by Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998. From this notification, the nature of services was made more explicit as compared to Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998. But this is not all which happens to these professionals. Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 was amended by Notification No. 15/2002-ST, dated 1-8-2002 w.e.f. 1-8-2002 by inserting an Explanation under this notification. This Explanation provides that, "Nothing contained in this notification shall apply to the services provided by a practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant which may fall in any other taxable services as defined in clause (105) of section 65 of the said Act". Also, the same was clarified by the following illustration:

"The service provided by a practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant in connection with the management of any organisation in any manner or recruitment of manpower in any manner shall be deemed to be the taxable service provided under the category of management consultant or manpower recruitment agency, as the case may be. Therefore, no exemption under this notification shall be applicable to such practising chartered accountant, a practising company secretary or a practising cost accountant."

HEADNOTE: Section 73, read with section 86, of the Finance Act, 1994 - Recovery of service tax not levied or paid or short levied or short paid or erroneously refunded - Appellant, engaged in manufacture and sale of castings on specific rate of contract, paid service tax on account of services of goods transport operator - On basis of Chartered Accountant’s Certificate, said amount of service tax was refunded to it - However, Commissioner in exercise of its revisional power demanded back amount of refund sanctioned - It was case of appellant that it paid service tax which was not payable by it and said amount was not recovered from customers and so, doctrine of unjust enrichment did not arise in its case - It was found that said service tax amount had not vitiated contract price in any way - Commissioner in his order had not relied on any contradictory certificate of another professional - Whether certificate issued by a professional generally, should not be challenged without having contradictory certificate from another professional and in absence of such a contradictory certificate, it was to be held that appellant had a strong prima facie case in its favour for waiver of requirement of pre-deposit of service tax for hearing appeal - Held, yes

FACT: The appellant was sanctioned a refund by the adjudicating authority on basis of the factual situation prevailing and certificate given by the Chartered Accountant. However, the Commissioner reviewed the order of adjudicating authority and demanded the refund amount back on the ground that the certificate of the Chartered Accountant only stated that amount had been debited to expenses account in profit and loss statement. In appeal, the appellant contended that the amount had been paid as service tax which was not payable by the appellants and since they had not recovered the said amount from their customers. Therefore, the question of doctrine of unjust enrichment did not arise.

HELD: The Chartered Accountant’s Certificate was a detailed certificate which had been considered in depth by the adjudicating authority. The appellant was engaged in the manufacture and selling of casting on specific rate of contract. The amount of service tax paid by the appellant was on the goods transport operator. That had not vitiated the contract price in any way. Further, the certificate issued by the professional, generally should not be challenged without having contradictory certificate from another professional. The Commissioner in his order had not relied on any contradictory certificate of another professional. In the absence of which, it was to be held that the appellant had made out a prima facie case for waiver of pre-deposit of amount of service tax. [Para 5]

Eligibility of small service provider

1. A Firm of chartered accountants has the gross billing for the year ending on 31-3-2006 as under:— Since the service provided by the firm with respect to audit was only 2.30 Lakh hence the firm is not collecting and paying service tax in the year 2006-07 on the assumption that it is eligible for the benefit of exemption available to the small service providers as per Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) up to the value of 4 Lakh of collection. Please advise properly.

The total taxable service rendered by this firm of Rs.4.30 Lakhs in the previous year ended on 31-3-2006 hence the firm is not eligible for the exemption scheme available to this firm.

For this purpose there is clear provision in the Notification No.6/2005-ST, dated 1-3-2005 (F.No.334/1/2005-TRU) in the form of conditions mentioned in clause 2 of the scheme. The exact wording of clause 2(viii) is as under:—

"(viii)The aggregate value of taxable services rendered by a provider of taxable service from one or more premises, does not exceed rupees four lakhs in the preceding financial year."

Here, to be eligible for exemption scheme available to small service providers, the aggregate value of taxable service should not be more than Rupees 4 Lakh in the preceding financial year and both the Audit services and taxation services were part of taxable service though the tax was exempt on the taxation services. Let us see the exact wordings of the Exemption Notification No. 59/98-ST, dated 16-10-1998 in this respect:—

In exercise of the powers conferred by section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994(32 of 1994); and in suppression of the notification of the Government of India in the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) No. 57/98 Service tax, dated 7-10-1998, the Central Government, being satisfied that it is necessary in the Public interest so to do, hereby exempts the taxable service provided by a practising chartered accountant, in his professional capacity to a client, other than the taxable service related to—

(i)Accounting and auditing; or

(ii)to (xi) Various services Like certification etc. mentioned,

from whole of the service tax leviable thereon.

Services provided by a practising CA/CWA/CS in his professional capacity are taxable with effect from 16-10-1998. Till 28-2-2006, all non-statutory services provided by practising CA/CWA/CS were exempt from service tax. This exemption was withdrawn w.e.f. 1-3-2006. The practising CA/CWA/CS are providing non-statutory services like tax consultation and acting as representatives of clients before various statutory authorities. If the same service is provided by other professionals like an advocate or a non-qualified person, the services will not be taxable. This created discrimination. Many representations were made to Government by ICAI, ICWAI, ICSI and other bodies. Writ petitions were filed by many practising members in their personal capacity.

Finally, partial relief has been granted and service relating to representing clients before any statutory authority has been exempted vide Notification No. 25/2006-ST, dated 13-7-2006. However, there is no relief in case of other services like tax consultation, preparation and filing of tax returns and accounts writing work.

Background

1. Services provided by a practising CA/CWA/CS in his professional capacity are taxable with effect from 16-10-1998.

Any service provided or to be provided to a client, by a Practising Chartered Accountant, Practising Cost Accountant or Practising Company Secretary in his professional capacity in any manner, is a taxable service [section 65(105)(s), section 65(105)(u) and section 65(105)(t) of Finance Act, 1994].

Thus, this covers statutory as well as non-statutory services provided in his professional capacity.

However, services of firms of CA/ICWA/CS will be taxable, since the word used in inclusive part is ‘any concern’.

1.1 Distinction between tax on services of professional and other services - In case of all other taxable services, the service tax is on a specified service, while in case of practising CA/CWA/CS, the service tax is based on person who is providing the service and not the type of service.

This creates discrimination, since the service provided by practising CA/CWA/CS will be taxable while same service provided by others (like advocate, non-professionals) will not be taxed.

Under Chapter X of the Income-tax Act Special Provisions relating to avoidance of tax are provided. Section 92(1) stipulates that any income arising from international transaction shall be computed having regard to the arm's length price. As per Explanation under section 92(1), allowance for any expenses or interest arising from an international transaction shall also be determined having regard to the arm's length price. Section 92A defines the term 'associated enterprise' for the purpose of sections 92,92B, 92C, 92D, 92E and 92F. Section 92B defines the term of 'international transactions' for the purpose of sections 92, 92C, 92D and 92E. [Para 33]

Section 92C(1) specifies the method to be applied for determining the arm's length price in relation to international transaction and it is provided under section 92C(2) that the most appropriate method having regard to the nature of transaction is to be applied for computing the arm's length price. It is further provided under section 92C(3) that primarily it is the duty of the Assessing Officer to compute the arm's length price on the basis of material or information or documents in his possession for which the Assessing Officer is duty bound to give an opportunity to the assessee to show cause as to why the arm's length price should not be so determined on the basis of the material or information or documents in the possession of the Assessing Officer. Under sub-section (4) of section 92C it is provided that where arms's length price is determined by the Assessing Officer under sub-section (3) the Assessing Officer may compute total income of the assessee having regard to such determination. It is further provided that no deduction under section 10A or 10AA or 10B or under Chapter VI-A is to be allowed in respect of the said amount which is included in the total income of the assessee. However, where the Assessing Officer considers it necessary or expedient, he may, with the previous approval of the Commissioner, refer the computation of arm's length price in relation to the international transaction to the Transfer Pricing Officer, as per the provision of section 92CA(1). Sub-section (2) of section 92CA entails where reference is made under sub-section (1), the TPO shall serve a notice to the assessee requiring him to produce evidence in support of the computation made by him of arm's length price in relation to the international transactions referred to in sub-section (1) to section 92CA. Sub-section (2A) to section 92CA has been inserted by the Finance Act, 2011 with effect from 1-6-2011, under which it is provided that where any international transaction other than the one referred to by the Assessing Officer, comes to the notice of the TPO, the provisions of Chapter shall apply to such other international transactions as to an international transaction referred to him under sub-section (1). [Para 35]

From the combined reading of provisions of Chapter X of the Act it is clear that it is the duty of the Assessing Officer to compute any income arising from an international transaction having regard to the arm's length price. The Assessing Officer may determine the arm's length price of an international transaction on its own or where the Assessing Officer considers it necessary, subject to the approval of the Commissioner, he may refer the said computation of arm's length price in relation to international transaction under section 92CA to the TPO. In view of the relevant provisions of the Act the Assessing Officer is to determine whether the transaction involved is an international transaction and he may either determine the arm's length price of the said transaction on its own or where necessary, subject to approval of the Commissioner, refer the same to the TPO. [Para 36]

10E.3 The meaning of "accountant" now applies for the definition of an "authorised representative" u/s 288(2). As a result, in order to be appointed as an authorised representative for an assessee for any proceedings under the Act, a Chartered Accountant must have a certificate of practice. However, a Chartered Accountant having any other qualification specified in section 288 may be appointed as an authorised representative. Therefore, after this amendment, a Chartered Accountant who does not satisfy both the following conditions cannot be appointed as an authorised representative for an assessee:—

(i)

He/she does not have a certificate of practice; and

(ii)

He/she does not have any other specified qualification.

Though the section refers to the accounts being examined by an accountant, which means a Chartered Accountant, the examination can also be done by a firm of chartered accountants. This has been a recognised practice under the Act. In such a case, it would be necessary to state the name of the partner who has signed the report on behalf of the firm. The accountant signing the report as a partner of a firm or in his individual capacity should give his membership number below his name.

As per the decision taken by the Council of the ICAI, all attest functions undertaken by the members have to bear a UDIN issued by the ICAI. The same needs to be mentioned on the document being signed/attested by the member.

Section 92E does not stipulate that only the statutory auditor appointed under the Companies Act or other similar statute should perform the examination. The examination can, therefore, be conducted either by the statutory auditor or by any other Chartered Accountant in practice having certificate of practice.

The issue of a report u/s 92E, being a recurring assignment for expressing a professional opinion, the accountant accepting the assignment should communicate with the accountant who had done the examination in the earlier year, as provided in the Chartered Accountants Act. In the case of a person whose accounts of the business or profession have been audited under any other law (i.e., a company, a co-operative society, etc. which is required to get the accounts audited under a statute), it is not necessary to communicate with the statutory auditor if he had not done the examination in the earlier year.

The accountant should obtain from the assessee a letter of appointment for conducting the examination as mentioned in section 92E. It is advisable that such an appointment letter should be signed by the person competent to sign/verify the return of income in terms of the provisions of section 140 or by any person who has been authorized by the company to make such an appointment. The accountant should get the statement of particulars, as required in the annexure to the report, authenticated by the assessee before he proceeds to verify the same. The accountant is required to submit his report to the person appointing him, viz., the assessee.

The appointment of the accountant in the case of a company need not be made at the general meeting of the members. It can be made by the Board of Directors or even by any officer, if so authorised by the Board in this behalf. The appointment in the case of a firm or a proprietary concern can be made by a partner or the proprietor or a person authorised by the assessee. It is possible for the assessee to appoint two or more Chartered Accountants for carrying out the examination, in which case, the report will have to be signed by all the chartered accountants. In case of disagreement, they can give their reports separately.

The Act prohibits a relative or an employee of the assessee being appointed as an accountant under section 92E. Also, as per a decision of the Council (reported in the Code of Ethics under clause (4) of Part I of Second Schedule), a Chartered Accountant who is in employment of a concern or in any other concern under the same management cannot be appointed as an auditor of that concern. Therefore, an employee of an assessee or an employee of a concern under the same management cannot examine the accounts and records of an assessee u/s 92E.

An accountant responsible for writing or the maintenance of the books of account of the assessee should not examine such accounts. This principle will apply to the partner of such an accountant as well as to the firm in which he is a partner. In view of this, an accountant who is responsible for writing or the maintenance of the books of account, his partner or the firm in which he is a partner should not accept the examination assignment u/s 92E in the case of such an assessee.

Section 65(105)(j) - Clearing and Forwarding Agent’s Services - Whether service receiver can deduct amount of service tax from service provider’s bill

6.2 Facts The respondent, a transport contractor, entered into a contract with the appellant for handling of its materials. During the pendency of the said contract, section 65 was substituted by section 88 whereby 5 per cent service tax was introduced on various services including ‘clearing and forwarding (C&F) agent’. The appellant, consequently, deducted 5 per cent service tax from the respondent’s bills on the assumption that the respondent was a C&F agent from 31-10-1997 in spite of respondent’s objections. On reference, the sole arbitrator dismissed the respondent’s objection. On petition filed by the respondent, the Single Judge of the High Court allowed the same by setting aside the impugned award.

Decision of Bombay High Court:

u The High Court held that the constitutional validity with regard to the extension of service tax in view of the amendment to the Finance Act, 2000, section 116(a) and section 65(6) to treat the recipients of the services as an assessee in case of services rendered by goods transport operators and clearing and forwarding agents, was upheld by the Supreme Court in Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd. v. Union of India [2005] 1 STT 41.

u The High Court further held that Single Judge had set aside the award passed by the arbitrator by which the arbitrator held that the appellant was entitled to deduct the service tax amount from the amount payable to the respondent. Admittedly, the appellant was recipient of the service of the respondents as per the agreement-in-question. The appellant, pursuant to the provisions of service tax was registered and recognized as an ‘assessee’ and had also filed returns as contemplated accordingly. The appellant, therefore, was liable to pay the service tax being the recipient of the services from the respondent. Admittedly, there was no specific agreement with regard to payment of service tax-in-question by the respondent to the extent the appellant would be entitled to deduct the amount so paid or payable under the service tax, though the respondent was not an assessee and/or not liable to pay service tax under the law. There was no specific clause that such service tax liability would be deductible from the amount payable by the appellant to the respondent pursuant to the contract-in-question. The deduction as claimed and as directed by the award in absence of any agreement or clause, therefore, was not correct. The department, on application filed by the applicant, already rejected the specific claim of refund of that amount.

u The High Court further observed that there was nothing to show even from the plain reading of the agreement and the clauses thereof that, payment of service tax, though payable by the ‘assessee’, yet it would be the respondent, the service provider, to re-pay the same to the appellant and, therefore, the appellant was entitled to deduct service tax from the bills of the respondent in terms of the clauses of the agreement. The Single Judge, therefore, was right in reversing the award passed by the arbitrator. The agreement nowhere entitled the appellant to deduct and/or to recover such service tax from the respondent. Therefore, the High Court held, as rightly held by the Single Judge, that the award was, on the face of it, illegal and erroneous.

[Rastriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. v. Dewan Chand Ram Saran [2008] 14 STT 328 (Bom.)]

Section 65(105)(s) - Chartered Accountant’s services - Scope of services

6.3 Service tax on practising chartered accountants was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998 by the Notification No. 53/98-Service Tax, dated 7-10-1998. But there were protests against this levy by the CA community all over India. One of the main causes of protest was that, while the service tax was levied on chartered accountants’ services, but the same was not levied on the similar services provided by an advocate. Thus, due to protest against the levy by chartered accountants and certain Court decisions, the levy was restricted by Notification No. 57/98-ST, dated 7-10-1998 only on auditing and accounting services. So, the services provided by CAs and advocates, which can be of similar nature, remain out of service tax. But the later developments are of crucial nature and patently of a discriminatory nature.

The method chosen by the assessee to justify his declared price to be arm’s length price should be ‘the Most Appropriate Method (MAP) under section 92C(2)’, since proviso to section 92C recognises that there may be circumstances, where there can be more than one appropriate method in which case arithmetical means of the arm’s length price so arrived at can be taken, subject to variation of 5 per cent at the option of the assessee. Section 92E requires certification by way of a report from a chartered accountant in the prescribed Form 3CEB. It is understood that chartered accountant is not responsible for the choice of the method but only for the working on the basis of which the choice is made by the assessee. In the result, the choice is left to the assessee with no requirement on the part of the chartered accountant to certify that the method chosen is the MAP. This is a glaring defect, since the assessee is not likely to have the necessary expertise. Again, column 13 of the Form requires certification of the arm’s length price as computed by the assessee on the single method chosen by him and does not provide for arithmetical means of more than one method, so as to require certification of application of two methods, where more than one arm’s length price is available with option of the assessee to vary the same by 5 per cent. The result is that, the Assessing Officer, it can be said, does not get all the assistance that may be expected from such a certificate.

Not surprisingly, the choice of the method is a disputed issue in almost every case. In the decision of the Special Bench in Aztec Software Technology Services Ltd.’s case (supra ), it was pointed out that the selection of the MAP depends on the nature of transactions or availability of relevant data and the possibility of making the appropriate adjustment from the available data to arrive at arm’s length price on a reasonable basis.

The TPO, however, considered CUP method as the most suitable one. But then, the problem was in selecting comparable cases for application of this method.

There is considerable discussion as to the computation with reference to each of the methods by the Special Bench. Adoption of Nasscom average hourly rate, it was found, does not meet the requirement of CUP method to justify the mark-up rate over the assessee’s cost. The Special Bench pointed out OECD Guidelines on International Transfer Pricing, 2006, which required adjustments for

-Differences in the quality of the products;

-Differences in the geographic markets;

-Differences in the level of the market; and

-Differences in the amount and type of intangible property involved.

The Special Bench had set out the guidelines and set aside the assessment, while pointing out, that the burden of proof vested on the assessee to prove the declared price to be the arm’s length price. The Special Bench after referring to OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines would not consider TNMM as the most appropriate method. For purposes of Bench marking under this method, it was pointed out that it is necessary to arrive at net margin earned by comparable uncontrolled transaction, so as to require the data necessary for CUP method. The manner in which net margin was worked out was also faulted as it took into consideration only the net margin earned by the associated enterprise on its entire business activities. The cases chosen by the Assessing Officer for comparability was also found to be not completely reliable. Incidentally, it was found that the RPM was not applicable, since the assessee was not a reseller of goods or services. The CPM requires verification of cost. PSM was rejected, because it was not a case of ‘unique intangibles or multiple inseparable transactions’ apart from the fact that this method is rarely used. TNM method, on the other hand, requires consideration of the specified transactions and not overall business. It is under these circumstances, that the matter was restored to the Assessing Officer on the basis of the guidance thus offered.

On appeal: HELD: The TPO has alleged that the assessee failed to furnish any evidence to substantiate its claim that the payment is made to the AE for availing Information System Services, however, the material on record reveal that the assessee has not only undertaken a benchmarking process for determining the arm's length price of the transaction in the transfer pricing study report which was filed before the TPO, but, other relevant and necessary documents like copy of the agreement, invoices raised, certificate from independent Chartered Accountant Firm, (KPMG), details of users were also furnished before the TPO. Therefore, the allegation of the TPO that the assessee has not furnished the necessary details is not totally correct. In any case of the matter, non-furnishing of certain documentary evidences, as alleged by the TPO does not empower him to embark upon determining the arm's length price of the international transaction on estimation basis. Further, a reading of the TPO's, order makes it clear that his finding on the issue is contradictory. On the one hand, he has observed that the assessee has failed all the three tests, including, whether the services have actually been provided, on the other hand, he has accepted that the AE has provided the software. Thus, ultimately, what the TPO disbelieves is the quantum of payment. Accordingly, he has proceeded to estimate the price of the services rendered by the AE at Rs. 1,62,05,000. Though, the TPO has observed that he has applied CUP method for determining the arm's length price, however, he has not brought on record even a single comparable to support the arm's length price determined by him even on estimate basis. The estimation of service charges on so-called man hour basis is without any supporting material. Similarly, the estimation of cost of software was without any basis. Thus, it is very much clear that the determination of arm's length price by the TPO is not as per any one of the methods prescribed under section 92C read with rule 10B. Such determination of arm's length price on ad hoc/estimation basis is not permissible under the scheme of the Act as the Transfer Pricing Officer is duty bound to determine the arm's length price by following any one of the most appropriate method prescribed under the statute. It is relevant to observe, that the DRP has approved the determination of the arm's length price by the TPO without properly appreciating the implication of the relevant statutory provisions. As regards the observations of the DRP regarding the report of the KPMG, it is necessary to observe that the KPMG report is not an audit report but was furnished by the assessee to support the attribution of cost. Therefore, it cannot be said that it is a qualified report. It is further relevant to observe, the material that submitted indicates that the cost of the software has been allocated to 40 group companies across the globe who are using the software and related services and assessee's share in cost allocation works out to 2.3 per cent. Moreover, when the TPO himself agrees that the AE has provided software and certain services, there is no reason for not accepting the payment made to the AE to be at arm's length in the absence of any contrary evidence brought on record and by simply applying the benefit test. If the TPO did not agree to the arm's length price shown by the assessee is it open for him to determine the arm's length price by applying one of the most appropriate methods being backed by supporting material. Without complying to the statutory provisions, the TPO certainly cannot determine the arm's length price on ad hoc/estimation basis. Accordingly, the adjustment made to the arm's length price of payment made towards availing information system services from AE was deleted. [Para 21]

Under section 92CA(1) where any person being the assessee has entered into an international transaction in any previous year, and the Assessing Officer considers it necessary or expedient to do so, he may, with the previous approval of the Commissioner refer the computation of arm's length price in relation to the said international transaction under section 92C to the Transfer Pricing Officer. Under section 92CA(2) where a reference is made under sub-section (1) of section 92CA, the Transfer Pricing Officer shall serve a notice on the assessee requiring him to produce or cause to be produced on a date to be specified therein, any evidence on which the assessee may rely in support of computation made by him of the arm's length price in relation to international transactions referred to in sub-section (1). On plain reading of provisions of sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) of section 92CA it is clear that the TPO has to compute the arm's length price in relation to the international transactions referred to him by the Assessing Officer. Sub-section (2A) to section 92CA was inserted by Finance Act, 2011 with effect from 1-6-2011, according to which where any other international transaction [other than an international transaction referred under sub-section (1)] comes to the notice of TPO during the course of the proceedings before him, the provisions of this chapter shall apply as if such international transaction is an international transaction referred to him under sub-section (1). Therefore, prior to 1-6-2011 the TPO could not have selected any transaction suo motu for computation of arm's length price. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer made reference under section 92CA(1) in respect of three international transactions and the TPO in his order dated 17-3-2005 had found those international transactions at arm's length. Suo motu, he cannot take cognizance of any international transaction for suggesting adjustment in arm's length price. [Para 7]

Thus, TPO cannot take cognizance suo motu of any international transaction for computation of arm's length price under section 92C. 6.2 Power to Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) to identify international transactions

Section 92CA(1) provides that the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) can determine the ALP only in relation to an international transaction, which has been referred to him by the Assessing Officer.

This was recognized by the CBDT vide its Instruction No. 3 of 28-3-2003 as follows: “In terms of section 92CA this role is limited to the determination of arm’s length price in relation to the international transaction(s) referred to him by the Assessing Officer. If during the course of proceedings before him it is found that there are certain other transactions, which have not been referred to him by the Assessing Officer, he will have to take up the matter with the Assessing Officer so that a fresh reference is received with regard to such transactions”.

Further, in Amadeus India Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT [2011] 10 taxmann.com 88 (Delhi - Trib.) it was held that TPO has jurisdiction only in respect of international transactions referred to him by the Assessing Officer.

Section 92CA has now been amended with effect from 1-6-2011 so as to specifically provide that the jurisdiction of the TPO shall extend to the determination of the ALP in respect of other international transactions noticed by him subsequently, in the course of proceedings before him. Such international transactions would be in addition to the international transactions referred to the TPO by the Assessing Officer.

It is now well-settled that a procedural amendment is generally retrospective and applies even to pending proceedings [CWT v. Sharvan Kumar Swamp & Sons [1994] 210 ITR 886 (SC); CIT v. Synergy Financial Exchange Ltd. [2007] 288 ITR 366 (Mad.)]. Now, the amendment could be consi- dered as a procedural amendment and hence it could apply to all assessments including pending assessments in respect of years up to assessment year 2010-11, which are pending before the TPO.

6.3 Power to TPO under section 133A

Section 92CA(7) provides that for the purpose of determining the ALP, the TPO can exercise powers available to an Assessing Officer under section 131(1) and section 133(6). These are powers of summoning or calling for details for the purpose of inquiry or investigation into the matter. Section 92CA(7) has now been amended with effect from 1-6-2011 to enable the TPO to also exercise the power of survey conferred upon an income-tax authority under section 133A.

Section 133A provides for the power of an income-tax authority to enter a place of business or profession and inspect books of account and obtain such other information as he may require as to any matter which may be useful for, or relevant to, any proceeding under the Act.

HELD: It is cardinal rule of interpretation that where the language used by the legislature is clear and unambiguous then plain and natural meaning of those words should be applied to the language and resort to any rule of interpretation to unfold intentions is permissible where the language is ambiguous. [Para 9]

Now, the controversy in the instant case is disguised in the question as to whether the provisions of chapter X shall be invoked in a situation where the assessee is enjoying tax exemption under section 10A and/or where there is no motive to avoid tax. The purpose of enacting transfer pricing provisions was to put a stop to the avoidance of tax by shifting taxable income outside India. Similarly, extending the fundamental of intendment to section 10A it is comprehended that this particular section is purported to boost the business of those undertakings which are situated in free trade zones (FTZ) and engaged in export of article or things or computer software services etc. by exempting their income from levy of tax. Thus, here the question arises as to whether the transfer pricing provisions can be invoked concerning the international transaction carried out by the assessee with its AE where the former is enjoying exemption under section 10A. It is because, in such a situation, the assessee might not have any motive to shift the income from India to a foreign country as the same has already been exempted under section 10A [Para 9.8]

In this connection, section 92C has direct bearing on the controversy on hand. Therefore, it is imperative upon to take note of this section. On the perusal of the provision, of section 92C it is very clear that the purpose behind the provision of transfer pricing is to determine true profits/income as if such international transaction has been entered with an unrelated party or non-AE, irrespective of the fact that the income of the assessee was eligible for exemption. [Para 9.9]

A. Emergence of concept of service tax :

While on the manufacture of goods, tax is levied in the name of excise duty and on sale of goods tax is levied in the name of sales tax, there are number of activities, falling in the category of 'service sector' which constitute 40 per cent of National GDP, which are not subjected to tax. This has kept a number of activities, which in fact are an important part of the national economy, outside the tax net. It is of course true that the persons rendering such services are subjected to income-tax covered by Entry 83 in List I of Schedule VII of the Constitution, but that by itself is not sufficient as the persons manufacturing goods pay excise duty on the manufacture of goods and pay sales tax on sale of goods and are also liable to pay income-tax on the income earned by them. The professionals rendering services for remuneration and similarly other persons rendering service in a larger number of fields for remuneration can only be subjected to professional tax by the State Legislature by virtue of Entry 60 in List II but subject to the maximum limit of Rs. 2,500 per annum in view of the provisions of article 276(2) of the Constitution of India. Such tax is on profession/trade/calling/employment irrespective of the fact whether they were earning any income or not. In these circumstances, the Parliament decided to tax the services being rendered by the professionals and by other trades and callings. Thus, the service tax is absolutely distinct and separate from the tax on profession/trade/calling/employment. [Para 4]

B. Legislative history :

The Government of India has notified service tax on 12 new services added in the service tax net by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1998, vide notification dated 7-10-1998. The liability has been made effective from 16-10-1998. Further, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 93, the Central Government had exempted in the public interest the taxable services other than that of auditing and accounting provided by a practising chartered accountant in his professional capacity to a client. Vide notification dated 16-10-1998 certain exemptions have been given to the Chartered Accountants, Company Secretaries and Cost and Works Accountants. Thus, the net result was that the service tax was leviable on chartered accountants in relation to accounting, auditing and certification services provided by them, in their professional capacity. As section 12B of Central Excise Act, 1944 has been made applicable in relation to the impugned service tax, the direct legal consequence is that there is a presumption that service tax has been passed on to the customer, who is the beneficiary of the service, and that is the reason why the service tax is levied on the service provider himself. It is open to the service provider to pass on the tax to the beneficiary of the service and reimburse himself. Thus, it is evident that the service provider does not pay the tax and the tax falls on the service receiver. [Para 6]

C. Legislative competence :

The subject-matter of taxation available to the Parliament is enumerated in Entries 80 to 97 of List I. Entries 45 to 66 of List II are available to the State Legislature. Under article 246(1), the Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters and that includes the power to impose tax enumerated in List I. Where the case does not fall either in the State List or the Concurrent List, the Parliament has residuary power under Entry 97 of List I. [Para 7]

The Parliament has power to levy tax on the manufacture of goods as per Entry 84 in the Union List, and also to levy tax on the services being rendered by a professional. Thus, if the tax on a trade or calling would also include the power to tax the transactions being entered into by a person carrying on any trade or calling, there would not have been a separate entry to confer the power to levy tax on sale of goods. A trader carrying on his business of buying and selling goods and subjected to tax under Entry 60 in the State List is also liable to pay taxes on the sale or purchase of goods under Entry 54 in the State List. Thus, it is evident that the two taxes are separate and distinct and they cannot be merged merely because a person liable to pay tax under Entry 60 in the State List and also liable to collect and pay tax on sale of goods under entry 54 in the said list is one and the same person in both the cases. [Para 8]

Thus, what the Gujarat High Court has upheld as reasonable classification is classification between services rendered by a qualified professional and services rendered by a non-qualified person in same or similar field. 6.2 It has been brought to the notice that the provision requiring payment of service tax after receipt of payment are used for tax avoidance especially when the transaction is between associated enterprises. There have been instances wherein service tax has not been paid on the ground of non-receipt of payment even though the transaction has been recognized as revenue/expenditure in the statement of profit and loss account for the purpose of determining corporate tax liability. 6.3 As an anti-avoidance measure, it is proposed to clarify that service tax is leviable on taxable services provided by the person liable to pay service tax even if the amount is not actually received, but the amount is credited or debited in the books of account of the service provider. In other words, service tax is required to be paid after receipt of payment or crediting/debiting of the amount in the books of accounts, whichever is earlier. However, this provision is restricted to transaction between associated enterprises. This provision shall also apply to service tax payable under reverse charge method (Section 66A) as taxable services received from associated enterprises. For this purpose section 67 and rule 6(1) are being amended.

6.4 The term 'associated enterprise' has the same meaning as assigned to it in section 92A of the Income Tax Act, 1961. It is a relative concept i.e. an enterprise is an associated enterprise when it is viewed in relation to other enterprises. This concept is used in the Income Tax Act for applying transfer pricing provisions. An enterprise which participates, directly or indirectly, or through one or more intermediaries, in the management or control or capital of the other enterprise is considered as associated enterprise. It also covers an enterprise in respect of which one or more persons who participate, directly or indirectly, or through one or more intermediaries, in the management or control or capital of the other enterprise.

6.5 Section 92A(2) of the Income Tax Act specifies various situations under which two enterprises shall be deemed to be associated enterprises. Enterprise means a person who is engaged in the provision of any services of any kind. For details, relevant provisions of Income Tax Act may be referred to.

HELD: The assessee is required to prepare the documents to prima facie to prove the above tests depending upon the nature of services, the manner of allocation of the cost, functional analysis etc. It is required to be proved in the TP study report itself the detailed business overview and the industry analysis of the group and the associated enterprises as well as the assessee. The onus is on the assessee to show with documentation with regard to functions, performance with regard to rendition of the service and at least prima facie require to establish benefit test. There has to be some objective analysis of each and every service which are required by the assessee and rendered by the AE resulting into some qualitative and quantitative benefit if it can be measured. Another important factor is to examine whether the services have not been resulted into duplicative services. Further, assessee is also required to show it was for the business purpose and is not carried out by the shareholder as its own activity. [Para 29]

Not only that, the charging method, i.e., direct or indirect charge should also be based on proper allocation key which should be commensurate in the nature of services and the impurity of such services and utilization thereof by the assessee. Here in the instant case from the record, it is not discernable whether any such documentation was prepared by the assessee or was ever asked by the TPO. [Para 30]

The assessee submitted that in the subsequent year, the assessee had filed voluminous details before the Commissioner (Appeals) when asked by him. It has also been submitted that in the assessment year 2007-08, based on perusal of those documentation, the Commissioner (Appeals) has held that the payment for intra-group services is justified. [Para 31]

From the perusal of the TPO's order as noted above, it is seen that, he has merely noted that assessee had various employees and therefore, there was no requirement or need for such services. Nowhere he is questioned or asked about the rendition of the services or to demonstrate whether there was any duplicative service. Once assessee has given the details, then the TPO should have at least asked for the documentation of proving the aforesaid tests and cannot simply determine ALP at nil. Since the TPO has not brought anything on record, therefore, the earlier year orders even though none of the orders of the Tribunal have considered this aspect is to be followed. Accordingly, it is to be held that the TPO cannot substantiate the disallowance of ALP at nil. [Para 32]

[Para 32] Now, addressing the issue relating to 'benefit test'. The revenue alleged that the assessee had failed to satisfy the 'benefit test' in respect of payments made by the assessee under the CCA (Agreement) for receiving purchase services, order handling services and sales services. The assessee has submitted before the TPO, the detailed nature of the aforesaid services and copies of documentary evidences of receipt of services on sample basis. The assessee submitted, a brief chart to prove the benefit test. This chart explains the nature of services, main functions, and documentary evidences for receipt of services along with paper book reference. This chart also explains the relevant para of the Cost Contribution Agreement (CCA). The assessee received the purchase & order handling services and sales services and documented them properly. The assessee also submitted the certificate issued by PWC Austria, about the costs allocated to AT&S India Pvt. Ltd. The copies of 78 chains of e-mail, job description sheets of 10 individual employees of the CCA team, evaluation reports of 6 global customers and flow chart of quotation processing services prove that assessee has received benefit from these services. The revenue has not disputed that these services have not been received by the assessee, he disputed only the 'benefit test', that assessee did not get the benefit out of these services. Assessee has proved that he had received the benefit from these services, by way of submitting a brief chart containing the services obtained. Therefore, the assessee has satisfied the 'benefit test', and for that rendering of intra group services by AE and payment made thereon were in the nature of third party, which would willing to pay. [Para 33]

The Assessing Officer in the draft assessment order under section 143(3) read with section 144C(1), has not made any adverse comment under section 37 in respect of the services received under the CCA, for purchase services, order handling services and sales services. During the course of scrutiny assessment proceedings, the assessee submitted before the Assessing Officer the same evidences of receipt of purchase services, order handling services and sales services as those submitted to the TPO, as per the direction of the Assessing Officer. It is pertinent to note that the Assessing Officer, after examining the aforesaid details, did not make any adverse comment under section 37. As per the provision of sub-section (1) of section 37, the Assessing Officer is authorized to examine whether an expenditure (not being expenditure of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 and not being in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee) is incurred by an assessee wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business in the matter of computation of the income chargeable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'.

In the assessee's case under consideration, the Assessing Officer has not disallowed the benefit of services received by the assessee under the Cost Contribution Agreement. The authority of the TPO would be to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine the arm's length price ('ALP') and not to determine whether there is a service or not from which the assessee benefits. That exercise of actual verification would be left to the Assessing Officer under section 37. The Assessing Officer could, therefore, determine under section 37 that the expenditure claimed was not for the benefit of the business, and thus, disallow that amount, this does not restrict or in any way bypass the functions of the TPO. The jurisdiction of the TPO is specific and limited i.e. to determine the arm's length price of an international transaction in terms of Chapter X read with rules 10A to 10E of the Income-tax Rules. Therefore, the assessee has derived benefits from these services as per CCA agreement and hence the arguments advanced by the revenue is not acceptable. [Para 34]

HELD: From Circular No. 6-B, dated 6-7-1968 of the CBDT, it is clear that the provision was made specifically to check tax avoidance. Thus when there is no tax avoidance, the applicability of this section would not be appropriate. [Para 12.4]

[2009] 15 STR 262 (Bangalore - CESTAT)[15-01-2009] Chethana Consultants vs. Commissioner of Service Tax, Bangalore

The jurisdiction High Court in the case of CIT v. Cushman & Wakefield (India) (P.) Ltd. [2014] 367 ITR 730/46 taxmann.com 317 (Delhi) held that TPO cannot determine arm's length price of the payments made by the assessee to its AE at 'NIL' for the reason that assessee did not derive any benefit from services rendered by AE. [Para 11]

The High Court categorically held that the TPO is to conduct a transfer pricing analysis to determine the arm's length price (ALP) and not to determine whether there is a service from which assessee has derived benefit or not. The Court held that the exercise to determine whether assessee had derived any benefit or not from payment of such management fee is to be examined by the Assessing Officer and appropriate disallowance under section 37 is called for.

In the instant case, the TPO had determined the ALP of payment of management fees at 'NIL' by holding that the assessee did not derive any benefit from services rendered by the AE. Therefore, keeping in view the dictum laid down by the judgment of the jurisdictional High Court, necessarily Assessing Officer has to determine whether the assessee has derived any benefit from payment of professional fees and if any benefit had derived, whether such payment is commensurate to comparable transaction has to be examined by the TPO.

For the above said purpose, the Transfer Pricing issue is restored to Assessing Officer/TPO for de novo consideration. [Para 12]

Reference to Transfer Pricing Officer [Section 92CA]

Section 92CA of the Income-tax Act provides that the Assessing Officer may refer the computation of arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or specified domestic transaction to a Transfer Pricing Officer. Such a reference can be made where:—

(a)

The Assessing Officer considers it is necessary or expedient to do so, and

(b)

The Assessing Officer has taken previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner to refer the computation to Transfer Pricing Officer.

This section specifies the entire process through which the arm's length price is determined by the Transfer Pricing Officer.

With effect from 1-11-2020, the Amendment Act, 2020 has inserted a new sub-section (8) in section 92CA to empower the Central Government to frame a scheme for the purpose of determination of arm's length price to impart greater efficiency, transparency and accountability by:—

(a)

Eliminating the interface between the Transfer Pricing Officer and the assessee or any other person to the extent technologically feasible;

(b)

Optimising utilisation of the resources through economies of scale and functional specialisation; and

(c)

Introducing a team-based determination of arm's length price (ALP) with dynamic jurisdiction.
